en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Birth Stories in the Minor Collection.
(The Sixth Portion) 22.
Mahānipāta [538] 1.
The Commentary on the Mūgapakkha Jātaka
"Do not display your cleverness"—this was said by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
One day, indeed, the bhikkhus were sitting gathered in the Dhamma hall, praising the Blessed One’s perfection of renunciation.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you sitting here gathered now?"

When they asked, "Is it by this one? and he replied, "Yes," he said: "Monks, for me now, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), it is no wonder that I have renounced my kingdom and made the Great Renunciation.
For even in the past, while still fulfilling the perfections before my knowledge was fully matured, I likewise renounced my kingdom and went forth.
Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, at Bārāṇasī, a king named Kāsirāja ruled righteously.
He had sixteen thousand women, yet not one among them obtained either a son or a daughter.
The citizens, gathering in the royal courtyard and thinking, "There is not even a single son to preserve our king’s lineage," spoke according to the method described in the Kusajātakaya.
They spoke thus to the king: "Your Majesty, pray for a son. Having heard their words, the king commanded his sixteen thousand women, "May you all pray for a son.

Although they performed invocations and services to deities such as Canda and others, and prayed, they obtained neither a son nor a daughter. His chief queen, however, was the daughter of the King of Madda.
The queen named Candā was endowed with virtue. The king said, "My dear lady, you too should pray for a son.
On the full-moon day, having undertaken the Uposatha vows, she lay upon her small couch;
reflecting upon her own virtue, she performed an act of truth, saying: "If my virtue is unbroken, by this truth may a son be born to me!"
Through the power of her virtue, the abode of Sakka manifested a state of heat. Sakka, reflecting and understanding the cause, thought:
“Queen Candā desires a son; well then, I shall grant her a son. While searching for a son suitable for her, he beheld the Bodhisatta.
At that time, the Bodhisatta had been ruling the kingdom of Bārāṇasī for twenty-two years.

Having had this done, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Ussada Hell. After being cooked there for eighty thousand years, he passed away from that state and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan, he passed away from there and desired to go to the higher celestial worlds.
Sakka went to him and said, "Venerable sir, when you were born in the human world, the perfections..."
"And they shall be fulfilled; there will be prosperity for the great multitude.
This Queen Canda-devī, the chief consort of the King of Kāsi, yearns for a son; descend into her womb.
Having said this, and having obtained the promise of five hundred other sons of gods subject to death, he returned to his own place. He [the god] accepted, saying, "Very well."
Having descended from the world of the gods together with five hundred sons of the gods, he took rebirth in the womb of Queen Candā herself.
The other sons of the gods, however, took rebirth in the wombs of the wives of the ministers.
At that time, Queen Candā’s womb was as if filled with thunderbolts (*vajira*). Having realized that the embryo had been conceived, she...
She informed the king. Upon hearing this, the king provided for the care of her pregnancy.

When her pregnancy was full term, after ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit. On that very same day, five hundred sons were born in the houses of the ministers.
At that moment, the king was seated on the great terrace, surrounded by his assembly of ministers. Then [the announcement was made]: "A son..."
"Your Majesty, he is born," they announced. Upon hearing their words, love for his son arose in the king;
it pierced through his skin and other layers until it reached the marrow of his bones. An inner joy arose, and his heart became cool. He asked his ministers, "Are you satisfied?
Has a son been born to me? "What else could we say, Your Majesty? A son has been born to us!"
"Previously we were without a protector, but now we have become protected; we have found a husband," they said.
The king summoned Mahāsenagutta and commanded him: "A retinue must be obtained for my son;
go and investigate among the houses of the ministers how many children have been born today. Having agreed, saying "Very well," he went to the houses of the ministers.
Having gone there and looked about, he saw five hundred youths; returning, he reported this to the king.
The king sent ornaments for the five hundred boys and further provided five hundred nurses.
For the Great Being, however, he assigned sixty-four nurses who were free from defects such as being too tall, and who possessed ample breasts and sweet milk.
He gave nurses. For if a child drinks milk while sitting on the side of a woman who is too tall, his neck becomes long;
if he drinks milk while sitting on the side of one who is too short, the child’s spinal vertebrae become compressed;
if he drinks milk while sitting on the side of one who is too thin, the child’s thighs ache; [and if he does so] with one who is too stout...
When a child sits on the side and drinks milk, he becomes crooked-legged; if the milk is too early, it is too cold;
if it is too late, the milk is too hot; when sitting on the side of a woman with long breasts, the child’s nose becomes pressed flat.
Furthermore, the milk of women from Kāsi is too sour, and that of women from Sāsā—
However, the milk of women varies, being characterized by excessive bitterness and other such qualities;
therefore, having avoided all those defects and provided sixty-four nurses with sweet breast-milk and hanging breasts, he performed a great honor and granted a boon even to Queen Candā.
She, for her part, accepted it and set it aside.

On the day of the naming ceremony for the prince, the king summoned the brahmins who were experts in the science of marks (*lakkhaṇa-pāṭhaka*), honored them with great hospitality, and asked them whether there would be any obstacles to the prince’s life. Having observed his perfection of marks, they replied:
“Great King, this prince is endowed with the marks of merit and fortune. Let alone one continent; [he will rule] over two thousand [worlds].”
"He is capable of exercising sovereignty over all four great continents, and no obstacle whatsoever is seen for him," they said.

Having heard their words, the king was pleased; while bestowing a name upon the prince, he reflected that on the day the prince was born, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi, and because the hearts of both the king and his ministers became cool.
Because he was born while trembling (*temayamāna*), they gave him the name "Prince Temiya.
Then, when he was one month old, the nurses adorned him and brought him into the presence of the king.
The king embraced his beloved son, kissed him on the head, seated him on his lap, and sat there delighting in him.
At that moment, four thieves were brought before him. Seeing them, the king commanded:
"Inflict a thousand lashes with thorny whips upon one thief; place another in fetters and cast him into prison;
strike another’s body with spears; and impale the last on a stake. Then the Great Being—
Having heard his father’s words, he became terrified and thought, "Alas! For the sake of the kingdom, my father has committed an exceedingly grave deed that leads to hell.
On the following day, they laid him down upon a decorated, glorious couch beneath a white parasol.
After sleeping for a short while, he woke up; opening his eyes and gazing at the white parasol, he beheld a vast splendor and wealth.
He saw it. Then, although he was already terrified by his own nature, an even greater fear arose within him.
Reflecting, "From where indeed have I come to this house of thieves?", he perceived through the knowledge of recollecting past births that he had come from the world of the devas.
Looking further back than that, he saw that he had been cooked in the Ussada hell; looking further still, he saw [himself] in that very same place.
In that city, he recognized his royal status.
Then he thought: "Having exercised sovereignty over Bārāṇasī for twenty years, I suffered in the Ussada Hell for eighty thousand years;
now once again I have been reborn in this very house of thieves, for yesterday my father [was among] four thieves."
As he reflected, "When they were brought before me, I spoke such harsh words that lead to rebirth in hell;
if I were to exercise sovereignty, I would again be reborn in hell and experience great suffering," a great fear arose within him.
The Bodhisatta’s golden-colored body withered like a lotus crushed by the hand.
He became disfigured. Lying there, he thought, "How indeed might I escape from this house of thieves?
Then, a daughter of the gods who had previously been his mother in another existence, dwelling in the royal parasol, comforted him, saying:
"Dear Prince Temiya, do not fear, do not grieve, do not worry. If you wish to be released from here, even though you are a cripple..."
“Be like a cripple; though not deaf, be as if deaf; though not mute, be as if mute.
Having resolved upon these three qualities, do not reveal your own wisdom,” he said, and spoke this first verse:
“Do not manifest your cleverness; be considered a fool by all living beings.”
“Let all those people pick it out; in this way, your welfare will be secured.
In this context, *paṇḍiccayantī* means wisdom (*paṇḍicca*); or rather, this is the reading *pāṇḍicca*. *Bālamato* means one who is regarded as a fool.
*Sabbo jano* means the entire company, both those within and those outside. *Ocināyatu* means: “Take this ill-omened one away!”
"Let him despise me"—this means "let him disregard me.
Having gained encouragement by her words, he said:
"I shall do that word of yours which you speak to me, O deity."
“O Mother, you desire my welfare; O deity, you desire my well-being.
Having spoken this verse, he resolved upon those three limbs [of the body]. Then that daughter of the gods vanished.
And the king, so that his son would not feel longing, stationed those five hundred youths right there in his presence. They...

The other children wept and lamented for the sake of milk, but the Great Being, terrified by the fear of hell, did not weep nor lament, thinking, "It is better for me to die having withered away from the kingdom.
Then his nurses, having learned of this occurrence, reported it to Queen Candādevī; she, in turn, informed the king. The king summoned the brahmins who were skilled in interpreting signs.
He asked. Then the brahmins said, “Your Majesty, it is appropriate to give the prince milk after his usual time has passed;
thus, while crying, he will grasp the breast firmly and drink by himself.
From then on, the nurses gave the prince milk after his usual time had passed. And while giving it, sometimes once—
They give [the milk] after having passed [the time], and sometimes they do not give milk for the entire day.
The Chapter on Investigation:
Tormented by the fear of hell, he does not cry or lament even while withering away for the sake of milk. Then him—
Even seeing him not weeping, his mother would think, "My son is hungry," and give him breast-milk, or sometimes the nurses would feed him.
While the other children wept and wailed at the very moment they did not receive milk, the Mahāsatta—terrified by the fear of hell—neither wept nor wailed;
he neither slept, nor flexed his hands and feet, nor made a sound.
Then his nurses thought, "The hands and feet of those who are cripples are not like this;
the jaw of those who are mute is not like this; the ear canals of those who are deaf are not like this.
There must be a reason for this; we shall investigate him. Having thought, "We shall first investigate him with milk," they [tried it] all day long.
They gave him no milk. Although he was wasting away, he did not cry out for milk.
Then his mother, thinking, "My son is hungry," would herself give him her breast-milk. Thus, by withholding milk at intervals, they tested him for one year, yet they could find no flaw in him.
Then the ministers and others informed the king: "Children of one year of age are fond of cake-snacks; therefore, we shall test him.

Having seated five hundred princes right there in his presence and having presented them with various cake-snacks, they placed them not far from the Bodhisatta and said, "Take those cake-snacks as you please."
They stood in a concealed place. The other boys, quarreling and striking one another, seized various things and ate them.

But the Great Being, admonishing himself, thought, "Dear Temiya Kumāra, if you desire the fear of hell, then desire this cake to eat," and being goaded by the fear of hell, he did not even look at the cake. Thus...
Even while testing him at intervals for one year by offering him cakes of rice flour, they did not find any lapse in his conduct.
Then, thinking, "Children of two years old love various fruits;
we will test him with that," they presented him with various kinds of fruit, set them down not far from the Bodhisatta, and tested him. The other children, having started a quarrel, were fighting.
They would seize him and eat him. Terrified by the fear of hell, he did not even look at them.
Thus, for one year, they tested him repeatedly with various fruits, yet they could find no opening in him.
Then, thinking, "Children of three years old love playthings; let us test him with those," they [prepared] various objects made of gold.
Having had figures of elephants, horses, and other such things made, they placed them not far from the Bodhisatta. The other boys seized them, plundering one another;
but the Great Being did not look at anything. Thus, even with these playthings, they tested him from time to time for the course of a year, yet they did not find any opening in him.
Then, thinking, "Children of four years of age love food; let us test him with that," they presented him with various kinds of food.

While the other children ate by making small morsels of the food, the Great Being admonished himself, saying, "Dear Prince Temiya, there is no counting the number of your past lives in which you failed to obtain food."
Terrified by the fear of hell, he did not even look at it. Then his mother herself, as if her heart were breaking and unable to endure it, fed him with her own hands.
In this way, they tested him with food for one entire year, looking for an opening, yet they found no flaw in him.
Then [the king thought], "Children of five years of age are afraid of fire; therefore, we shall test him.
Having had a large house with many doors built in the royal courtyard and thatched with palm leaves, he had the boy sit in its center surrounded by the other children and set the house on fire.
When the other children saw the fire, they fled, crying out in terror.

But the Great Being thought, "This heating by fire is far better—a hundredfold, a thousandfold, even a hundred-thousandfold better—than the torment of the fires of hell," and he remained perfectly motionless, like a great elder who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpanna).
Then, as the fire approached him, they seized him and moved him away. Thus, for one year, from time to time, even by means of fire...
While investigating him, they saw no flaw whatsoever.
Thereupon, thinking, "Children as young as this boy are afraid even of a rutting elephant;
therefore, we shall test him with one," they trained a single well-disciplined elephant and had the Bodhisatta sit in the royal courtyard surrounded by the other children.
They released that elephant. Letting out a trumpeting cry and striking the ground with its trunk, it approached displaying terror.
Seeing it, the other children, terrified by the fear of death, fled in all directions. But the Great Being, seeing the intoxicated elephant approaching, thought:
"Rather than being cooked in the fierce hell, [it is better to face] a fierce elephant..."
"Death in my hand is better," he thought, and terrified by the fear of hell, he sat right there.
The well-trained elephant, lifting the Great Being up like a bouquet of flowers, carried him back and forth without tiring at all.
Thus, for one entire year, the elephant tested him from time to time, yet they could find no flaw in him.

Then, thinking, "Children of seven years of age are afraid of snakes; therefore, we shall test him with one," they had the Bodhisatta sit in the royal courtyard together with the other children and released a snake that had its fangs extracted and its mouth bound.
When the other children saw it, they fled, crying out in terror. But the Great Being, reflecting upon the fear of hell, [thought]: "This fierce snake..."
"Death in the mouth is indeed better," he thought, and like a great elder who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpanna), he remained perfectly motionless.
Then the snake coiled its entire body around him and spread its hood over his head, and even then he remained motionless.
Thus, although the snake tested him from time to time for the space of one year, it could find no opening in him at all.
Then, thinking, "Children of eight years of age love theatrical performances;
therefore, we shall test him," they had him seated in the royal courtyard together with five hundred other boys and put on a theatrical performance.
When the other boys saw the performance, they cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! and laughed with loud laughter. But the Great Being—
“Even at the moment of being reborn in hell, you will have not even a moment’s smile or joy.

Having contemplated this fear of hell, he remained motionless and did not look back. Thus, even with the theatrical performance, though they tested him from time to time for a whole year, they did not find any lapse in him.
Then [the king thought], "Children of nine years of age are afraid of a sword; therefore, we shall test him.

Having had him seated in the royal courtyard together with five hundred boys, at the time when the boys were playing, a man took up a sword the color of crystal and, wandering about, shouting, crying out, terrifying them, leaping, and clapping his hands, made a great noise.
“The King of Kāsi, it seems, has an only son who is a bringer of ill-fortune; where is he? I shall cut off his head!
he cried, rushing forward. Upon seeing that man, the remaining children became terrified and fled in all directions, crying out.
But the Great Being, reflecting upon the terrors of hell, sat there as if unaware. Then that man [approached him] with a sword...
Having touched his head and threatened him, saying, "I shall cut off your head," he departed, unable even to frighten him.
Thus, even with a sword, they tested him at intervals for one year, yet they did not find any vulnerability in him.
Then, when he reached the age of ten, in order to test his deafness, they had him seated upon a splendid couch and [surrounded] by a curtain...
Having had it surrounded and made openings at the four corners, they did not show it to him;
instead, they seated the conch-blowers beneath his bed and blew the conches all at once, creating a single, resonant sound.

Although the ministers stood at the four corners and looked through the openings of the curtain, they could not perceive even for a single day any lapse in the Great Being’s mindfulness or any movement of his hands or feet.
Nor did they see even as much as a quiver. Thus, for one year, testing him at intervals even with the sound of conchs, they saw no opening in him whatsoever.
Thereafter, when he was eleven years old, for another year they likewise tested him with the sound of kettledrums, yet they still saw no opening in him.

Then, when he was twelve years old, thinking, "We shall test him with a lamp," they lit lamps in jars and extinguished all other lamps, laying him down for a short while in the darkness. They wondered, "Will he move his hand or foot in the middle of the night's darkness?
Having lifted the lamps from the jars and created light all at once, they observed his posture.
They examined him. Thus, even with the aid of a lamp, they investigated him at intervals for one year, yet they did not see in him even the slightest movement.

Then, when he was thirteen years old, thinking, "We shall test him with molasses," they smeared his entire body with molasses and laid him down in a place swarming with many flies. The flies rose up; they surrounded his entire body.
They ate him as if he were being pierced by needles. Yet, having attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*), he remained perfectly motionless like a great elder (*mahāthera*).
Thus, even when they tested him at intervals with molasses for an entire year, they did not see in him even the slightest flicker of movement.
Then, when he reached his fourteenth year, [they thought]: "Now he has grown old; he is fond of cleanliness and loathes impurity."
“Let us examine him with impurity,” they said; from then on, they neither bathed him nor made him rinse his mouth.
Having evacuated his bowels and urine, he lay there smeared in filth. Because of his foul odor, it was as if the time had come for his internal humors to emerge;
flies swarmed over him, feeding on the stench of the impurity. He remained motionless. Then—
The nurses standing around him said, "Dear Prince Temiya, you have grown old;
who will look after you always? Are you not ashamed? Why are you lying there? Get up and attend to your own body!
Thus they reviled and reproached him. Although he was submerged in such a repulsive heap of excrement, because of its foul odor...
Even after reflecting upon the foul stench of the Gūthaniraya hell— which is capable of making the hearts of those standing even a hundred yojanas away leap up—
he remained motionless. Thus, though they probed him with filth from time to time for an entire year,
they did not find any opening in him.

Then, when he was fifteen years old, [the king] thought, "We shall test him with charcoal," and so they placed charcoal-heaps beneath his bed, thinking, "Perhaps, oppressed by the heat and unable to endure the painful sensation, he will show signs of agitation.
Then pustules broke out on his body. The Great Being thought, "The torment of the Avīci hell is a hundred yojanas away."
"It is better for this suffering to spread from that [other] suffering a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold," he said,
and having thus resolved, he remained motionless. Then his parents, as if their hearts were breaking,
had the people cleared away and removed him from that exposure to the heat of the fire, saying, "Dear Temiya Kumāra, we [know] your state of being a cripple..."
“We know. For they do not have such hands, feet, ears, and noses as these. You are a son obtained by us through our prayers;
do not destroy us! Do not deliver us to the reproach of the kings dwelling throughout all of Jambudīpa,” they entreated him.
Although thus entreated by them, he remained lying there motionless, as if not hearing them at all.
Then his parents, weeping and lamenting, withdrew. At times the mother would approach alone and entreat him;
at other times the father alone would approach and entreat him. Thus, testing him from time to time for the space of a year, they did not find any opening in him.
Then, when he reached the age of sixteen, the ministers, brahmins, and others thought:

"Whether he be a cripple, or mute, or deaf, when one has reached an age that is ripe for passion, there are none who do not feel desire; when one has reached an age that is ripe for anger, there are none who do not feel hatred.
For this is the natural law, like the blossoming of flowers when the time arrives—even for him [the Prince], there are actors..."
“Having brought them here, we shall test him with them. Then, having summoned dancing girls endowed with grace, like celestial maidens possessing supreme beauty, he said:
“Whichever among you is able to make the prince laugh or to bind him with passions, she shall become his chief queen.
Having thus spoken, he bathed the prince with scented water.
Having adorned him like a son of the gods and placed him upon a well-prepared couch of splendor within a magnificent inner chamber resembling a celestial mansion,
they made the interior of the room a single mass of fragrance with garlands of perfumes, garlands of flowers, incense, scents, powders, and so forth, and then departed.
Then those women surrounded him and entertained him in various ways with dance and song, as well as with sweet words and other such means.
They sought to delight him. Because of his perfection of wisdom, he did not look at those women;
rather, resolving, "May these women not experience the touch of my body," he suppressed his inhalations and exhalations, and his body became rigid.
Not experiencing the touch of his body, they [perceived] that his body was rigid.
"This is not a human; he must be a *yakkha*," they said, and becoming terrified and trembling, unable to steady themselves, they fled.
Thus, for one year, the troupe tested him from time to time, yet they did not find any opening in him.
In this way, although they tested him for sixteen years with sixteen great tests and many minor tests, they were unable to fathom his mind.
The Section on Investigation is finished.
The Section on Soliciting the Kingdom:
Then the king, feeling remorse, summoned the brahmins who were experts in the science of marks and said, "Regarding the prince..."
“At the time of his birth, you told me, ‘This prince is endowed with the marks of grain and merit; no obstacle whatsoever is seen for him.
But now he has been born a cripple on a wooden chair, mute and deaf. Does your word not agree with this?
The brahmins replied, “Great King, there is nothing that the teachers have not seen. Nevertheless, however—”

“Your Majesty,” they replied, “we did not say this because we thought, ‘If it is said that a son obtained through the royal family’s prayers is a bringer of misfortune (kāḷakaṇṇī), you might feel dejection. Then the king asked them, “What should be done now?
“Great King, while this prince remains in this house, three obstacles will manifest: to his life...”
“...or there will be an obstacle for the white parasol, or an obstacle for the chief queen.

“Therefore, Your Majesty, without making a delay, have an inauspicious chariot yoked with inauspicious horses, have him laid down therein, carry him out through the western gate, and it is fitting to dig a four-walled pit in the raw cemetery and bury him there,” [said the ministers]. The king—
Fearing the danger of obstacles, he accepted their words, saying, "Very well.
Then Queen Candā, having heard of this occurrence, approached the king alone in great haste;
after paying homage, she said, "Your Majesty, you granted me a boon, which I have set aside as something to be claimed; grant it to me now."
She entreated him. “Take it, Queen,” he said. “Your Majesty, grant the kingdom to my son,” she replied.
“That cannot be, Queen,” he said. “For what reason, Your Majesty? “Because, Queen, your son is a bringer of misfortune.
“In that case, Your Majesty, even if you do not give it for as long as I live, grant it for seven years. “That cannot be, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant it for six years.”
“It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me five years.
“It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me four years. “It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me three years.
“It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me two years. “It is not possible, Queen.”
“In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the kingship for one year. “That is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the kingship for seven months.
“That is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the kingship for six months.
“That is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the kingship for five months. “That is not possible, Queen.”
“In that case, Your Majesty, grant us the sovereignty for four months. “It is not possible, Queen.
“In that case, Your Majesty, grant us the sovereignty for three months. “It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant us the sovereignty for two months.
“It is not possible, Queen. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant us the sovereignty for one month. “It is not possible.”
“Queen,” he said. “In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the sovereignty for half a month. “That is not possible, Queen.
“In that case, Your Majesty, grant me the sovereignty for seven days. The king said, “Very well, Queen, take it.
At that moment, she had her son adorned and had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, “This kingdom belongs to Prince Temiya.”
Having had the entire city decorated, he placed his son upon the back of an elephant, caused a white parasol to be held over his head, and after circumambulating the city, returned once more.
Having led him into the inner city and laid him upon a splendid couch, he entreated his beloved son throughout the entire night: "Dear Temiya Kumāra, on account of you, for sixteen years..."
“Having failed to obtain sleep, my eyes have become inflamed from weeping; through grief, my heart feels as if it is breaking.
I know your condition as one who is paralyzed from the waist down and so forth; do not leave me without a protector.
By this very means, she entreated him for five days—on the second day, and again on the third, and so on.
The Chapter on the Request for the Kingdom is finished.
Then, on the sixth day, the king summoned his charioteer named Sunanda and said, "Dear Sunanda, charioteer, tomorrow morning at dawn,
having yoked an inauspicious chariot with inauspicious horses and having laid the prince down therein, [drive him] out by the western gate..."

“Take him out, dig a four-walled pit in the raw-carrion ground, throw him in there, break his skull with the back of a spade, deprive him of life, cover him over with earth, perform the rite of increasing the earth, bathe, and then come back,” he commanded.
He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and accepted the order. Then, during the sixth night—
The queen, having entreated the prince, said: "Dear Temiya-kumāra, your father, the King of Kāsi, has ordered that you be buried tomorrow morning in the raw charnel ground;
you will meet your death tomorrow morning, my son. Upon hearing this, the Great Being thought:
"Dear Temiya-kumāra, the effort you have exerted for sixteen years has now reached its culmination."
Rapture arose within him. His mother’s heart felt as if it were breaking; nevertheless, thinking "my desire will reach its fulfillment," he did not speak with her.
Then, at the end of that night, early in the morning, while the charioteer Sunanda was harnessing the chariot, through the power of the deity, [he saw] the Great Being...

Through the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*), he yoked auspicious horses to the auspicious chariot, placed the chariot at the palace gate, ascended the great terrace, entered the inner chamber, and having paid homage to the queen, spoke thus: "Queen, do not be angry with me;
this is the king’s command. Having said this, he embraced his son, and pushing the queen aside with the back of his hand, he [took] the bundle of flowers.
Lifting up the prince as if he were a garland, she descended from the palace. Then Queen Candā, beating her breast and lamenting with a great cry, remained upon the main floor.
Thereupon the Great Being, looking at her, thought: "If I do not speak, my mother will die of a broken heart.
Thus, although he desired to speak, [he reflected]: "If I were to speak, for sixteen years..."
"Otherwise, my effort will be in vain; but by not speaking, I shall become a source of support for myself, my parents, and the great multitude," he thought, and so he consented.
Then the charioteer, having helped him onto the chariot, thought, "I shall drive the chariot toward the western gate."
He sent forth the chariot. Then, through the power of the Great Being’s perfections (*pāramitā*), a deity took possession of him, caused the chariot to turn back, and sent it toward the eastern gate;
however, the wheel of the chariot struck against the threshold stone.
Hearing that sound, the Great Being thought, "My heart's desire has reached its fulfillment," and his mind became even more filled with joy.
The chariot, having departed from the city, traveled three yojanas by the power of the deities.
There, a dense forest appeared to the charioteer like a raw cemetery.
Perceiving that this place was convenient, he turned the chariot off the road, parked it by the side of the path, and alighted from the chariot to take the Great Being’s ornaments.
Having unfastened his bundle and set it aside, he took up a spade and began to dig a four-walled pit in a spot not far from the chariot.
Then the Bodhisatta thought: "This is the time for my exertion; for sixteen years I have not [moved] my hands and feet."

"I wonder, do I have strength, or not? Having risen, touching his right hand with his left and his left hand with his right, and massaging both feet with both hands, he resolved to descend from the chariot.
At that very moment, the great earth, at the spot where his feet had fallen, sank down like a leather bag filled with wind.
Having leaped up, it stood pressing against the rear of the chariot.
The Great Being descended from the chariot and, after walking back and forth several times, realized: "By this very means, I have the strength to travel even a hundred leagues in a single day.
He then thought: "Sārathi, if he were to contend with me, would there be any [strength] left in him?"
Reflecting, "I have the strength to contend with him," he seized the rear of the chariot,
lifted it up like a toy carriage for children, and stood there, causing the chariot to spin around. Then, perceiving,
"I indeed have the power to contend with him," the thought arose in him to adorn himself.
At that very moment, the abode of Sakka manifested a state of heat. Sakka, reflecting and understanding the cause, thought:
"Prince Temiya’s wish has reached its fulfillment; now the desire for adornment has arisen in him.
What need has he for human ornaments? Having thus reflected, he had the divine ornament-maker, Vissakamma, take celestial ornaments.
Having summoned him, he commanded: "Dear Vissakamma, son of the gods, go and adorn Prince Temiya, the son of the King of Kāsi.
Accepting with the words "Very well," he descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, went into his presence, wrapped him in ten thousand cloths, and [adorned him] with both divine and human ornaments.

Having adorned him like Sakka himself, he returned to his own place. Then, with the grace of a king of the gods, he gave the charioteer an opportunity and, standing on the bank of the pit, asked him while speaking the third verse:
“Why indeed, O charioteer, do you dig this pit in such a hurry?”
“Tell me truly when asked, what will you do with the *kāsū*?”—
here, *kāsū* means a pit.
Having heard that, the charioteer, while digging the pit, spoke the fourth verse without even looking upward:
“A son has been born to the king who is mute and lame, devoid of consciousness;
I have been requested by the king: ‘Bury my son in the forest.
In this context, “lame” (*pakkha*) means one who is paralyzed from the waist down (*pīṭhasappī*). By the word “mute” (*mūga*), his state of being deaf is also established, for one who is deaf...
For he was unable to give a reply. "Became mindless" means he became as if without consciousness. He spoke thus because he had not been told [anything] for sixteen years.
"Was requested" means he was commanded or sent. "Dig it up in the forest" means you should dig it up in the forest.
Then the Great Being said to him:
“I am neither deaf nor mute, neither lame nor crippled;
yet you, O charioteer, would do what is unrighteous by casting me away in the forest.
Behold my thighs and my arms, and listen to my words.”
"O charioteer, you might do what is unrighteous by burying me in the forest.

In this context, "I am not deaf" means: "O good charioteer, if the king were to command that such a son as I be executed, I would demonstrate that I am not like that. "If you bury me in the forest" means: if...
The meaning is: "If you were to bury me in the forest in such a state, free from deafness and other ailments, you would be performing an unrighteous act.

Regarding the word "thighs" (*ūrū*): even after hearing that previous verse, seeing that he was still not looking at her, she thought, "I shall show him his body adorned with ornaments," and spoke thus.
Its meaning is: "O dear charioteer, these [thighs] of mine, which resemble the trunks of golden plantain trees..."
“Behold my thighs and my golden-hued arms, and listen to my sweet speech.
Then the charioteer thought to himself, “Who indeed is this who, from the moment he arrived, has been praising only himself?
Abandoning the digging of the pit and looking upward, he beheld the perfection of his physical form and thought, “Who is this man?”
Not knowing whether he was a human or a deva, he spoke this verse:
“Are you a deity or a gandhabba? Or perhaps Sakka, the first-born?
Who are you, whose son are you, and how may we know you?”
Then the Great Being, having identified himself and teaching the Dhamma, said:
"I am neither a god nor a gandhabba; I am not Sakka, the first-giver.
I am the son of the King of Kāsi, whom you are crushing with your tusks."
“I am the son of that king whom you serve for your livelihood;
O charioteer, you would be acting unrighteously if you were to bury me in the forest.
Under the shade of whichever tree one might sit or lie down—”
One should not break its branch, for he who betrays a friend is evil.
"As is the tree, so is the king; as is the branch, so am I;
as is the person who comes for shade, such are you, O charioteer."
"O charioteer, you would commit an unrighteous act if you were to bury me in the forest.
Therein, "nihañnasi" means "you will bury. He points out that although you dig a pit with the perception, "I shall bury him here," it is indeed "me" whom you intend to bury.
Even when told, "I am the prince," he still did not believe it because of his sweet speech.

Having been caught, he stood there listening to the Dhamma. One who betrays a friend is a base person who destroys his own friend by breaking a leaf, a branch, or a sprout of a tree whose shade he has enjoyed;
how much more so, then, one who kills the son of a master?
Like a man who has approached for the sake of enjoying the shade, [he approached] the king.
"Living by depending on you," he said.
Even though the Bodhisatta spoke thus, the man still did not believe him.
Then the Great Being, thinking, "I shall cause him to believe," began the ten verses known as the *Mittapūjā-gāthā*, making the forest resound with the applause of the deities and his own voice.
“He becomes one who has abundant food, well-provided with his own kinsmen;
many depend upon him—he who does not betray his friends.
Whatever country he goes to, whether a market town or royal capitals,”
He is honored everywhere who does not betray his friends.
Thieves do not overpower him, nor do the nobles despise him;
he overcomes all enemies who does not betray his friends.
“Unangered, he returns home; welcomed in the assembly;
he becomes the best among his kinsmen—he who does not deceive his friends.
Having honored others, he is honored in turn; being respectful, he becomes respected.”
One who does not betray friends is supported by praise and renown.
“The one who honors receives honor; the one who salutes receives a salutation;
and he attains fame and glory, who does not betray his friends.”
“Like a blazing fire, he shines like a deity;
he is never deprived of glory—he who does not betray his friends.
Cattle multiply for him, and what is sown in his field grows abundantly.”
He who does not betray his friends enjoys the fruit of what has been spoken [by them]:
"Whether a man falls from a precipice, from a mountain, or from a tree,
he who does not betray his friends finds a firm footing upon falling."
“Just as the wind cannot shake a banyan tree whose roots are deeply established, so enemies cannot overcome one who does not betray his friends.

In this context, *sakagharā* means “one’s own home”; alternatively, *ayameva pāṭho* (this very reading) may be used. *Na dubbhatī* means “he does not bear malice toward. *Mittānaṃ* [means “toward friends”].
“He does not offend the virtuous friends, such as the Buddha and others. Regarding the phrase “He is honored everywhere,” this should be illustrated by the story of Sīvali.
“They cannot overpower him” means they are unable to act with violence; this should be explained by the story of the novice Saṅkicca.
“The kṣatriyas do not despise him” should be illustrated by the story of the merchant Jotika. “He crosses over” means...

He transcends [this]. "Sagharan" means his own home. While one who betrays friends comes even to his own home with a troubled mind and as if angry, this person, however, returns to his own home without anger.
"Welcomed" (paṭinandita) means that when many people have gathered together, they speak of the virtues of one who does not betray enemies; he is welcomed by that, his mind being joyful.
"Having honored others, one is honored": by honoring others, one is also honored by others. "Being venerable, one is respected":
by being respectful toward others, one is also held in high esteem by others. "Possessing honor, praise, and devotion":
this means one who moves about having raised up both virtue and a reputation for praise; that is, one who honors friends. "A worshiper": being a worshiper of friends...
He also receives honor. As a "worshipper" (*vandaka*), having become a worshiper of virtuous friends such as the Buddhas, he receives homage in future existences.
And he attains both "glory and fame" (*yasokitti*): namely, the retinue of sovereignty and the renown of his virtues.
Regarding this verse, the story of the householder Cittagahapati should be told.
“Blazes forth” means he blazes forth with a retinue of sovereignty. “He is not deprived of glory”: here the story of Anāthapiṇḍika should be told.
“He eats” means he enjoys. “He gains a foothold”: this should be illustrated by the Cūḷapaduma Jātaka.
“One whose continuity has deep roots” means one whose root-sprouts have increased. “Enemies do not prevail over him”: here—
The story of the thief who entered the house of the Elder Kuraraghariyoṇa’s mother should be told.
Even while Sunanda the charioteer was teaching the Dhamma with so many verses, he did not recognize him;
thinking, "Who might this be?", he left the digging of the pit, went near the chariot, and there [found] both him and the articles of adornment.
Having seen him again after he had returned, and recognizing him as he looked upon him, he fell at his feet, raised his joined palms in reverence,
and while entreating him, spoke this verse: "Come, prince, I shall lead you back to your own home."
“Rule the kingdom, O Blessed One; what will you do in the forest?
Then the Great Being said to him:
“I have no need for that kingdom, nor for kinsmen or wealth.”
"O charioteer, if by my unrighteous conduct I were to obtain the kingdom.
In this context, "no" (alaṃ) is a word of refusal.
The charioteer said:
“Give me a full bowl of alms, Prince, as you pass by here;
for when you have gone, my father and mother will give to me, Prince.
“Eunuchs and princes, merchants and brahmins,” he said.
They too, being delighted, gave [offerings], O Prince, when you had departed.
The elephant-riders, the cavalrymen, the chariot-warriors, and the infantry—
they too, being delighted, gave [offerings], O Prince, when you had departed.
“The countryside is rich in grain, and the townspeople have gathered together;
let them give me offerings, Prince, now that you have gone.
In this context, “full bowl” means a vessel of satisfaction. “Let them give” means: as if raining down a shower of the seven treasures, may they fulfill my heart’s desire.
“They might give him a gift of satisfaction. Having thought, “Perhaps he will go out of compassion for me,” he said this.
“Vesiyānā” means merchants. “Upāyanāni” means presents.
Then the Great Being said to him:
“I have been abandoned by my father and mother, and by the kingdom and the town;
furthermore, among all the princes, I have no home of my own.
I have been dismissed by my mother and completely forsaken by my father.”
“Having gone forth into the forest, I shall not long for sensual pleasures.
In this context, “by father and mother” means I was sent away by my father and my mother. The same applies to the others as well.
“By my mother” means, O charioteer, I have been permitted by my mother, who has set a limit of seven days for my sovereignty and is now choosing a boon.
"Name. *Sañchatta* means "completely abandoned. *Pabbajito* means "having gone forth," that is, having departed for the purpose of dwelling in the forest.
As the Great Being was thus speaking of his own virtues, joy arose within him. Then, through the force of that joy, uttering an inspired utterance (*udāna*), he said:
"Even for those who are not in a hurry, the hope for fruit is indeed fulfilled."
“I have ripened the holy life; know this, O charioteer.
Even for those who do not hasten, the goal is fully realized. I have ripened the holy life;
having gone forth, I am free from fear on every side.”

In this context, "the fruit of my aspiration has ripened" means he spoke thus to show that the fruit of his aspiration had been accomplished for him, who had exerted himself for sixteen years without delay. "I have ripened the holy life" means one whose desire has reached its fulfillment.
"The purpose rightly ripens" means that the task to be performed by means of the correct method and cause succeeds.
The charioteer said:
“Being thus one who speaks with such pleasant discourse and with words so relaxed,
why did you not speak in that way then in the presence of your father and mother?”
In this context, "discourse on factions" refers to a friendly discourse.
Then the Great Being said:
"I am not a partisan because of my lack of connection, nor am I deaf because of my lack of hearing."
"I am not tongueless nor mute; do not consider me a fool.
I remember a former birth where I exercised sovereignty;
having ruled there, I fell into a most terrible hell."
“For twenty years indeed I ruled there, but for eighty thousand years I burned in hell.
Fearing that [repetition of] kingship, I thought: ‘Let them not consecrate me to the kingship.’”
Therefore, I did not speak then in the presence of my father and mother.
My father, having seated me on his lap, instructed me in the matter:
"Kill one and bind the other; have one flogged with salt-smeared leather."
“Pierce him on a stake!”—thus he instructs him.
Having heard those harsh words uttered by her, though not deaf, I appeared as if deaf;
though impartial, I was regarded as partial.
I was immersed up to my neck in urine, feces, and pus.
"Life is precarious, meager, and joined with suffering;
why, for the sake of such a life, should one harbor enmity toward anyone?"
“Through the failure to obtain wisdom and through not seeing the Dhamma,
why should one, for the sake of this wretched life, create enmity with anyone?
Even for those who do not hasten, the hope for fruit is fulfilled.”
“I have ripened the holy life; know this, O charioteer.
Even for those who do not hasten, the goal is fully realized. I have ripened the holy life;
having gone forth, I am free from fear on every side.”
In that context: "without joints" means by the absence of joints; "without ears" means by the absence of ears;
"without a tongue" means by the absence of a tongue capable of turning [to taste], [saying] "I am not mute. "Where" means in whichever birth I exercised sovereignty in the city of Bārāṇasī.
"Into evil" means into a state of evil. "I have fallen" is what he says. "They consecrated me in the kingdom" means they anointed me for the kingship. "Having seated him" means...
"Having had him sit down. "He instructs on the meaning" means he instructs regarding the purpose. "The scourging with salt" means:
having struck him with spears, make him a victim for the scourging with salt. "Pull him out" means: tear him apart. "Thus he instructs him" means:
in this way he instructs him regarding the matter. "By those words" means: by those very speeches. "I was esteemed as a partisan" means: I was considered to belong to one side.
*Acchāhanti acchiṃ ahaṃ*: they cover their eyes; *avasinti*: the meaning is "they dwell. *Samparipluto*: surrounded;
the meaning is "having become submerged. *Kasiraṃ*: suffering. *Parittaṃ*: small. This is what is meant:
O skillful charioteer, even if the life of beings were long-lasting despite being suffering, one would still desire it; and even if it were small... [the rest of the sentence follows].
If it were happiness, one would desire it; but this [state] is painful and meager, connected with the entire suffering of saṃsāra, present, and oppressive.
"What" (ko) means who? "Enmity" (veraṃ) refers to the fivefold enmity beginning with the taking of life.
"By anyone" (kenaci) means by some cause. "By wisdom" (paññāya) means by the non-attainment of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). "Of the Dhamma" (dhammassa)...

Because he had not yet seen the path of stream-entry. Again, he spoke these verses of inspired utterance (*udāna*) for the purpose of demonstrating the firmness of his resolve through his lack of desire to return.
Having heard this, the charioteer Sunanda thought: "This prince has cast aside such royal splendor as if it were a corpse;
having not broken his own determination, he has entered the forest thinking, 'I shall go forth. What is the use of this miserable life of mine?"
"What is the use? I too shall go forth with him," he thought, and spoke this verse:
"I too shall go forth, O Prince, in your presence;
Summon me, O Blessed One, for the going-forth pleases me."
In that context, "in your presence" means *tava santike*. "You shall summon me" means you shall call out, "Come, go forth into homelessness.
Although thus entreated by him, the Great Being thought: "If I were to ordain him right now, my parents would not come here;
consequently, their welfare would suffer. Furthermore, these horses, this chariot, and these articles of adornment would be lost right here."
Thinking, “He is a yakkha; will I not incur reproach, thinking that the charioteer has been devoured by him?
and considering both his own release from blame and the prosperity of his parents, he gave the horses, the chariot, and the ornaments as a loan to the man, and spoke this verse:
“Having returned the chariot, come debt-free, O charioteer;
for the going forth of one who is debt-free is praised by the seers.
In this context, “this” refers to this act of going forth, which has been praised, extolled, and lauded by the seers such as the Buddha.
Having heard this, the charioteer thought, "If I go to the city and he should go elsewhere, my master might hear of this occurrence and say, 'Show me my son.
If I do not see him upon returning, he will impose a royal penalty upon me.
Therefore, I shall speak of my own merit and obtain his promise not to go elsewhere. Thinking thus, he spoke these two verses:
“Since you have done exactly what I told you— may it be well with you—
you ought to do for me that very thing I now request.
Stay right here until I have brought the king.”
“Perhaps your father, upon seeing you, will be delighted and glad at heart.
Then the Great Being said:
“I shall do as you say, O charioteer, according to what you tell me.”
“I too wish to see my father who has come here.
‘Come, friend, turn back; you should report well-being to our kinsmen.
When you have been told to do so, you must offer salutations to my mother and father.’”
In that context, *karomi te taṃ* means "I shall do this for you"; it refers to these words. *Ehi samma nivattassu* means "Come, my dear friend charioteer;
having gone there, come back, and turn back from right here immediately. *Vutto vajjāsī* means "Being addressed by me, you should speak the greeting, saying:
'Your son, Prince Temiya, pays homage. This is the meaning.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being bowed like a golden plantain tree;
prostrating himself with the five points of his body toward the city of Bārāṇasī, he paid homage to his parents and gave his message to the charioteer.
Having received the message, the charioteer circumambulated the prince, mounted the chariot, and set out toward the city. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having grasped his feet and performed a circumambulation, the charioteer mounted the chariot and approached the palace gate.
The meaning of this is: monks, having been addressed thus, that charioteer grasped the prince’s feet, circumambulated him, mounted the chariot, and approached the palace gate.
At that moment, Queen Candā opened the window-lattice and, thinking, "What indeed is the news of my son?", she watched the path by which the charioteer was returning.
Seeing him coming alone, she beat her breast and lamented.
Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Seeing the empty chariot and the lone charioteer who had arrived, the mother,
her eyes filled with tears, gazed at him while weeping:
‘This is that very charioteer who comes, having slain my own son.’”
"Surely my son, the increaser of the earth's realm, has been slain.
Surely my enemies rejoice, surely my foes are exultant,
now that they see the charioteer returned after having killed my own son."
Seeing her empty chariot and the charioteer who had returned alone, she, weeping with eyes full of tears, questioned him:
“Why was he mute? Why was he crippled? Why did he lament then?”
“Being struck down upon the ground, tell me that, O charioteer!
How did he who was like a mute bird avoid [harm] with his hands and feet while being struck down upon the ground? Being asked, tell me that.”
In this context, "mother" refers to the mother of Prince Temiya. "The increaser of the earth" means:
surely that son of mine, having become an increaser of the earth, has been slain upon the earth. "Weeping, she questioned him":
having set the chariot aside to one side and ascended the great terrace, she paid homage to Queen Candā and questioned the charioteer standing at one side. "What indeed? means...
"Was my son indeed mute and wingless? 'Tadā' means when you had thrown him into the *kāsuya* pit and struck him on the head with a spade—at that time.
'While being struck upon the ground' means while you were striking him down upon the earth—what did he cry out?
Tell me all of that without omitting anything. 'He avoided it' means: 'Go away, charioteer!'"
"Tell me how he, writhing with his hands and feet, drove him away, saying, 'Do not kill me!
Then the charioteer said:
"I shall tell you the narrative, noble lady; grant me safety."
"Whatever I have heard or seen, I shall tell it in the presence of the prince.

In this context, "If you would grant me safety": if you were to grant me safety, then he [the prince] might say, "If I were to say, 'Your son is neither mute nor lame, but is sweet-spoken and a preacher of the Dhamma,' then why have you not come back taking him with you?"
The king, becoming angry, thought, "He might even inflict royal punishment upon me; I shall first beg for his safety," and so he spoke.
Then Queen Candādevī said to him:
"I grant you safety, my dear; speak without fear, charioteer."
"Whatever you have heard or seen in the presence of the prince.
Then the charioteer said:
"He is not mute, nor is he lame; his speech is fluent and clear."
“Fearing indeed for his kingdom, he committed many misdeeds in his dwelling.
He remembered a former birth in which he had exercised sovereignty;
having ruled there, he fell into a terrible hell.”
“For twenty years he ruled there, yet for eighty thousand years he fell into hell.
Fearing that kingdom, he thought: ‘Let them not consecrate me to the kingship.’”
Therefore, he did not speak then in the presence of his father and mother:
"Endowed with all limbs and members, possessed of perfect proportions,
eloquent in speech and wise, he stands upon the path to heaven."
“If you wish to see the prince, your own offspring, come, I will lead you to where Temiya lies.
In this context, *visaṭṭhavacano* means one whose speech is unimpeded. *Akarā ālaye bahū* means there are many deceptions on your part.
"He is wise" means he possesses wisdom. "If you both," addressing the king as the primary party, he spoke thus to them both:
"Where Temiya dwells"—meaning, "I will bring him to wherever your son remains, having given his word to me;
it is fitting now that you go quickly without delay"—he said this.
But the prince, having sent the charioteer away, desired to go forth into the homeless life.
Then Sakka, knowing his mind, at that moment summoned the divine son Vissakamma and sent him, saying: "Dear Vissakamma, Prince Temiya desires to go forth;
you must create for him a leaf-hut and the requisites for one who has gone forth, and then return. He replied, "Very well."
Having accepted [the invitation], he went with speed and, by the power of his own psychic potency (*iddhi*), created a delightful hermitage within a forest grove three *yojanas* away;
he fashioned night-quarters, day-quarters, a lotus pond, a reservoir, and trees bearing out-of-season fruit.
Having constructed a walking path (*caṅkama*) measuring twenty-four cubits near the leaf-hut, he made it the color of crystal throughout the length of the walkway.
Having strewn beautiful sand and prepared all the requisites for the going-forth, he inscribed these words upon the wall: "Whoever desires to go forth, let them take these and go forth.
Then, having driven away all the beasts and birds with fierce cries and unpleasant sounds, he returned to his own place.
At that moment, the Great Being, having seen him and recognized his status as a gift from Sakka, entered the leaf-hut, removed his garments,
put on a red bark-cloth as an undergarment and another as an upper robe, draped a deerskin over one shoulder, bound his circle of matted locks,
placed a carrying-pole on his shoulder, took up a wooden staff, and emerged from the leaf-hut, manifesting the splendor of one gone forth.
Pacing back and forth, he uttered the inspired exclamation, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!
He entered the leaf-hut, sat upon a bed of wood-chips, and having realized the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, he emerged from the leaf-hut in the evening.
Taking leaves from a *kāra* tree standing at the end of his walking path, he placed them in the bowl given by Sakka.
Having soaked [the food] in saltless, unfermented, and smokeless water, he consumed it as if it were the Deathless (*amata*);
then, having cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he took up residence there.
King Kāsī, too, having heard the words of the charioteer Sunanda, summoned Mahāsenagutta and, appearing in great haste, spoke to him to prepare for the journey:
“Harness the horses to the chariot; bind the girths upon the elephants.
Let the conchs and drums resound; let the *ekapokkhara* lutes be played.
Let the armored kettledrums be struck; let the sweet-sounding *dundubhī* drums resound.”
"Let the merchants follow me as I go to announce the birth of my son.
Let the household slaves, the princes, the courtesans, and the brahmins quickly harness their carriages; I am going to announce the birth of my son."
“Let the elephant-riders, the chariot-warriors, and the foot-soldiers quickly harness their vehicles; let us go to announce the news of our son.
The people of the countryside have gathered, and the merchants have also assembled.”
"Quickly harness the vehicles; I am going to announce the news of my son.
In this context, *udīrayantu* means "let them emit sound"; *vādantu* means "let them strike"; *ekapokkhara* means "single-headed drums"; *sannaddha* means "well-strung";
*vaggū* means "sweet-sounding"; *gacchaṃ* means "I am going"; and *puttanivedako* means "one announcing the news of the son."

"I am going as one who informs and instructs my son. Having instructed him and caused him to accept my word, I shall go to bring him back after placing him right there upon that heap of jewels and consecrating him"—with this intention he spoke thus.
"Negamas" refers to householders; "assembled" means having gathered together.
Thus commanded by the king, the charioteers harnessed the horses, placed the chariot at the palace gate, and informed the king. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“The charioteers, having yoked the horses— The Sindhu steeds, swift of pace— Arrived at the royal gate and announced: ‘O King, these horses are ready.’”
Therein, *asseti* means having taken horses that are of the Sindhu breed, swift-carriers, and endowed with speed.
*Sārathīti* means charioteers. *Yutteti* means harnessed to the chariots. *Upāgacchun’ti*: having taken those horses harnessed to the chariots, they arrived;
and having arrived, they announced, "The horses are harnessed, Your Majesty."
Then, having heard the words of the charioteers, the king spoke this half-verse:
“The stout waste away through speed; the thin waste away through lack of food.
Having heard that, the charioteers also spoke this half-verse:
“Having avoided those that are lean and fat, the horses have been yoked together in harmony.
The meaning of this is: “O King, having not taken such horses as are lean or fat, horses that are equal in age, color, speed, and strength have been yoked.
Then the king, proceeding toward his son, [took] the four divisions, the eighteen regiments, and the entire army.
He caused them to assemble. While he was still in the process of assembling them, three days had passed.

Then, on the fourth day, the King of Kāsi departed from the city, had the necessary provisions gathered, went to the hermitage, and being greeted by his son, exchanged friendly greetings with him. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
Then the king, hurrying, mounted his harnessed chariot and addressed the women of the harem: “All of you follow after me!
Take the yak-tail fan, the sunshade, the sword, and the white parasol.”
Mounting his chariot adorned with gold,
the king then set forth, placing the charioteer in front;
he quickly arrived at the place where Temiya was resting.
“Having seen him approaching, blazing as if with splendor, surrounded by a multitude of kshatriyas, Temiya spoke this:
‘I hope all is well with you, dear father; I hope you are free from illness, dear father?’”
"And all the princesses are healthy, my mothers.
"It is well with me, my son, and likewise, my son, I am free from illness;
and all the princesses are healthy, your mothers."
“I hope, dear son, that you do not drink liquor; I hope that wine is not dear to you.
I hope your mind delights in truth, in the Dhamma, and in generosity.
“I do not drink liquor, father, nor is wine dear to me.”
Moreover, my mind delights in truth, in the Dhamma, and in generosity.
“I hope you are healthy and fit; I hope your draft animals are carrying their loads well;
I hope you have no ailments that cause such torment to your body.”
“Moreover, my body is healthy and fit; moreover, my mount carries me well;
moreover, I have no diseases that afflict the body. Are your extremities flourishing and your middle thick?”
“Are your storehouses and treasury well-supplied?
“Both my ends are flourishing and my middle is abundant;
my storehouses and treasury are all fully supplied.”
“Welcome to you, Great King, and a most hearty welcome;
let them set up the couch where the king shall sit.
In this context, the phrase *upādhī rathamāruhyā* means “let them place the golden sandals upon the chariot. These are the three feet.
The king spoke, commanding: "Take the five royal insignia for the purpose of performing the consecration of my son right here.
He said, "Adorned with gold," referring to these sandals. "He approached" means he had arrived. At what time?
At the time when the Great Being was sitting, having cooked and extinguished the *kāra* leaves. [It was] as if blazing.
"Shining with splendor" means blazing as it were with royal majesty.
"Surrounded by a host of nobles" means attended by a circle of ministers who are at ease in conversation, or surrounded by a multitude of kshatriyas. "He said this":
having had the King of Kasi lodge outside the camp, [the Buddha] approached the leaf-hut on foot, paid homage to him, and sat down while exchanging friendly greetings.
He spoke these words.
By both phrases—“kusalaṃ” (well-being) and “anāmayaṃ” (health)—he asks specifically about health. “Kacci amajjapo” means he asks, “I hope you do not drink liquor.
There is also a reading, “appamatto,” which means, “I hope you are not negligent regarding wholesome qualities.”
Meaning: *Suramappiyaṃ* means that the drinking of liquor is unpleasant. There is also a reading, *suramappiyā*, which means that liquor is unpleasant.
*Dhamme* refers to the tenfold duties of a king (*rājadhamma*). *Yoggaṃ* means that which is to be yoked to the yoke—your horses, oxen, and so forth.

*Kacci vahati* means "does it carry [the load]?"—that is, does it carry it while being free from illness? *Vāhanaṃ* refers to all vehicles, such as elephants, horses, and the like. *Sarīrassupatāpanā* means...

They cause affliction to the body. "The borders" refers to the frontier provinces. "Prosperous" means flourishing, well-supplied with food, or full of clothing, ornaments, food, and drink, and densely populated.
"And in the middle" means in the center of the kingdom. "Dense" refers to villages and market towns that are thickly settled.
"Well-sheltered" means covered, protected, or fully provided. "Where the king resides."
"Let them prepare the throne upon which the king shall sit," he said.
Out of reverence for the Great Being, the king did not sit upon the throne.
Then the Great Being said, "If he will not sit on the throne, then prepare a spread of leaves," and having had it prepared, he spoke this verse to invite the king to sit upon it:
“Sit right here on this well-prepared mat of leaves;
taking water from here, wash your feet.
In that context, *niyata* means well-spread. He said *etto* while pointing to the water for use.

Out of reverence for the Great Being, the king did not sit even on the leaf-mat, but sat upon the ground itself. The Great Being, having entered the leaf-hut and brought out that *kārapaṇṇaka* fruit, invited the king to partake of it and spoke this verse:
“This *kārapaṇṇaka* fruit of mine, O King, is cooked and without salt;
Eat it, Great King, for you have come as my guest.”
Then the king said to him:
"I do not eat leaves, for this is not my food;
I eat rice from the paddy field, pure, with meat as a sauce."
In this context, "na ca" is a word of negation.
Having described his own royal food in such a manner, out of respect for that Great Being,
the king placed a small amount of leafy greens on the palm of his hand and engaged in a friendly conversation with his son, saying, "Dear, you eat such food as this?"
He sat down and spoke. At that moment, Queen Candā, surrounded by her retinue of women, arrived along the same path;
having reached the Bodhisatta’s hermitage and seeing her beloved son, she fell right there and lost consciousness.
Then, regaining her breath, she rose from where she had fallen, approached the Bodhisatta, firmly grasped his feet, and paid homage with eyes filled with tears.
Having wept with a clear mind, she rose from the place of prostration and sat down to one side.

Then the king said to her, "Bhadde, look at the food for your son," and placing a small amount of leafy greens in her hand, he gave a little bit to each of the other women as well. They all said, "Master, you eat such food as this! and [addressed] him...
Taking it and placing it upon their own heads, they said, "You are doing something exceedingly difficult, Master," and sat down paying him homage.
The King spoke again, saying, "Dear son, this appears to me as a marvel," and he uttered this verse:
"A marvel occurs to me, even though I am alone and in seclusion."
“While eating such food as this, by what means does his complexion become so radiant?
In that regard, “alone,” dear one, means that even when he is alone and retired in seclusion, seeing him sustaining himself on this kind of food, it appears to me as something marvelous.
“Such as this” (edisaṃ) means of this sort: unsalted, unseasoned, free from smoke, and boiled.
He asked, "For what reason does the complexion of those who eat from leaf-plates become serene?
Then, explaining it to him, he said:
"One king lies down upon a spread of leaves when he is about to depart."
"Because of that solitary sleep of mine, O King, my royal complexion is serene.
Nor do I have the tethering ropes of kinship, nor is there royal protection established for me;
because of that peaceful sleep of mine, O King, my royal complexion is serene."
“I do not grieve for the past, nor do I long for the future;
I maintain myself with the present, and thereby my complexion becomes serene.
Through longing for the future and grieving for the past—”
“By this fools wither away, like a green reed that has been cut down.

In this passage, *nettisaṃbandhā* means those bound by swords. *Rājarakkhā* means those protected by the king. *Nappajappāmi* means I do not long for. *Harito* means green-colored. *Luto* means like a reed that has been pulled out and cast into the sun.
Then the king, thinking, “I will take him away after anointing him right here,” spoke, inviting him to the kingship:
“I give you, my son, an elephant corps, a chariot corps, cavalry, and infantry clad in armor;
I give you delightful dwellings,
and I give you a harem adorned with every ornament.”
“O son, follow this path; you shall become our king.
‘There are four women, skilled in dance and song and well-trained;
they will delight you in sensual pleasures—what will you do in the forest?’”
“I shall bring you daughters from rival kings, adorned with ornaments;
having fathered sons by them, you may then go forth into the religious life.
You are young, a mere lad, in the prime of your first youth.”
"Rule the kingdom, venerable sir; what will you do in the forest?
In this context, "an elephant corps" refers to a body of elephants starting from ten elephants; likewise for a "chariot corps.
"Armored" means brave warriors clad in armor. "Skilled" means clever. "Trained" means trained in other women’s duties as well.
"Cāturitthiyo" means women who are clever and graceful; or alternatively, women who are clever like city-dwellers; or alternatively, "cāturiyo" refers to female dancers.
"Paṭirājūhi te kaññā" means I shall bring those princesses of yours from other kings.
"Yuva" means one who has reached youth. "Dahara" means young. "Paṭhamuppattika" means having arisen in the first stage of life.
He had just emerged. He was very young.
From this point on, there is a discourse on the Dhamma by the Bodhisatta:
“A youth should practice the holy life; as a youth, one should be a practitioner of the holy life.”
For the going forth of one who is young is praised by the seers:
"A youth should practice the holy life; let him be a practitioner of the holy life while young.
'I shall practice the holy life; kingship is not my highest aim.'"
“I see, mother and father, a young man, a speaker of words;
I see my beloved son, obtained with such hardship, dead before reaching old age.
I see, too, a young maiden, beautiful to behold.”
Like a tender bamboo shoot, it withers at the end of life.
"For both men and women die even while young;
in this regard, what person can place trust in life, thinking, 'I am still young'?"
“For one at the end of whose night life may be shorter,
what childhood can there be therein, like that of fish in shallow water?
The world is constantly assailed and constantly besieged.”
"While the infallible [days] are passing away, why do you consecrate me to the kingdom?
The King of Kāsi replied:
"By what is the world struck down? By what is it surrounded?"
“Bodies go unrewarded; tell me that when you are asked.
The Bodhisatta said:
“The world is struck down by death, surrounded by old age;”
“O Khattiya, know this: the nights pass not in vain.
Just as when a loom is stretched out, whatever thread is woven upon it becomes less and less to be woven; such is the life of mortals.”
"Just as a full river current flows on and does not turn back,
so too the life of human beings flows on and does not turn back.
Just as a full river current carries away trees born upon its banks..."
“Thus all living beings are swept away by old age and death.
In this context, “one who lives the holy life (brahmacārī) should be young” means that one practicing the holy life should be youthful.
“Praised by the seers (isīhi vaṇṇitaṃ)” means extolled and commended by the seers such as the Buddhas and others. “I am not desirous of kingship” means that I do not have a need for sovereignty.
"I am not. When they say, "Mother, Father," it refers to one who is speaking thus. "Torn away" means seized and dragged off by death.
"For whom the night has passed," O Great King, means for whom life is shorter as days and nights elapse from the moment of conception in the mother’s womb.
"What will youth avail in that state? means what will the condition of being young accomplish at that stage of life?
"By what is one struck down? means "by what is one afflicted? The King asks this without understanding the meaning of what was spoken in brief.

"Nights" means nights. For it should be understood that these nights are called "not in vain" because they pass away only by exhausting the lifespan, beauty, and strength of these beings. "Whatever is sown" means whatever...
It is woven upon that loom. "To be woven" means that while the weaving is underway, the remainder to be woven becomes so small;
such is the life of sentient beings. "It does not turn back" means that at each and every moment, what has passed is simply gone and does not return.
"One might carry it on a tree growing near the bank" means one might carry it on a tree growing near the water's edge.
Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king became deeply disenchanted, thinking, "What use have I for the household life?
Desiring to go forth, he thought, "I will not return to the city for now; I shall go forth right here.
However, if my son should go to the city, I would grant him the white parasol. Having reflected thus, in order to test him, he invited him once more to the kingship and said:
“An elephant corps, a chariot corps, horses, infantry, and armored men;
delightful dwellings, my son, I give to you.
I also give you a harem, adorned with every ornament.”
"So, my son, follow this path; you shall become our king.
'There are four women, skilled in dance and song and well-trained;
they will delight you in sensual pleasures—what will you do in the forest?'"
“I shall bring you daughters from rival kings, adorned with ornaments;
having fathered sons by them, you may then go forth into the religious life.
You are young, a mere lad, in the prime of your youth.”
“Rule the kingdom, O venerable one! What will you do in the forest?
I shall give you storehouses and treasuries, vehicles and armies, and delightful dwellings, my son.”
“Surrounded by a circle of cows, preceded by a host of slave-girls, rule the kingdom, O Blessed One! What will you do in the forest?
In this context, “surrounded by a circle of cows” means preceded by a circle of beautiful-limbed royal maidens.
Then the Great Being, declaring his lack of interest in kingship, said:
“What is the use of wealth that must be exhausted? What is the use of a wife who will die?
What is the use of youth that ends in old age, since it is overcome by decay?”
“In this matter, what delight, what play, what pleasure, or what longing for wealth could there be?
What use have I for sons or wives, O King? I am released from bondage.
Since I understand this—‘Death does not spare me’—”
For one seized by the End-maker, what pleasure is there?
What is the pursuit of wealth? Just as ripe fruits are always in fear of falling, so for mortals who are born, there is constant fear of death.
“Some are not seen in the evening, yet many people are seen in the morning;
these are not seen in the morning, yet many people are seen in the evening.
One should exert oneself this very day; who knows if death will come tomorrow?”
“We have made no compact with that Great Army, Death.
Thieves long for wealth, O King, but I am released from bondage.
Come, O King, turn back; I have no need for kingship.”
In this regard, O Great King, when you say, "What if it were to be exhausted," what are you inviting me with wealth? For that which is exhausted would go to destruction.
Indeed, either wealth abandons a person, or a person, having abandoned that wealth, departs; in every way, it is subject to exhaustion.
Why then do you invite me with that wealth? And as for "what if it were [lost] by a wife"—[it refers to] a wife.
"What shall I do? She will die even while I am still standing. "By the aged" means by one who is surrounded and overcome by old age. "Is overcome" means it will be surpassed.
"Therein" means in this very world-dwelling characterized by the nature of aging and death.
"What joy? means what kind of satisfaction? "Sport" means play. "Delight" means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Bondage" means the bondage of sensual desire.
"I am free, O Great King," he said thus because death had been suppressed by means of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Death does not neglect me" means: "Death is never negligent;
it is always intent upon my destruction. For one such as I who understands this—being assailed and slain by the Ender (Antaka)—what joy could there be?
What pursuit of wealth could there be? "Constantly" means from the time of birth onwards, always [subject] to aging and death.
Fear itself arises.
"Exerting" (*ātapan*) refers to the energy of wholesome action (*kusalakamma*). "Duty" (*kicca*) means that which is to be done.

"Who would know death tomorrow?"—who could know whether death or life will occur tomorrow or the day after? "Appointment" (*saṅgara*) means a rendezvous. "By the great army" refers to the twenty-five fears, the thirty-two types of criminal acts, the ninety-eight diseases, and so forth.
"By a multitude of people. "Thieves for the sake of wealth" means that thieves, giving up their lives for the sake of wealth, are said to long for wealth;
however, I am released from the bondage called the longing for wealth, and the meaning is: "I have no need for wealth.
"Turn back" means: turn back properly according to my word, and having abandoned kingship, take renunciation as your refuge.
"Having done this, go forth into homelessness. As for what you thought, 'I shall establish him in the kingdom,' do not think that; I have no need for kingship.
Thus the Great Being’s teaching of the Dhamma reached its conclusion with a continuous flow of reasoning.
