Having heard this, the sixteen thousand women of the harem, beginning with King [Vessantara] and Queen Candā, as well as the ministers and others, [were moved].
All desired to go forth. The king also caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, saying, "Let those who wish to go forth in the presence of my son do so.
And having opened the doors of all the gold treasuries and other stores, he had it proclaimed on golden tablets:
"There are great jars of treasure in such-and-such places; let those who need them take them."
Having had the letters inscribed, he caused them to be fastened upon a great pillar.

Those citizens, leaving their shops as they were and their houses with doors wide open, departed from the city and came into the presence of the king. Together with the great multitude, the king went forth and took ordination in the presence of the Great Being.
The hermitage, three *yojanas* in extent and established by Sakka, became fully populated.
The Great Being inspected the leaf-huts; he assigned the leaf-huts situated in the middle to the women.
Why was this? Because they were of a timid nature. However, he assigned the leaf-huts on the outskirts to the men.
All those leaf-huts were constructed by the divine son Vissakamma himself. And as for the fruit-bearing trees, the divine son Vissakamma himself [provided them].
He had them constructed by means of his supernormal power (*iddhi*).

On the Uposatha day, they would all take the fruits that had fallen to the ground from the fruit-bearing trees fashioned by Vissakamma, and having consumed them, they practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Among them, if anyone conceived a thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*), a thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*), or a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*), [the deity] would know his mind.
The Great Being sat in the air and preached the sweet Dhamma.
Having heard the Bodhisatta’s sweet Dhamma, those people became one-pointed in mind and very quickly produced the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
At that time, a neighboring king [heard] that the King of Kāsi had indeed departed from the city of Bārāṇasī and entered the forest.
Having heard that [the prince] had gone forth, he thought, "I shall seize Bārāṇasī. Departing from his city, he reached Bārāṇasī;

having entered the city and seen it adorned, he ascended the royal palace, surveyed the seven kinds of excellent treasures, and thinking, "There must be some danger for the King of Kāsi because of this wealth," he summoned those addicted to liquor.
He asked, "Has fear arisen here in your city for your king? "No, Your Majesty," they replied. "For what reason?
"Because our king’s son, Prince Temiya, thinking, 'I will not rule the kingdom of Bārāṇasī,' though not deaf, acted as if he were deaf;
having departed from this city and entered the forest, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*. Because of that..."
They reported, "For this reason, our king, together with a great multitude of people, has departed from this city, gone into the presence of Prince Temiya,
and gone forth into the religious life. Upon hearing their words, the neighboring king was pleased and,
thinking, "I too shall go forth," asked, "Dear son, by which gate did your king depart?"
When he said, “Your Majesty, by way of the eastern gate,” the king, together with his own retinue, went out by that very eastern gate and proceeded along the riverbank.
The Great Being, having learned of his approach, came into the midst of the forest, sat in the air, and taught the sweet Dhamma.
He, along with his retinue, went forth right there in his presence. In this same manner, seven other kings also [did so].
They arrived thinking, "We shall seize the city of Bārāṇasī. Those kings, too, having abandoned their seven kingdoms, went forth into homelessness in the very presence of the Bodhisattva.
The elephants became wild forest elephants; the horses became wild forest horses; the chariots were destroyed in the wilderness itself;
and in the treasuries, they scattered the coins, making them like sand in the hermitage grounds. All of them—
Having attained the superknowledges (abhiññā) and meditative absorptions (samāpatti), they became destined for the Brahma-world at the end of their lives.
Even the elephants and horses among the animals, having gained confidence in the company of the seers, were reborn in the six worlds of sense-sphere gods (kāmāvacara).
Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and proclaimed the Truths (saccāni), the Teacher said: "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well..."
"Having renounced the kingdom, he indeed went forth," he said, and then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the goddess dwelling in the parasol was Uppalavaṇṇā;
the charioteer Sunanda was Sāriputta; the parents were the royal families;
the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's assembly; and as for the wise Mūgapakkha, I myself was that Perfectly Enlightened One."
The First: The Commentary on the Mūgapakkha Jātaka.
[539] 2. The Commentary on the Mahājanaka Jātaka.
"Who is this in the midst of the ocean?"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation.
He related it. For one day, the monks were sitting gathered together in the Dhamma hall, praising the Great Renunciation of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata [undertook] the Great Renunciation."
Having said, "He has indeed gone forth," he was requested by them to relate a past event.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, in Mithilā, a king named Mahājanaka reigned.
He had two sons, Ariṭṭhajanaka and Polajanaka. Among them, the king gave the vice-regency to his eldest son.
He gave the position of general to his younger brother. Later, Mahājanaka passed away.
After performing the funeral rites for him, Ariṭṭhajanaka became king upon the death of the monarch and granted the vice-regency to the other.
A certain attendant minister of the latter went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, the viceroy intends to have you killed. The king [heard] him...

Having heard these words again and again, he broke his affection for his younger brother, had Polajanaka bound with shackles, and placed him in a house not far from the royal palace, stationing guards there. The prince thought:
"If I am indeed an enemy to my brother, let not even these shackles leave my hands and feet, nor let the door be opened; if it is not so..."
"I hope that my shackles will fall from my hands and feet, and that the door shall be opened," he said, making an act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
At that very moment, the shackles broke into pieces, and the door was opened.
Having gone out, he went to a certain border village and made his dwelling there.
The inhabitants of the border village recognized him and attended upon him. Even the king was unable to capture him.
Having gradually brought the border province under his control, he became possessed of a great retinue.
Thinking, "Previously I was not an enemy to my brother, but now I am," he went to Mithilā surrounded by a large multitude and established his camp outside the city.

Having established his residence there, he took up his abode. When the warriors living in the city heard that "the prince has arrived," the majority of them, taking elephants, horses, chariots, and other mounts, came into his presence;
other citizens also arrived. He sent a message to his brother, saying:
"Formerly I was not your enemy, but now I am your enemy; give me either the royal parasol or battle."
Having heard this, the king, desiring to wage war, addressed his chief queen: "My dear lady, victory or defeat in battle cannot be known for certain;
if any misfortune should befall me, you must protect the fetus.
Having said this, he departed from the city surrounded by a vast army.
Then, in battle, the warriors of Polajanaka brought him to his death. At that moment, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city, crying, "The king is dead!
When the queen learned of his death, she quickly took gold, silver, and other valuables, placed them in a basket, covered the top with a soiled rag, and scattered rice grains over it.
Having dressed herself in soiled rags and made her body unsightly, she placed a basket upon her head and went out every single day;

no one recognized her. Having departed through the northern gate, because she had never been anywhere before, she did not know the way and was unable to determine the direction, thinking only, "There is a city named Kālacampā."
Because she was pregnant, she sat alone in the hall while asking, "Is there anyone going to the city of Kālacampā?
However, the being conceived in her womb was neither ordinary nor common; it was a Great Being who had fulfilled the perfections.
Through his splendor, the palace of Sakka trembled. Sakka, reflecting upon this, understood the cause and [saw] that within her womb—
Thinking, "A being of great merit has been reborn;

it is fitting that I go," he prepared a carriage, arranged a couch therein, and driving the carriage like an elderly man, he stood at the door of the hall where she was seated and asked, "Is there anyone going to the city of Kālacampā? "I shall go, dear sir," she replied.
“In that case, mother, mount the chariot and sit there. “Dear son, I am far along in my pregnancy;
it is not possible for me to mount the chariot. I shall go behind you, but please give me room in this basket.
“Mother, what are you saying? There is no one equal to me in knowing how to drive a chariot. Mother, do not—”
“Fear not, climb up and sit down. She replied, “Very well, dear father.
As she was climbing, by his own supernatural power, he caused the earth to rise up like a leather bag filled with wind and made the chariot strike its rear end against it.
Having climbed up and lain down upon the couch, she realized, “This must be a deity,” and as soon as she had settled upon that divine bed, she fell fast asleep.
Then Sakka, having brought her to a river thirty *yojanas* away, woke her up and said, "Mother, descend and bathe in the river;
there is a pair of cloths at your head—put them on—and there is a meal in a bag within your robe—eat it.
She did so, lay down again, and reached the city of Kālacampā in the evening.
Seeing the gates, watchtowers, and walls, he asked, "Father, what is the name of this city?
"It is the city of Kālacampā, mother," he replied. "What are you saying, father? Is not the city of Kālacampā sixty yojanas away from our own city?
"That is true, mother; however, I know the direct path. Then, near the southern gate—
Having helped her down, he said, "Mother, our village is ahead;
you go on and enter the city," and like one who had already gone forward, Sakka vanished and returned to his own place.
The queen sat alone in the hall. At that moment, a world-renowned teacher residing in the city of Kālacampā arrived.
A Brahmin who was devoted to the study of mantras, while traveling with five hundred young disciples for the purpose of bathing,
saw from afar that the Great Being was seated there, handsome and having attained the pinnacle of beauty; at the mere sight of him, through the power of the Great Being,
he felt a sense of affection for his younger sister as soon as he beheld him, and setting the young disciples outside, he went alone.
Having entered the *sālā*, he asked, "Sister, which village do you inhabit? "Dear son, I am the chief queen of King Ariṭṭhajanaka in Mithilā.
"Mother, why have you come here? "Dear son, King Polajanaka has been killed;
therefore, being afraid, I have come here thinking, 'I shall protect my womb. "Mother, but in this city of yours..."
“Is there anyone who is a relative? “There is no one, dear brother,” she replied. “In that case, do not worry.
I am a high-born brahmin of great wealth, a teacher renowned throughout the land; I shall take you under my care, placing you in the position of a sister.
You should call me ‘brother,’ grasp my feet, and lament. She raised a great cry, grasped his feet, and wept.
The two of them lamented for one another.
Then his pupils, hearing the great noise, ran quickly forward and asked, "Teacher, what is the matter with you?
He replied, "This is my younger sister; at such-and-such a time, she was born without me. Then...
The young brahmins said, "Teacher, do not worry about your sister from now on that you have seen her.
He had the young brahmins bring a suitable disguise, seated her there, and sent them home, saying, "Sons,
go and tell the brahmin woman that she is my younger sister, and ask her to perform all the necessary duties."
Having gone there, they told the brahmin woman. Then the brahmin woman bathed him with warm water, prepared a bed, and laid him down.
When the brahmin returned from his bath at mealtime, he had her summoned, saying, "Call my sister," and after eating together with her, he looked after her right within the house.
Before long, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion. His grandfather gave him the name Mahājanaka-kumāra.

As he grew up, while playing with other children, those who provoked him would be seized firmly by him—due to his birth in an unbroken lineage of Khattiyas and because of his great strength and pride—and struck with force. At that time, they raised a great clamor.
Weeping, when asked "By whom were you struck?", they replied, "By the son of a widow.
Then the boy thought, "They are constantly calling me 'the son of a widow. Very well, I shall ask my mother.
One day he asked his mother, "Mother, who is my father? Then his mother said to him, "Dear one, the brahmin is your father."
He deceived her. On the following day, while he was beating the children, when they called him "the son of a widow," he said, "Is my father not a brahmin?
When they asked, "What does a brahmin have to do with you? he thought, "They are constantly asking me, 'What does a brahmin have to do with you?
My mother has not told me this matter as it truly is; she is acting according to her own whim toward me."

"He will not tell; very well, I shall make him tell. While drinking from her breast, he bit the breast with his teeth and said, "Mother, tell me about my father; if you do not tell, I will cut off your breast.
Unable to deceive her son, she said, "Dear child, you are the son of King Ariṭṭhajanaka in Mithilā; your father was killed by Polajanaka..."
"He was killed; protecting him, I came to this city, and this brahmin, having placed me in the position of a sister, looks after me," she said.
Having heard this, from that time forward he did not become angry even when addressed as "the son of a widow.
Within the space of sixteen years, he mastered the three Vedas and all the arts; at the age of sixteen—
However, he possessed a most excellent form. Then, thinking, "I shall take the kingdom belonging to my father," he asked his mother:
"Mother, do you have any wealth in your hand, or not? I will engage in trade, acquire wealth, and then take the kingdom belonging to my father. Then his mother said to him: "Dear son, I do not..."
“I have come empty-handed; however, I possess three treasures in my hands: a treasure of pearls, a treasure of gems, and a treasure of diamonds.
Each of these is the size of a king’s scepter. Take them and rule the kingdom; do not engage in trade.
“Mother, give me even this wealth as my own half-share. Having taken that, I shall go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi.”
“Having brought back much wealth, I shall seize the kingdom.
Having had half of it brought back and made into a bundle, he loaded the goods onto a ship along with merchants traveling to Suvaṇṇabhūmi;
then, turning back again, he paid homage to his mother and said, “Mother, I am going to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. Then his mother said to him, “Son, the ocean—”
“Your name is of little success and full of obstacles; do not go. You have much wealth for the taking of the kingdom.
He replied, “I shall certainly go, mother,” and having paid homage to his mother, he departed from his home and boarded a ship.
On that very day, a disease arose in the body of Polajanaka, and he lay upon his bed unable to rise. At that time, seven...
Hundreds of people boarded the ship. After seven days, the ship had traveled seven hundred yojanas.
Moving with excessive speed, it was unable to carry itself; the planks broke apart, water surged up from all sides, and the ship sank in the middle of the ocean.
The great multitude wept and lamented, paying homage to various deities. The Great Being—
But he neither wept nor lamented, nor did he pay homage to the deities;
rather, realizing that the boat was about to sink, he crushed sugar with ghee, ate his fill, soaked two fine cotton cloths in oil, and put them on tightly.
Then, standing by the well, he climbed into the well at the very moment the boat was sinking.
The great multitude became feeders upon fish and turtles; for a distance of half a league all around, the water turned to blood.

Standing at the edge of the pit, the Great Being determined the direction, thinking, "In this direction lies the city of Mithilā," and leaping from the top of the pit, he passed over the fish and turtles and, by virtue of his great strength, landed at the distance of a league.
On that very day, the father of Pōla passed away. From then on, the Great Being crossed the ocean like a mass of gold as he rolled amidst the jewel-colored waves.
Just as he had done for one day, he continued crossing for seven days;
however, observing the time and thinking, "Today is the full moon day," he would rinse his mouth with salt water and observe the Uposatha fast.
And at that time, the four World-Guardians had appointed a divine maiden named Maṇimekhalā as the guardian of the ocean, with these instructions:
"Rescue those beings who are endowed with virtues such as filial devotion to their mothers and who are unfit to perish in the sea.
For seven days she did not look toward the ocean; it is said that her mindfulness was forgotten while she was enjoying celestial splendors.
Some say, "She has gone to the assembly of the gods. Then she thought, "Today is the seventh day for me not having looked upon the ocean;
what indeed is the news? As she looked out, she saw the Great Being.
Thinking, "If Prince Mahājanaka had perished at sea, I would not have gained entry into the assembly of the gods," she [stood] not far from the Great Being with her body adorned.
Standing in the sky and testing the Great Being, she spoke this first verse:
“Who is this that, seeing no shore, strives in the midst of the ocean?
Knowing what purpose do you exert yourself so intensely?”
There, "not seeing the shore, he exerts himself" means that not seeing the shore, he exerts his energy and makes an effort.

Then, having heard her words, the Great Being thought: "Today is the seventh day of my crossing the ocean; I have never before seen a second being. Who could this be that speaks to me? Looking up into the sky, he saw her and spoke the second verse:
"Having considered the course of the world, O deity, and the nature of exertion..."
"Therefore, not seeing the shore in the midst of the ocean, I strove on.
Therein, "having reflected upon the course of the world" means: having seen and considered the activity of the world's course, I dwell;
this is the meaning. "And of effort" indicates that I dwell having carefully weighed the benefit of effort. "Therefore" [refers to the following].
“Because I dwell with careful attention, knowing that ‘what is called human effort does not perish;
it establishes one in happiness,’ therefore, even though I do not see the shore, I exert myself and apply energy; I do not grow weary.
Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma, she became desirous of hearing more and spoke this verse again:
“In this deep and immeasurable [ocean], whose further shore is not seen, your human effort is in vain;
you will die without having reached it. In this context, “without having reached” means without having reached the shore.
Then the Great Being said to her, "O deity, what is this you say? Even if I were to die by exerting myself, I shall be freed from blame," and he spoke this verse:
"Free from debt toward his kinsmen, and toward the gods and his father, a man who performs his duties does not suffer remorse hereafter."
In this regard, "free from debt" means that by exerting effort, one becomes free from debt toward one's relatives, deities, and Brahmās, remaining blameless and beyond reproach.
"Performing the duties of a man" means that just as a person who performs the tasks to be done by men does not later regret them nor grieve over them,
so too I, while exerting energy, [shall act] at a later time...
"I do not regret it, I do not grieve for it"—this is the meaning.
Then a goddess spoke this verse to him:
"That action which cannot be led across, which is fruitless and results in exhaustion;"
"In that case, what is the use of effort, when death has already overtaken one?

Here, "not to be brought to the further shore" means not to be brought to the ultimate goal by means of effort. "Death has overtaken one"—for whom the exertion of effort is applied to the wrong place, for such a person only death is the result;
therefore, "what is the use of effort? When the goddess had spoken thus, the Great Being, making her speech unanswerable, spoke the following verses:
“O deity, one who has understood that this world is ultimately beyond guidance—
if he does not protect his own life, one should know that he would be failing [in his duty].
O deity, some say that in this world the fruit is according to one's intention.”
“Actions bring about results, yet they may or may not succeed.
O deity, do you not see the visible fruit of action?
Others are merely names, but I cross over them; and I see that very fruit right here before me.”
“Thus I shall strive, according to my power and according to my strength;
going to the further shore of the ocean, I will perform manly deeds.
In this context, “absolutely” (*accantaṃ*) refers to that which cannot be accomplished even by exerting effort and energy.
Having understood that [the situation] is "unavoidable," one does not protect one's own life by failing to avoid fierce elephants and the like.
"He would know if he were to neglect"—if he were to neglect his energy (*vīriya*) in such circumstances, he would know the fruit of that state of indolence (*kusīta*).
This illustrates that you are saying whatever is useless. However, in the *Pāḷi* it says: "He would know if... [and so forth].
They omit what has been written; that is not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding the "fruit of one's own intention":
observing the fruit of their own intention, some men engage in such works as agriculture and trade, which may or may not succeed.
However, [the effort] consisting of physical and mental energy directed with the thought, "I will go there," or "I will master this,"...
He shows that for one who practices it, that very thing succeeds; therefore, it is indeed fitting to do it.
"Others have sunk elsewhere"—other people, having sunk into the great ocean, failed to exert effort and became food for fish and turtles, whereas I alone cross over.
"And see that near at hand"—"see this fruit of my effort; by me..."
"In this present body, I have never before seen what is called a deity;
yet here I am, seeing him standing in my presence in this divine form. "According to my power and according to my strength" means in accordance with one's own capability and power.
"What shall I do? means "I will perform it. Then, having heard those firm words of his, the deity spoke this verse in praise:
“Since you have thus crossed the flood, the immeasurable great ocean,
and are endowed with the exertion of the Dhamma, you do not sink because of your karma;
therefore, go right there where your mind finds delight.”
"In that very place where it has gone" means in such a deep and vast great ocean.
"Endowed with the effort of the Dhamma" means possessed of the exertion of the Dhamma. "By action" means by one's own manly effort.
"You do not sink" means you do not founder. "Wherever your mind delights" means go right there.
Having spoken thus, she asked, "O wise one of great prowess, where are you taking him?

When he replied, "To the city of Mithilā," she lifted the Great Being up like a bouquet of flowers, cradled him with both hands, laid him across her breast, and leaping into the air as if carrying her beloved son, she departed. For seven days, the Great Being—
Having his body smeared with salt water, he fell asleep while touched by a divine touch.
Then she led him to Mithilā, laid him down on his right side upon an auspicious stone slab in the mango grove park,
and having had the park deities take charge of his protection, she returned to her own place.
At that time, Polajanaka had no son; however, he had a daughter named Sīvalidevī, who was wise and clever.
When the ministers questioned him as he lay upon his deathbed, "Great King, once you have passed away, to whom shall we give the kingdom?
the king then said to them, "Sirs, [you must] win over my daughter, Sīvalidevī."

“Give the kingdom to one who is capable; or else, give the kingdom to whoever knows the head of the four-legged couch, or whoever is able to string the thousand-fold-strength bow, or whoever is able to bring forth the sixteen great treasures,” he said.
The ministers replied, “Your Majesty, please tell us the inventory of those treasures. Then the king—
“There is a treasure at sunrise, and also a treasure at sunset;
there is a treasure within and a treasure without, and a treasure neither within nor without.
There is a great treasure at the ascent, and also a treasure at the descent.”
In the four great sāla trees, there is a treasure extending for a league all around.
At the tips of the tusks is a great treasure, and at the tips of the hairs and the feathers;
at the tops of the trees is a great treasure—these are the sixteen great treasures.
“A couch with a thousandfold strength, and through the propitiation of Sīvalī.
Thus he recited the summary verse (*uddāna*) along with the great treasures. Having spoken these words, the king passed away.
After the king’s death, the ministers performed his funeral rites and, having assembled on the seventh day, held a consultation.
“O, it has been said by the king that the kingdom should be given to whoever is capable of winning over his daughter;
who will be able to win her over? They replied, “The commander-in-chief is the favorite,” and sent him a message.
Having heard the message and accepted it, saying, “Very well,” he went to the palace gate for the sake of the kingdom and announced his arrival.
He informed the princess. When she learned that he had arrived, she wondered, "Does he have the fortitude to bear the glory of the white parasol?
To test him, she said, "Let him come quickly.
Hearing her message, desiring to please her, he came with great speed starting from the foot of the stairs and stood before her.
Then, testing him, she said, "Run with speed on the great floor. He, thinking, "I shall satisfy the princess," sprang forward with great velocity.
Then she said to him, "Come back again. He returned once more with speed.
Knowing his lack of steadfastness, she said, "Come here, friend, and massage my feet. For the sake of pleasing her, he sat down.

She massaged his feet. Then, having struck him in the chest with her foot and cast him down on his back, she gave a signal to the female slaves, saying, "Bind this blind, foolish man, who is devoid of fortitude, beat him, seize him by the neck, and carry him out! They did exactly as she commanded.
When they asked him, "What is it, General?", he replied, "Do not speak; she is no human woman, she is a *yakkhinī*."
He said: "Then the treasurer went, and he too was put to shame in that very same way.
Likewise the merchant, the umbrella-bearer, and the sword-bearer—all of them were indeed put to shame.
Then the ministers assembled and said, 'There is no one capable of winning the favor of the king’s daughter; [she requires] a bow of a thousand-fold strength.'"
“Give the kingdom to one who is capable of mounting [the throne],” he said; yet no one was able to mount it.
Then he said, “Give the kingdom to one who knows the head of the four-legged couch (caturassapallaṅka)”; yet no one knew it.
Then he said, “Give the kingdom to one who is capable of extracting the sixteen great treasures (mahānidhi)”; yet no one was able to extract them. Then he said, “O sirs...”
"It is impossible to protect a kingdom that is without a king; what indeed should be done? they deliberated.
Then the chaplain said to them, "Sirs, do not worry. It is proper to release the 'Phussa-chariot';
for one who wins the Phussa-chariot is capable of ruling the entire Jambudīpa. They replied, "Very well."

Having accepted [the request], they had the city decorated, yoked four lotus-colored horses to an auspicious chariot, spread out a supreme coverlet, and placed upon it the five royal insignia; then, surrounded by a fourfold army, they set out.
Musical instruments were played in front of the chariot while its owner was present, but behind it when he was absent.
“Let them go; therefore, let all the musical instruments play behind you,” he said.
Then, having consecrated both the yoke and the goad with the golden pitcher, he released the chariot, saying, “Let it go to the presence of whoever has the merit to rule the kingdom.
Thereupon, the chariot circumambulated the royal palace and swiftly ascended the main street.
The general and the others thought, "Let Phussaratha come into my presence.
Having passed by the houses of them all, he circumambulated the city, departed through the eastern gate, and set out toward the park.
Then, seeing him proceeding with speed, they said, "Turn back! The chaplain replied, "Do not turn him back."
“Let him go even a hundred yojanas if he wishes; do not stop him,” he said. The chariot entered the park, circumambulated the auspicious stone slab, and stood ready for his mounting.
Seeing the Great Being lying there, the chaplain addressed the ministers, saying, “Sirs, a man is seen lying upon the stone slab; he is worthy of the white parasol.”
"We do not know whether he possesses courage or not. If he is a man of merit, he will not look at us;
but if he is possessed by an evil omen, he will rise up trembling in fear and look [at us].
Therefore, quickly strike all the musical instruments! she said. At that very moment, many hundreds of musical instruments were struck.
Then the sound of the musical instruments was like the roar of the ocean.
Awakened by that sound, the Great Being uncovered his head and looked out;
seeing the great multitude, he thought, "It must be that I have arrived with the white parasol," and having covered his head again, he turned over onto his left side.
He lay down. The chaplain, having uncovered his feet and examining the marks, thought, "Let this one island suffice;
he is capable of ruling over all four great islands," and so he had the musical instruments played once more.
Then the Great Being opened his mouth, turned over, and lay down on his right side, [addressing] the great multitude.
He looked around. Then the chaplain, having cleared the assembly, raised his joined palms, and bowing down, said, "Arise, O King;
the kingdom has come to you. Thereupon the Great Being asked him, "Where is your king?
When told, "The king has passed away," he asked, "Does he have no son or brother? When told, "There is none, Sire," [he continued].
Saying, "In that case, I shall indeed exercise sovereignty," he rose and sat cross-legged upon a stone slab.
Then they consecrated him right there. He became the king named Mahājanaka.
Having mounted his excellent chariot and entered the city with great splendor and majesty, as he was ascending to the royal palace, [he addressed] the commander-in-chief and the others...
Having reflected, "Let these very places be so," he ascended to the Great Terrace (Mahātala).
But the princess, by virtue of her previous perception, commanded a man for the purpose of testing him:
"Dear one, go, approach the King, and say: 'Sire, Queen Sīvalī summons you.'"

"Let him come quickly! He went and reported it accordingly. Although the wise king heard his words, he acted as if he had not heard them and praised only the palace, saying, "Oh, how magnificent this palace is!
Unable to make him hear it, he went and reported the matter to the princess: "Noble lady, the king does not heed your words."
"He hears [you], yet he praises only the palace; he does not value your words as even a blade of grass.
Having heard his words, she thought, "That man must be one of great aspiration," and she sent her again a second and a third time.
The king, according to his own desire and natural inclination, ascended the palace, stretching out like a lion. In him—
As he was approaching, the king’s daughter, unable to maintain her composure due to his splendor, came forward and offered him a hand to grasp.
He took her hand, ascended the great terrace, and sat upon the royal couch beneath a raised white parasol;
then, addressing his ministers, he said: "Friends, did the king, when he passed away, leave you any instruction?"
Having asked, "Has it been given? and being told, "Yes, Your Majesty," he said, "In that case, speak. [The other replied:
"Your Majesty, tell him to give the kingdom to one capable of winning over Queen Sīvalī.
When Queen Sīvalī came and was given a hand to hold, she was indeed considered won over; "Speak something else," [he said]. "Your Majesty, the headboard of the square couch..."
"Give the kingdom to one who is capable of knowing [this]," he said. The king thought, "This is difficult to know;
it can be known by means of a stratagem," and having drawn a golden needle from his head, he placed it in the hand of Queen Sīvalī, saying, "Place this down.
She took it and placed it at the head of the couch. Some even say, "He gave her a sword."
Thus, perceiving through that sign, "This is the pillow," as if not hearing their words, he said, "What are you saying?
When they spoke again in the same manner, he said, "It is no great matter to know this; this is the pillow. Then he said, "Say something else.
"Your Majesty, grant the kingdom to one capable of stringing the thousand-fold-strength bow," he was told by him.

It was said: "In that case, bring them here. Having had them brought, while still seated cross-legged on the couch, he strung the bow—just as women string a cotton-carding bow—and said, "Say something else.
He replied, "Your Majesty, grant us the kingdom for one capable of extracting the sixteen great treasures. It was asked, "Is there some summary (uddāna) of them?"
Having asked, when they replied, "Yes, Your Majesty," he said, "In that case, explain it to me.
They recited the summary verse: "At sunrise, the treasure. As he listened to it, that meaning became as clear to him as the full moon in the sky.
Then the king said to them, "There is no time today, my men; we shall take the treasure tomorrow. On the following day, he...
Having assembled his ministers, he asked, "Did your king feed the Paccekabuddhas? They replied, "Yes, Your Majesty.
He thought, "This is not the sun; rather, because they resemble the sun, the Paccekabuddhas are called 'Sūriyas.
There must be a treasure hidden at the place where they were welcomed. Then the king [inquired] regarding those Paccekabuddhas...
He asked, "When they were coming, while you went out to meet them, to what place did they go?
When he was told, "To such-and-such a place, O King," he had them dig up that spot and bring forth the treasure.
He then asked, "When they were departing, while you followed after them, from where did you dismiss them? When he was told, "From such-and-such a place," [he likewise had that spot dug up].
"Have the treasure brought out! he commanded, and had the treasure brought out.
Then the great multitude, raising thousands of shouts of joy, wandered about digging in the direction of the sun’s rising because it was said, "The treasure is at the rising of the sun.
Furthermore, because it was said, "The treasure is at the setting," they wandered about digging in the direction of the sun’s setting. "But this wealth..."
"It exists right here! Oh, how wonderful! they exclaimed, giving rise to joy and gladness.

"A treasure within" means he had the treasure brought out from inside the threshold of the great gate at the royal palace. "A treasure without" means he had the treasure brought out from outside the threshold.
"Neither within nor without" means he had the treasure brought out from below the threshold. "A treasure on the ascent" refers to the auspicious elephant.
At the time of ascending, he had the treasure brought out from its place of concealment by means of a golden ladder.
Likewise, upon descending, he had the treasure brought out from the place where he descended from the elephant's back. Regarding "the four great sal trees":
in the place where they were made into a service for the ground, the four legs of the royal couch were made of sal wood; beneath them were four...
He had the treasure-pots brought forth. Regarding "treasure for a league all around": a "league" (*yojana*) is the measure of a chariot-yoke;
he had the treasure brought forth from a distance of one chariot-yoke’s length all around the royal couch. Regarding "great treasure at the tips of the tusks":

at the place where the auspicious elephant stood, he had the treasure brought forth from the position facing its two tusks. Regarding "at the tips of the hairs": at the place where the auspicious elephant stood...
He had the treasure extracted from the spot directly in front of its tail. Regarding "Kepuka": *kepu* means water;
having had water drawn from an auspicious lotus pond, he showed him the treasure. Regarding "great treasures at the tops of trees":
in the park, at the foot of a great *sāla* tree, at the time of midday when the tree’s shadow was perfectly circular, [he saw] the treasure within it.
He had them brought out. Having thus had the sixteen great treasures brought out, he asked, "Is there anything else?
They replied, "There is nothing, Your Majesty. The great multitude was joyful and delighted.
Then the king, thinking, "I shall distribute this wealth through the channels of giving," [went] to the center of the city and to the four city gates.
Having had five alms-halls constructed at five locations, he established a great distribution of gifts (*mahādāna*).
He summoned his mother and a brahmin from the city of Kālacampā and accorded them great honor.
Even while he was still in his youth, the entire kingdom of Videha proclaimed: "It is said that the son of King Ariṭṭhajanaka, a king named Mahājanaka, [has ascended] the throne."
"He is indeed wise and skilled in means; we shall see him. Thus, the people were stirred up for the sake of seeing him.
From here and there, many people arrived bringing abundant offerings, and the citizens prepared a great festival.

In the royal palace, carpets and other furnishings were spread out, perfumed garlands and flower wreaths were hung, and it was filled with the appearance of scattered parched grain, flowers, incense, and the scent of perfumes.

Having had various kinds of food and drink prepared, they presented them [to the King]. For the sake of the King’s gift-offering (*paṇṇākāra*), they took many varieties of hard and soft foods, honey, molasses, fruits, and so forth, in silver and golden vessels; taking these, they stood surrounding him here and there.
On one side the circle of ministers sat down, on one side the group of brahmins, and on one side the guild-leaders (*seṭṭhi*) and others sat down.
On one side, female dancers possessing supreme beauty sat down; Brahmins also recited auspicious verses for the sake of well-being;
those skilled in dance, song, and the like performed dances and songs; and hundreds of musical instruments were struck.
At that time, the royal palace resounded with a single unified noise, like the depths of the ocean when struck by the force of a Yugaṇdhara wind.
The place where he looked around trembled.

Then the Great Being, while seated upon the royal throne beneath the white parasol, observed that great splendor and majesty resembling the glory of Sakka, and recollected the exertion he had made in the great ocean. To him, [the thought arose]: "Virtue indeed..."
Thinking, "This is what ought to be done; had I not exerted effort in the great ocean, I would not have obtained this success," joy arose in him as he recollected that exertion.
With the surge of that joy, uttering an inspired exclamation, he said:
"A wise man should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent."
"I see myself as I have become just as I desired.
A wise person should indeed aspire and not despair;
I see myself as one who has been pulled out of the water onto dry land."
“A person should indeed strive; a wise one should not despair.
I see myself now as I have come to be, just as I desired.
A person should indeed strive; a wise one should not despair.
I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
"Even when brought to suffering, a wise person should not cut off hope for the arrival of happiness;
for many contacts, both harmful and beneficial, come upon one before death has arrived."
“Even that which is not thought of comes to pass, and even that which is thought of perishes;
for riches, whether of a woman or a man, do not arise from mere thought.
In this context, “one should indeed hope” means that one should simply form the hope for one’s own work without performing an act that cuts off hope. “One should not despair” means:
Exerting energy, one should not become despondent nor indolent.
"Just as I wished"—that is, just as I desired the state of kingship—"so indeed have I become a king. "Extracted" means removed. "Brought to suffering" means touched by bodily and mental suffering.
"Harmful and beneficial": harmful contacts are those that result in suffering; beneficial contacts are those that result in happiness. "Without thought" means those who do not think.

"Those who do not reflect. This is what is meant: among those contacts, beings touched by an unwholesome contact do not exert energy, failing to consider that "there is also wholesome contact; by exerting energy, one may attain it.
Not reflecting on this matter, they fail to obtain wholesome contact and, succumbing to death, they meet their end.
"Therefore, energy must indeed be exerted.
Regarding the phrase "even the unthought": for these beings, even what was not thought occurs, and even what was thought perishes.

For instance, my own thought—"I shall obtain the kingdom without even fighting"—was something unthought; whereas [the thought] "having brought wealth from Suvaṇṇabhūmi and having fought with my father... [was thought].
"I thought, 'I shall seize the kingdom that belongs to me,' but now my thought is lost and what was unintended has come to pass.
For wealth is not 'made of thought' (cintāmaya) because the wealth of these beings is not produced by mere thinking;
therefore, one must simply exert effort. For for one who possesses effort, even that which was not intended comes to be."
From that time forth, he ruled his kingdom righteously and justly without violating the ten duties of a king, and he attended upon the Paccekabuddhas.
Later, Queen Sīvalī gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit;
they gave him the name Prince Dīghāvu. When he reached maturity, the king bestowed upon him the position of viceroy and ruled for seventy thousand years.
He had it done. One day, when the park-keeper brought various fruits and diverse flowers, the king saw them and was delighted;
having shown him honor, he said, "Good park-keeper, I shall visit the park; you must decorate it.
He accepted, saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," and having done so, he informed the king.
Thus, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant and accompanied by a great retinue, he departed from the city and reached the gate of the pleasure grove.
There were two mango trees there with a dark-blue luster; one was fruitless, while the other bore fruit.

That fruit, however, was exceedingly sweet, and because the king had not yet tasted the finest fruit, no one dared to take any from it. The king, still seated upon the back of the noble elephant, [proceeded].
Then, taking one fruit, he ate it; as soon as it was placed upon the tip of his tongue, it appeared to him like divine food.
He thought, "I shall eat many when I return. Knowing that the king had consumed the best fruit, the viceroy and all the others, down to even the elephant and horse castrati, took a fruit and ate it.
Others, failing to obtain fruit, broke the branches with sticks and made him lie down.
The tree stood there broken and shattered, while the other remained radiant like a mountain of jewels.
When the king emerged from the park and saw this, he asked his ministers, "What is this? [They replied,] "By the King’s supreme fruit..."
"It has been plundered by the multitude, O King," they said. "My good man, why is it that neither its leaves nor its color have faded?
"Because it is fruitless, O King, it has not faded. Hearing this, the king was moved with a sense of spiritual urgency and said, "This tree stands here with a lush appearance because it is fruitless;
but this other one, because it bears fruit, is broken down and shattered."
“Firmly established. This kingship is like a tree bearing fruit, whereas the life of renunciation is like a tree without fruit.
Fear belongs only to one who possesses something; there is no fear for one who possesses nothing. Therefore, rather than being like a fruit-bearing tree, I shall become like a tree without fruit;
having abandoned this prosperity and gone forth, I will take up the homeless life. Having thus made a firm resolve and fixed his mind, he—
Having entered the city, while still standing at the door of the palace, he summoned the commander-in-chief and said:

"Great Commander, from this day forward, let no others see me except for one attendant appointed to bring my food and to provide water for my mouth and tooth-sticks; take the former judges and ministers and rule the kingdom."
"From now on, I shall practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) upon the upper terrace of the palace," he said, and having ascended the palace, he practiced the duty of a recluse all alone.
When time had passed in this manner, the great multitude gathered in the royal courtyard;
not seeing the Great Being, they said, "Our king is not as he was before," and spoke these two verses:
“Indeed, sir, King Disampati, the lord of all lands, has never before been thus:
today he pays no heed to dancing, nor does he set his mind on song.
He gazes neither upon the deer, nor the pleasure gardens, nor the swans.”
“Like a mute, sitting in silence, he does not instruct on what is beneficial.
In this context, “deer” is a term inclusive of all [animals]; the meaning is that previously he would have them fight elephants and fight rams, but today he does not even look at them.
“In the park” means he no longer enjoys the pleasures of the park. “Swans” refers to those [ponds] covered with five kinds of lotuses...
He did not even look at the flocks of swans in the park lotuses. Thinking he was a fool, they asked the food-bearer and the attendant, "Sire, is the king consulting with you on some matter?
They replied, "He is not consulting. Therefore, they spoke thus.
The king, without clinging to sensual pleasures and with a mind inclined toward seclusion, recollected the paccekabuddhas who were his family preceptors.
“Who indeed will point out to me the dwelling place of those who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline, who possess nothing, and who are free from worldly attachments?
Thus he uttered this inspired utterance in three verses:
“Those who desire happiness, whose conduct is secluded, who have desisted from killing and binding;”
“Who are those young and old who dwell today in the monastery?
“They are wise ones who have transcended the forest of worldly existence; homage to those great seers who, while the world is in a state of agitation, dwell free from agitation.”
“Having cut through the net of Death, which is spread wide and firm, those who have severed their attachment go forth;
who can reach the destination of such as these?

In this context, “desirous of happiness” means desirous of the happiness of Nibbāna. “Of secret virtue” means they possess concealed virtue and do not proclaim their own qualities. “Both young and old” means both the youthful and the elderly. “They dwell” means they reside [in that state].
As he was thus recollecting their virtues, a great rapture arose within him.
Then the Great Being rose from his cross-legged seat, opened the northern lion-window, and facing the northern direction, placed his palms together in reverence at his head.
Paying homage with the thought, "The Paccekabuddhas are endowed with such virtues," he spoke the verses beginning with, "They have transcended the forest-thicket."

In this context, "those who have transcended the forest" refers to those who have abandoned craving. "The Great Seers" refers to those who stand having sought the great qualities, such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).
"In the world that is eager" means in the world that has fallen into the agitation of passion and the like. "The net of Death" is the net of craving spread out by the Māra of the defilements.
"Those who are deceitful" means those who are exceedingly deceitful. "Who shall find their path? means: who shall find mine?
The meaning is that he would take them and go to bring them to the dwelling place of those Paccekabuddhas.
While he was practicing the duties of a recluse right there in the palace, four months passed.
Then his mind inclined exceedingly toward the life of renunciation; the household appeared to him like the hell of the world-intervals, and the three realms of existence appeared as if set ablaze.
Thus, with a mind intent on renunciation, he thought, "When indeed will it be my time to leave this city of Mithilā— adorned and prepared like the abode of Sakka—
and entering the Himālaya mountains, to take up the garb of one who has gone forth?
Having thus reflected, he began the description of Mithilā.
“When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, divided into sections, and well-measured?
When indeed will that time come? When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, vast, and radiant on all sides?”
"Having abandoned it, I shall go forth; when will that ever be?
When shall I, having abandoned Mithilā, prosperous with its many walls and gate-towers, go forth? When will that ever be?"
“When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, with its strong watchtowers and ramparts, and go forth into homelessness? When will that day surely come?
When shall I [leave] Mithilā, so prosperous, with its well-laid-out great highways?”
"Having abandoned it, I shall go forth— when indeed will that be?
When shall I abandon Mithilā, so prosperous,
with its well-arranged marketplaces, and go forth— when indeed will that be?"
“When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, crowded with cattle, horses, and chariots, and go forth into homelessness? When indeed will that time come?
When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, adorned with groves and forests?”
"Having abandoned it, I shall go forth—when indeed will that be?
When shall I, having abandoned Mithilā, prosperous and garlanded with park-forests, go forth? When indeed will that be?"
“When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, adorned with palaces and groves of trees, and go forth into homelessness? When indeed will that time come?
When shall I renounce Mithilā, so prosperous, the triple city belonging to the kinsmen of kings?”
Built with joy by the illustrious Vedeha,
when will that time come when, having abandoned it, I shall go forth? "When,
in the prosperous Videha kingdom, crowded and protected by the Dhamma..."
"Having abandoned [the world], I shall go forth; when will that ever be?
When the Vedehas are prosperous, invincible, and protected by Dhamma;
having abandoned [the world], I shall go forth—when will that ever be?"
“When shall I renounce the delightful inner palace, so well-apportioned and measured, and go forth into homelessness? When will that day indeed come?
When shall I leave the delightful inner palace, plastered with lime and clay?”
“Having abandoned it, I shall go forth; when will that ever be?
‘When shall I abandon the delightful inner palace, fragrant and enchanting;
having abandoned it, I shall go forth—when will that ever be?’”
“When shall I, having abandoned these gabled houses—divided into sections and measured out—go forth into homelessness? When indeed will that time come?
When shall I [abandon] these gabled houses plastered with lime and clay?”
"Having abandoned [this], I shall go forth— when will that ever be?
When shall I abandon these gabled houses,
fragrant and delightful, and go forth— when will that ever be?"
“When shall I leave this gabled chamber, anointed and smeared with sandalwood paste, and go forth into homelessness? When will that time ever come?
When shall I [leave] the golden couch, spread with woolen blankets and embroidered cloth?”
"Having abandoned [this], I shall go forth; when will that ever be?
When, upon a jeweled couch, spread with woolen rugs and covered with fine cloth;
having abandoned it, I shall go forth—when will that ever be?"
“When shall I renounce fine cotton cloth, silk, linen, and Koṭumbara cloth, and go forth? When will that time ever come?
When shall I [bathe] in a delightful lotus pond resounding with the cries of ruddy geese?”
Covered with mandārava flowers and with lotuses and water-lilies;
when shall I ever leave this behind and go forth into homelessness?
When shall I [see] the elephant herds, adorned with every ornament?
When the Mātaṅga elephant, with golden girths and clad in golden trappings,
has been mounted by village chiefs bearing spears and goads in their hands—
when shall that time come when I have abandoned him and go forth into homelessness?
“When shall I be mounted upon swift-drawing Sindhu horses, noble by birth like thoroughbreds, adorned with every ornament,
and led by village headmen carrying quivers and bows?”
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth— when will that ever be?
When shall I see the chariot-warriors, armored and with banners raised,
and the elephants and tigers, adorned with every ornament?"
“When the village chiefs, with bows in hand and clad in armor, have mounted [their chariots],
I shall abandon [this life] and go forth into homelessness— when will that time ever be?
When shall I [ride] in a golden chariot, equipped and with its banner raised high?”
“Even when I am mounted upon elephants and tigers, adorned with every ornament,
and accompanied by village chiefs clad in armor and holding bows in their hands—
when shall that time come when I shall renounce all this and go forth?”
“When shall I [see] the chariot ready, with its armor fastened and its banner raised;
with elephants and tigers, adorned with every ornament;
and mounted by village chiefs, clad in mail and holding bows in their hands?”
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth into homelessness;
when will that time ever be? When shall I see horse-chariots equipped with armor, their banners raised high, and likewise elephants and tigers, adorned with every ornament?"
“When the village headmen, with bows in hand and clad in armor, have mounted [their chariots]—having abandoned them, I shall go forth into homelessness. When will that time ever be?
When will I see the war-chariots yoked, armored, and with banners raised?”
"Furthermore, when I am mounted upon a noble elephant adorned with every ornament,
surrounded by village chiefs clad in armor and holding bows in their hands—
when will that time come when I shall renounce it all and go forth?"
“When shall I [be mounted] upon a chariot drawn by bulls, armored and with banners raised high;
or likewise upon an elephant adorned with all ornaments,
accompanied by village chiefs bearing bows in their hands and clad in mail?”
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth into homelessness—
when will that time ever come? When shall I see the Aja-ratha, armored and with its banner raised,
as well as the Dīpa and Veyyaggha, adorned with every ornament?"
“When the village chiefs, with bows in hand and clad in armor, have mounted [their chariots]—having abandoned them, I shall go forth into homelessness. When will that time ever be?
When will I see the rams’ chariots, equipped and with banners raised?”
“Even if I were mounted upon a noble elephant adorned with every ornament,
surrounded by village chiefs clad in armor and holding bows in their hands—
when will that time come when I shall renounce all this and go forth?”
“When shall I mount the deer-chariot, armored, with its banner raised high,
together with the lions and tigers, adorned with every ornament;
[mounted] by village chiefs wearing armor and holding bows in their hands?”
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth; when will that time ever be?
When shall I [see] those elephant-riders, adorned with every ornament, brave warriors clad in blue armor, holding lances and hooks in their hands?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth— when will that ever be?
When shall I [see] those horsemen, adorned with every ornament,
wearing blue armor, heroic, and bearing *illiya* bows?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth into homelessness—
when will that time ever be? When shall I [see] those who mount chariots,
adorned with every ornament, brave warriors wearing blue armor, holding bows and quivers in their hands?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth— when will that ever be?
When shall I [see] those archers, adorned with every ornament,
wearing blue armor, heroic, with bows in hand and quivers at their sides?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth;
when will that time ever be? When shall I see the princes, adorned with every ornament, wearing variegated armor, heroic, and bearing golden ear-rings?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth; when will that time ever be?
When shall I [dwell] among the noble ones, who are observant of their vows, well-adorned, their limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood, and wearing the finest Kāsī cloth?"
"Having abandoned [this life], I shall go forth into homelessness—
when will that ever be? When shall I see my circle of ministers,
all adorned with ornaments, wearing yellow armor, brave, and garlanded, walking before me?"
"Having abandoned [them], I shall go forth; when will that ever be?
When shall I, having abandoned my seven hundred wives, all adorned with every ornament, go forth? When will that ever be?"
“When shall I, having abandoned my seven hundred wives—those well-proportioned women of slender waists—go forth into homelessness? When indeed will that time come?
When shall I, having abandoned my seven hundred wives—who are obedient and speak with affection—go forth?”
"Having abandoned it, I shall go forth— when indeed will that be?
When shall I abandon a bronze bowl weighing a hundred palas, adorned with a hundred gold stripes,
and go forth— when indeed will that be?"
"When indeed shall I [be borne] by herds of elephants, adorned with every ornament—
elephants with golden girths, clad in gold-trimmed cloths,
mounted by village chiefs holding spears and goads in their hands?"
When will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
“When will my thoroughbred mares, adorned with every ornament,
like noble Sindhava horses of swift carriage and high birth, [follow] me?”
“When will that time come when those village leaders, armed with spears and bows,
no longer follow me as I drive? When will that time come when the ranks of chariots,
armored and with banners raised, [will surround me]?”
“Moreover, women adorned with every ornament— Dīpās and Veyyagghās alike—
mounted upon elephant-drivers who carry bows in their hands and wear armor:
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me as I go?”
“When shall I indeed [ride] golden chariots, armored, with banners raised high—
those adorned with ivory and tiger-skins, decorated with every ornament;
mounted by village chiefs, clad in mail and holding bows in their hands?”
When will that time come when they will no longer follow me? “When will my chariots be yoked,
with their warriors girt for battle, their banners raised high—
chariots adorned with leopards, tigers, and all manner of ornaments?”
“When will that time come when I shall not be pursued by the village chiefs, those armored men with bows in their hands? When will that time come when I, mounted on horse-drawn chariots,
clad in mail and with banners raised high, shall no longer be followed?”
“Women adorned with every ornament— Dīpās and Veyyagghās alike—
mounted upon elephant-drivers who carry bows in their hands and wear armor:
when will that time come when they no longer follow after me?”
“When will the charioteers bring me forth— clad in armor, with banners raised high,
adorned with all ornaments, and mounted upon elephants of the Dīpa, Veyyaggha, or Oṭṭha breeds,
led by village chiefs who carry bows in their hands and wear breastplates?”
"When will that time come when they will no longer follow me? When will it be that ox-carts,
yoked with bulls, equipped with armor, raised with banners—
whether adorned with leopards or tigers, and decorated with every ornament— [shall follow me]?"
“When will that time come when the village leaders, armed with bows and clad in armor, will not pursue me as I drive the chariot? When will those who have mounted my unaging chariot,
armored and with banners raised high, [pursue me]?”
“Even women adorned with every ornament— Dīpās and Veyyagghās alike—
mounted upon village chiefs who are armored and hold bows in their hands,
will never follow me as I go to the chariot. When will that time ever come?”
“When will I [be drawn] by chariots with deer-skin covers, yoked with horses adorned with raised banners—
some from Dīpa, others from Veyyaggha— all decorated with every ornament;
and when will I be mounted by village chiefs, clad in armor and holding bows in their hands?”
When will that time come when they no longer follow after me?
“When will it be that deer-drawn chariots, armored and with banners raised—
some drawn by leopards and others by tigers, all adorned with every ornament— [shall follow me]?”
“When will that time come when I shall not be pursued by village chiefs mounted on elephants,
armed with bows and clad in armor? When will that time come when I,
adorned with every ornament, shall be followed by elephant-riders?”
“When will it be that the brave warriors,
wearing blue garments and holding spears and goads in their hands, will not follow me as I ride?
When will it be that horsemen, adorned with every ornament, [will follow me]?”
When will that time come when the brave warriors,
wearing blue turbans and bearing bows made of *illiyā* wood, will no longer follow me as I ride?
When will that time come when the chariot-riders, adorned with every ornament, [will follow me]?
When will those heroes, wearing blue garments,
with bows in hand and quivers at their sides, no longer follow after me? When will archers,
adorned with every ornament, [no longer follow me]?
When will that time come when the brave warriors, wearing blue turbans,
with bows in hand and quivers at their sides, will not pursue my chariot?
When will the princes, adorned with every ornament, [come to seek me]?
When will that time come when the brave warriors,
wearing variegated garments and bearing golden earrings, will no longer follow me as I go?
When will the noble hosts, virtuous and adorned, [follow me]?
"When will that time come when those whose limbs are anointed with yellow sandalwood and who wear the finest Kāsī cloth will no longer follow me? When will the assembly of ministers,
adorned with every ornament, [no longer follow me]?"
"When will it be that those heroes wearing yellow garments,
adorned with garlands, walking in front, will no longer follow me as I travel?
When will it be that my seven hundred wives, all adorned with every ornament, [will likewise no longer follow]?"
When will that time come when those seven hundred wives of mine—well-proportioned and slender-waisted—will no longer follow after me?
When will that time come when they will not pursue me? When will that time come?
“When will my seven hundred wives, obedient and sweet-spoken,
no longer follow after me as I go? When shall I, having taken up the bowl, shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe, [enter the homeless life]?”
"I shall wander for alms from house to house; when will that ever come to pass?
When shall I wear a saṅghāṭī robe made of rags discarded on the great highway; when will that ever come to pass?"
“When shall I, shrouded in wet robes during a seven-day downpour, go about for alms? When indeed will that time come?
When shall I, having gone everywhere—from tree to tree and forest to forest—[wander]?”
“Free from longing, I shall go— when will that ever be?
When shall I go alone through mountain fastnesses, having abandoned fear and terror— when will that ever be?”
“When shall I, like a lute-player, straighten my mind—so delightful with its seven strings? When indeed will that come to pass?
When shall I, like a wheelwright, repair a worn-out sandal?”
“May I cut off the fetter of sensual desire, both that which is divine and that which is human.
In this context, “when” (*kadā*) is a reflection on time. “Prosperous” (*phītaṃ*) means well-flowered with garments, ornaments, and so forth.
“Divided and measured into parts” means divided according to gates and streets by skilled city-planners, by way of royal palaces and other structures.
Measured by its divisions (*koṭṭhāsato*). "When will that be? means: when indeed will it be for me to go forth, having abandoned such a city?
"Radiant on all sides" means endowed with the splendor of ornaments everywhere.
"With many walls and gate-towers" means possessed of both thick and broad ramparts as well as gate-towers. "With strong watchtowers and fortresses."
It was provided with strong watchtowers and gatehouses. "Besieged" (pīḷita) means crowded. "Tipura" means possessed of three cities;
the meaning is "having three walls. Alternatively, "tipura" means filled three times over.
"Filled with royal kinsmen" (rājabandhunī) means filled with those closely related to the king. "By Somanassa" refers to the King of Videha who bore that name.
"Nicita" means endowed with accumulations of wealth, grain, and so forth. "Ajeyya" means not to be conquered by adversaries.
"Candanaphosita" means sprinkled with red sandalwood. "Koṭumbarāni" refers to garments produced in the kingdom of Koṭumbara.
"Hatthigumba" means herds of elephants. "Hemakappanavāsase" refers to both a golden ornament known as a *kappana* for the head and [fine cloth].

"And endowed with golden nets. "By village leaders" means by elephant trainers. "Like thoroughbreds by birth" means like thoroughbreds indeed, by virtue of their birth and their capacity to understand what is to be done and what is not to be done; [it refers to] herds of such horses.
"By village leaders" means by horse trainers. "Carrying quivers and bows" means carrying both quivers and bows. "Chariot-arrays" means rows of chariots. "He causes to resound."
"Suṭṭhu naddhe" means well-fastened. "Dīpe athopi veyyaggheti" means surrounded by the skins of leopards and tigers.

"Gāmaṇīyehīti" means by chariot-drivers. "Sajjhuratheti" means on silver chariots. They yoke them to goat-chariots, antelope-chariots, and deer-chariots for the sake of beauty. "Ariyagaṇeti" means among groups of brahmins;
it is said that at that time they were of noble conduct, and therefore he spoke to them in this way. "Haricandanalittaṅgeti" means with limbs smeared with yellow sandalwood.
His body was anointed with sandalwood paste the color of gold. "Seven hundred wives" refers specifically to his beloved wives.
"Well-perceived" means being very mindful. "Obedient" means those who carry out the husband's word.
"A hundred-pala" means made of a hundred palas of gold. "Kaṃsa" means a bowl. "With a hundred lines" means endowed with a hundred lines on its back surface.
"When you go alone, wandering through the Anitthigandha forest grove, when will they not follow after me?
"Seven days of rain" (*sattāhasammegha*) means when a great cloud has arisen for seven days; the sense is "seven days of heavy downpour. "Ovaṭṭha" means with the head bowed down.
"In all places" (*sabbattha*) means in every direction. "Rujjaka" means a lute player. "Fetter of sensual desire" (*kāmasaṃyojana*) means the fetter that is sensual desire.
He divines the divine; he divines the human.

It is said that he was born during a time when the lifespan was ten thousand years; having ruled for seven thousand years, he went forth into homelessness when three thousand years of his life remained.
From the moment he saw the mango tree at the gate of the pleasure garden upon going forth, however—
Having lived for four months in the household, he thought, "The life of a renunciant is more excellent than this royal attire; I shall go forth.

Having thought thus, he secretly instructed his attendant: "Dear son, without letting anyone know, go and buy saffron robes and an earthen bowl from the market and bring them back. He did so. Then the king summoned his barber.
Having had his hair and beard shaved off, he gave a choice village to the barber and dismissed him;
then, having put on one saffron robe, draped another over his shoulders, and placed a third over his shoulder, he tucked even his clay bowl into its bag and slung it over his shoulder.
Next, taking up his mendicant’s staff, he walked back and forth several times upon the great terrace in the manner of a Paccekabuddha.
He paced back and forth. Having stayed there that very day, on the following day at the time of sunrise, he began to descend from the palace.
Then Queen Sīvalī, having summoned those seven hundred favorite women, said: "It has been a long time since we have seen the King;
four months have passed. Today we shall see him. Adorn yourselves with all your ornaments and display, according to your strength, the graceful movements, laughter, and charms of women."

Having said, "Show him and strive to bind him with the fetters of the defilements," she ascended the palace with those women, who were fully adorned and prepared, thinking, "We shall see the king. Even though she saw him descending, she did not recognize him.
Thinking, "This must be a Paccekabuddha who has come to give counsel to the king," she paid homage and stood to one side.

He stood there. The Great Being also descended from the palace. The other woman, having ascended the palace and seen the honey-colored hair and the articles of adornment upon the royal couch, thought, "This is not a Paccekabuddha; he must be our beloved husband.
Come, let us entreat him and make him turn back. She descended from the great terrace and reached the royal courtyard. Having arrived, she—

Then, having loosened her hair along with all those women, she scattered it over her back and beat her breast with both hands, crying out most piteously, "O Great King, why do you perform such an act?
As she pursued the king, the entire city was thrown into commotion. They too thought, "The king, they say, has gone forth into homelessness."
"But from where shall we obtain such a righteous king? they cried, following after the king while weeping.
There, the Teacher, describing both the lamentation of those women and the king's departure as he left them behind, said:
"And those seven hundred wives, adorned with every ornament..."
“Raising your arms, you cried out: ‘Why will you abandon us?
Those seven hundred wives of yours—well-proportioned and slender-waisted—raised their arms and cried out: ‘Why will you abandon us?’”
“Those seven hundred wives of yours, obedient and sweet-spoken, have raised their arms and cried out: ‘Why will you abandon us?
Those seven hundred wives of yours, adorned with every ornament,”
Having abandoned his prosperity, the king went forth, preceded by the life of renunciation.
And those seven hundred wives— well-proportioned and slender-waisted—
he too abandoned, as the king went forth, preceded by the life of renunciation.
“Those seven hundred wives, obedient and sweet-spoken,
the king abandoned and fled from prosperity, preceded by his renunciation.
Abandoning the bronze vessel weighing a hundred palas, adorned with a hundred gold bands;”
"He took up a clay bowl; that was his second consecration.
In this context, "stretching out his arms" means raising his arms. "They lamented," monks, refers to King Mahājanaka and those seven hundred wives who, even as they were wailing, cried out:
"O Lord, why do you go away, abandoning us? What fault is ours?"
"Having abandoned [the world], he went forth"; the meaning is that he went while being escorted as if urged, "Go forth into the religious life.
"That, monks, was his second consecration": having performed that taking up of the clay bowl as a second consecration, that king went forth.
Queen Sīvalī, lamenting and unable to turn the king back, thought, "There is this expedient," and having summoned Mahāsenagutta, she commanded him:
"Dear son, set fire to dilapidated houses, ruined halls, and the like in the direction where the king is traveling;
gather grass and leaves and create smoke in various places along the way."
So he did accordingly. She went into the presence of the king, fell at his feet, and announcing the state of Mithilā’s being ablaze, she spoke these two verses:
“Terrible are the flames like fire; the treasuries are burning apart.
Silver and gold, pearls, and many beryl gems—”
“Jewels, conch shells, pearls, cloth, yellow sandalwood;
antelope skins, ivory goods, and much iron and black metal—come, O King, turn back; let not this wealth of yours perish.”
In this context, *bhesma* means terrifying. *Aggisamā jālā* means that fires seized the houses of various people;

the meaning is that this is a great conflagration. *Kosa* refers to gold, silver, treasuries, and so forth. *Bhāgaso* means that even though these are well-portioned into sections, they are not being consumed by fire, O King.
*Loha* refers to copper, bronze, and so on. May these not perish for you.
"Do not lament over this wealth; let this wealth perish. Come, extinguish it, and you shall depart later.
Otherwise, there will be reproach for you, saying, 'Mahājanaka departed without even looking back at the burning city.
Because of that, you will experience shame and remorse. Come, give orders to your ministers and extinguish the fire, O King."
Then the Great Being, demonstrating, "Queen, what are you saying? That which belongs to those who possess something is consumed by fire, but we are without possessions," spoke this verse:
"Truly, we live in great happiness, we for whom there is nothing at all;
while Mithilā was burning, nothing of mine was consumed."
In this context, "possessions" (*kiñcana*) refers to those defilements known as obstacles;
since we have no such possessions, we live in great happiness by virtue of that state of having nothing. For that very reason, he says:
"Even while Mithilā was burning, nothing of mine burned; I did not see even the slightest bit of my own belongings being consumed."
Having spoken thus, the Great Being departed by the northern gate. His seven hundred wives also went out after him.
Then Queen Sīvalī, having devised a stratagem, commanded her ministers, "Show yourselves as if you were plundering the country and destroying the villages.
At that very moment, men with weapons in their hands began running and rushing about from here and there.

They showed the king those who were plundering the bodies as if pouring lac juice over them, who were lying on planks as if they had received mortal wounds, and who were drifting along like the dead. The great multitude cried out, "Great King!
While you yourself are still alive, they are plundering the kingdom and slaughtering the people! Then the queen, having paid homage to the king, spoke this verse for the sake of his turning back:
“‘The forest-dwellers have arisen; they are destroying that kingdom.
Come, O King, turn back; let not this kingdom perish.

Therein, ‘forest-dwellers,’ O Great King, means that while you yourself were still reigning, forest-thieves arose and emerged; they are now destroying that kingdom of yours which was protected by Dhamma.”

Having heard this, the king thought, "While I am still alive, there can be no such thing as thieves rising up to ravage the kingdom; this must be the doing of Queen Sīvalī. Thinking thus, he spoke to her without offering a rebuttal:
"Very happily indeed we live, for us there is nothing at all;
while the kingdom is being plundered, you have not stolen anything from me."
“Truly we live in great happiness, for we possess nothing at all;
we shall subsist on rapture, like the Ābhassara deities. In this context, *vilumpamānamhi* means while it is being plundered.

*Yathā te brahmāno pītibhakkhā hutvā samāpattisukhena vītināmenti, tathā vītināmessāmāti*: “Just as those Brahmās, having become consumers of rapture, spend their time in the bliss of meditative attainment, so too shall we spend our time.”
Even when this was said, the great multitude continued to follow the king. Then it occurred to him:

"This great multitude does not wish to turn back; I shall make them turn back. When they had gone about half a league, he turned around and, standing on the main road, asked his ministers, "To whom does this kingdom belong?
When they replied, "To you, Your Majesty," he said, "In that case, this..."
"Inflict the royal punishment upon anyone who attempts to intervene in this decree," he said, and with his sword he drew a horizontal line across it.
No one was able to intervene in the decree issued by that powerful king.
The great multitude, placing the decree upon their heads, wailed with intense lamentation. The queen also, unable to intervene in that decree, [addressed] the king...
Seeing him departing with his back turned, she was unable to restrain her grief;

striking her breast, she fell across the great highway and proceeded rolling about. The great multitude, saying, "The letter has been intercepted by the owners of the letter," followed the very path the queen had taken.
Then the Great Being also set out toward the northern Himalayas. The queen too—
Taking the entire army and its mounts, they departed together with him. The king, unable to turn back the great multitude, traveled sixty yojanas along the road.
At that time, an ascetic named Nārada, having lived in a golden cave in the Himālayas, possessed the five supernormal powers and was dwelling in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna).
Having spent seven days and emerged from the bliss of *jhāna*, he uttered this inspired exclamation: "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!
Looking with his divine eye to see if anyone on the surface of Jambudīpa was seeking such bliss, he beheld the Great Being, the sprout of a Buddha, and thought:
"Even though King Mahābhinikkhamana has gone forth, with Queen Sīvalī at his head..."
