Thinking, “I cannot turn back the great multitude, and it might even cause him an obstacle; therefore, having gone now,
I shall give him exhortation for the sake of making his resolve even more firm and steadfast,” he went by the power of psychic potency and, standing in the air before the king,
spoke this verse to inspire his enthusiasm:
“What is this great clamor? What festival is being held in the village?
We ask you, O ascetic: where has this multitude come from?
Having heard this, the king said:
“While I am departing, leaving this place where these people have gathered,
as I cross the boundary to attain the state of a Sage, why do you ask me,
knowing full well that I am departing while still mingled with worldly pleasures?”
In that context, "What is this? means: what is this sound of a great multitude in the form of a body of elephants and so forth, and for what reason is it occurring?
"What sport is this in the village? means: what kind of sport is this, like that in a village, belonging to those who are coming along with you? "Where is it? means:
for what purpose has this great crowd set out and gathered together, and why is it coming while surrounding you? Thus he asked.
"Mamaṃti" means "me," who am leaving this people behind as I go; "taṃ maṃ ohāya gacchantan" means me, while going after having left them behind.
"Ettha" means in this place; "eso mahājano abhisato anubandhanto āgato" means this great multitude has come, having pursued and followed after me.

"Sīmātikkamanaṃ yan tan" means you, however, [think] of me as one who is departing, having transcended the boundary of defilements for the sake of attaining *mona*—which is to say, the wisdom of the homeless sage.
"Do you ask this knowing that [the mind] continues to be mixed with the delights arising moment by moment, without having abandoned the joy of thinking, 'I have indeed gone forth'?
Or do you ask without knowing? Have you not heard that Mahājanaka, it is said, went forth after abandoning the kingdom of Videha?"
Then, for the sake of making his resolve firm, he spoke this verse again:
“Do not think, ‘I have crossed over,’ while still maintaining this body;
for that which remains to be crossed is vast, for there are many obstacles.”

In this context, "Do not think, 'I have crossed over,'" means that while wearing this body clothed in saffron robes, you must not think, "By the mere assumption of this outward mark of renunciation, I have crossed over and transcended the boundary of the defilements.
"This is not to be crossed over" means that these so-called defilements cannot be fully traversed by such means alone. For there are many obstacles on the path to heaven.
"Many obstacles of defilement stand blocking your path.
Then, having heard his words, the Great Being asked about those obstacles:
"Who indeed is the obstacle for me, who am dwelling in such a state?"
“He who desires neither what is seen nor what is unseen of sensual pleasures.

Therein, “he who desires neither what is seen nor what is unseen” means: “I, who desire neither the sensual pleasures seen in the world of humans nor those unseen in the world of devas—what obstacle could there possibly be for me, who thus dwell alone? Thus he speaks.
Then, pointing out that very obstacle to him, he spoke this verse:
“Sleep, lethargy, yawning, discontent, and drowsiness after eating—these many obstacles dwell within the body. In this context, *niddā* refers to the sleep of a monkey.
*Tandī* means laziness. *Aratī* means restlessness or dissatisfaction. *Bhattasammado* means the feverish indigestion following a meal.
This is what is meant: when it is said, "Ascetic, you are handsome and golden-hued; having renounced kingship, you have gone forth," they will give you choice, nutritious almsfood.
Taking a bowl full of it, you will eat as much as you require, enter a leaf hut, lie down on a bed of wood shavings, and fall asleep while snoring.
Having fallen asleep and waking up in the middle of the night, you will roll over again and again, stretch out your hands and feet, and stand up;

yet, having taken hold of the robe-pole, you will put on the robe that was hanging there, and becoming indolent, you will neither take up the broom to sweep nor fetch water, but will lie down again and sleep, and will give rise to thoughts of sensual desire. At that time—
"You will grow weary of the life of renunciation; you will suffer from the fever of hunger.
By saying "They dwell within the body," he shows that these many obstacles dwell having become inhabitants of his body, arising right within his body itself.
Then the Great Being, offering him praise, spoke this verse:
“Truly it is good that the venerable one instructs me, O Brahmin;
Brahmin, I ask you this: who indeed are you, dear sir?
In this context, “Brahmin, instructs me” means: O Brahmin, truly it is good that the venerable one instructs me.
Then the ascetic said:
"My name is Nārada, and I am known as Kassapa;
I have come into your presence, for it is good to meet with the virtuous."
“May all that joy attend you in your dwelling;
may you fulfill whatever is lacking through patience and tranquility.
Straighten out what is crooked, and straighten out what is elevated.”
“Having honored kamma, true knowledge, and the Dhamma, one should wander forth.
In this context: “Vidū” means that by clan they know me as “Kassapa. “Sabbhī” means that I have come because association with the wise (paṇḍita) is indeed good.
“Ānanda” means that for you there is joy, satisfaction, and gladness regarding this going-forth.
"Let it be; do not be distressed. "The abodes" refers to the fourfold divine abode (brahmavihāra). "Let it proceed" means let it arise.
"Whatever is deficient" means whatever is lacking in you by way of virtue, the preparation of the kasiṇas, and meditative absorption—fill that with these [qualities] such as virtue and so forth.
"And with patience and tranquility" means without conceit, thinking "I am one who has gone forth from royalty," but rather through the patience of endurance.
And may you be endowed with the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesūpasama*). "Spread out" means do not lift up, do not stretch out; the meaning is "abandon.

"The depressed and the elevated" refers to the self-deprecation (*omāna*) that occurs in the manner of "Who am I? and so forth, and the overweening pride (*atimāna*) that occurs in the manner of "I am well-born" and so forth.

"Action" (*kamma*) refers to the ten paths of wholesome action. "True knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Dhamma" refers to the ascetic practice known as the preliminary work on the *kasiṇas*. "Having honored it, one should wander forth" means:
having honored these qualities, you should conduct yourself accordingly; or, having honored these qualities, go forth by firmly undertaking them—protect your renunciation;
do not become disenchanted. This is the meaning.
Having thus exhorted the Great Being, he departed through the air for his own abode.

When he had gone, another ascetic named Migājina likewise emerged from meditative absorption; looking about, he saw the Bodhisatta and thought, "I shall give him instruction in order to turn back the great multitude.
He came to that very spot, manifested himself in the air, and said:
“Having abandoned many elephants and horses, cities and provinces,
you went forth as a renunciant, O Father, yet found delight in a begging bowl.
Are your subjects, friends, ministers, and kinsmen well?”
“O Father, why did you find pleasure in that which is so loathsome?”—in this context, he says “in that bowl” (*kapāle*) referring to the clay alms-bowl. This is what is meant:
“Great King, having abandoned such sovereignty and lordship, you went forth into homelessness; yet in this bowl you have found delight. Thus he states the reason for his renunciation.
Questioning him, he spoke thus: "What indeed have these evil-minded ones done to you?
For what reason did you abandon such sovereignty and happiness as yours, and find no pleasure in this mere skull?
Then the Great Being said:
“O Migājina, at no time whatsoever have I ever conquered any kinsman by unrighteous means, nor have my kinsmen ever conquered me.
In this context, “O Migājina,” means: O Migājina, at no time whatsoever (*jātucche*)—absolutely—I have never [conquered] any kinsman.
"At no time have I ever conquered anyone by unrighteousness; nor indeed have those kinsmen ever conquered me by unrighteousness—thus, the meaning is that no one has ever done me wrong.
Having thus rejected his question, he now spoke, showing the reason for which he had gone forth:
“Having seen the course of the world, being devoured and turned to mud;
where the foolish worldling perishes and is bound—
having made this a simile, I am a mendicant, Migājina.”
In this context, "Having seen the world’s way of life" means: "I saw the way of life, the tradition, the lineage of the foolish world that follows the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*);

having seen that, I have gone forth"—this he indicates. "Devouring and made into mud" means: having seen the world being devoured by defilements (*kilesa*) and made into mud by those very same [defilements].
"Wherein the worldling sinks" means: wherein, in the basis of defilement, the worldling sinks.
The worldling clings there; many beings cling there and are both slain and bound by fetters, bonds, and the like.
"If I too am bound here, I shall be both slain and bound just like these beings"—thus, making this very reason his own analogy, seeing the world made into a mire, the mendicant...
The meaning is "born. He addresses him by name as "Migājina. But how did he come to know his name?
Because he had asked it first at the time of their greeting.
The ascetic, wishing to hear the reason in detail, spoke this verse:
“Who indeed is your Blessed One as teacher? Whose word is this so pure?
For it is not by abandoning either [cosmic] eons or knowledge, O bull among charioteers, that they call one a recluse who has transcended suffering.”
In this context, "whose" refers to the pure speech you have uttered; it means whose speech is it?

It refers to the ascetic who proclaims the efficacy of action (*kamma-vādī*) and is an attainer of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that proceed through repeated cultivation. "The one with true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the Paccekabuddha, who is endowed with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
This is what is meant: O Great King, O Bull among Charioteers, for indeed, [the Dhamma] is not merely for a monk of conventional practice.
It is not possible to practice in such a way as to transcend suffering without relying on a true ascetic or his instruction;

for it is said that one is a true ascetic when one conducts oneself in a manner that leads to the overcoming of suffering. However, having heard their words, it is indeed possible to practice accordingly;
therefore, tell me: who is your Blessed One, the Teacher?
The Great Being said:
“O deer-skin wearer, never at any time have I entered [the city] after having paid homage to any ascetic or brahmin whatsoever.”
In that context, "having honored" means having paid homage for the purpose of inquiring about the virtues of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"I have never entered before" means he says: "I have never previously entered [any such place], nor have I ever questioned any other ascetic.
For even while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Paccekabuddhas, he had never at any time inquired specifically about the virtues of the going-forth; therefore, he spoke thus.
Having spoken thus, he said, illustrating from the very beginning the reason for which he had gone forth:
“Going forth with great majesty, radiant with glory,
while songs were being sung and sweet melodies were being played.”
“In that place resounding with the beating of cymbals and drums,
and hushed by the rhythmic clapping of hands, I saw a deer-skin spread out,
a ripe mango fruit beyond a curtain, and a person being struck by men seeking meat.”
“Thus, having abandoned that glory and descended from my deer-skin seat,
I approached the foot of both a fruit-bearing and a fruitless mango tree.
Seeing the fruit-bearing mango tree struck down, shattered, and reduced to a withered stump, I— ”
Then he saw another mango tree, blue in luster and beautiful.
“In this very way, surely we too— though under a lord who has many thorns—
our enemies will slay us, just as this fruitful mango tree was struck down.”
“The leopard is killed for its skin, the elephant for its tusks;
the wealthy man is destroyed for his riches, yet the homeless one who has no attachments—
both the fruitful mango tree and the fruitless one are alike to me as teachers.”
In that context, "in the midst of the *vaggus*" means while sweet-sounding musical instruments (*tūriya*) were being played.

"Resounding with the beating of musical instruments" means in a pleasure grove (*uyyāna*) filled with the sounds of those instruments being struck. "Accompanied by clapping and rhythmic beats" means endowed with both claps and rhythmic beats.
"That deer-skin" refers to the deer-skin; I saw it. "The mango tree has fruit" means the mango tree has borne fruit.
"Tirocchada" means a mango tree growing outside the wall, supported by the wall, located within a garden beyond the enclosure.
"Haññamānaṃ" means being struck. "Orohitvā" means having descended from the back of the elephant. "Vinaḷīkataṃ" means made into a bed of reeds.
"Evameva" means just so. "Phalī" means one who has attained fruit. "Ajinamhi" means for the sake of skin, for the purpose of leather. "Dantehi" means by the tusks.
"By one's own teeth" means it is killed by the cause of being bitten; "kills" is the same as "is killed. "Homeless and without intimacy":
one who has abandoned the home because of having gone forth is called "homeless";

and because of the absence of intimacy with craving—which has the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) of sentient beings as its basis—one is called "without intimacy. The intention is: "Who could kill that one who is homeless and without intimacy? "Those teachers..."
He said, "Those two trees were my teachers.
Having heard this, Migājina gave the king this advice: "Be heedful," and then he departed for his own place. When he had gone, Queen Sīvalī fell at the feet of the king and said:
"All the people are distressed, thinking the king has gone forth into homelessness."
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalrymen, and infantry—
having reassured these people, having established a defense,
and having installed your son in the kingdom, you may then go forth into homelessness afterwards.”

In this context, "distressed" means frightened and terrified. "A shield" means that he established a protection and a defense for the distressed populace by saying, "Even though we are being burned and plundered, the king does not look upon us," and then, having installed his son Prince Dīghāvu on the throne and consecrated him, [said]:
"Afterwards, you shall go forth into homelessness. This is the meaning.
Then the Bodhisatta said:
“I have four provinces, friends, ministers, and kinsmen;
there are sons of the Videhas, Dīghāvu the increaser of the kingdom.”
“They shall exercise sovereignty over Mithilā, O Pajāpatī.

Regarding this, the phrase “there are sons” means that there are no sons of the ascetics named Sīvalī; however, there is Dīghāvu, the son of those who dwell in the kingdom of Videha, and they shall exercise sovereignty. “Pajāpatī” is how he addresses the queen.
The queen said, “Lord, now that you have gone forth, what am I to do? Then he said to her, “My dear lady, I shall instruct you; do as I say,” and spoke this verse:
“Come, I shall instruct you in that speech which is pleasing to me:
You rule the kingdom, yet you commit much evil and misconduct through body,
speech, and mind, by which you go to a state of misery.”
“Sustain yourself with alms-food that has been given by others and prepared by others; this is the way of the wise. In this context, “you” means:
having raised the parasol for your son and ruling the kingdom under the thought, “This is my son’s kingdom,” you will commit much evil.
“You go” means: by means of the great evil committed through body and so forth, you will go to a state of misery.
"This is the duty of the wise: one should subsist on alms-food; this is the way of the learned.
Thus the Great Being gave her this advice. As they were conversing with one another while walking along, the sun set.
The queen had the army camp pitched in a suitable location. The Great Being, too, [set out] alone...
He went to the foot of a tree. Having stayed there for the night, on the following day he attended to his bodily needs and set out upon the road.
The queen, saying, "Let the army follow behind," remained right behind him.
At the time for alms-round, they reached a city named Thūṇa. At that moment, within the city, one...
A man, having bought a large piece of meat from a butcher, had it roasted over coals on a spit;
then, setting it down on the edge of a wooden board to let it cool, he stood by. While his attention was elsewhere, a dog seized the meat and ran off with it.
The man, realizing this, pursued it as far as the outer southern gate, where he turned back in despondency. And the King...
As the queen walked ahead of the dog, she split into two parts. Out of fear, the dog dropped the piece of meat and fled.
Seeing this, the Great Being thought: "This dog has abandoned it and fled without looking back;
no other owner for it is to be seen. There is no such blameless alms-food of rag-robes as this; I shall consume it."
So, having taken out the clay bowl, he took that piece of meat, wiped it clean, placed it in the bowl, went to a place near water, and began to eat it.

Then the queen thought: "If he were interested in kingship, he would not eat such a loathsome thing, smeared with dust and the leavings of a dog. If he eats this, then now he is [no longer fit for the throne]."
Thinking, "He will have no husband," she said, "Great King, you eat such a loathsome thing.
He replied, "Queen, through your blind folly you do not know the excellence of this alms-food.
Having said this, he looked back at the place where it had fallen, consumed it as if it were the Deathless (*amata*), rinsed his mouth, and washed his hands. In that [moment]...
At that moment, the queen, reproaching him, said:
“Even one who does not eat at the fourth mealtime might die of hunger like a woman struck by a sudden plague;
yet a true man of noble birth, possessing the character of a virtuous person, would never consume such unrefined, ignoble food.”
"This is not good; this is not right; O Father, you are eating the leavings of a dog.

In that context, "untimely death" (*ajuṭṭhamārī*) means precisely death without a protector. "Smeared" (*luḷita*) means covered with dust. "Unnoble" (*anariya*) means unsightly. "One should not practice" (*na sevetha*):
the particle *na* is used here for the purpose of inquiry. This is what is meant: even at the time of the fourth meal...
"He might not eat and die of hunger; surely, even if this were so, a true man of noble family would never consume such alms-food. "Tayidaṃ" means "this very thing.
The Great Being said:
“Moreover, Sīvālī, that which is not edible for me is not what has been relinquished by a householder or a dog;
whatever wealth is righteously acquired here, all that is said to be edible and blameless.
In this context, “not edible” means that such alms-food is not called inedible for me. “Whatever” refers to what [has been relinquished] by a householder...
Or whatever has been discarded by a dog or a crow—that is called "refuse-rags" (*paṃsukūla*); because it is ownerless, it is indeed blameless. "Whatever there may be":
therefore, whatever other wealth has been obtained in accordance with the Dhamma, all that is edible. "Without deficiency" (*anavaya*) means *anu-avaya*;

even when looked at again and again, it is without deficiency, possessing complete virtues, and is blameless. However, what is obtained through unrighteous means (*adhammaladdha*), even if it is worth a thousand pieces of gold, is truly loathsome.
As they were thus conversing with one another, they arrived at the gate of the city of Thūṇa.
There, while some girls were playing, one young girl was scattering sand with a small winnowing fan. On one of her hands she wore a single bracelet, and on the other two bracelets;
these struck against each other, while the other remained silent. The king [observed] this occurrence.
Having understood this, he thought: "Queen Sīvalī follows behind me; and a woman is indeed a stain upon one who has gone forth.
People will reproach me, saying, 'Even after going forth, she was unable to abandon her wife. If this young girl is wise, she will tell Queen Sīvalī the reason for her turning back.
Having heard her words, I shall dismiss Queen Sīvalī. Having reflected thus, he said:
“O maiden Upasenī, always adorned with unloosened ornaments;
why does one of your arms produce sound, while the other arm of yours does not produce sound?

In this context, *Upasenī* means one who has approached her mother as a servant (*senikā*). *Niggaḷamaṇḍite* means one whose nature is to adorn herself with ornaments that do not fall off. *Janati* means it makes a sound.
The maiden said:
“O ascetic, these two bracelets are fastened upon this hand of mine;
when they strike together, a sound is produced, for that is the nature of a pair.”
“In this hand of mine, O ascetic, is fastened a single garment;
it has no companion and knows nothing of duality; it stands as one who has become a sage.
When there is a second person involved in dispute, how can one alone dispute with anyone?”
“May you, who desire heaven, find delight in solitude.
In this context, *dunīvara* means two bracelets. *Saṅghāta* means from being joined together or from clashing;

the meaning is that such a rebirth occurs for the second time. *Gati* means arising or birth. The meaning is that for the second time, such a rebirth occurs. *So* refers to that *nīvara*. *Munibhūto vā* means having become a sage.
He stands like a noble person (ariyapuggala) who has abandoned all defilements (kilesa).

"Having fallen into dispute" means that one who is called a "second ascetic" (samaṇa dutiyaka) has entered into a dispute, engages in quarreling, and adopts a contrary view. "With whom will he dispute alone? means: being alone, with whom indeed will he dispute?
"May solitude be pleasing to you" means: may the state of being alone be agreeable to you. For those called ascetics, even taking a sister along...
“They do not practice [the holy life]; why then do you wander about having taken such a wife of supreme beauty?
She will create an obstacle for you; take her away and perform the work of a recluse alone. Thus he exhorted him.
Having heard the words of that young woman and having gained an opportunity, he spoke while conversing with the queen:
“Listen, Sīvalī, to this discourse proclaimed by the young maiden:
‘Pesī reviled me, and her destination shall be that of her second [husband].
O Bhaddā, this is the twofold path practiced by those who wander the world.”
“Of these, you take one; I shall take another.
“Do not call me ‘your husband,’ nor shall I call you ‘my wife.
In this context, “proclaimed by the maiden” means spoken by the girl. “Pesiyā” means: “If I were to rule the kingdom...”
"This servant of mine would have been obedient to my word; she would not even have dared to look at me.
But now she regards me as if I were her own servant, and she instructs me, saying, 'That is indeed the second course. *Anuciṇṇo* means followed or practiced. *Pathāvīhi* means by travelers.
*Ekaṃ* means take one path that is pleasing to you; as for me, however, I shall take what remains after you have chosen."
"I shall take another. Do not say to me again, 'Sīvalī, from now on you are my wife';
neither did I ever say to you, 'You are my wife.
Having heard his words, she said, "Your Majesty, you are supreme; please take the right-hand path, and I shall take the left-hand path."
Having said, "I shall take her," she walked a short distance; then, unable to restrain her grief, she returned and entered the city together with the king, conversing with him all the way.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke this half-verse:
"Conversing thus, they approached the pillar at the entrance of the city."
In that context, "they entered the city" means they had gone into the city.
Having entered, the Great Being, wandering for alms, arrived at the door of an arrow-maker’s house.
Queen Sīvalī also stood to one side. At that time, the arrow-maker had heated an arrow on a brazier of glowing coals and was moistening it with sour gruel.
Closing one eye and looking with the other, he straightened it.
Seeing this, the Great Being thought, "If this man is wise, he will explain the reason for my condition; I shall question him.
He approached and asked. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“In the workshop of an arrow-maker, when the time for his meal has arrived,
there the arrow-maker has made one shaft straight;
having fixed one eye, he looks with the other to see if it is crooked.”
"In that regard, monks, 'at the fowler's hut' means that when it was time for his own meal, the king stood at the fowler's hut.
And there, he—meaning at that very hut. 'Having suppressed' means having closed [his eyes]. 'With one squinting' means he looked with one eye at the arrow as it was curved."
Then the Great Being said to him:
"It is well that you see it thus; listen to me, fletcher!
Why is it that you press one eye shut and look crooked with the other?"
The meaning of this is: "O fletcher, do you truly see well in this way—that by closing one eye, you look at the curved arrow with the other?
Then, as he was explaining it to him, he said:
"With both eyes, O ascetic, it appears broad."
“Without having reached the supreme mark, it is not possible for one to be straight.
But when one has reached the supreme mark, it is possible for one who looks with one eye turned away and the other squinting to become straight.”
“When a second person has entered into dispute, with whom can one person dispute? For you who desire heaven, take delight in solitude.
In this context, “as if wide” means it appears as if broad. “Without reaching the supreme mark” means beyond...
"Without reaching the point of curvature. "For the sake of straightness" means not for the sake of straightness. This is what is meant:
when a wide space is being dug, one would not reach either the point of straightness or the point of curvature further on;

while that [point] has not been reached and is not visible, it is not possible and does not succeed to effect straightness. "Having reached" means having reached with the eye; the meaning is "having seen. "Fallen into dispute" means...
Just as when the second eye is opened, there arises a dispute because no sign is perceived—
where a crooked place appears straight, and a straight place appears crooked— in the same way, a companion of a recluse also falls into dispute,
engages in quarreling, and adopts differing views. But with whom would one who is alone dispute?
"May you approve of solitude; may you take pleasure in being alone. "Monks, sister, do not wander about taking even their own sisters with them;
why then do you wander about taking such a wife as this, who possesses the most excellent beauty? She will create an obstacle for you.
Take her away and practice the duty of a recluse all by yourself," he thus exhorted her.
Having thus given him this exhortation, he became silent. The Great Being, too, having wandered for alms and gathered mixed food, departed from the city;
sitting down at a place convenient by water, he finished his meal, rinsed his mouth, placed the bowl into its bag, and addressing Queen Sīvalī, said:
“Listen, Sīvalī, to this story as told by the fowler:
‘Pesī reviled me; such is the destiny of a second [offender].
O Bhaddā, this is the forked path practiced by those who wander the world.’”
“Take one of them; I shall take another.
“Do not call me ‘husband,’ nor shall I call you ‘wife.

In this context, *suṇāsī* means “listen,” referring to what you say. However, the phrase “of a servant girl” (*pesiyā maṃ*) was spoken specifically with reference to the admonition of the young woman.
It is said that although she was told, "Do not say to me, 'He is my husband,'" she nevertheless followed the Great Being.
The king was unable to turn her back, and the great multitude followed as well. Not far from there lay a forest;
seeing a line of dark green woods, the Great Being, wishing to turn her back, while still walking along, [cut] muñja grass by the side of the path.
He saw it. Then, having pulled out a reed from the sheath, he said, "Do you see this, Sīvalī? It is no longer possible to join this here again;
even so, it is no longer possible for me to live together with you again. Having said this, he spoke this half-stanza:
"O Sīvalī, you who were drawn from a reed-sheath, dwell alone!"
Therein, she gave her this instruction: "I shall dwell alone; you too, dwell alone.

Upon hearing this, Queen Sīvalī, unable to restrain her grief at the thought, "From now on, I shall have no more companionship with the great king Mahājanaka," struck her breast with both hands and fell upon the high road.
The Great Being, perceiving her unconsciousness, stepped aside and entered the forest.
The ministers arrived, sprinkled her body with water, rubbed her hands and feet, and restored her consciousness.
She asked, "Dear ones, where is the king? "Do you not know yourself? she replied, "Search for him, dear ones. They [searched] here and there...
Though they ran and searched, they did not see the Great Being. The queen, having lamented with great wailing, had a shrine built at the place where the king stood;
she worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and then returned.
The Great Being, too, having entered the Himalayas, within seven days alone attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
She did not return to the human realm again. The queen, having had shrines constructed at all those places— where she had conversed with the fowler, where she had conversed with the young girl,
where she had consumed the meat, where she had conversed with Migājina,
and where she had conversed with Nārada— and having worshipped them with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, was surrounded by her army divisions.
Having reached Mithilā, he had his son consecrated in the Ambavana grove and sent him to the city surrounded by his army.

He himself went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and dwelling right there in the grove, he performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and became destined for the Brahma-world.
The Great Being (*Mahāsatta*) also, without falling away from his absorption, became destined for the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata went forth on the Great Renunciation," and he then identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the goddess who protected the ocean was Uppalavaṇṇā;
Nārada was Sāriputta; Migājina was Moggallāna; the young girl was the Bhikkhunī Khemā; and the fletcher was Ānanda."
“Queen Sīvalī was Rāhula’s mother; Prince Dīghāvu was Rāhula; his parents were members of a great royal family;
and as for the Great King Mahājanaka, he was none other than myself, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This concludes the second commentary, the Mahājanaka Jātaka.
[540] 3. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka:
"Who has pierced me with an arrow? The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain bhikkhu who supported his mother.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, there was an only son of a wealthy merchant family possessing a fortune of one hundred and eighty million.
He was dear and pleasing to his mother and father. One day, having gone to the excellent palace and opened the lion-window, he looked out upon the street;
seeing the great multitude with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings going to Jeta’s Grove to hear the Dhamma, he thought, "I too shall listen to the Dhamma.
Having paid homage to his parents and had them take perfumes, garlands, and so forth, he went to the monastery.

Having gone there, he had the community of monks provided with robes, medicines, drinks, and so forth; and having honored the Blessed One with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he sat to one side.
Having heard the Dhamma, he perceived the danger in sensual pleasures and recognized the benefits of going forth.
When the assembly had risen, he requested the Blessed One for the going forth, [saying], "Without the permission of my mother and father..."
Having heard that "the Tathāgatas do not ordain their own sons," he paid homage to the Blessed One and returned home again.
With great reverence, he paid homage to his mother and father and said, "Mother and father, I shall go forth in the presence of the Tathāgata.
When his parents heard these words of his, their hearts broke into seven pieces because he was their only son.
Trembling with affection for their son as if he were their own child, they spoke thus:
“Dear beloved son, dear sprout of the family, dear eye, dear heart, dear one as our very life—how shall we live without you? Our lives are bound up in you.
For we, dear one, are worn out by old age, aged, and infirm; today, tomorrow, or the day after, we shall meet our death.”
"Therefore, do not go away abandoning us. Dear son, renunciation is indeed exceedingly difficult. When there is need for cold, one finds heat;
when there is need for heat, one finds cold. Therefore, dear son, do not go forth.
Having heard this, the noble youth sat down, distressed and dejected, with his head bowed, brooding for seven days without food.
Then his parents thought thus: "If our son does not receive permission, he will surely die;
we shall never see him again. But if he lives after going forth, we shall see him again.
Having reflected, they gave their consent, saying: "Dear beloved son, we grant you permission to go forth; go forth! Hearing this, the noble youth—
With a joyful mind, he bowed his entire body, paid homage to his mother and father, and went to the monastery where he requested the Blessed One for ordination.
The Teacher summoned a bhikkhu and commanded, "Ordain this youth.
He ordained him. From the time of his ordination onwards, great gain and honor accrued to him.

Thus, having pleased his teacher and preceptor and received full ordination, and having mastered the Dhamma for five years, he thought, "I am living here in a crowded place; this is not suitable for me.
Desiring to fulfill the task of insight meditation (*vipassanādhura*), he took a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from his preceptor, paid homage to him, and departed from Jetavana.
He lived in a forest hermitage dependent upon a certain frontier village.
There, although he applied himself and strove for twelve years, increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he was unable to produce any distinction.
As time passed, his mother and father also fell into poverty; those who managed their fields or their trade [said]: "In this..."
"There is no one in the family, whether son or brother, who would demand and collect the debt," they said;
thus, each taking what was in their own hands, they fled as they pleased. Even the slaves, laborers, and others in the house took the gold, silver, and other wealth and fled.
Later on, the two men became so destitute that they could not even get water poured into their hands, and having sold the house—
Having become wretched and overcome by compassion, they dressed themselves in rags and wandered for alms with bowls in their hands.
At that time, a certain bhikkhu, having departed from Jetavana, arrived in due course at the place where they lived.
After he had performed the duties for a guest and they were seated comfortably, he asked him, "Venerable sir, from where have you come?"
When it was said, “I have come from Jetavana, friend,” he inquired after the health of the Teacher, the Great Disciples, and others, and then asked about the condition of his parents:
“Venerable sir, is there well-being in Sāvatthī for the merchant family named so-and-so?
“Friend, do not inquire after the condition of that family. “Why not, venerable sir? “Friend, [the reason is this:]”
"It is said that this family had one son who went forth into the Buddha’s dispensation;
from the time he went forth, this family has completely declined, and now these two people, having reached a state of extreme pitifulness, are wandering for alms.
Upon hearing his words, unable to maintain his composure, with eyes filled with tears—
He began to weep. “Friend, why do you weep? “Venerable sir, those were my mother and father;
I am their son. “Friend, your mother and father have met their destruction because of you; go and look after them.
He thought, “For twelve years I strove and exerted myself, yet I was unable to realize either the path or the fruit.”

Thinking, "I am incapable [of success]; what is the use of my going forth? Having remained a householder, I shall support my mother and father, give gifts, and be destined for heaven," he entrusted his forest dwelling to that elder.
On the following day, departing from the forest and traveling by stages, he reached the Jetavana Piṭṭhivihāra, not far from Sāvatthī.
He arrived there. There were two roads: one led to Jetavana and the other to Sāvatthī.
Standing right there, he reflected, "Shall I see my parents first, or rather the One of Ten Powers?
Then he thought, "My parents have been seen by me for a long time; however, from now on, seeing the Buddha will be difficult for me."
"It will happen; therefore, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One and heard the Dhamma this very day, we shall see our mother and father tomorrow morning.
Having thus abandoned the road to Sāvatthī, he entered Jetavana in the evening.
On that day, however, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, perceived the excellence of this clansman's spiritual potential (*upanissaya*).
Thus, at the time of his arrival, he praised the virtues of parents by means of the *Mātuposaka Sutta*.

That bhikkhu, however, standing at the edge of the assembly and listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, thought: “I used to think that while remaining a householder, I would be able to look after my mother and father;
but now the Teacher says that it is precisely as one who has gone forth that one is a caregiver and benefactor to one’s parents.”
He said: "If I had gone without seeing the Teacher, I would have fallen away from such a going-forth as this.
But now, while remaining a renunciant rather than a householder, I shall support my mother and father.
Having gone to the hall where the tickets were distributed, he took his ticket for rice and his ticket for gruel, and for twelve years lived in the forest.
The monk who had returned to the community became like one who had committed a *pārājika* offense.
Early in the morning, having entered Sāvatthī, he thought, "Shall I first take rice-gruel, or shall I see my parents?
Then, thinking, "It is not fitting to go before my poor parents with empty hands," he took rice-gruel and [went] to them.
He went to the door of his old house. His mother and father, having gone out to beg for alms of rice-gruel, were living against a neighboring wall.
He approached and saw them sitting there; overcome with grief, he stood not far from them with eyes filled with tears.
Although they saw him, they did not recognize him. Then his mother thought, "He must be standing here for the sake of begging."
Saññā said, "Venerable sir, there is nothing suitable for you to receive; please pass on.
Hearing her words, he was seized by a sorrow that filled his heart; with eyes full of tears, he stood right there.
Although he was told "pass on" a second and a third time, he remained standing. Then his father said to his mother, "Go, lady..."
"Know this: is he not indeed our son? She rose, approached him, and looking at him, recognized him;
falling at his feet, she lamented, and her father did likewise. There was great compassion.
He too, seeing his mother and father, being unable to maintain his composure, shed tears. He [suppressed] his grief...
Having consented, he reassured his parents, saying, "Mother and Father, do not worry; I shall support you.
He gave them rice-gruel to drink, seated them to one side, and after bringing more alms-food and feeding them, he sought alms for himself.
Then, having gone back to them and asked for permission regarding the meal, he later partook of it himself.
From then on, he looked after his parents according to this method.
Having given them whatever fortnightly meals and such he himself obtained, he would go for alms himself; if he received anything, he ate it, but if he received nothing, he did not eat.
Whatever he obtained—whether the rainy-season robes or anything else—he gave to them alone. He wore only the worn-out rags that they had used.
Having taken it, he would fix the bolt, dye it, and then use it himself.
However, there were many days when he received no alms compared to the days he did receive them. Consequently, his lower and upper garments became exceedingly coarse.
Thus, while looking after his mother and father, he later became emaciated, pale and sallow, with his veins showing all over his body.
It happened thus. Then the monks who were his close friends and companions asked him: "Friend, formerly your bodily complexion was radiant;
but now you are emaciated, pale, and jaundiced, with your veins showing all over your body.
Has some illness arisen in you? He replied: "Friends, no illness has arisen in me; however, there is an obstacle for me," and he related that situation.
He reported this. Then those bhikkhus said to him, "Friend, the Blessed One does not permit the squandering of what has been given out of faith;
yet you, having accepted what was given out of faith, are doing what is improper by giving it to householders.
Having heard their words, he was ashamed and withdrew. Not satisfied with that much, they went into the presence of the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir,..."
“Such-and-such a monk, having squandered what was given in faith, is supporting householders,” they reported to the Teacher.
The Teacher summoned that monk and asked, “Is it true, monk, that you have taken what was given in faith and supported householders?
When he replied, “It is true, Bhante,” and the Teacher desired to praise that deed and [relate] his own former conduct, he said:
Desiring to make it known, he asked, "Monk, while supporting a householder, whom did you support?
When he replied, "My mother and father, venerable sir," the Teacher, in order to inspire him with enthusiasm, gave three times the cry of approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent, monk!
You stand upon the path I have traveled; I too, while practicing my former conduct, supported my mother and father."
He replied: "She regained her breath. Being requested by those bhikkhus to reveal her former conduct, the Teacher related a past event.
In the past, not far from the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a village of hunters on the near bank of a river, and on the opposite bank...
There was one village of hunters. In each village lived five hundred families.
In both villages, there were two chief hunters who were friends. While still young, they made a formal agreement:
"If one of us has a daughter and the other has a son, we shall arrange their marriage. Then, on the near bank...
A son was born in the house of Gāmajeṭṭhaka; because he was received by means of a *dukūla* cloth at the very moment of his birth, they gave him the name "Dukūla.
A daughter was born in the other's house; because she was born on the opposite shore (*paratīra*), they gave her the name "Pārikā.
Both of them were handsome, pleasing, and golden-hued. Although they were born into a family of hunters (*nesāda*), they did not commit the act of taking life.
In the course of time, when their son Dukūla Kumāra was sixteen years old, his parents said to him, "Son, we shall bring a maiden for you.
However, he, being a pure being who had come from the Brahma-world, covered both his ears and said, "Mother and father, I have no need for the household life;
do not speak such words to me. Even though he was told as many as three times, he remained firm.
She did not desire it either. When her mother and father said to her, "Dear child, we have a son who is a friend of ours;
he is handsome and golden-colored; we shall give you to him," she spoke in the same way and covered both her ears.
She too, having come from the Brahma-world, did not desire the life of a householder. However, Prince Dukūla sent a secret message to her, saying, "If..."
"If you have need for sexual intercourse, go to another's house; I have no desire for sexual intercourse.
She likewise sent him that same message.
Then their parents, even though they were unwilling, performed the marriage ceremony for them both. Both of them [remained] in the ocean of defilements...
Having descended, the two great Brahmās lived together on one side like brothers. But Dukkūla Kumāra did not kill fish or deer;

he did not even sell meat that had been brought to him. Then his parents said to him, "Dear son, although you were born into a family of hunters, you neither desire the life of a householder nor do you commit the slaughter of living beings. Why is this?"
“...will you perform the formal act of ordination? “Mother and Father, if you grant us permission, we shall go forth.
Hearing this, the parents said, “In that case, go forth,” and they gave their consent to the two people.
With hearts full of joy and satisfaction, they paid homage to their parents, departed from the village, and in due course entered the Himalayas by way of the banks of the Ganges.
Having gone to the place where the river named Migasammata, descending from the Himālaya, joins the Gaṅgā, they left the Gaṅgā and ascended toward the Migasammata.
At that moment, the palace of Sakka manifested a sign of heat. Sakka, looking out and perceiving the cause, [acted].
Having addressed Vissakamma, he said, "Dear Vissakamma, two Great Beings have departed from their village and entered the Himālaya mountains;

it is necessary to find a dwelling place for them. Within half a *kosa* of the Migasammata River, go and construct leaf-huts and the requisites for those who have gone forth, and then return. He accepted, saying, "Very well."

Having made all the necessary arrangements in the manner described in the Mūgapakkha Jātaka, he drove away the animals and birds that made unpleasant noises, constructed a narrow footpath, and returned to his own place. They too, seeing that path, traveled by it and reached the hermitage.
Having entered the leaf-hut, the wise Dukūla [prepared] the requisites for one who has gone forth.

Seeing him, and knowing that he had been given to her by Sakka, she removed her garment, put on a red bark-cloth as a lower robe and another as an upper covering, placed an antelope skin over her shoulder, tied a circle of matted hair upon her head, and assuming the appearance of an ascetic, she granted the going-forth to Pārikā as well.
Both of them dwelt there, having cultivated sense-sphere loving-kindness. Of those two—
Through the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*), all the beasts and birds attained a mind of mutual loving-kindness;
no one harmed anyone else. From then on, Pārikā brought drinking water and water for washing, swept the hermitage grounds, and performed all the necessary duties.
Both of them, having gathered various fruits and eaten them, [remained] themselves...
Having entered their own leaf-hut, they took up residence there while practicing the duties of a recluse.

Sakka would come to attend upon them. One day, while observing them, he perceived an obstacle, thinking, "Their eyesight will fail," and so he approached the wise Dukūla, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and spoke thus:
“Venerable sir, an obstacle is perceived for you; it is fitting that you obtain a son to look after you.
Please partake in the ways of the world. Then Dukkūlapaṇḍita said to him: “Sakka, why do you say such a thing?
Even while living in the midst of a household, we loathed these worldly ways as if they were a heap of maggots and excrement; but now, in the forest—”
“Having entered [the city] and gone forth into the ascetic life of a seer, how could we do such a thing?
Then Sakka said to him, “Venerable sir, if you will not do it in this way, you should touch the navel of the female ascetic Pārikā with your hand during her fertile period.
The wise Dukūla agreed, thinking, “This can be done. Sakka paid homage to him and returned to his own abode.
The scholar Dukūla also explained the reason to Pārikā and, during her period of heat, touched her navel with his hand.
At that moment, the Bodhisatta, having descended from the deva-world, took rebirth in her womb.
After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion; therefore, they gave him the name Suvaṇṇasāma. While Pārikā was out for the sake of gathering fruits...
When they had gone into the forest, the kinnaris performed the duties of nurses for them within the mountain ranges.
Both of them, having bathed the Bodhisatta and laid him down to rest in a leaf-hut, would go into the forest to gather various fruits.
At that moment, the kinnaras took the boy, bathed him in mountain caves and other places, and having ascended to the summit of the mountain, [adorned him] with various flowers.
Having adorned him and ground yellow orpiment, realgar, and other substances upon a stone, they applied a tilaka mark on his forehead;
then, bringing him back, they had him lie down in the leaf-hut. His mother also arrived and gave her son breast milk.
Later, while protecting him as he grew until he reached the age of sixteen, his parents sat him down in the leaf-hut.
They themselves would go into the forest for the sake of roots, fruits, and other forest produce.
The Great Being, thinking, "Perhaps some obstacle might befall my parents at any time," observed the path by which they traveled.
Then one day, as they were returning from the hermitage in the evening after gathering roots, fruits, and other forest produce, [he saw them]...
Not far away, a great cloud arose. They entered the root of a tree and stood upon the top of an anthill.
Inside it there was a venomous snake. Water mixed with the scent of their sweat flowed down and entered its nostrils.
It became enraged and struck them with the wind from its nose. Both of them became blind and [could not see] one another.
They did not see him. The wise man Dukūla addressed Pārikā, saying, “Pārikā, my eyes have failed me;
I do not see you. She spoke in the same way. Thinking, “There is no life for us now,” they stood lamenting, unable to find the path.
But what was their past karma? It is said that in the past they had been members of a family of physicians.
Then that physician attended to the eye disease of a certain wealthy man.
That man gave him no wealth at all. Thereupon, the physician, becoming angry, went to his own home, informed his wife, and said:
"My dear, I have been attending to his eye disease, but now he gives me no wealth; what shall we do?"
She too, becoming angry, said, "We have no need for what belongs to him; give him a medicinal preparation that will make his eyes blind.
He agreed, saying, "Very well," went to him, and did so.
Before long, he became blind. By this very deed, the eyes of both of them became blind.
Then the Great Being thought, "On other days my parents arrive at this hour;
now I do not know their whereabouts, so I shall go along the path toward them. Having gone to the path, he made a sound.
Recognizing his voice, they responded with an echo, and out of affection for their son, [they cried], "Dear Suvaṇṇasāma, here..."

“There is an obstacle; do not come,” they said. Then he gave them a long staff, saying, “In that case, take hold of this tip of the staff and come to me. They took the tip of the staff and came into his presence.
Then he asked them, “For what reason have your eyes been ruined? Thereupon his parents said to him:
“Father, we were standing here at the foot of this tree on top of an anthill while it was raining;
that is the reason. Having heard his parents’ words, he understood: “There must be a venomous snake there;
it must have been provoked by him and released a nasal spray. Upon seeing his parents, he both wept and laughed. Then, [he said] to him:
They asked him, "Dear son, why do you both weep and laugh?

He replied, "Mother and father, I wept because I thought, 'Your eyes have been ruined even while you were still young. I laughed because I thought, 'Now I shall be able to look after them. Mother and father, do not worry; I will look after you."
Having thus comforted his parents and brought them to the hermitage, he tied ropes for them in all places— their night-quarters and day-quarters,
on the walking-path, in the leaf-hut, at the place for defecating, and at the place for urinating— and from that time forth, having established them in the hermitage,
he himself would gather roots, fruits, and other provisions from the forest, set them down in the leaf-hut, and depart early in the morning.
Having swept their dwelling place and paid homage to his parents, he took a water jar, went to the Migasammata River, and brought back drinking water and water for washing;
having provided tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, and so forth, he gave them sweet fruits.
When they had finished eating and rinsed their mouths, he himself ate and [then attended] to his parents.
Having paid homage, surrounded by a herd of deer, he entered the forest for the sake of gathering fruits.
At the foot of the mountain, accompanied by a retinue of *kinnaras*, he gathered fruits and returned in the evening;
having brought water in a jar, he bathed them according to their desire with warm water, washed their feet, and, having brought a bed of glowing coals, warmed their hands and feet.
Having given various fruits to them while they were seated and having had them eat, he himself ate at the end and set aside what remained.
In this very manner, he looked after his parents.
At that time, a king named Pīḷiyakkha reigned in Bārāṇasī. Out of greed for deer meat, he...
Having caused his mother to hand over the kingdom, he entered the Himavat mountains equipped with his five weapons.
While killing deer and eating their flesh, he reached the Migasammata River; proceeding by stages, he arrived at the ford where Sāma used to fetch water.
Seeing the tracks of the deer and having constructed a shelter from branches the color of jewels, he took up his bow and fixed a poisoned arrow.
Having girded his quiver, he remained there as if hidden. At the time of evening, the Great Being, having gathered various fruits and placed them in the hermitage, paid homage to his parents.

Thinking, "I shall fetch water," he took his water-jar and, surrounded by a herd of deer, drove two deer together; placing the water-jar upon their backs and holding it with his hand, he went to the river ford.
He arrived. The king, standing at the gate, saw him approaching in that manner and thought:
"Even though I have been wandering about for so long, I have never before seen a human being. Is this a god or a nāga?
If I approach and question him, should he be a god, he will fly up into the sky; if he is a nāga..."
He will enter the earth. However, I shall not wander only in the Himalayas for all time; I will go to Bārāṇasī.
There they will ask me, ‘Great King, while dwelling in the Himalayas, have you ever seen anything extraordinary? There I will say, ‘I have seen such a being. ‘Who...’
He thought: "If I am asked 'Is this he? and I say 'I do not know,' then they will reproach me; therefore, having pierced him and weakened him, I shall question him.
Then, as soon as those deer had descended, drunk their fill of water, and emerged, the Bodhisatta, having mastered his role...
Descending slowly like a great elder, his agitation calmed, he stepped back up,
put on his red bark garment as an underrobe and another as an upper robe, placed an antelope skin over his shoulder, lifted the water-jar, wiped away the water,
and set it upon the tip of his left shoulder. At that moment, thinking, "Now is the time to strike," the king raised his poisoned arrow toward the Great Being.
It pierced his right flank, and the arrow emerged from his left side. Realizing he had been struck, the herds of deer fled in terror.
But the wise golden monkey, though wounded, did not spill the water-jar as it might have fallen;
instead, establishing mindfulness, he lowered himself slowly, cleared away the sand, and set it down.

Having determined the direction and lying down like a golden statue upon sand the color of a silver plate— with his head toward the direction where his parents lived— he established mindfulness and spat out blood from his mouth,
saying: "In this region of the Himālayas, there is no one who is my enemy, nor is there anyone who is an enemy of my parents."
Without having seen the king, he first spoke this verse:
"Who indeed has pierced me with an arrow while I was distracted carrying water?
Is it a khattiya, a brahmin, or a vessa? Who are you that pierce me and then hide?"

In this context, "negligent" (*pamatta*) refers to one whose mindfulness is not established in the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*). For it was with reference to this that he, at that moment, made himself "negligent. "Pierced" (*viddha*) means having pierced.
Having spoken thus, he then uttered the second verse in order to demonstrate that the flesh of his own body was not considered fit to be eaten:
"Meat is not for me to eat; there is no need for my skin; ... [and so forth] ..."
"By what mark, then, did you think me to be a woman?
Having spoken this second verse, he asked him about his name and so forth:
"Who are you, whose son are you, and how shall we know you?"
“O friend, being questioned by me, tell me: why do you remain hidden after having pierced me?
Therein, *amaññatha* means: “This man thought, ‘For what reason should I be pierced?’”—this is the meaning.
Having spoken thus, he remained silent. Hearing that, the king [thought], “This man has been pierced by me with an arrow smeared with poison...”
"Even though I have been cast down, he neither reviles nor insults me; rather, as if stroking my heart, he addresses me with kind words.
I shall go into his presence. Having thought thus, he went and, standing before him, spoke these two verses:
"I am the king of the Kāsīs, known to me as Pīḷiyakkha."
“Having abandoned the kingdom out of greed, I wander about hunting deer.
I am renowned as one skilled in archery and firm in my aim;
even a nāga would not escape me when I have come within range of my arrow.”
In that regard, the thought occurred to him: "I am the king. He thought: "Even the gods and the *nāgas* speak in the human tongue;
I do not know whether this one is a god, a *nāga*, or a human. If he should become angry, he might destroy me.
But when it is said 'king,' there is no one who does not pay homage. Therefore, in order to make his own status as king known, first—
“I am a king,” he said. “Out of greed” means out of greed for the deer’s flesh. “Seeking the deer” means searching for the deer.
“I wander” means I am wandering. As for the second verse, however, he spoke thus desiring to demonstrate his own strength.
In that context, “archery” refers to the science of the bow. “Firmly trained” means one capable of both lowering and raising a firm bow, such as the *sahassatthāma* (the thousand-fold-strength) bow.
Having thus praised his own power, the king, asking for his name and clan, said:
"Who are you, or whose son are you? How shall we know you?
Proclaim the name and clan of both your father and yourself."
Therein, *pavedayāti* means "tell.

Having heard this, the Great Being thought: "If I were to say, 'I am one among the devas, nāgas, kinnaras, or kṣatriyas,' he would indeed believe me; however, it is right for him to speak only the truth. Having reflected thus, he spoke as follows:
"O venerable sir, I am the son of a hunter; my kinsmen know me as Sāma."
They addressed him while he was still alive: "I have gone to lie down as if embraced by my own kin.
I am pierced by a broad arrow, like a deer by one laced with poison;
O King, look, I lie here drenched in my own blood."
“The arrow has gone sideways; I see blood flowing from me.
I am afflicted, so I ask you: why do you hide after having struck me?
A leopard is slain for its skin; an elephant is slain for its tusks.”
“Now, for what reason indeed did you think of me as one who should be pierced?
In this context, “while I was living” means that previously, while I was alive, my relatives would address me, saying, “Come, Sāma! Go, Sāma!
“Today I have gone” means that today I have thus gone; the meaning is that I have arrived at the mouth of death, I have entered [it].
"Sayeti" means "I lie down. "Paripluto" means submerged. "Paṭivāmagataṃ" means having entered by the right side, it has emerged by the left side;
this is the meaning. "Passa" means look at me. "Dhimhāmi" means I spit;
having established mindfulness and being unshakable, he said this after spitting blood from his mouth. "Āturo tyānupucchāmī" means "I, who am gravely ill, inquire after you."
Having sacrificed, I question him: "You are hiding" means you are staying hidden in this forest thicket.
"Viddheyyaṃ" means that which is to be pierced. "Amaññatha" means you thought.
Having heard his words, the king, without declaring the truth as it was and speaking a falsehood, said:
“A deer appeared, come to the place where arrows fall;
seeing it, I was terrified, and by that my anger took possession of me.
In this context, *āvisī* means it overwhelmed him. He thereby indicates: “By that cause, anger arose in me.”
Then the Great Being said to him, “What do you say, Great King? In this Himalaya, there is no such thing as a fleeing deer upon seeing me,” and he continued:
“Since I remember myself, since I have attained the state of reason, the wild animals do not fear me, even those with claws and fangs in the forest.”
“Since I have avoided the treasure-hoard and since I have reached youth,
the deer do not fear me in the forest, even when they are pursued by hunters.
O King, the timid Kimpurisas on Mount Gandhamādana— ”
“Greeting one another, we go among the mountains and the forests.
‘The deer do not fear me, even though I am in the forest with my weapons;
by what reason, then, do the deer now tremble before me?’”

In this regard, "The deer do not fear me," O Great King: from the time I first remember myself, from the moment I attained and came to possess consciousness, ever since that time, upon seeing me, the deer do not become terrified.
"Even those with feet" means even the predatory wild beasts. "From which [time] the treasure": from the time [I first remember it].
"I wore bark garments. 'O Great King, let alone the timid kimpurisas; for kimpurisas are exceedingly cowardly.
Even those who dwell on this Gandhamādana mountain do not tremble upon seeing me;
rather, we go about greeting one another with joy. It is the deer who are terrified of me.'"
"Seeing me, the deer would be terrified; for what reason would you cause me to be believed?
This he said to point out [the danger]. Hearing that, the king thought, "By piercing this innocent creature, I have spoken a falsehood; I shall speak only the truth," and said:
"O Samanera, it is not that the deer is afraid of me; why then should I speak a lie?"
"Overcome by anger and greed, I discharged that arrow at you.
In this context, *na taṃ tasā* means "the deer was not terrified upon seeing you"; the sense is that it was not afraid.
*Kiṃ tāhaṃ* means "how could I possibly speak a falsehood in the presence of one so beautiful to behold? *Kodhalobhābhibhūtāhaṃ* means "overcome by anger..."
"And having been overcome by greed"— for he, having first raised his bow with the thought "I shall pierce the deer" due to anger arising toward the deer,
and later, upon seeing the Bodhisatta, not knowing whether he was a deity or some other being,
gave rise to greed with the thought "I will ask him"; therefore, he spoke thus.
Having spoken thus, he thought, "This Sāma will not live alone in this forest; he must have relatives. I shall question him. Having reflected thus, he spoke the other verse:
"From where have you come, Sāma? By whom were you sent?
'O water-carrier, go to the river,' so you were told, O Migasammata, when you arrived."
In this context, "Sāmi" (Sir) is an address to the Great Being. "Having come" means:

having come from what region to this forest, or having been sent by which person who said, "Go to the river to fetch water for our water-carrier," have you arrived here at this place honored as a deer? This is the meaning.
Having heard his words, and enduring great painful sensations, he spat out blood from his mouth and spoke this verse:
“My mother and father are blind; I support them in the great forest.
I have come, Migasammata, to provide them with water.”
Therein, "I support them" means I nourish them by bringing back roots, fruits, and so forth.
Having spoken thus, the Great Being, lamenting for his parents, said:
"They have their own strength, yet he [the son] is their very life."
“Lacking water, they will surely die blind,” he thought.
“This suffering is not as great for me as that which is obtainable by a man:
that I do not see my mother—that is a suffering more bitter than this.”
“This suffering of mine is not so great, for such a thing could indeed be found by a man;
but that I do not see my father—that is a sorrow for me greater than this.
Surely my poor mother must be weeping for a long time.”
"At midnight or at night, he empties out like a river.
'Surely that father of mine is wretched; he weeps for a long time;
at midnight or at night, he empties out like a river.'"
“Because of their practice of walking on foot and massaging one another’s feet,
they will wander through the Great Forest, lamenting for me, their father.
This too is the second arrow that shakes my heart.”
"And since I do not see [anyone] in this blindness, I think I shall lose my life.
In this context, "usāmattaṃ" means a measure of food. For "usā" is a name for food, and it exists because of that.
"Sāhassa jīvitaṃ" means his life would last for only six days; this refers to the various fruits that have been brought and set aside.
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Alternatively, *usā* means heat (*usmā*). By this he shows: "There is still a measure of warmth in their bodies;
therefore, they have life remaining along with the fruits and food I have brought.

"They will die" (*marissare*) means "I think they will die. "By a man" (*pumunā*) means by a male person; the sense is that such suffering must indeed be experienced by a man. For a long time (*cirarattāya*).
"Rucchatīti" means she will weep for a long time. "Aḍḍharatte vā" means in the middle of the night; "ratte vā" means in the latter part of the night.
"Avasucchatīti" means she will dry up like a small stream—this is the meaning.
"Uṭṭhānapādacariyāyā" means, O Great King, that twice or thrice both by night and by day, having risen, I [observed] their walking about through my own energy of exertion.
"I shall massage his hands and feet; now, not seeing me, they will wander and roam about this forest region for my sake, crying out 'Sāma!
like those whose vision has been lost and who are being pierced by thorns.
Regarding the "second dart": it is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even a hundred-thousandfold more painful than the first dart, which was struck and poisoned.
This second arrow of grief at not seeing them is even more painful for them.
Having heard his lamentation, the king thought: "This man is an absolute celibate, established in the Dhamma, and supports his mother and father;
even now, though fallen into such suffering, he laments only for them. What an offense I have committed against one so endowed with virtues!"
Having thought, "What indeed can I do? How shall I comfort him? he made this resolution: "When one is being cooked in hell, what will sovereignty avail?
I shall care for my parents in the very same manner that he has cared for them;
thus his death will be as if it were not death. Having thus resolved, he said:
"Do not lament so bitterly, Sāma of auspicious appearance;
having become a laborer, I will support you in the great forest.
I am skilled in the art of archery and am renowned as one of steadfast character."
“Becoming a laborer, I will support you in the Great Forest.
“Seeking the remains of prey among the deer, and gathering roots and fruits from the forest;
becoming a laborer, I will support you in the Great Forest.”
“What is that forest of yours, my dear, where your mother and father dwell?
I shall support you in such a way as your parents supported you.
In this context, “I shall support you” means I shall support your mother and father. “Of deer” refers to lions and other such wild animals.
"Seeking the remains of food. This was said by him after he had spoken thus: "I am skilled in archery;

having slain large game, I shall support your parents with sweet meat," and when [the king] replied, "Great King, do not commit the slaughter of living beings on our account," he spoke as follows: "Just as you supported them, so too shall I support them."
Then the Great Being said, "Very well, Great King, in that case, please support my parents," and pointing out the way, he spoke:
"Great King, this is the footpath at my head;
having gone from here for half a league, there is their little house."
“Wherever my mother and father are, support them from here on.
Therein, “one-footed path” means a path of a single step. “At the top” refers to that place which is the region of my head. “Half a kos” means within half a kos.

Having thus pointed out the way to him, and having endured such intense pain due to his powerful affection for his parents, he raised his joined palms in supplication for their support and spoke again as follows:
"Homage to you, O King of Kāsi! Homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!
My mother and father are blind; support them in the Great Forest.
I extend my hands in reverent salutation to you; homage be to you, O King of Kāsi!"
"Tell my mother and father, 'He bids you pay him homage.
Therein, "tell [them]" means: "Your son, Suvaṇṇasāma, has been pierced by a poisoned arrow on the riverbank;
lying on his right side upon the sandy bank which resembles a silver plate, he extends his joined palms and pays homage at your feet. Thus [he said].
"Great King, the meaning is: 'Having spoken thus, you should offer salutations on my behalf to my mother and father.
The king accepted, saying, 'Very well. The Great Being, having sent the salutations to his parents, fell unconscious. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
'Having said this, that youth Sāma, beautiful to behold, ...'"
“Fainting from the force of the poison, he fell into unconsciousness.
In this context, “he fell into [unconsciousness]” means he became senseless.
For while speaking thus far below, he was as if breathless; now, however, he was overwhelmed by the force of the poison.
The stream of life-continuum consciousness proceeded supported by the heart-base;
speech ceased, the mouth was closed, the eyes were shut, the hands and feet became rigid, and the entire body was smeared with blood.
The king thought, "Just now he was conversing with me; what can this be? and he observed his breathing.

When they had passed away, the body became stiff. Seeing this, and unable to restrain his grief, thinking, "Sāma has now passed away," he placed both hands upon the head and lamented with a great cry.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
That king lamented at great length with words full of compassion:
“I was one who knew neither aging nor death; today I know it, though not before.
Having seen one who has passed away by his own hand, I realize there is no escaping death.”
“He who addresses me as if I were possessed by poison—now that such a time has come, he does not say anything at all to me.
Surely I am going to hell; of this there is no doubt.”
"For evil committed at that time is a source of misery for a long night.
There will be those who speak of me, saying, 'He was a doer of evil in the village.
But in the forest, where there are no humans, who is fit to speak against me?"
“Karma indeed brings one back to mind; young men gather together in the village.
But in the forest, where there are no humans, who indeed will bring me back to mind?
Therein, “I was” means that for so long a time I had the perception, “I am ageless and immortal. “Today” means today I...
"Having seen this Sāma deceased, [he laments: 'Neither for me nor for others is there any escaping the arrival of Death;
today I know that arrival of Death, whereas previously I did not know it. Thus he wails.
"Now that time has come thus, he who was struck by a poisoned arrow is now addressing me; now that time has come thus, at such a time of death..."
When [the opportunity] arrives, he does not say even the slightest thing. "Then indeed" (*tadā hi*) means: at that moment, evil was committed by me myself through my own piercing.
"A misdeed for a long time" (*cirarattāya kibbisaṃ*) means: that which is capable of ripening over a long period, being dreadful and harsh.
"Of him" (*tassa*) means: of one who wanders about having committed such an evil deed. "Censurers" (*vattāro*) means: they become those who revile him.
“Where in the village is this evildoer? But here in this forest, devoid of humans, who is there that ought to speak to me?
If anyone were present, they would surely speak—thus she laments. “They remind him”: in the villages or market towns, young men meet together;
there, many men gather and say, “O murderer of a man, your deed was cruel!”
"Thus you have been charged with such-and-such a penalty"—in this way they remind and accuse him of his past deeds.
But lamenting and accusing himself, he thinks: "In this desolate forest, who will remind me?
At that time, a celestial maiden named Bahusundarī, a resident of Mount Gandhamādana, [appeared] during the Great Being's seventh existence.
She had previously been his mother. Out of maternal affection, she was constantly mindful of the Bodhisatta;
however, on that day, while experiencing celestial splendor, she did not turn her attention toward him. Some even say, "She had gone to a divine assembly.
When he fell unconscious, she became mindful, wondering, "What is the condition of my son? and saw that this King named Pīḷiyakkha—my...
Having pierced her son with an arrow smeared with poison and killed him on the sandy bank of the Migasammata River, she wailed with a great cry.
"If I do not go, my son Suvaṇṇasāma will die right here;
the king’s heart will burst, and Sāma’s parents, deprived of food and unable to find even water, will wither away."
They will die. But when I have gone there, the king will take a water-jar and go to his parents;
having arrived, he will say, "I have killed your son. When he has said this, and they have heard his words, they will bring him back to their son's side.
Then both they and I will perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*), and by the power of that truth—
“Sāma’s poison will be destroyed. In this way my son will regain his life, and his parents will regain their sight;
and the king, having heard Sāma’s teaching of the Dhamma, will go to the city, give a great almsgiving, and become destined for heaven.
Therefore, I shall go there. Having gone, she stood on the bank of the Migasammata River, invisible—
Standing in the air with his body, he conversed with the king. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having vanished from the Gandhamādana mountain, that deity, out of compassion for the king alone, spoke these verses.”
“O Great King, it is said that those who had come here committed a wicked deed;
though innocent, three people, including father and son, were killed by a single arrow.
‘Come, I shall instruct you so that you may attain a happy rebirth.’”
"O blind one in the forest, support yourself through the Dhamma;

I believe you will go to a happy destination. In this context, "of the king" means "of the king alone. "They have come, it is said, O Great King," means: "You have committed a great offense, a great evil. "A misdeed" means:
whatever has been done that is a misdeed, you have performed that base action. "Harmless ones" means: those who are faultless. "Father and son" means: [the father and the son].
Mother, father, and son—these three people were killed in a single fire. For when he was killed, his mother and father, being dependent upon him, were as good as killed too.
"I am training after him" means I am training in accordance with him; I am instructing.
"Support them"—standing in Sāma’s place and manifesting affection, support those two blind ones just as Sāma did. "I believe they will go to a happy destination."
"By this very means, by that [practice], one shall surely go to a happy destination"—this is what I think.
Having heard the words of the deity, he believed, "I shall indeed support his parents and go to heaven.
Resolving firmly, "What use have I for kingship? I myself shall support them," he uttered a powerful lamentation.

Lamenting and diminishing his grief, thinking, "Suvaṇṇasāma must be dead," he honored his body with various flowers, sprinkled it with water, circumambulated it three times keeping it to his right, and prostrated at four points.
Then, taking a water-pot filled by him, overcome with dejection, he set out facing the southern direction. Regarding this matter:
Explaining this, the Teacher said:
“Having lamented at length with words full of compassion,
that king took a water-pot and departed facing the south.”
By his very nature a man of great power, the king entered the hermitage, striking it as he went while carrying a water-jar;

having reached the door of the leaf-hut of the wise Dukūla, the wise Dukūla, while still sitting inside, heard the sound of his footsteps and, wondering, "This is not the sound of Sāma’s steps; whose could it be? he spoke these two verses:
“Whose voice is this sound of footsteps? It sounds like that of a human being.
This is not the cry of Sāma; who then are you, dear sir?
For Sāma walks with composure, and his feet move with composure.”
“This is not the voice of Sāma; who indeed are you, dear sir?
In this context, “of a human being” means that this sound of footsteps belongs to a human being as he approaches, and not to a lion, tiger, leopard, wolf, nāga, or kinnara;
“this is not the voice of Sāma. “Santam hi” refers precisely to one endowed with tranquility. “Vajati” means he walks to and fro. “Neyati” means he establishes [others].
Having heard that, the king thought: "If I do not disclose my own royal status and say, 'I have killed your son,' they will become angry and speak harshly to me.
