In this way, anger would arise in me toward them, and then I would harm them, which would be unwholesome for me. However, if I am called 'the King,' they will not fear."
"There is no other way; therefore, I shall first explain my royal status," he thought.
Then, having placed the water-jar in the water-shed and standing at the door of the leaf-hut, he said:
"I am the king of the Kāsīs; I am known as Pīḷiyakkha."
“Having abandoned the kingdom out of greed, I wander about seeking deer.
I am renowned as one skilled in archery and firm in my aim;
even a nāga would not escape me when I have come within range of my arrow.”
The scholar Dukūla, exchanging greetings with him, said:
“Welcome to you, O Great King; your arrival has not been ill-timed.
You have come as a lord; declare what it is that you seek here.”
“Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhuka, and kāsumārī;
eat these small fruits, O King, one by one, the best of each.
This too is cool drinking water, brought from the heart of the mountain.”
“Then drink from it too, O Great King, if you so desire.

The meaning of this was explained in the *Sattigumba Jātaka*. Here, however, the phrase “from the mountain clefts” (*girigabbharā*) refers to the Migasammata River; for that river, having issued from a mountain cleft, became known simply as the “Mountain Cleft.

When he had thus offered such hospitality, the King thought, “It is improper for me to say at the very outset, ‘Your son has been killed by me. Instead, I shall initiate the conversation as if I were unaware,” and he said:
“You blind ones are not able to see anything in this forest; who indeed has brought fruit for you?
This well-placed provision of mine is surely being eaten by someone who is not blind.
In this passage, “nālaṃ” means that you blind ones are not capable of seeing anything in this forest. “Ko nu vo phalamāharī” means: who indeed has brought fruit for you?
"Who indeed brought these various fruits for you? This 'store' (nivāpa)— prepared through right method, skillful means,
and cause as a collection and accumulation of pure fruits fit for eating—
appears, is perceived, and presents itself to me as if it were not blind."
Having heard that, the wise Dukūla spoke two verses, showing: “Great King, we do not bring fruits and flowers; rather, it is our son who brings them”:
“Young and youthful, not yet full-grown, dark-skinned and beautiful to behold;
his long hair is black and curls beautifully at the tips.”
“Thus, having gathered fruit and taken a water-pot from here, the water-carrier has gone to the river; I think he has not gone far.
Therein, *nātibrahā* means neither too tall nor too short. *Sūnaggavellitā* means [a woman] with hair like the edge of a butcher’s block—that is, a hide used for pounding meat.
"Bent like the peak [of a mountain]. "Kamaṇḍalu" means a water-pot. "Not come from afar" means: "I think he has not come from a distance now; he must have come from a nearby place.
Having heard that, the king said:
“I myself slew that executioner who was your attendant,
that youth whom you described as being of beautiful appearance.
His long hair was black, and moreover, it was curled at the tips.”
"Upon those [arrows] smeared with blood, the dark-skinned great one lies slain.
Therein, "pierced" means I killed him by piercing him with an arrow soaked in poison. "Proclaim" means speak. "He lies" means he lies upon a sandbank on the shore of the Migasammata River.
Now, not far from the wise Dukūla was the leaf-hut of Pārikā; she was sitting there when the king—
Having heard those words and desiring to hear the account of what had occurred, she emerged from her own leaf-hut and,
taking him for the rope-maker, went into the presence of the wise Dukkula and said:
"With whom, O Dukkula, do you converse, speaking as one who says, 'Sāma has been killed'?"
“Having heard that Sāma is slain, my heart trembles.
Like the tender sprout of an assattha tree shaken by the wind,
having heard that Sāma is slain, my heart trembles.”
In this context, "the proponent" refers to one who says, "I have killed Sāma. "Coral" means a sprout. "Stirred by the wind" means struck by the breeze.
The wise Dukūla, offering advice, said:
"This king of Kāsi is like a deer; he has himself [slain] Sāma, who was regarded as a deer."
“He pierced me with the arrow of anger; may we not seek evil from him.

In this context, “at Migasammata” means on the bank of the river Migasammata. “With anger” means with the anger arisen toward the deer. “May we not seek evil from him” means that neither of us two should seek evil from him.
Again, Pārikā said:
“The beloved son, obtained with difficulty, who supported his blind parents in the forest—
how could my mind not be provoked to anger when that only son has been slain?
In this context, *ghātimhi* means “by the slayer.”
The wise Dukūlapaṇḍita said:
“A beloved son, obtained with difficulty, who supported his blind parents in the forest—
when that only son was slain, the wise say he remained without anger.”

In this regard, "non-anger": anger indeed leads to hell; therefore, the wise have said and declared that instead of giving way to anger toward one who has slain his own son, one should practice non-anger.
Having spoken thus, they struck their chests with both hands, extolled the virtues of the Great Being, and lamented bitterly. Then the king, comforting them, said:
"Do not lament excessively, saying, 'Sāma is dead!'"
“Having become a laborer, I will support you in the Great Forest.
I am skilled in the art of archery and renowned as one of firm character;
having become a laborer, I will support you in the Great Forest.”
“Seeking the remains of deer and forest roots and fruits, I shall become a laborer and support you in the great forest.
Therein, by saying “O speakers,” he means: “By me who says ‘Sāma has been killed,’ [you were addressed] together with me thus: ‘By you, one so endowed with virtues as this...’”
“Your son has been killed; who now will support us? Having said such things, [the king] said: “Do not lament excessively.
I shall become your servant and support you just as Sāma did.
Thus the king comforted them, saying: “Do not worry; I have no need for the kingdom; I shall support you all my life. As they conversed with him, they said:
“This is not our custom, O Great King; this is not fitting for us.
You are our king; we pay homage at your feet.
In this context, *dhamma* means nature or reason. “This is not fitting for us” means that this performance of service toward you is not appropriate for us.

"It is not fitting for us, nor does it become us. As for the words, "We pay homage at your feet," they spoke them because, although they remained in the outward signs of those who have gone forth, they were overwhelmed by grief for their son and their pride had been humbled;
some also say they spoke thus in order to inspire confidence in the king.

Having heard this, the king was exceedingly pleased and thought, "Oh, how wonderful! Even toward me, who has committed such an offense, there is not even a harsh word; they only show me favor. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
"O hunter, you speak the Dhamma; you have shown us honor.
You are our father, O Pārikā, you are our mother."
In that context, speaking of each one individually, he said: "Father" refers to the wise Dukkūla; "From today onwards, you shall stand in the place of my father.
"Mother Pārikā," he said, "you too shall stand in the place of my mother.

"But I, standing in the place of your son Sāma, shall perform all duties such as washing his feet and so forth; do not regard me as the king. Thus he spoke, without considering himself to be the king.
"‘Sāmo’ means ‘one should observe.

Having raised their joined palms and paid homage, they said, ‘Great King, we have no need for you to perform labor for us; nevertheless, please take us by the tip of your staff and bring us back yourself so that we may see you,’ and making this request, they spoke these two verses:
“Homage be to you, O King of Kāsi! Homage be to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!

By the truth that this Sāma was formerly a practitioner of the holy life— ”

“By that truth that this Sāma was formerly a practitioner of Dhamma,

Amidst their many piteous lamentations, [he spoke thus:]

Therein, "from the mountain" means on the mountain. "All the forests are made of fragrance" means all the trees are made of fragrance;
for there is not a single tree there that is without fragrance. "Of them," O monks, refers to those two while they were still lamenting.
At the conclusion of the deity’s act of truth, Sāma rose up immediately; as water is repelled from a lotus leaf, the poison was turned back and his affliction vanished.
Neither the place where he had been pierced nor even the wound itself could be discerned, asking, "Was he pierced here? Was he pierced there?

The manifestation of all four of these occurred in that very hermitage at one and the same moment.

In this context, “I have arisen safely” means I have arisen in safety and well-being. “Address me as ‘Mañcu’” means address me with a sweet voice.

"Welcome to you, O Great King; you have come well indeed.

“Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhūka, and kāsumārī;

I have cool water brought from the heart of the mountain.”
"Then drink from it as well, O Great King, if you so desire.
Having seen that marvel, the king said:

Therein, “I saw you as a ghost” means, “Sāma, I saw you dead. “How indeed do you” means he asked, “How indeed have you regained life?
The Great Being, thinking, “This king perceives me as ‘dead’; I shall make known my state of being undying,” said:

whose mind and intentions have been withdrawn, is considered dead while still living.
Even though he is alive, O Great King, a man in intense pain...”
“Though he has reached cessation and is peaceful, they imagine him who is living to be dead.

In this context, *api* means “even though he is living. *Upanītamanasaṅkappaṃ* means one whose mental activity has descended into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). *Jīvantaṃ* means while he is indeed living;

"While I am thus absorbed in meditation and existing, the world regards me as if dead, even though I am living.

be my support, and make the path leading to the world of the gods.

"A marvel indeed in the world!"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling near Mithilā in the Maghadeva Mango Grove, concerning the manifestation of a smile.
For one day, in the evening, the Teacher was with a large company of bhikkhus...
While wandering on a walking tour together in that mango grove, the Blessed One, seeing a certain delightful spot of ground and desiring to recount his own former conduct, manifested a smile.
When asked by the Venerable Ānanda Thera for the reason for manifesting the smile, he said:
"Ānanda, in the past, during the time of King Makhādeva, while I was sporting in the play of meditation (*jhānakīḷha*) upon this very spot of ground..."
Having said, “I have previously dwelt here,” and being requested by him, he sat upon the prepared seat and related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, in the city of Mithilā, a king named Maghadeva reigned.
He played at the games of a prince for eighty-four thousand years, served as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years, and [reigned as king] for eighty-four thousand years.
While exercising his sovereignty, he said, "My dear barber, when you see grey hairs upon my head, then you must inform me.
Later, having seen the grey hairs, the barber informed the king. The king had the grey hair pulled out with golden tweezers;
placing it in the palm of his hand and gazing at the grey hair, he thought: "The King of Death has come and stood upon my forehead."
Perceiving death as if it were already clinging to him, [the king] thought, "Now is the time for my renunciation.
Having given a choice village to his barber and summoned his eldest son, he said, "Dear son, accept the kingdom; I shall go forth.
When [the son] asked, "For what reason, sire?"—
“Grown upon my head, these hairs have taken away my youth;
they have appeared as messengers from the gods. It is time for me to go forth.
Having said this, he anointed his son in the kingdom and said, “Dear son, you too, upon seeing such grey hair, should likewise go forth.”

Having exhorted him, he departed from the city and, having gone forth as an ascetic in the mango grove, cultivated the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) for eighty-four thousand years and was reborn in the Brahma-world. His son also, by that very same means, went forth and became destined for the Brahma-world.
Likewise his son, and likewise his son; in this manner, [there were] two less than...
When eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas saw grey hair upon their heads, they went forth in this mango grove and,
having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra),
were reborn in the Brahma-world. Among them, King Makhādeva, who was the very first to be reborn, while remaining in the Brahma-world, looked back upon his own lineage.
Seeing that eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas minus two had gone forth into homelessness, he became joyful in mind.
Looking ahead to see whether the lineage would continue beyond this point or not, he realized it would not continue.
Thinking, "I alone shall sustain my lineage," he passed away from there and was reborn in the city of Mithilā as the son of the king’s chief queen.
Having taken rebirth in the womb, he emerged from his mother’s womb after the lapse of ten months.
On the day of the naming ceremony, the king summoned the brahmins skilled in interpreting signs and questioned them.
Having examined his physical characteristics, they said, "Great King, this prince has been born to continue your lineage; for your lineage is one of those dedicated to the religious life."

"He will not come after this one," they said. Hearing this, the king thought, "This prince was born to continue my lineage like the rim of a chariot wheel; therefore, I shall give him the name 'Prince Nimi.
Having thus reflected, he gave him the name "Prince Nimi."
Thus, from his childhood onwards, he was devoted to giving, to virtuous conduct, and to the observance of the Uposatha.

Then, his father, seeing the grey hair as before, gave a choice village to his barber, handed over the kingdom to his son, and having gone forth into homelessness in a mango grove, became destined for the Brahma-world. King Nimi, however, due to his inclination toward generosity, [established] in the four...
Having caused five alms-halls to be built at five locations—namely, at the city gates and in the center of the city—he established a great distribution of gifts.
Allocating one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for each alms-hall, he relinquished five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas every day;
he constantly observed the five precepts and kept the Uposatha on the fortnightly days.

He himself undertook these practices and exhorted the great multitude to perform meritorious deeds such as giving. Having explained the path to heaven and intimidated them with the fear of hell, he taught the Dhamma.
Abiding by his instruction, people performed acts of merit such as giving; when they passed away from there, they were reborn in the world of the gods.
Thus the realm of the gods became completely filled, while hell became as if empty. At that time, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven...
The hosts of devas, having assembled in the Sudhamma hall of the divine assembly, exclaimed, "Oh, how wonderful!
It is because of our teacher, King Nimi, that we enjoy this celestial prosperity which cannot even be measured by the knowledge of a Buddha," and thus they praised the virtues of the Great Being.
Even in the world of men, [his fame spread] like oil poured upon the surface of the great ocean.
The discourse on the virtues of the Great Being spread abroad. The Teacher, having made that matter manifest, spoke to the community of monks, saying:
“Truly a marvel in the world, do those with clear vision arise!
When there was King Nimi, wise and seeking what is skillful.”
“The King, the subduer of enemies, gave gifts to all the people of Videha.
As he was giving those gifts, this intention arose in him:
‘Between giving and the holy life, which is more fruitful?’”
In that regard, "when he was," monks, means when the wise Nimī, desiring the welfare of both himself and others, was King Nimī;
at that time, gods and humans said: "It is indeed wonderful, sirs!

Even though the knowledge of a Buddha has not yet arisen, such a person—who performs the work of a Buddha for the great masses and appears as one with vision in the world—has arisen. Thus they spoke of him.
The meaning is: "They tell the story of his virtues. There is also a reading: *yathā ahū*. Its meaning is as follows:
"Just as King Nimi was wise and sought only what is wholesome, so too do such far-sighted ones arise, accomplishing the Buddha-work for the great masses of people.
That which has arisen for them is indeed a marvel in the world! Thus the Teacher himself [spoke].
Filled with wonder, he spoke thus: "Of all Videhas" means of all those dwelling in the kingdom of Videha. "Which is it?
means: of these two, which indeed would bear great fruit?
It is said that on the day of the fifteenth-day Uposatha, having observed the Uposatha and removed all his ornaments, he [lay] upon the surface of his royal bed.

Having fallen asleep for two watches while lying down, he woke up during the final watch, sat cross-legged, and thought, "I give immeasurable gifts to the great multitude and I also guard my virtue; now, does the fruit of giving have the greater result, or that of the holy life?
Having thus reflected, he was unable to sever his own doubt. At that moment—
He manifested a state of heat within the abode of Sakka. Sakka, reflecting on this, saw him thinking such thoughts and thought, "I shall sever his doubt.

Coming alone and swiftly, he made the entire residence one mass of light, entered the inner chamber, pervaded it with radiance, and standing in the air, he answered when questioned. Regarding that matter:
Explaining this, the Teacher said:
“Knowing his intention, Maghava, the elephant among gods,
The thousand-eyed one appeared, dispelling the darkness with his radiance.”
“Salomahaṭṭha, lord of men, Nimi spoke to Vāsava:
‘Are you a deity, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka, the first-born?
‘Such a complexion as mine has never been seen or heard of by me.’”
"Tell me, venerable sir, how we may know you.
Knowing him to be thrilled with hair standing on end, Vāsava said to Nimi:
"I am Sakka, the lord of the gods; I have come into your presence."
“Alomahaṭṭha, lord of men, ask whatever question you desire.
Having been granted leave by him, Nimi spoke to Vāsava:
“I ask you, O Great King, Lord of all beings.”
“Between giving and the holy life, which is of greater fruit?
Thus questioned by the god among men, Vāsava spoke to Nimi;
knowing the ripening of the holy life, he explained it to the one who knew.
“By an inferior holy life one is reborn as a kshatriya;
by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified.
Indeed, these bodies are not easily obtained by anyone through mere supplication.”
“Those who are born in the body, homeless ascetics.
In this context, “with his hair standing on end” means, monks, that King Nimi, having seen the radiance and looking up at the sky, saw [the being] adorned with celestial ornaments;
becoming terrified, his hair stood on end, and he asked, “Are you a deity? Are you a gandhabba? and so forth. “Without his hair standing on end” means...
"Free from fear and with the hair on his body standing on end, ask, O Great King," he said. "He spoke to Vāsava" means that, being delighted in mind, he spoke to Sakka.

"Knowing, he told it to one who did not know" means, monks, that Sakka, knowing the ripening of the holy life (brahmacariya) which he had previously seen for himself in the past, declared it to him who did not know.
Regarding the passage beginning with "By the inferior," etc.: in various sectarian systems, mere abstinence from sexual intercourse is called "inferior" virtue (*sīla*);
by means of that, one is reborn in a noble warrior family (*khattiya-kula*). Mere access concentration (*jhāna-upacāra*) is called "middling"; by means of that, one is reborn among the devas.
However, the production of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) is called "superior"; by means of that, one is reborn in the Brahma-world. Outsiders describe that as "Nirvana."

Therefore he said, "it is purified. However, in this Buddha’s dispensation, for a bhikkhu of pure virtue who aspires to one or another of the divine hosts, the volition of the holy life (*brahmacariya-cetanā*) is called "inferior" due to its lowness;
by that, he is reborn in the world of gods as he has aspired. For a bhikkhu of pure virtue, the production of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is "middling."
By that [merit], one is reborn in the Brahma-world. For one of pure virtue, the arising of Arahatship through the development of insight is called "supreme";

by that, one is purified. Thus Sakka praises it, saying: "Great King, the dwelling in the holy life (brahmacariya) is of great fruit—hundredfold, thousandfold, and even hundred-thousandfold more than giving. *Kāyā* means jars for the Brahmās. *Yācayogena* means...
“By one engaged in begging” or “by one engaged in sacrifice”—in both cases, this is a name for the donor himself. “Ascetics” means those who depend upon austerity.

Having thus illuminated the great fruitfulness of living the holy life (*brahmacariya*) by means of this verse, he now speaks, pointing out those kings of the past who, despite giving great gifts, were unable to transcend the sensual sphere (*kāmāvacara*):
“Dudīpa, Sāgara, Sela, Mujakinda, Bhagīrasa;”
“Usindara, Kassapa, and Asaka the worldling—
these and many other kings, kshatriyas, and brahmins,
having performed various sacrifices, did not transcend the state of a peta.”

The meaning of this is as follows: Great King, in the past in Bārāṇasī, a king named Dudīpa, having given gifts, was cut off by the wheel of death and was reborn in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) itself.

Likewise, Sāgara and the other seven—these eight and many other kings, kṣatriyas, and brahmins, having performed various sacrifices and given manifold kinds of gifts, [were reborn] in what is known as the plane of the sense-sphere realm.

The meaning is that they did not transcend the state of being a *peta*. For the deities of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are called "hungry ghosts" (*petā*) because of their wretchedness, owing to their dependence on others for the sake of the objects of defilement such as forms. And this has been said:
“Those who, being alone, do not find delight, and who do not obtain the joy born of seclusion;”
“Even though they possess enjoyments equal to those of Indra, they are indeed wretched, for their happiness is dependent on others.

Having thus shown the greatness of the fruit of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) over the fruit of giving, he now spoke to show how ascetics, by dwelling in the holy life, transcend the realm of ghosts (*petabhavana*) and are reborn in the Brahma-world:
“But as for these who have lived the homeless life, ascetics...”
Sattisaya, Yāmahanu, Somayāma, Manojava;
Samudda, Māgha, Bharata, and the seer Kālapurakkhata;
Aṅgīrasa, Kassapa, Kisavaccha, and Akatti.

In this context, "they departed" means they transcended the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). "Ascetics" refers to those who rely on both the austerity of moral virtue (*sīla-tapa*) and the austerity of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-tapa*).
"The seven Sati brothers" is said with reference specifically to the seven brothers beginning with Yama and Hanu.
Together with the four beginning with Aṅgīrasa, these eleven departed—that is, they transcended—such is the meaning.

Having thus first praised the great fruitfulness of living the holy life (brahmacariya) by way of its result as a gift through the power of what he had heard, he now spoke, bringing forward what he himself had previously seen:
“To the north is the river Sīdā, deep and difficult to cross;
The golden mountains, with the color of the tips of reeds, shine forever.”
“In the past, there were ten thousand ancient seers dwelling there in the Parūḷhakaccha, Tagara, Rūḷhakaccha, Vana, and Naga forests. Among them,
I was the foremost in generosity, self-restraint, and self-mastery.”
“Having performed the supreme vow, wandering alone and concentrated in mind,
I shall pay homage for a long time to the upright man— whether he be of noble birth or not—
since young men are bound by their own actions.”
“All castes that stand upon unrighteousness fall downward into hell;
all castes are purified by practicing the supreme Dhamma.
In this regard, O Great King, in the past, in the Northern Himalayas, between two golden mountains—
The river named Sīdā was deep and difficult even for boats to cross. For what reason? Because its water was exceedingly fine;
due to the fineness of the water, even something as small as a peacock feather that fell into it would not remain on the surface, but would sink and go to the bottom.
For that very reason, it was called Sīdā. Moreover, on its banks were golden mountains.
Always having the color of the tip of a reed, they shine and radiate light. Regarding "the thickets on its banks are tagara":
on the banks of that river, the thickets were overgrown with *tagara* plants, fragrant with the scent of *tagara*. Regarding "the forests and mountains have grown thickets":
as for the other mountains there as well, the thickets between them had grown dense forests, being covered with trees bearing flowers and fruit.
The meaning is as follows: "There" (*tattha*) means that in that very delightful region of land there were ten thousand seers (*isi*).
All of them had attained the superknowledges (*abhiññā*) and the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). Among them, at the time for going on alms-round, some would go to Uttarakuru;
some would bring back rose-apple fruits from the great Jambudīpa; and some, having brought sweet fruits from the Himālaya itself, [would provide for the community].

Some ate [the fruit], while others went to various cities throughout the land of Jambudīpa. Not a single person was overcome by craving for flavors; they spent their time solely in the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
At that time, a certain ascetic traveled through the air to Bārāṇasī, and being well-clad and well-robed, he entered the city for alms and arrived at the door of the royal chaplain’s house.
Having gained confidence in his tranquility, the chaplain invited him inside the residence.
Having brought him back and fed him, and having looked after him for several days until trust had arisen, [the man] asked:
"Venerable sir, where do you dwell? "In such-and-such a place, friend. "But do you dwell there alone, or are there others as well?
"What are you saying, friend? Ten thousand seers dwell in that region; they are all possessors of the higher knowledges and the attainments."
Having heard of their virtues, his mind inclined toward the going-forth.
Then he said to him, “Venerable sir, please take me there as well and ordain me. “Friend, you are a royal official; it is not possible to ordain you.
“In that case, venerable sir, I shall ask the king for permission today; may you come tomorrow. He consented.
On another occasion, having finished his morning meal, he approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, I wish to go forth into the homeless life.
"For what reason do you wish to go forth? "Because I have seen the fault in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation.
"In that case, go forth; even when you have gone forth, you should come to see me. He agreed, saying "Very well," and went to his own home.

Having gone there, he instructed his wife and children, showed them all his property, and taking his own requisites for the life of a renunciant, sat down while watching the path by which the ascetic would arrive.
The ascetic likewise came through the air, entered the city, and went into his house. After the man had served him with great hospitality, he said, "Venerable sir, by me—"
"How should it be done? he asked. He led him outside the city, took him by the hand, and by his own supernatural power transported them there;
having ordained him, on the following day he provided him with food, gave it to him, and instructed him in the preliminary practice of the kasiṇas.
Within just a few days, he had developed the supernormal powers and attainments, and began to wander for alms by himself.
Later on, thinking, "I gave my word to show myself to the king;
now I shall show myself to him," he paid homage to the ascetics and traveled through the air to Bārāṇasī. While wandering for alms, he arrived at the king’s gate.
When the king saw him, recognized him, and had him enter his palace, he honored him and asked, "Venerable sir, where do you dwell?"
He asked, “Great King, on the banks of the Sīdā River, which flows between golden mountains in the northern region of the Himālaya.
“But, venerable sir, do you dwell there alone, or are there others as well? “What do you say, Great King?
Ten thousand seers dwell there, all of whom have attained the superknowledges and the meditative absorptions. The king [inquired] about them...
Having heard of their virtues, he desired to give alms-food to all of them. Then the king said to him:
"Venerable sir, I wish to give alms-food to those seers; what should I do? "Great King, those seers are not greedy for tastes perceivable by the tongue;
it is not possible to bring them here. "Venerable sir, relying on you, I shall feed them; please tell me a means."
“In that case, Great King, if you wish to give them a gift, go forth from here and, while staying on the banks of the Sīdā River,
give them the gift.
Having accepted this with the words “Very well,” he had all his requisites gathered and set out together with a fourfold army.
Having departed, he reached his own kingdom’s border. Then the ascetic, by means of his supernatural power, led him along with his army to the bank of the Sīdā River;
having caused a military camp to be established on the riverbank, he went through the air to his own dwelling place and returned on the following day.
Then the king, having honored him with a meal, said: “Tomorrow, Bhante, ten thousand...”
“O seers, take [the provisions] and come right here,” he said. Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he went and on the following day, at the time for alms-round, announced to those seers:

“Sirs, the King of Bārāṇasī, having come and sat on the bank of the Sīdā River with the intention, ‘I shall give alms to you,’ invites you for tomorrow; out of compassion for him, go to the royal camp.”
“Accept almsfood. Having consented with the words, “Very well,” they traveled through the air and descended not far from the royal camp.
When the king saw them, he went out to meet them, led them into the camp, and had them sit on prepared seats.
After satisfying the group of seers with excellent food, he became inspired by their deportment and [invited them] for the following day as well.
He invited them. By this means, he gave alms to ten thousand ascetics for ten thousand years.
While giving, he established a city in that very place and carried out agricultural work there.
But, Great King, that king was not someone else at that time; rather, I was the foremost in giving, for it was I myself who was then preeminent in generosity.
"Having performed that great sacrifice and given that gift, I was unable to transcend this world of ghosts and be reborn in the Brahma-world.
But those ascetics, having consumed the gift I gave, all transcended the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara) and were reborn in the Brahma-world.
By this it should be understood: 'Only the life of the holy life (brahmacariya) is of great fruit.'"
Having thus manifested his own preeminence through generosity, he manifests the virtues of those seers (isīnaṃ) by means of the other three terms.
Therein, "by restraint" means by virtue (sīla). "By self-control" means by the control of the sense faculties (indriyadama).

"Unsurpassed" means having practiced a vow (vata) and undertaking of observances that are continuously supreme by means of these qualities. "Wandering apart" means having cast aside and rejected the group (gaṇa).

"Having abandoned [companionship] and gone into solitude" means having attained a state of being alone. "Concentrated" means with a mind concentrated by access-concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption-concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).

This shows that I attend upon such ascetics. "I am upright" means, O Great King, among those ten thousand seers (*isī*), I am even a single person who is upright due to the absence of physical crookedness and so forth, though I may be of low birth.
"Whether he be of high birth or not, without considering their birth, I shall, with a mind full of confidence in their virtues, pay homage to all of them excessively;
I shall pay homage to them at all times," he says. For what reason? "For young men are bound by karma.
Indeed, these beings are bound by karma and have karma as their refuge; for that very reason, they should be understood as being of all castes.
Having spoken thus, he advised him, saying: “Great King, although the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is indeed more fruitful than giving, both of these are thoughts of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*).
Therefore, being diligent in both, give gifts and guard your virtue.
Having given this counsel, he returned to his own place. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having said this, Maghavā, the king of the gods and lord of the Sujās, having instructed the King of Videha, departed for the heavenly realm.
In that context, “departed” (apakkamī) means he went away; the sense is that even while remaining seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods, he made himself appear [to have left].
Then the hosts of devas said to him, "Great King, was it not seen that you had gone? Where have you been?
He replied, "Sirs, a doubt arose in King Nimī of Mithilā; having explained the answer to his question and freed that king from his doubt, I have returned.
Having said this, he spoke again in verse to explain the reason for his departure:
“Listen to this, sirs, as many as are gathered here:
the manifold and extensive praise of righteous men.
Just as this King Nimi was wise and sought after what is skillful...”
The King, the subduer of enemies, gave gifts to all the people of Videha.
As he was giving that gift, a thought arose in him:
"Between this gift and the holy life (brahmacariya), which one is more fruitful?"

In this context, "this" means: listen and hear this praise being spoken by me concerning those righteous people of virtuous nature—praise that is high by way of their virtue and vast by way of their generosity. "Just as this" means:
just as this King Nimi was exceedingly wise.
Thus, without omitting anything, he spoke in praise of the king. Hearing this, the hosts of devas desired to see the king and said, "King Nimi is our teacher;
it was by abiding in his instruction and relying upon him that we obtained this divine prosperity.
We wish to see him; summon him, O Great King! Sakka replied, "Very well."

Having accepted the request, he summoned Mātali and said, "Friend Mātali, harness the Vejayanta chariot, go to Mithilā, place King Nimi in the celestial vehicle, and bring him here. He consented, saying "Very well," harnessed the chariot, and set out.
However, while Sakka was conversing with the devas and giving orders to Mātali, the chariot—
And as he was thus engaged, a month passed by according to human reckoning.

So it happened that on the full-moon day of the Uposatha, King Nimi—having opened the eastern lion-window, seated himself upon the great terrace, and surrounded by his assembly of ministers—was reflecting upon his own virtue when that chariot appeared together with the lunar disc rising from the eastern world-system. The people...
Having finished their evening meal and sat down at the doors of their houses, they spoke pleasant conversation, saying, "Today two moons have risen.
While they were thus conversing, the chariot became visible. The great multitude said, "This is not a moon;
it is a chariot," and gradually [they beheld] the Vejayanta chariot, yoked with a thousand Sindhava horses and driven by Mātali.
When it became visible, they thought, "Whose divine vehicle is this that is coming? Then, [realizing], "It belongs to no one else;
our king is righteous, so this must be the Vejayanta chariot sent by Sakka;
it is worthy of our king alone," they were joyful and delighted, and spoke this verse:
“Truly wonderful in the world has arisen that which makes the hair stand on end!
A divine chariot has appeared for the illustrious Videhan.
Therein, “wonderful” (*abbhuta*) means it has never happened before. They spoke thus because of its marvelous nature.
While that great multitude was speaking thus, Mātali arrived with the speed of the wind, turned the chariot around,
and having placed it behind the threshold of the lion-window, made it ready for mounting and invited the king to ascend.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“The divine son Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, possessed of great psychic power,
invited King Vedeha of Mithilāggaha: ‘Come, O best of kings,
Lord of Disampati, mount this chariot.’”
“The gods of the Thirty-three, together with Indra, desire to see you;
for mindful of you, those gods are gathered in the Sudhamma hall.

In this context, “the house established in Mithilā” means the dwelling situated in Mithilā, or one who is held in affection in Mithilā by means of the four bases of sympathy. “They are gathered” means they are seated there discussing only your own virtues.
Having heard this, the king thought, "I shall see the world of the devas, which I have never seen before, and Mātali will have rendered me his service;
I shall go. Having reflected thus, he addressed the women of the inner court and the great multitude, saying, "I shall return before long;
you must remain diligent and perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms. Having spoken, he ascended the chariot. Regarding this matter:
Explaining this, the Teacher said:
“Then King Vedeha, hastening to seize Mithilā,
rose from his seat and mounted his chariot at the head of the procession.”
Having ascended the divine chariot, Mātali said this:
“By which path shall I lead you, O best of kings, Lord of Disa—
by the path of those who perform evil deeds, or by that of those men who perform meritorious deeds?”
In this context, *pamukha* means "foremost" or "facing forward"; the meaning is that he has mounted [the vehicle] with his back turned toward the great multitude.
*Yena vā* means: by whichever path one goes, it is possible to see the place where those of evil deeds dwell;
or, by whichever path one goes, it is possible to see the place where those people of meritorious deeds dwell—it is among these two [options].
“By what path shall I lead you? This he said even though uncommanded by Sakka, in order to demonstrate his own excellence as a messenger.
Then the king, thinking, “There are two places I have never seen before; I shall see both,” said:
“O Mātali, charioteer of the gods, lead me by both paths.”
“Or by what means do those people go who have performed evil deeds, and those who have performed meritorious deeds?
Then Mātali, thinking, “It is not possible to show both groups at once; I shall ask him,” spoke this verse again while questioning:
“By what means, O best of kings, Lord of Disampati, do I first take you?”
“Or by what [means] do those people who perform evil deeds and those who perform meritorious deeds [go]?
Thus ends the section on hell.
Then the king, thinking, “I shall certainly go to the world of the gods; first, however, I will see hell,” spoke the following verse:
“I see first the hell, the dwelling place of those who commit evil deeds;
I see the states of those of cruel actions and the destination of the immoral.
In this context, “the destination” means that I see their rebirth as well.
Then he showed him the Vetaraṇī River. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Mātali showed the king the difficult-to-cross Vetaraṇī River, boiling, filled with caustic lye, scorching, and like a crest of flame.”
Therein, monks, having heard King Māra’s words, Mātali drove the chariot toward the hells and first showed him the Vetaraṇī River, which has arisen through the seasonal conditions of kamma.
There, the hell-wardens, seizing weapons such as flaming swords, spears, lances, javelins, clubs, and mallets, strike and pierce the beings in hell.
They torment them. Unable to endure that suffering, they fall into the Vetaraṇī River.
It is covered above with thorny creepers of *vetra* grass as thick as javelins. There they are tormented for many thousands of years.
As those thorns, which are as sharp as razor-edges, blaze forth, they are torn into pieces. Beneath them [are pits] as deep as the trunks of palm trees.
Blazing iron spikes arise. After spending a vast duration of time there, the hell-beings fall from the *vetta* creepers onto the spikes;
with their bodies pierced and impaled upon the spikes like fish on a spit, they burn for a long time.
Those spikes blaze, and the hell-beings also blaze. Beneath those spikes, upon the surface of the water, [the fires] are aflame.
The sharp iron lotus petals are like the edges of razors.
Having been pierced by spears, they fall onto the iron lotus petals and experience painful sensations for a long time. Then they fall into alkaline water;
the water blazes, the hell-beings themselves blaze, and smoke rises. Beneath the water, however, is a riverbed with razor-sharp edges.
It is completely covered over. Thinking, "What is it like below?", they dive into the water and are cut into pieces by razor-edged blades.
Unable to endure that great suffering, they wander about crying out with a great, terrifying roar.
Sometimes they are carried downstream, sometimes against the current. Then, the hell-wardens standing on the bank [attack them] with spears, javelins, lances, and so forth.
Having lifted them up, they pierce them like fish; having fallen into painful sensations, they let out great cries of distress.
Then, having pulled them out with blazing iron forks and dragged them about, they lay them down upon the blazing iron ground and thrust red-hot iron balls into their mouths.
Thus King Nimi, seeing the beings in hell tormented by great suffering in the Vetaraṇī River, became terrified and his heart trembled;
he asked Mātali, "What evil kamma did these beings commit? He explained it to him as well. To illustrate this matter, he said:
"Nimi indeed addressed Mātali, having seen the people falling into the difficult-to-cross [river]."
"Indeed, fear seizes me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil did these mortals commit, that these people fall into the Vetaraṇī?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
"Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
'Those of very wicked nature in this world of living beings— who, being powerful, oppress and provoke those who are weak—
having committed such cruel deeds and produced evil, those people fall into the Vetaraṇī River.'"
In that context, "he finds" means: having become one who is no longer master of himself, he has become like a vessel of fear.
"Having seen" means having seen it falling. "Know, monks"—Mātali, knowing for himself, declared this to him who did not know.
"Weak" means devoid of physical strength, the strength of wealth, and the strength of command. "Powerful" means endowed with those strengths. "They harm" means...
They torment them with blows of the hands and so forth. "They revile" means they abuse and strike them with various grounds for reproach.
"Having produced" means having generated; the sense is "having made.
Having thus answered the king's question, Mātali caused that region—where the Vetaraṇī hell had been seen by the king—to disappear.
Having sent a chariot ahead and pointed out the place where the dogs and other animals were devouring [the king],
the Teacher spoke this verse to explain the matter as it was answered by the king who,
having seen it, was terrified: “Black vultures, brindled vultures, and carrion-eating hawks, along with flocks of crows, are devouring him in a terrifying manner.”
“Fear indeed seizes me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, the divine charioteer:
What evil did these mortals commit, that these hosts of people are being eaten by crows?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Whosoever among these are miserly, stingy, and revilers of recluses and brahmins;
who are harmful, wrathful, and of very wicked nature—having performed those cruel deeds and produced evil, [they shall suffer the fruit thereof]."
“They fear the flocks of crows that devour them.
This same method applies to the subsequent questions and answers as well. In this context, *sāmā* refers to those of red color;
*soṇā* refers to dogs; and *sabālā* refers to those of brindled color—that is, those of white, black, yellow, and red colors—thus referring to dogs of five colors.
[The Buddha] shows this. It is said that those [beings], as large as great elephants, pursue the hell-beings upon the blazing iron ground like deer;

they bite into their fleshy humps, cast their bodies—three-quarters of a league in height—down upon the blazing iron ground, and while the victims cry out with loud screams, they trample their chests with two forefeet, tearing away the flesh until only the bones remain.
They devour. "Vultures" refers to vultures with iron beaks as large as great carts laden with merchandise;
these pierce the bones with their beaks, which resemble spikes, and devour the marrow. "Flocks of crows" refers to swarms of crows with iron beaks;
they are exceedingly terrifying and devour every being they see. These flocks of crows produce those very beings who are the denizens of hell.
"They are eating [these beings]; what evil indeed have these mortals committed? he asked. "They were stingy," meaning they were non-givers to others.
"They were miserly," meaning they were stubbornly stingy who would even refuse when others were giving. "To the recluses and brahmins," meaning to those who have stilled and cast out evil.
"Blazing with fire, they trample the earth and strike it with their burning limbs."
“Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil have these mortals done, that these people lie here with their limbs shattered?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Those of very wicked nature in this world of the living, who harm and provoke men and women of blameless character—
those of wicked nature, having committed cruel deeds, produce evil for themselves."
“People tremble, lying there with their bodies shattered.
In this context, “blazing” means having bodies set ablaze. “The earth” refers to a blazing iron ground nine yojanas thick.
“Treading” means stepping upon it. “And striking with trunks” means that the hell-wardens, having pursued them, [strike] with [trunks] the size of palm trees.
Striking them with blazing logs on their shanks and other limbs, they knock them down and crush them with those very logs until they are reduced to powder.
"Supāpadhammino" means having themselves become exceedingly evil-natured. "Apāpadhammaṃ" refers to one endowed with virtue, conduct, and so forth, or one who is innocent.
"Others shovel glowing coals over men who, with their limbs scorched, are weeping."
"Indeed, fear seizes me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil have these mortals done, that these people are scattering burning coals?
Being thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows: "Those who,
for the sake of wealth, make others their witnesses and compel them to pay debts—
having thus compelled the people, O Lord of Men, those doers of cruel deeds produce evil for themselves."
"People tremble at the pit of glowing coals.

Therein, "the pit of glowing coals" means: O Mātali, who are these others who, like cows entering a cow-pen, are surrounded on all sides by hell-wardens and, being beaten with blazing iron balls, fall into the pit of glowing coals? And there, for them, as far as...
They seize those who are submerged up to their waists with large iron tongs and pour glowing embers over them;
then, unable to endure the embers, they weep and, with their limbs burnt, they scatter and shake [the ashes].
Or, by the power of their karma, they themselves scatter and pour embers upon their own heads—this is the meaning. "For the sake of a guild's wealth" means giving when there is an opportunity.

For the sake of wealth belonging to a guild that was collected and set aside with the intention, "We shall give [this], or we shall perform a ceremony, or we shall build a monastery," they cause it to be made known;

that is, having consumed that wealth according to their own desire and having given bribes to the guild elders, they say, "In such-and-such a place, this much profit has been realized; in such-and-such a place, this much was given by us."
Having acted as false witnesses, they cause that debt to be paid and bring about ruin.
“Blazing with flames, glowing, and aflame, a great iron cauldron appears.
O charioteer, fear seizes me upon seeing it; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer.”
“What evil have these mortals done that these people fall head-first into the iron cauldron?
Being thus questioned, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, answered him;
knowing the ripening of evil deeds, he spoke to one who already knew.
“Those of very evil nature who harm and provoke a virtuous ascetic or brahmin—having produced that evil through their cruel deeds, those people fall headlong into the iron cauldron.
In this context, *padittā* means set ablaze. *Mahatī* means as large as a mountain, filled with molten iron that remains solid for an eon (*kappa*).
Being cast head-first and feet-upwards by the terrifying guardians of hell, they fall into that iron cauldron.
"Virtuous" means endowed with the qualities of moral conduct and behavior.
"Having wrapped [the victim's] neck, they tear it out, and having drenched it in hot water..."
“Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil have these mortals done, that these people lie here with their heads shorn?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Those in this world of the living who are of very wicked nature seize birds and torment them;
having tormented the bird, O Lord of Men, those hunters, having produced evil through their cruel deeds..."
“They lie there, people, with their heads torn off.
In this context, “tearing out” means pulling out [the hair]. “Then having wrapped them” means having wrapped them head-downwards with glowing iron cords.
“In hot water” means in boiling iron water that has remained so for an eon (*kappa*). “Having drenched them” means having soaked them and then thrown them [in]. This...
It was said: "O Mātali, those for whom these hell-wardens wrap their necks with glowing iron cords,
bend their bodies to the measure of three gavutas, twist that neck around, tear it out, seize them with glowing iron rods,
and cast them into a mass of glowing molten iron while being joyful and delighted— by that very neck being torn out..."
Furthermore, the neck indeed arises together with the head. What deeds did these people perform?

"Because fear arises in me upon seeing them. "Having seized birds and tormented them, O Great King"—meaning those who, in this world of the living, seize birds, pluck their feathers, twist their necks, bring them to the end of their lives, and then eat or sell them.
"Or else, these people lie here with their heads cut off.
"This river flows with abundant water, its banks not shallow, and it has excellent landing places;
men, tormented by the heat, drink from it, and for them, that water becomes a great relief when drunk."
“Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil have these mortals done, that their drink becomes so turbid?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, he spoke to one who understood:
“Those of impure conduct who give pure grain mixed with chaff to buyers,
when those who are parched with thirst drink it because they are scorched by the heat, that very husk becomes their drink.”
In that context, "with non-shallow banks" means having shores that are not deep. "Well-established" means endowed with beautiful landing places.
"It becomes *bhusa*" means it turns into rice-straw (*vīhibhusa*). "Pāni" means drinking water. It is said that in that region a delightful river flows with abundant water;
the beings of hell, scorched by the heat of the fires and unable to endure their thirst, [stretch out] their arms...
Having taken up the glowing iron ground, they enter that river while trampling upon it;
at that very moment, the banks burst into flames, and the water turns into burning chaff and straw.
Unable to endure their thirst, they eat that burning chaff and straw; having consumed their entire bodies, it passes out through their lower parts.
Unable to endure that suffering, they raise their arms and weep. "Pure grain" refers to the seven kinds of perfectly pure grain, such as rice and so forth.
"Mixed with chaff" means having mixed it with chaff, or with husks, or with sand, clay, and the like.
"Impure deeds" refers to defiled actions of body, speech, and mind. Regarding the word *kāyino*: "pure grain..."
Thinking, "I will give it," they take the price from the hand of the buyer and give such impure grain.
"With spears, lances, and javelins, they pierce both sides of the one who is crying out;
for fear seizes me upon seeing this, O Sūta. I ask you, Mātali, the divine charioteer."
“What evil have these mortals done that these people lie here slain by swords?
Being thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer,
explained the ripening of their evil deeds, proclaiming what he knew to one who already knew.
“Those in the world of the living who perform unwholesome deeds, making their livelihood by taking what is not given—
grain, wealth, silver, gold, goats, sheep, cattle, and even buffaloes—
those people of cruel deeds, having produced evil, lie down pierced by swords.”
In this context, "both" (*ubhayāni*) means both [sides]. "Piercing" (*tudanti*) means they strike through. "Of those wailing" (*kandantānaṃ*) refers to those who are crying out.
The harsh hell-wardens, having surrounded them on all sides like hunters in the forest surrounding a deer, pierce both sides with various weapons such as arrows;
their bodies appear perforated and mangled like a withered leaf. "Having taken what was not given" (*adinnam ādāya*) means belonging to another.
They maintain their livelihood by seizing both conscious and unconscious beings through such means as cutting the umbilical cord and by deception:
“Bound by the neck, why do these some lie here, while others, cut to pieces and hacked apart, lie there?
O Charioteer, fear seizes me upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer.”
"What evil have these mortals done, that these people lie here so terrified?
To him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, being questioned, replied—
knowing the ripening of evil deeds, he explained it to one who knew:
“The deer-hunters, the pig-trappers, and the fishers, having killed the cattle, the buffalo, and the goats and sheep,
spread them out on their stakes; having committed these cruel deeds and produced evil,
those people lie down, having entered the pit.”
There, having seen them bound by the neck with great glowing iron chains, dragged along, cast down upon the iron ground, and being hacked with various weapons, he asked.
"Others are being cut apart" means that others, moreover, were cut into pieces.
"Roasted" means that, having been placed upon glowing iron plates, they were pounded like meat with a mallet.
They lie down having formed a heap. "Fishers" means those who kill fish. "Cows" refers to cattle.
"They spread them out on the butcher's blocks" means that, for the sake of making a living by selling meat, they placed them at the butcher stalls.
"This pond is full of urine and excrement; it is foul-smelling, impure, and reeks with putridity."
"Devoted to God, these men eat; for fear seizes me, O Sūta, upon seeing them.
I ask you, Mātali, charioteer of the gods: what evil have these mortals done, that these people must feed on urine and excrement?"
Questioned by him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, explained;
knowing the ripening of evil deeds, he spoke as one who knows.
“Those who are litigants and quarrelsome, always intent on harming others;”
"Having brought about those cruel deeds, these fools, who were betrayers of friends,
eat filth. In this context, "these humans, overcome by hunger, eat" means that these beings in hell, afflicted by starvation and unable to endure their hunger,
eat a mass of old filth that is boiling, smoking, and blazing, which has remained there for an eon.
"Making a lump," they mean they eat and consume [the food] together as one mass. "Litigants" means those who initiate legal suits. "Harassers" means those who cause harm even to friends and kinsmen.

"Traitors to friends" refers to those fools who, having eaten and feasted in their very homes, having sat upon seats prepared for them and slept there, subsequently demand a copper coin (māsaka-hāpaṇa) or take bribes; these are the betrayers of friends.
"Great King, they eat such filth as this.
"This lake is filled with blood and pus; it is foul-smelling, impure, and stinks of rot.
Men drink from it when tormented by the heat; for even I, O charioteer, feel fear upon seeing it."
“I ask you, Mātali, charioteer of the gods: what evil did these mortals commit, that these people here must feed upon blood and pus?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Those in the world of the living who commit a defeat against their mother or father, or who kill an Arhat—
having produced such cruel karma and evil, those people shall become eaters of blood and pus."
In this context, "tormented by heat" means oppressed by suffering.
"Defeated" (*pārājikā*) means those who, having killed their aged parents, have fallen into a state of defeat even while remaining householders. "Arhats" refers to those worthy of special honor.
"Kill" means they put to death their parents who perform difficult deeds. Furthermore, by the term "Arhats," one also includes the disciples of the Buddha.
Furthermore, in another Ussada hell, the hell-wardens pierce the tongues of the denizens with glowing iron spikes as large as palm trees;
having dragged them out and cast those beings onto the glowing iron ground, they spread them out like ox-hide and strike them with hundreds of spears.
They writhed like fish thrown onto dry land, and they were unable to endure that suffering.
Unable to do so, weeping and lamenting, they discharge saliva from their mouths. When Mātali showed this to the king, the king said:
“Behold the tongue pierced by the hook, like leather split by a hundred spikes;
like fish cast upon dry land, they quiver—why are these people weeping and spitting saliva?”
“Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil have these mortals done, that these people lie here with their hands clasped?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Whatever people in Sandhāna, for the sake of profit, sell what is valuable at a low price;
through fraud they deceive the honest, driven by greed for wealth, just as one might kill a fish hidden beneath the water."
“There is no refuge for the deceiver, who is overtaken by his own deeds;
having brought forth evil through their cruel actions, those people lie down with crooked hooks [in their throats].
In this context, *kimete* means “for what reason are these? *Vaṅkaghaṭṭā* means “those whose hooks have been swallowed. *Sandhānagatā* refers to the *sandhāna*.
"Reached the limit" means they stand at the place where the price is determined.
"They value by price" means that, having taken a bribe, they devalue the respective prices of elephants, horses, and so forth, or gold, silver, and so forth—whether animate or inanimate.
"They devalue by body" means that while devaluing those things, they devalue the bodily [commodity]; for instance, when one hundred should be given, they give fifty.

They cause [others] to give; as for the other [portion], they take it after dividing it with them. "By means of fraud" (*kūṭena kūṭanti*) refers to various forms of deception, such as fraudulent scales and the like.
"On account of greed for wealth" (*dhanalobhahetu*) means they perform this fraudulent act out of greed for wealth.

"As one who moves in the water [is hidden] by a net for the sake of slaughter" (*channaṃ yathā vāricaraṃ vadhāya*): even while performing that deed, they conceal the fact that it has been done by means of sweet speech.
Just as those who approach to kill a water-dwelling fish do so by concealing their hook with bait, even so they perform that deed having concealed it.
For there is no refuge for a cheat who thinks, "My deed is concealed; no one knows of it."
Thus, preceded by those deeds, he finds no foothold.
“These women, their limbs mangled, are crying out as they are seized by the arms by those of low birth;
smeared with blood and gore, they are like cows slaughtered at the place of execution.”
These [women] are always buried in the ground, their trunks protruding and aflame.
"Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What evil did these women commit, that they are always buried in the ground?"
The aggregates were transcended, becoming like a blazing fire.
To him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, being questioned, replied;
knowing the ripening of evil kamma, he spoke as one who knows.
“Women here in this world of the living, who performed impure deeds and acted unrighteously— those women, beautiful in form,
having abandoned their husbands for the sake of pleasure and sport, committed other unrighteous acts;
having caused delight in the world of the living, they pass beyond the aggregates, becoming like blazing flames.”
In this context, "women" (*nārī*) refers to females. "With limbs completely shattered" (*samparibhinnagattā*) means their bodies are thoroughly broken all over.

"Of foul birth" (*dujaccā*) means of low origin, deformed, and loathsome. "At the place of slaughter" (*āghātane*) means at the site where cattle are killed. "Mangled" (*vikantā*) means having their heads cut off like cattle, covered in pus and blood.
"Always buried" (*sadā nikhātā*) means [buried] waist-deep in the eternally blazing earth of iron.
Having been laid down and buried, they remain as if fixed in place.
"They overtop the mountain peaks," O Mātali, means that those women pass beyond these mountain summits.

It is said that when they have entered and stand there at the height of their waists, a blazing iron mountain rises up from the eastern direction and, coming toward them with a roar like a thunderbolt, strikes their bodies.
He goes along grinding them like a sugar-cane presser. When he has passed beyond that and stands on the western side, their bodies become visible once more.
Unable to endure the suffering, they raise their arms and wail.
The same applies to the blazing mountains that arise in the other directions. Two mountains rise up and crush them like a stalk of sugarcane.
They press down as if crushing them, and boiling blood flows forth. Sometimes three mountains arise and press down;
sometimes four mountains arise and press down upon their bodies. Therefore he said, "The aggregates overwhelm.
"Of noble women" means daughters established in noble families. "They acted unseemly" means they performed improper deeds.
"Dittarūpā" means having coarse forms, being of a dissolute nature. "Patiṃ vippahāya" means having abandoned their own husbands.
"Acāruṃ agamaṃsu" means they went [to others]. "Ratikhiḍḍahetu" means for the sake of sensual pleasure and for the sake of sport.
"Ramāpayitvā" means having delighted their own minds with other men, they were reborn here. Now, as for their bodies...
"These aggregates pass beyond, becoming aflame.
"Having seized them by the feet, for what reason do they throw these others back down into hell head-first?
Fear indeed comes upon me, O Charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer."
“What evil have these mortals done that they cause these people to fall headlong into hell?
Questioned thus, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods, explained it;
knowing the ripening of evil deeds, he spoke to one who knew.
“Those in the world of the living who perform unwholesome deeds and violate the wives of others—
such thieves of the highest treasure, those people are cast headlong into hell.
For many a succession of years, they experience painful sensations there in the hells.”
"For there is no refuge for the evildoer who is pursued by his own deeds;
having brought forth evil through their cruel actions, those people cast themselves headlong into hell.
In this context, "hell" refers to a great pit filled with blazing embers. It is said that they enter it like cows entering a pen.
When they approach that hell, being pierced and beaten by the hell-wardens who have taken up various weapons, those wardens then cast them down there, throwing them with their feet upwards.
Seeing them being thus cast down, he asks and says this: "Thieves of the finest goods" means those who steal the excellent articles beloved by people.

Having spoken thus, Mātali the charioteer made that hell disappear, drove the chariot forward, and showed him the hell that is the place of burning for those with wrong views. Being questioned by him, he explained:
“Various and diverse tortures of many kinds, most terrible in appearance, are seen in the hells.
Fear indeed comes upon me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine driver.”
"What evil have these mortals done, that these people experience such excessive,
sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations of pain?
To him, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied when questioned:
Knowing the ripening of evil deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Those in the world of the living who hold very evil views, yet out of delusion perform acts of trust;
and who incite others toward those same views—they, having produced that evil view, produce evil."
“People tremble while experiencing sensations that are excessive, painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter.
In this context, *uccāvacā* means high and low; the sense is that they are both small and great. *Upakkamā* means applications of means or causes.
*Supāpadiṭṭhino* means those who possess extremely evil views, such as the ten-based wrong view beginning with “there is no giving.”
"Deeds of betrayal" means that, out of trust in that view, people rely upon it and perform various kinds of evil deeds.
"They are tormented" means that these people experience such suffering.
Thus he described the Paccaṇa hell for the king’s wrong-views. Even in the world of the gods, the hosts of deities [blocked] the path of the king’s arrival.
While looking about, they sat down right there in the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods. Sakka, wondering, "Why is Mātali delaying?", investigated and understood the reason.

He thought, "Mātali is wandering about showing the hells to demonstrate his own excellence as a messenger, saying, 'Great King, having committed such-and-such an action, one is reborn in such-and-such a hell,' to King Nimi."
"But his life would be exhausted in a mere moment, and there would be no end to his witnessing of hell.
He then dispatched a divine son of great speed, saying, "Tell Mātali: 'Take the king and return quickly.
He consented, saying, "Very well," and having gone with great speed, he reported this. Upon hearing his words, Mātali said, "No..."
"Is it possible to remain [here] for long? Having thus shown the king many hells in all four directions in a single instant, he spoke this verse:
"O Great King, you have already seen the abodes of those who commit evil deeds, the places of those who perform cruel acts, and the destiny of the immoral."
"Depart now, O lord of kings, into the presence of the King of the Gods.

Its meaning is this: "Great King, having seen this abode of beings who have committed evil deeds, and having understood the places of those who have performed cruel acts, you also know the destination and rebirth of those who are immoral. Now, go into the presence of the King of the Gods."
"Go forth, go out, Great King, for the sake of seeing divine prosperity.
The Section on Hell is finished.
The Section on Heaven.
Having spoken thus, Mātali drove the chariot toward the world of the gods. As the king was traveling to the celestial realm,
he saw the sky-dwelling palace of the goddess Bīraṇī— a twelve-league structure made of jewels, featuring five spires, adorned with every ornament,
endowed with pleasure gardens and lotus ponds, and surrounded by *kappa*-trees— and he beheld that goddess as well.

Seeing her seated on the couch within the inner chamber, surrounded by a thousand nymphs, opening the jeweled lion-lattice window, and looking out, he asked Mātali, and the latter explained it to him with this verse:
“This celestial mansion has five pinnacles; in the midst of the couch, she is adorned with garlands.”
There dwells a woman of great majesty, manifesting various kinds of psychic power.
"O Charioteer, upon seeing her, a sense of wonder has come over me; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
what good deed did this woman perform, that she rejoices here, having attained heaven in this celestial mansion?"
Questioned by him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods,
explained the ripening of meritorious deeds, proclaiming what he knew to one who wished to know:
"If you have heard of Bīraṇī in the world of the living, she was once a slave-girl belonging to a brahmin."
"Recognizing that the guest had arrived at the proper time, she rejoiced in him just as a mother does for her son;
being self-restrained and generous, she now delights in a celestial mansion.
In this context, "five-pinnacled" means endowed with five gabled chambers. "Adorned with garlands" means [adorned] with all ornaments, such as garlands and the like.
The meaning is "adorned. "Dwells therein" means she dwells in that celestial mansion (*vimāna*). "Displaying various kinds of psychic power" means exhibiting manifold divine miracles (*iddhi*).
"Having seen" means: having seen me standing there, she finds joy; she obtains it;
the sense is that I become as if possessed of wealth through being overwhelmed by extreme satisfaction. "A slave-girl of deceit" means [born] from the womb of a domestic slave-girl.
"Born-a-slave. Regarding "she was a brahmin's [slave]": it is said that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, she was the slave of a certain brahmin.
When the time was right, eight *salākabhatta* (tickets of food) were assigned by that brahmin for the Saṅgha.
Having gone home, he [said]: "From tomorrow onwards, for each individual monk, [one ticket] worth one kahāpaṇa..."
“Having prepared eight tickets for meals, you should provide them,” he said to the brahmin woman. She refused, saying, “Master, a monk is a rogue;
I will not be able to do it. Her daughters also refused. He then said to his slave girl, “Can you do it, mother?
She agreed, saying, “I can do it, Master,” and she carefully prepared rice gruel, hard food, cooked rice, and so forth.
Having prepared [the offerings] and received the voting ticket, he recognized that it was the proper time for the guest who had arrived;

having smeared the ground with fresh cow dung and offered flowers, and having provided well-prepared seats, he welcomed him at all times— just as a mother delights upon seeing her son returned from abroad— and served him with great care, even offering his own possessions.
She gives something. Because she was both restrained and generous, she was possessed of virtue and possessed of generosity;
therefore, by means of that very virtue and that generosity, she rejoices in this celestial mansion (*vimāna*). Alternatively, "restrained" refers to the taming of the sense faculties.
Having spoken thus, Mātali drove the chariot forward and [showed] the seven golden celestial mansions of the devaputta Soṇadinnaka.
He showed them to him. Having seen those [palaces] and his glorious majesty, he asked about the deed performed by him. The other explained it to him:
“Seven magnificent, radiant, fashioned palaces shine forth;
therein dwells a powerful *yakkha*, adorned with all ornaments.”
He wanders about on all sides, preceded by a host of women.
“O charioteer, upon seeing him, a sense of wonder comes over me; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What good deed did this mortal perform, that he rejoices, having reached heaven and attained a celestial mansion?”
Questioned by him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods,
explained the ripening of meritorious deeds, proclaiming what he knew to one who sought to know.
“This householder Soṇadinna was a master of giving.”
With the goal of the life of renunciation, he had seven monasteries built.
There, the monks who resided there attended upon him with great care,
providing them with clothing, food, lodgings, and lamps.
He gave with a mind full of serene confidence to those who had become upright:
on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, he offered [the meal] fully endowed with the eight factors.
“He who observes the Uposatha, always restrained in his virtues, and who is self-controlled and generous—he rejoices in a celestial mansion.
In this context, *daddallamānā* means shining brightly. *Ābhenti* means they illuminate, like the rising sun. *Tattha* means among those [celestial mansions].
"In the seven celestial mansions standing in succession. A *yakkha* is a certain son of the gods. Regarding Soṇadinnaka, O Great King:
in former times, during the era of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was in a certain town in the kingdom of Kāsi a householder named Soṇadinnaka who was a patron of giving.
Having had seven monastic huts constructed for the sake of those who have gone forth, he provided dwellers therein..."
The meaning is that he served the monks properly with the four requisites, observed the Uposatha, and was constantly restrained in his moral conduct;
having passed away from there, he has been reborn here and rejoices.
And in this context, "the fortnight of miracles" refers to the seventh and ninth days by way of approaching and following the eighth Uposatha day, as well as the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
This was said with reference to the thirteenth and first lunar days, by way of both approaching and following after [the Buddha].
Having thus related the deed performed for Soṇadinna, he drove the chariot forward and showed him the crystal mansion.
That mansion was twenty-five yojanas in height and was adorned with many hundreds of pillars made of the seven precious gems.

It was adorned with many hundreds of gabled pavilions, surrounded by networks of tinkling bells, with banners made of gold and silver raised aloft, beautified by pleasure groves variegated with various flowers, provided with delightful lotus ponds, and crowded with celestial nymphs skilled in dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the like.
Upon seeing this, the king asked those nymphs about the deed they had performed; the other [the Elder] explained it to him as well.
“This celestial mansion shines, well-constructed of crystal;
it is crowded with throngs of excellent women and adorned with magnificent gabled chambers.
It is provided with both food and drink, and with both dance and song.”
“O charioteer, seeing them, wonder has indeed found me; I ask you, Mātali, the divine charioteer:
What good deed did these mortals perform, that they rejoice here in celestial palaces, having attained heaven?
Thus questioned by him, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, speak as one who knows:
"Whatever women there are here in this world of the living, who are virtuous female lay followers—
always delighting in giving with a clear heart, established in truth, and heedful in the observance of the Uposatha;"
"Self-restrained and sharing [their wealth], they rejoice in a celestial mansion (vimāna).
In this context, "byamha" means a celestial mansion; it is what is called a palace (pāsāda). "Phalikāsū" means on walls made of crystal.
"Nārīvaragaṇākiṇṇaṃ" means crowded with throngs of excellent women. "Kūṭāgāravarocitaṃ" means adorned, well-adorned, or increased by excellent gabled chambers (kūṭāgāra).

The meaning is: "by both" means by both [of them]. Although the phrase "whichever" was spoken without specific restriction, it should be understood that these women, having been laywomen in Bārāṇasī during the dispensation of Buddha Kassapa, performed these aforementioned types of meritorious deeds in groups and thereby attained that divine success.
Then, having driven the chariot before him, he showed him a delightful jeweled mansion situated on level ground.
It stood firmly established, endowed with great height, shining like a mountain of jewels, resounding with the sounds of celestial songs and music, and surrounded by many sons of the gods.
Seeing this, the king asked those sons of the gods what deed they had performed, and the other explained it to him:
“This celestial mansion shines forth, fashioned from beryl;”
It was endowed with various grounds, divided into sections and measured out.
“The sounds of *āḷambara* drums and *mudiṅga* drums, of dancing, singing,
and beautiful music— divine sounds, worthy of being heard and delightful— resounded forth.”
“Never before have I perceived such a sound, so exceedingly beautiful, whether seen or heard in the past, O Sūta.
For a thrill comes over me upon seeing it, O charioteer Mātali, driver of the gods; therefore I ask you.”
“What indeed did these mortals do that was so good, they who rejoice in celestial palaces having reached heaven?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods,
explained the ripening of meritorious deeds, he who knows declaring it to one who knows.
“Whatever lay followers here in this world of the living are virtuous,
who have respectfully provided for the Arhats who have become cooled— whether at monasteries, at wells, at water-stations, or at crossroads.”
“They gave robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings to those who have become upright, with a mind full of serene confidence.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,”
"And on the fortnight of miracles, they observed the Uposatha endowed with its eight factors. Always restrained in their virtues,
