self-controlled and generous, they now rejoice in that celestial mansion."
In that context, "on beryl [surfaces]" means on walls made of beryl. "Endowed with delightful ground-areas" means it is possessed of charming grounds.
"Cymbals and drums"—these two are what are meant here.
"Dancing, singing, and well-played music"—various kinds of dances and songs, as well as the well-played sounds of other musical instruments, proceed there. "Thus endowed."

Thus it became so delightful. As for the phrase "whosoever," although this was stated without specific restriction, it should be understood that they were lay followers (*upāsaka*) living in Bārāṇasī during the time of Buddha Kassapa;
having performed these meritorious deeds in a communal bond, they attained that excellence.
In that context, *paṭipādayuṃ* means "they presented" or "they gave"; the sense is that they gave to them. *Paccayaṃ* means "requisites," specifically the requisites for the sick.
"Adaṃsu" means they gave gifts of such various kinds.
Having thus explained to him the deed they had performed, he drove the chariot before him and showed him another crystal mansion.
That [mansion] was adorned with many gabled chambers, and its banks were adorned by divine young groves covered with various flowers.
It was surrounded by a river of pure water, resounding with the calls of various birds, and served as the dwelling place of a certain meritorious man who was attended by throngs of celestial nymphs.
Upon seeing it, the king asked about the deeds performed by that man, and the other explained them to him:
“This palace shines forth, well-constructed of crystal;”
It was crowded with throngs of excellent women and adorned with the finest gabled houses.
It was provided with both food and drink, as well as with dancing and singing on both sides;
and rivers flowed around it, filled with various flowering trees.
“Indeed, joy finds me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What good deed did this mortal perform, that he rejoices, having reached heaven in a celestial mansion?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, he spoke to one who knew:
"In Mithilā, O householder, there was this master of giving;
[he established] monasteries, wells, rest-houses, and crossroads."
I served with great care those who had become cool, the Arahants.
With a mind full of serene confidence, I gave robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings to those who were upright.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, one should observe the Uposatha fully endowed with its eight factors.
Always restrained in moral conduct, one should dwell in the observance of the Uposatha.
“Through self-restraint and sharing, he rejoices in a celestial mansion.
In this context, “najjā” is a grammatical inversion; the meaning is that a river flows surrounding that celestial mansion.
“Nānāpupphadumāyutā” means that river is joined with trees bearing various flowers. “Mithilāyaṃ,” O Great King—this...
"In the time of Buddha Kassapa, there was a certain householder and donor in the city of Mithilā.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as planting groves and so forth, he attained this prosperity.
Having thus explained the deed performed by him, [the deity] drove the chariot forward and showed another crystal mansion.
He showed it to him. It was endowed with a young grove that surpassed the previous celestial mansion and was covered with various flowers and fruits.
Having seen it, the king asked about the deed performed by the son of the gods who possessed such prosperity, and the other explained it to him.
“This celestial mansion shines forth, well-constructed of crystal;
it is crowded with throngs of excellent women and adorned with the finest gabled chambers.
It is provided with both food and drink, and with both dance and song.”
And rivers flow around it, filled with various flowering trees:
royal *nyagrodha* trees, wood-apple trees, mangoes, sal trees,
rose-apples, *tinduka* trees, and *piyāla* trees— many trees that bear fruit perpetually.
“O charioteer, a sense of wonder has come upon me upon seeing this; Mātali, divine charioteer, I ask you:
what good deed did this mortal perform, that he rejoices, having reached heaven in a celestial mansion?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied to him.
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, he spoke as one who knows:
"In Mithilā, there was a householder, a lord of giving;
he established monasteries, wells, rest-houses, and causeways."
I served with great care those who had become cool, the Arahants.
With a mind full of serene confidence, I gave robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings to those who were upright.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, one should observe the Uposatha well-endowed with its eight factors.
Always restrained in virtuous conduct, one should dwell in the observance of the Uposatha.
"Through self-restraint and sharing, he rejoices in a celestial mansion.

Regarding this, O Great King, at the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a certain householder and patron of alms in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha. Having performed these meritorious deeds, he attained this prosperity.

Thus, having explained the deed performed by that being, the chariot was driven forward; and after showing another beryl mansion just like the previous one, when asked about the deed performed by the young god who was enjoying such prosperity therein, [the Teacher] explained it.
“This celestial palace shines forth, fashioned from beryl;
it is endowed with various levels of ground, divided into sections and measured out.
There are tambourines and drums, and dancing, singing, and beautiful instrumental music.”
Divine sounds resounded, lovely and delightful to hear:
"Never before have I known such a sound,
so exceedingly beautiful, whether seen or heard in the past."
“Indeed, joy finds me, O charioteer, upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What good deed did this mortal perform, that he rejoices, having reached heaven in a celestial mansion?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied to him:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, speak as one who knows:
"In Bārāṇasī, there was a householder, a master of giving;
he established monasteries, wells, rest-houses, and causeways."
I respectfully served those who had become cool and were arahants.
With a mind full of serene confidence, I gave robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings to those who were upright.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, one should observe the Uposatha,
perfectly endowed with its eight factors, always restrained by virtue.
“Through self-restraint and sharing, he rejoices in a celestial mansion.
Then, having sent a chariot before him and shown him a golden mansion resembling the rising sun, he was asked about the prosperity of the young god dwelling there, and [the Buddha] explained:
“Just as the rising sun becomes crimson and great;”
"This celestial mansion is just like that, fashioned out of gold.
'O Sūta, upon seeing this, a sense of wonder has come over me; I ask you, Mātali, charioteer of the gods:
What good deed did this mortal perform, that he rejoices, having reached heaven in this celestial palace?'"
Questioned by him, Mātali, the charioteer of the gods,
explained the ripening of meritorious deeds, proclaiming what he knew to one who wished to know:
"In Sāvatthī, there was a householder who was a master of giving."
In monasteries, at wells, at rest-houses, and at crossroads,
she diligently provided for those who had attained arahantship and become cooled.
She offered robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings.
He gave with a mind full of serene confidence to those who had become upright.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, he offered [the gift] perfectly endowed with the eight factors.
“He who observes the Uposatha, always restrained in his virtues, and who is self-controlled and generous—he rejoices in a celestial mansion.
In this context, *udayamādicco* means the rising sun.

Regarding *Sāvatthiyaṃ*: during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a householder in the city of Sāvatthī who was a patron of almsgiving. Having performed these meritorious deeds, he attained this state of prosperity.
Thus, while he was speaking of these eight celestial mansions, Sakka, the king of the gods, thinking, "Mātali is taking far too long," dispatched yet another swift devaputta.
He went with great speed and reported the matter.
Upon hearing his words, [Sakka] thought, "It is no longer possible to delay," and simultaneously sent forth many celestial mansions toward the four quarters.
He showed them. When asked by the king about the deeds performed by the sons of the gods who were experiencing such prosperity there, he explained:
"Many [palaces] of ours are suspended in the air, fashioned from gold;
shining brightly, they gleam like lightning amidst the thick clouds."
“O charioteer, seeing me, my curiosity has been aroused; Mātali, divine charioteer, I ask you this:
What good deed did these mortals perform, that they now rejoice in celestial palaces, having attained heaven?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, speak as one who knows:
“With faith firmly established in the well-expounded True Dhamma,
they have carried out the Teacher’s word in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
"These are their locations, O King, which you behold.
Therein, "vehāyasāme" means these are established in the sky itself; he says, "these are celestial mansions situated in space.
"Like lightning amidst thick clouds" means like lightning flashing within dense rain-clouds. "Well-situated" means by way of the path.

Because they have arrived, they are well-established. This is what is meant: O Great King, these men, having gone forth in the past under the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa—which leads to liberation—practiced the duty of a recluse with perfectly pure virtue;

having realized the fruit of stream-entry, yet being unable to attain Arhatship, they passed away from there and were reborn in these golden celestial mansions. Of these disciples of the Buddha Kassapa...
“Those places, O Great King, which you see.
Having thus shown him the celestial mansions situated in the sky, he spoke to encourage him to go into the presence of Sakka:
“O Great King, you have seen the abodes of those who have committed evil deeds;”
"Furthermore, you have understood the locations of those with wholesome deeds;
arise now, O King of Kings, into the presence of the King of Devas.
Therein, "the abode," O Great King, refers to the abode of those in hell which you saw first, belonging to those of evil deeds.
"The places [of those who have performed evil deeds] were known; now, as you behold the celestial mansions situated in the sky, the places of those who have performed wholesome deeds are also known.
Now, go forth and proceed to see the splendor in the presence of the king of the gods.

Having spoken thus, he drove the chariot forward and showed him the seven concentric mountain ranges that stand surrounding Sineru. As the King saw them, the Teacher, revealing how the King had questioned Mātali, said:
“Mounted upon a divine vehicle drawn by a thousand horses, as the Great King was traveling along, he saw mountains within the ocean.
Having seen them, he asked his charioteer: ‘What are these mountains called?’”
Therein, "carried by horses" means being drawn by horses. "Standing upon a divine vehicle" means having stood upon a divine vehicle.
"He saw" means he beheld. "In the midst of the Sīdā" means in the middle of the great ocean called Sīdā.
It is said that in that great ocean the water is so subtle that even a single peacock feather placed in it cannot remain standing but sinks; therefore, it is called Sīdā.
“It is called the Great Ocean Sīdā. Within it, “mountains” (naga) means hills (pabbata).
When asked, “What are their names?”—that is, “What indeed are the names of these mountains?”—the divine son Mātali, being thus questioned by Nimi the king, said:
“Sudassana, Karavīka, Īsadhara, and Yugandhara;”
“Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the lofty mountain Giri—
these are the mountains within the Sīdantara ocean, rising up in succession;
they are the abodes of the Great Kings, O King, which you behold.”
In that regard, Great King, among these mountains, the one furthest out is called Sudassana;
next to it is the mountain called Karavīka, which is higher than Sudassana. Between those two, however, lies one Sīdantara Mahāsamudda ocean.
Next to Karavīka is the mountain called Īsadharo, which is higher than Karavīka. Between those as well lies another Sīdantara Mahāsamudda ocean.
Immediately adjacent to Īṣādhara is the mountain named Yugandhara; it is higher than Īṣādhara. Between those two is one great ocean called the Sīdantara-mahāsamudda.
Immediately adjacent to Yugandhara is the mountain named Nemindhara; it is higher than Yugandhara.
Between those two is one great ocean called the Sīdantara-mahāsamudda. Immediately adjacent to Nemindhara is the mountain named Vinataka.
It is higher than Nemindhara. Between those two as well is one great ocean, the Sīdantara.
Immediately adjacent to Vinataka is the mountain named Assakaṇṇa; it is higher than Vinataka. Between those two as well is one great ocean, the Sīdantara.
Regarding the phrase "rising up in succession": these seven mountains rise up in regular sequence from within the Sīdantara great ocean.
They stood there like a flight of stairs. "As for 'those which,' O Great King, these mountains that you see are the abodes of the Four Great Kings.
Having thus shown him the world of the gods of the Four Great Kings, he drove the chariot forward toward the realm of the Thirty-three.
Having surrounded the gateway-tower of the Citta peak, a statue of Indra stood there and showed itself. Seeing it, the king asked, and the other explained it to him:
“Of many forms and beautiful, it shines with various wonders;
It is crowded with those like Indra, and well-guarded as if by tigers.”
“O charioteer, a sense of longing has found me upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
what do they call this gate, so delightful even when seen from afar?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, speak as one who knows:
"That which they call Citrakūṭa, the entrance for the king of the gods,
is revealed here as the gateway to Mount Sudassana."
“Multiform and beautiful, it shines with various wonders;
crowded with those like Indra, well-guarded as if by tigers—
enter this place, O Lord of Kings, and tread upon the dustless ground.”
In this context, "of many forms" means of various kinds. "Variegated with many colors" means variegated with various jewels.
"It shines forth" means what indeed is this that is perceived? "Crowded" means completely filled.
"Well-guarded by tigers alone" means just as a great forest is guarded by tigers or lions, so too it is well-guarded by those who resemble Indra. And of those statues of Indra...
The fact that it was established for the purpose of protection should be understood according to the method described in the *Kulāvaka-jātaka* of the *Ekaka-nipāta*.
"What name do they call it? means what is its name? "An entrance" (*pavesana*) refers to that which is constructed for the purpose of exiting and entering.
"Of Sudassana" refers to Mount Sineru, whose appearance is beautiful. "Because it is the gate" means because this [gate] is established upon the summit of Mount Sineru.
"It illuminates the gate of the divine city measuring ten thousand yojanas; the meaning is that the gateway-tower becomes visible.
'Enter by this' means: enter the divine city through this gate. 'Tread upon the dustless ground' means:
O Great King, tread with a celestial vehicle upon the divine ground, which is free from dust, composed of gold, silver, and jewels, and strewn with various flowers."
Having spoken thus, Mātali led the king into the city of the gods. Therefore it was said:
“Mounted upon the divine vehicle drawn by a thousand horses, as the Great King drove along, he beheld this assembly hall of the gods.”
Thus, while traveling seated in the divine vehicle, he saw the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas and asked Mātali about it; Mātali then explained it to him:
"Just as a blue radiance appears in the autumn sky, so too is this celestial palace, fashioned from beryl, comparable to that."
“O charioteer, a sense of wonder has found me upon seeing this; I ask you, Mātali, divine charioteer:
What do they call this celestial mansion that appears so enchanting even from afar?
Thus questioned, Mātali, the divine charioteer, replied:
Knowing the ripening of meritorious deeds, speak as one who knows:
"That which they call 'Sudhammā'—this assembly hall is seen;
beautiful with its veḷuriya gems, variegated, well-constructed, and magnificent."
“Eight well-fashioned pillars, all made of beryl,
stand there where the Tāvatiṃsa gods, all with Indra as their priest, dwell.
Thinking of the welfare of both gods and humans, they converse together.”
"Let the King of Sages enter, for it is the gods' place of rejoicing.
In this context, *idam* is merely a particle; the meaning is "he saw the assembly hall of the gods. *Passesā* means "look at this. *Veḷuriyā rucirā* means "shining with beryl.
*Citrā* means "variegated," being adorned with various jewels. *Dhārayanti* means "these [beings] support" this assembly hall.
Well-constructed pillars, divided into eight-sided and other shapes, support [the structure].
"With Indra as their chaplain" means that they remain surrounding Indra, having made him their leader and precursor, contemplating the welfare of gods and humans.
"Enter by this way" means: enter that place where the gods remain mutually expressing their appreciation.

The gods remained seated, watching the path for his arrival. Hearing that the king had come, they took divine perfumes, incense, and flowers in their hands and went out to meet him as far as the gateway of the Cittakūṭa palace.
There, honoring the Great Being with divine perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they led him into the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods.
The king alighted from his chariot and entered the assembly hall. The gods [honored him] with a seat.
They invited him. Sakka also invited him with both a seat and sensual pleasures. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“The gods rejoiced upon seeing the king arrive:
‘Welcome to you, Great King! And a most gracious welcome to you!’”
“Sit now, O royal sage, in the presence of the king of the gods.
Sakka, the lord of the Vasus, welcomed Vedeha, the ruler of Mithilā,
and invited him with sensual pleasures and a seat.
“Excellent! You have truly arrived at the abode of those who wield power.
Dwell among the gods, O sovereign king, where all desires are fulfilled;
enjoy superhuman pleasures among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.”
Therein, *paṭinandiṃsu* means they rejoiced; being joyful and glad, they accepted [the invitation]. *Sabbakāmasamiddhisū* means in those places endowed with the perfection of all desires.
Thus, having been invited by Sakka both with celestial pleasures and with his throne, the King, declining it, said:
"Just as a borrowed vehicle, just as borrowed wealth;”
"It is indeed a great attainment that there is this support from the gifts of others.
Yet, I do not desire this support from the gifts of others;
the merits performed by myself—that is my unique wealth."
“Having gone among humans, I shall perform much wholesome merit through generosity,
righteous conduct, self-restraint, and self-mastery—
that by doing which one becomes happy and does not later regret it.”
In this regard, that which is obtained from another on account of a gift—that is, because it was given by that other person—is like something borrowed; therefore, I do not desire that.
But as for those merits performed by myself, that alone is my own exclusive wealth, since it is not shared with others.
“...the following wealth. Regarding “even conduct”: by means of even conduct through the three doors. Regarding “restraint”: by the guarding of virtue (*sīla*). Regarding “taming”:
by the taming of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the devas with a sweet voice. While he was teaching the Dhamma, according to the calculation of human beings—
Having remained for seven days and honored the host of devas, while standing in the midst of that assembly, he spoke in praise of Mātali’s virtues:
“Our lord Mātali, the charioteer of the devas, has been of great benefit to us,
in that he has shown me the consequences of both my wholesome and evil deeds.”

In that regard, "he who showed me the places of my good deeds and the evils [of my] bad deeds" means he who showed me the states of the gods for my wholesome kamma and the evil states of the denizens of hell for my unwholesome kamma.
The Section on Heaven is finished.
Then King [Vessavaṇa], having addressed Sakka, said: "Great King, I wish to go to the world of men. Sakka—
“Very well then, dear Mātali, take King Nimi right there to Mithilā,” he said. Having agreed with “So be it,” Mātali prepared the chariot.
After the king had exchanged greetings with the hosts of devas and sent the devas back, he mounted the chariot.
As Mātali drove the chariot, they reached Mithilā by way of the eastern direction. When the great multitude saw the divine chariot, they—

“King [Vessavaṇa] has come to us! he thought, and was filled with joy. Mātali, having circumambulated Mithilā clockwise, lowered the Great Being down through that very lion-window, and after taking leave, saying, “I shall depart now, Great King,” he returned to his own place.
The great multitude also surrounded the king and asked, “O Lord, what is the world of the gods like? The king [described] the world of the devas and of Sakka...

Having praised the prosperity of the king of the gods, he taught the Dhamma to the great multitude, saying, "You too should perform meritorious deeds such as giving; in this way, you will be reborn in that heavenly world.
Later on, when his barber informed him that grey hairs had appeared, he had the grey hair removed with a golden pair of tongs.
Having placed [his hand] in the barber’s hand and given him an excellent village, he, desiring to go forth, entrusted the kingdom to his son.
When the son asked, "Why, O King, will you go forth?", he replied:
"These hairs on my head, having grown, now take away my youth."
"The time for my going forth has come; the divine messengers have appeared.
Having spoken this verse, he went forth like the former kings and, dwelling in that very mango grove, developed the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and attained rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Revealing his state of having thus gone forth, the Teacher spoke this concluding verse:
“Having spoken this, King Nimi, the ruler of Videha and lord of Mithilā, having performed various sacrifices, entered into self-restraint.

In this context, “having spoken this” means having spoken this verse beginning with “The hairs of my head...”. “Having performed various sacrifices” means having given a great gift. “He entered into self-restraint” means he attained the restraint of virtue (sīla).
But his son, named Kāḷārajanaka, brought that lineage to an end.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, the Tathāgata went forth on the Great Renunciation," and he identified the Jātaka:
"At that time Sakka was Anuruddha, and Mātali was Ānanda."
“The assembly of the Buddha consisted of eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas, and King Nimi was none other than I myself, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This concludes the fourth narrative, the Commentary on the Nimi Jātaka.
[542] 5. Commentary on the Ummagga Jātaka.
"Pañcāla comes with his entire army"—this was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*).
One day, the bhikkhus, having gathered in the Hall of Truth, sat there praising the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom:
"Friends, the Tathāgata is of great wisdom, of vast wisdom, of profound wisdom, of radiant wisdom, and of swift wisdom."
Possessing sharp wisdom and penetrative wisdom, a crusher of the doctrines of others, he— by the power of his own wisdom—
tamed the brahmins such as Kūṭadanta, the wanderers such as Sabhiya, the bandits such as Aṅgulimāla, the yakṣas such as Āḷavaka, the devas such as Sakka,
and the Brahmās such as Baka, rendering them free from harmful activity; and having granted the going-forth into homelessness to a great multitude of people.
“...he established them in the fruits of the path; such is the great wisdom of the Teacher, friends.
The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?

When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is possessed of wisdom; in the past, too, while his knowledge was still unripened, he practiced conduct for the sake of the knowledge of enlightenment.”
"Even while wandering, one is truly wise only through wisdom. Having said this, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, in the kingdom of Videha, a king named Vedeha reigned in Mithilā.
He had four wise ministers who instructed him in matters of profit and righteousness: Senaka, Pukkusa, Kāminda, and Devinda. At that time, the King [consulted] the Bodhisatta...
On the day of his conception, at the time of dawn, he saw such a dream:
in the center of the royal courtyard, four masses of fire, as large as great city walls, arose from the four corners and blazed up.
In their midst, a mass of fire the size of a glowworm arose, and in that very instant, having surpassed those four masses of fire, it reached as far as the Brahma-world.
Having risen, it stood illuminating the entire Cakkavāḷa; yet when it fell upon the ground, not even as much as a mustard seed could be seen.
The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings;
the great multitude moved through its midst as if through a flame, and not even a hair’s breadth of heat was felt. Having seen this dream, the king arose, terrified and trembling.
Sitting there, thinking, "What indeed will happen to me?", he caused the dawn to break.
When the four wise men arrived in the morning, they asked about his comfortable sleep, saying, "Your Majesty, did you sleep well?
He replied, "How could I have obtained a comfortable sleep? and related everything, saying, "I saw such a dream as this."
Then the wise Senaka said to him, "Do not fear, Great King; this is an auspicious dream, there will be prosperity for you.
When asked, "For what reason, Teacher? he replied, "Great King, having surpassed us four wise men, another fifth wise man shall arise for you. For we four wise men are like four masses of fire."
“Another fifth wise man will arise among them like a mass of fire that has appeared;
he will be peerless in the world with its devas,” he said. When it was asked, “But where is he now?
he replied, “Great King, today he must either have taken rebirth-linking or have emerged from his mother’s womb,” by the power of his own craft.
He gave his explanation as if he had seen it with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). From that time forth, the king also remembered those words.
Now, in Mithilā, there were four villages at the four gates: Pācīnayavamajjhaka, Dakkhiṇayavamajjhaka, Pacchimayavamajjhaka, and Uttarayavamajjhaka.
Among them, in Pācīnayavamajjhaka, there was one named Sirivaḍḍhana.
A merchant lived there, and Sumanadevī was his wife. On that very day, at the moment the king saw the dream, the Great Being descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and took rebirth in her womb.
At that same time, another thousand sons of gods also descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and [took rebirth] in that very village.
They took rebirth in families of preeminent merchants and supreme nobles. After ten months had passed, Queen Sumanā gave birth to a son of golden complexion.

At that moment, Sakka, surveying the human world, perceived that the Great Being was about to emerge from his mother’s womb and thought, “It is fitting to make this sprout of a Buddha manifest throughout the world, including the realm of the devas.”

At the very moment the Great Being emerged from his mother’s womb, an invisible being approached, placed a small medicinal jar into his hand, and returned to its own place. The Great Being took it, closing his fist around it.
When he had emerged from the mother’s womb, she experienced not even the slightest pain; he came forth as easily as water from a water-pot.
Seeing the medicinal jar in his hand, she asked, "Dear son, what have you obtained?
"Medicine, mother," he replied, and he placed the divine medicine in his mother's hand.
Having placed it there, he said, "Mother, give this medicine to anyone who is afflicted by any illness whatsoever. Delighted and overjoyed, she informed the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana.
He, however, suffered from a headache that had persisted for seven years.
Becoming joyful and exultant, he thought, "This child, while being born from his mother's womb, came having taken medicine; at the very moment of birth, he spoke with his mother.
The medicine given by such a meritorious person must be of great power. Having reflected thus, he took that medicine.
Having crushed this *nisadā* plant, he smeared a little upon his forehead.
At that moment, his seven-year-old headache vanished like water from a lotus leaf. He was filled with joy, thinking, "This is a medicine of great power.
The fact that the Great Being had returned after taking the medicine became known everywhere. Whosoever were afflicted by illness—
Everyone went to the merchant’s house and asked for the medicine.

Having ground it on a grindstone for each person, he took a small amount, stirred it with water, and gave it to them. As soon as their bodies were anointed with that divine medicine, all their ailments were pacified.
The happy people praised it, saying, "The power of the medicine in the house of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana is truly great!"
They departed. On the day the Great Being’s name was being chosen, the Great Merchant said, “My son has no need for a name after his grandfather or others;
since he came taking medicine when he was born, let him have the name ‘Osadha’ alone.
Thus, they gave him the name “Prince Mahosadha.”
Then this thought occurred to him: "My son is of great merit; he will not be born alone, but must be accompanied by children born at the same time.

Looking into the matter, and having heard that a thousand children had been born, he gave ornaments to all the boys and provided nurses, thinking, "They shall be attendants upon my son. By the Bodhisatta...
Together with them, he performed auspicious rites at the place of blessing. Having adorned the children, they brought them to attend upon the Great Being.
Playing with them, the Bodhisatta grew up until, at the age of seven, he was as handsome as a golden statue.
Then, while he was playing with them in the middle of the village, elephants, horses, and other animals approached.
The playground was broken up; when the wind and sun struck them, the children grew weary.
One day, while they were still playing, an unseasonable cloud arose. Seeing it, the Bodhisatta Nāgabala ran and entered a single sala tree.
The other children, running after him, collided with one another's feet and stumbled.
They fell and suffered broken knees and other injuries. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "It would be fitting to build a play-hall in this place;
thus, when wind, rain, or heat come, we shall not suffer," said to those children:
"Friends, in this place let us build a single hall capable of withstanding standing, sitting, and lying down, even when wind, rain, or heat arrives."
“We shall have it built; each of you bring one kahāpaṇa. They did so.
The Great Being summoned the master builder and gave him a thousand [kahāpaṇas], saying, “Build a hall in this place.
He accepted, saying, “Very well,” and taking the thousand, he pounded the stumps and thorns and leveled the ground.
He stretched out the cord. The Great Being, finding the manner of his cord-stretching unsatisfactory, said, "Teacher, do not stretch it like that;
stretch it properly. "Master, I have stretched it according to my own craft;
I know nothing other than this. "If you do not even know this much, how will you build a hall for us after having taken our wealth?"
"Bring it; having stretched out the thread, I will show you," he said. Having had it brought, he himself stretched out the thread.
It was as if it had been stretched out by the divine son Vissakamma. Then he asked the carpenter, "Will you be able to stretch it out like this?
"I shall not be able," he replied. "But will you be able to do it according to my instructions? "I shall be able, Master," he replied. The Great Being [then proceeded] just as...
In one part of that hall was a dwelling place for the destitute; in another, a lying-in room for destitute women;
in another, a dwelling place for visiting ascetics and brahmins; in another, a dwelling place for visiting people;
and in another, a place for storing the goods of visiting merchants—all [of these were] likewise.
Having turned his face toward the exterior, he surveyed the hall. Right there he had a gaming arena constructed, right there a court of justice, and right there an assembly hall for the Dhamma.
When the hall was finished in just a few days, he summoned painters and, having personally supervised them, had beautiful paintings executed.
The hall became the very counterpart of the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods.
Then, thinking, "The hall does not shine by this much alone; it is fitting to have a lotus pond constructed," he had a lotus pond excavated.
He summoned a bricklayer, supervised the work himself, and had a lotus pond built with a thousand curves and a hundred bathing places.
It was covered with five kinds of lotuses and became like the Nanda Pond. On its banks grew trees bearing flowers and fruit.
Having caused various trees to be planted, he constructed a pleasure grove comparable to the Nandana Grove.

And relying upon that very *sālā* hall, he established a practice of giving for righteous recluses and brahmins, as well as for visitors, travelers, and others. His conduct became renowned everywhere;
many people flocked to him. Sitting in the *sālā*, the Great Being [instructed] those who arrived one after another regarding what was appropriate and what was inappropriate.
He spoke on what was appropriate and inappropriate and established a legal decision; it was as if the time of a Buddha’s appearance had arrived.

After seven years had passed, King Vedeha remembered, thinking, “The four wise men told me that after overcoming them, a fifth wise man would appear; where is he now? and [recalled] his place of residence.
"Know this! he said, and dispatched four ministers through the four gates. The ministers who departed from the other gates did not see the Great Being.

However, the minister who departed from the eastern gate, seeing the sal trees and so forth, thought, "There must be a wise man who either built or commissioned the building of these sal trees," and he questioned the people: "Who built these sal trees?"
“By which carpenter was this made? The people replied, “This was not made by a carpenter;
it was made by the wise Mahosadha, the son of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, after he had deliberated by means of his own power of wisdom.
“But how many years old is the wise man? “He is seven full years old. The minister [calculated] the age from the day the king saw the dream.
Having calculated it, [he thought], "This accords with the king's dream; this indeed is that wise man," and he sent a messenger to the king, saying:

"Your Majesty, in the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka, the son of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, a wise man named Mahosadha, though only seven years of age, has planned such a sal-tree grove and constructed a lotus pond and a park. This is that wise man."
“I shall take him and bring him here. When the king heard these words, his heart was filled with joy;
he summoned Senaka, informed him of the matter, and asked, “Teacher, shall we bring the wise man?
Being envious of the gain, Senaka replied, “Great King, one does not become a ‘wise man’ merely by having halls and such constructed; anyone can have these built.”

"This is a trivial matter," he said. Having heard his words, [the king] thought, "There must be a reason for this," and remaining silent, he dispatched a messenger to the minister with the instruction:
"While staying right there, let him test the wise man. Upon hearing this, the minister stayed right there and tested the wise man.
The Question of the Seven Boys.
Herein is the summary for investigation:
“Meat, ox, knot, thread, son, ox, and with the chariot.”
"The staff, the head, and the snake; the cock, the jewel, and the birth;
the rice, and the sand as well; the pond, the field, the donkey, and the jewel.
Regarding that, "flesh" refers to one day when the Bodhisatta was going to the playground, a hawk [seized] from a meat-slicer...
Taking the piece of meat, he soared into the sky. Seeing him, the boys pursued the bird, thinking, "We will make him drop the piece of meat.
The bird darted here and there; looking upward and following after him, they stumbled over rocks and such, becoming exhausted.
Then the wise man said to them, "I will make him drop it myself."
“Throw it away, Master! he said. “In that case, you watch,” he replied;
and without even looking up, he ran with the speed of the wind, stepped upon the shadow of the deer, struck it with his hand, and let out a great roar.
By the power of that sound, it was as if the noise had pierced right through the belly of the deer and issued out from within. Terrified, the deer dropped its meat. The Great Being—
Realizing that it had been discarded, [the wise man] watched its shadow and, not allowing it to fall to the ground, caught it in mid-air.
Seeing this marvel, the great multitude made a tremendous noise, shouting, cheering, and clapping their hands.
A minister, having learned of this occurrence, sent a messenger to the king, saying: "The wise man has caused this piece of meat to be discarded by this very stratagem."
"May Your Majesty know this. Having heard this, the king asked Senaka, "What is it, Senaka?
Shall we bring the wise man? He thought, "From the moment he arrives here, we shall be deprived of our luster;
the king will not even acknowledge our existence. It is not right to bring him. Out of intense envy for his gain, he said, "Great King,"
“By this much alone, one is not called wise; this is something quite trivial,” he said. The king, remaining neutral, sent him back again with the instruction, “Let him test him right there.
A man named Goṇa, a resident of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka, [set out] from another village thinking, “When the rains have fallen, I shall plow.”
Having purchased an ox, brought it home, and kept it there, he led it to a grassy field for grazing the following day.
Sitting upon the ox’s back, he became weary; dismounting, he lay down at the foot of a tree and fell asleep.
At that moment, a certain thief seized the ox and fled. Upon waking, not seeing the ox, he looked here and there and [saw] the ox...
Seeing a thief fleeing after having seized [the oxen], he rushed forward with speed and said, "Where are you taking my oxen?
"I am leading my own oxen to wherever I wish," he replied. Hearing their dispute, the great multitude gathered together.
When the wise man heard the sound of them passing by the hall door, he summoned both of them; and upon seeing their actions, he...
He recognized, “This is the thief; this is the owner of the ox. Even though he already knew this, he asked, “Why are you quarreling?
The owner of the ox said, “Sir, I bought these from such-and-such a person in such-and-such a village, brought them here, and kept them in my house.
When I led them to the grazing ground for pasture, seeing that I was negligent, this man seized the oxen and fled.”
“I, while looking here and there, saw this man; having pursued him, I seized him.
The inhabitants of such-and-such a village know that these were purchased by me. But the thief said, “These are my kinsmen from home; he speaks a lie.
Then the wise man said to them, “I shall judge your dispute according to the Dhamma; will you abide by my judgment?”
Having asked him, when he replied, "Yes, sir, I will stay," [the king] said, "It is necessary to win the favor of the public," and first questioned the thief:
"What did you have these oxen eat? What did you have them drink? "I had them drink rice-gruel, and I had them eat sesame flour and beans.
Then he questioned the owner of the oxen. He said, "Sir, how could I, being so poor..."
“Having received rice gruel and other such things, they were made to eat nothing but grass.
The wise man had the assembly take up their words, and having had piyaṅgu leaves brought, crushed, and kneaded with water, he gave them to the oxen to drink. The oxen discarded the grass entirely.
The wise man said, “Look at this! and showing it to the great multitude, he asked the thief, “Are you a thief?”
"Are you not a thief? he asked. "I am a thief," he replied. "In that case, from now on, do not do such a thing again," he advised him.
But the Bodhisatta’s retinue beat him with their hands and feet until he was weakened.
Then the Wise One said to him, "Even in this very life you receive such suffering; but in the future, in the hells and other realms, you will experience great suffering."
"You will experience [the consequences], friend; from this day forward, you must abandon such deeds," he said, and then gave him the five precepts.
The minister reported the matter to the king exactly as it had happened. The king asked Senaka, "What do you say, Senaka?
Shall we bring the wise man? "O Great King, there is one named Goṇa-aḍḍa; whoever settles disputes, wait for him."
When this was said, the king remained neutral and again sent the same message.
This should be understood in the same way for all instances. From here on, however, we shall present only the analysis of the summary verses (*uddāna*).
"A knot" (*ganthi*) refers to an ornament made of knotted threads, fashioned by tying together various colored threads, as worn by a woman of ill repute.
Having removed it from her neck and placed it upon her garment, she descended into the lotus pond prepared by the wise man to bathe.
Another young woman, seeing it, conceived a desire for it; she lifted it up and said, "Mother, this is exceedingly beautiful!
For how much was it made for you? I too shall have one like it made for myself; having fastened it around my neck, I shall see its measure..."
"I will wait for you," she said; and when the other, out of her straightforwardness, replied, "Wait for me," she put it around her neck and departed.
Seeing this, the other quickly climbed out, put on her wrap, ran after her, and seized the wrap, saying, "Where are you going, taking my jewelry and fleeing?
The first one replied, "I am not taking what belongs to you."
"This is indeed an ornament for my neck," she said. When the great multitude heard this, they gathered together.
While playing with the children, the wise man heard their quarreling as they were leaving through the door of the hall; hearing the sound, he asked, "What is that noise?
and upon hearing the cause of the two women's dispute, he had them summoned and, by their very appearance, distinguished the thief from the non-thief.
Even though he already knew the matter, he asked them, saying, "I shall judge you according to the Dhamma; will you abide by my judgment?
When they replied, "Yes, Master, we will abide by it," he first questioned the thief:
"When you were adorning yourself with this jewelry, what perfume did you anoint yourself with? She said, "I always anoint myself with *sabbasaṃhāraka*."
"Sabbasaṃhāraka" is a perfume prepared by blending all other perfumes. He then asked for the other one.
She said, "How could I, a woman of low station, have obtained *sabbasaṃhāraka*, Master? I always anoint myself with the scent of *piyaṅgu* flowers alone.
The wise man had a water bowl brought and had her place that ornament into it.
Having summoned a perfumer, he said, "Smell this fragrance and identify what kind of flower it is.
While smelling it, the perfumer recognized it as being *piyaṅgu* flowers and spoke this verse in the Ekakanipāta:
"There is no one who can gather [all scents]; pure *kaṅgu* grass wafts forth."
“The harlot spoke a falsehood; the old woman spoke the truth. In this context, *dhuttī* means a harlot (*dhuttikā*).
*Āhu* means she said; or rather, *āhu* is simply the reading.

Thus, having made the reason known to the great multitude, the Great Being asked, “Are you a thief, or are you not a thief? and caused her to confess her state as a thief. From that time forth, the wisdom of the Great Being became manifest.
Regarding the word *sutta*: there was a certain woman who guarded a cotton field.
While guarding the cotton field, she took some pure cotton right there, spun it into fine thread, made a ball of it, and placed it in her lap as she was returning to the village.
Thinking, "I shall bathe in the wise man’s lotus pond," she went to the bank, removed her garment, and [placed it] upon the garment.
Having placed the ball of thread down, she descended and bathed in the lotus pond. Another woman, seeing it, seized it out of greed and said, "Oh, what a lovely thread!
Mother, you have done well! She clapped her hands, looked as if in admiration, placed it in her lap, and departed.
The rest is to be detailed in the same manner as before. First, the wise one...
He questioned the first thief, asking, "What did you put inside when you were making the sugar-ball?
She replied, "Only cotton seeds, Master. Then he questioned the other. She said, "It was *timbaru* seeds, Master.
He had the assembly take both women's statements, and having had the string of the sugar-ball unwound, he saw the *timbaru* seeds and thus established her guilt as a thief.
The great multitude, joyful and delighted, cried out "Bravo! Bravo! a thousand times, saying, "The lawsuit has been well adjudicated.
Regarding the son: one day, a certain woman, taking her son with her, went to the wise man’s lotus pond to wash his face;
having bathed the boy and seated him on her own garment, she descended into the water to wash her own face. While she was there—
At that moment, a certain female spirit (yakkhinī), seeing the boy and desiring to devour him, assumed the guise of a woman and asked, "Friend, this boy is truly beautiful;
is he your son? When she was told, "Yes," she said, "I will nurse him.
Being told, "Nurse him," she took him, played with him for a short while, and then fled taking him away. The other [woman], seeing this, ran after her.
“Where have you taken my son? she cried, and seized him. The ogress replied, “From whom did you get this son? He is my son!
As the two of them were quarreling while walking through the door of the hall, the wise man heard the sound of their dispute. Having summoned them, he asked, “What is this?
They explained the matter to him. Upon hearing this, the Great Being—due to his unblinking eyes—[realized the truth].
Because of her dark complexion, her lack of apprehension, and the absence of a shadow, he recognized, "This is a female *yakkha*.

He said, "Will you abide by my judgment? When she replied, "Yes, we shall abide by it," he drew a line on the ground, laid the boy down in the middle of the line, and had the *yakkhinī* take hold of his hands and his mother take hold of his feet. Then, addressing both of them...
"Drag him away and seize him! Only one who is able to drag him can have this as a son," he said.
Both of them dragged him. As the boy was being dragged, he became overcome with pain and cried out.
His mother, as if her heart were splitting, released her son and stood there weeping. The wise man asked the great crowd, "O sirs!"
“O lady, is a mother’s heart tender, or is it not? “A mother’s heart is tender.
“But now, standing while holding the child, is she a mother, or is she one who has let him go?
“One who stands having let him go is wise, O lady. “But do you know this child-thief? “We do not know him, O wise lady.”
Then the wise man said to them, "This is a yakkhinī; she has seized him in order to eat him. "How do you know that, wise one?
"By her unblinking eyes, by their redness, by her lack of apprehension, by the absence of shadow, and by her mercilessness.
Then he asked her, "Who are you? "I am a yakkhinī, sir. "Why did you seize this boy?"
“I am taking it to eat, Master. “You blind fool! Having committed evil deeds even in the past, you were born as a female spirit (yakkhinī);

now you commit evil once again. Oh, what a blind fool you are! Having said this, he established her in the five precepts, told her, “From now on, do not commit such evil deeds,” and sent her away. The child’s mother also [took] the child...
Having obtained [the boon], and having praised the wise man, saying, "May my lord live long," he took his son and departed.
It is said that there was a certain man named Gotakāla; he was called "Gota" because he was a dwarf (*lakuṇḍaka*), and "Kāla" because of his dark complexion.
After working for seven years, he obtained a wife. Her name was Dīghatālā. One day, he addressed her:
Having said, "Bhadde, bake some cakes and solid food; we shall go to see our parents," he was refused by her when she asked, "What have you to do with your parents?
Even though he spoke thus up to three times, he had cakes and solid food baked, took provisions and gifts, and set out on the road together with her. On the way, he saw a river flowing shallowly.
Both of them were, however, by nature afraid of water; therefore, unable to cross it, they stood on the bank.
At that time, a certain poor man named Dīghapiṭṭhi, while wandering about, arrived at that place.
When they saw him, they asked him, "Friend, is this river deep or shallow? Having heard their words, he [perceived] their fear of water.
Having understood this, he said, "Friend, this river is deep and filled with many fierce fish.
"Friend, how will you go? He replied, "We have acquaintance with the crocodiles and sea-monsters;
therefore, they do not harm us. "In that case, friend, take us along as well. He consented, saying, "Very well. Then, for him—
They gave him hard food and soft food to eat. Having finished his meal, he asked, "Friend, whom shall I carry first?
He replied, "Carry your female companion first; carry me afterwards.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," he placed her on his shoulder, took provisions and gifts, and having descended into the river, walked a short distance.
Squatting on his haunches, he departed.
Gotakāḷa, while still standing on the bank, thought: "This river is deep; even though it is so long, it is of such a nature that for me it will surely be easy to cross.
The other one also led him into the middle of the river and said: "Bhadde, I..."
"I will support you; you shall wander about surrounded by male and female slaves, dressed in excellent garments and ornaments. What will this hunchbacked dwarf do for you?

Do as I say," she said. Upon hearing his words, she immediately broke her affection for her own husband and became attached to him at that very moment, saying, "Husband, if you will not abandon me..."
“I will carry out your word,” she replied, consenting. “My dear lady, what are you saying? I shall support you,” he said.
Having gone to the opposite shore, they both, living together in harmony and mutual affection, said, “Stay here, leaving Gotakāḷa behind!
and as he looked on, they departed while eating solid food right there. Seeing this, he thought, “These two have joined together and left me...”
"Thinking, 'They are fleeing after abandoning [me],' he ran back and forth;
having descended a short distance, he turned back in fear, and then, out of anger toward them, shouting, 'Whether I live or die! he leaped up and fell into the river.
Realizing his state [of being face-down], he swam across the river, reached him with speed, and cried, 'Ho, wicked thief! Where have you taken my wife?'"
The other said to him, "Hey, you wicked dwarf! Where is your wife? She is my wife!
Having said this, he seized him by the neck and threw him down. Grasping a long palm tree in his hand, he cried out, "Stop! Where are you going?
This wife was obtained by me after working for seven years! And so, he began to quarrel with him.
He arrived at the hall. A great crowd of people gathered.
The wise man asked, "What is this noise? and having summoned both of them, he listened to their words and counter-words.
He said, "Will you abide by my judgment? When they replied, "Yes, we will," he first [addressed] Dīghapiṭṭhi.
Having summoned him, he asked, "What is your name? "I am named Dīghapiṭṭhika, sir," he replied. "What is the name of your wife?
Not knowing her name, he said something else. "What are the names of your parents? "They are named so-and-so.
"But what are the names of your wife's parents? Not knowing, he again said something else. To him...
Having had the assembly take their seats and removed that man, he summoned another and, in the same manner as before, asked for the names of everyone.
Knowing the truth and not making any mistake, he spoke accordingly. Having removed him as well, he summoned Dīghatāla and asked, "What is your name?
"My name is Dīghatāla, sir. "What is your husband's name?"
Not knowing [the answer], she spoke of something else. "What are your mother and father's names? "They are named So-and-so, Master.
"But what are your husband's mother and father's names? She too, lamenting, spoke of something else.
Having summoned the other two, he asked the great crowd, "Does this accord with Dīghapiṭṭhi’s statement, or with Gotakāḷa’s?"
“Gotakāla is the wise one,” they said. “This man is her husband; the other is a thief.
Then he asked him, “Are you a thief? Are you not a thief? “Yes, master, I am a thief,” he replied, admitting his thievery.
By the judgment of the wise man, Gotakāla recovered his own wife, and after praising the Great Being, he took her and departed. The wise man—
Dīghapiṭṭhi said, "Do not do so again.
Regarding "and with a chariot": one day, a certain man sat in a chariot and went out for the purpose of washing his face.
At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw the wise man and [reflected upon] "the power of the wisdom of Mahosadha, the sprout of a Buddha."
Thinking, "I shall make it manifest," he approached in the guise of a human, took hold of the rear of the chariot, and set out.
The man seated in the chariot asked, "Dear sir, for what purpose have you come?
When told, "To attend upon you," he replied, "Very well," and descending from the vehicle, went to perform the funeral rites for his body. At that moment, Sakka [took] the chariot...
Having mounted it, he drove it off with great speed. But the owner of the chariot, having performed his bodily duties and come out, saw Sakka taking his chariot and fleeing;
he pursued him swiftly and cried out, "Stop! Stop! Where are you taking my chariot?
When the other replied, "Your chariot shall be another, but this is my chariot," he began to quarrel with him.
He arrived at the hall door. The wise man asked, "What is this? and had them summoned.
Seeing them approaching, and because of their fearlessness as well as the unblinking state of their eyes, he recognized, "This is Sakka; this is the chariot-owner.
Even so, he asked the cause of their dispute and said, "Will you abide by my judgment? To which they replied, "Yes, we will abide by it."

Having said, "I will drive the chariot; you two follow behind holding onto the chariot—the owner of the chariot will not let it go, but the other will," he commanded a man, "Drive the chariot! He did so.
The other two followed behind, holding on. After going a short distance, the owner of the chariot let go and stood still.
Sakka, however, went along with the chariot and returned with the chariot itself. The wise man pointed this out to the people:
"This man went a short distance, left the chariot, and stood still;
but this one ran along with the chariot and returned with the chariot itself, yet not even a single drop of sweat is upon his body, nor is there any inhalation or exhalation."
“There is none; he is fearless, with unblinking eyes—he is Sakka, the king of the gods. Then, having asked him, “Are you Sakka, the king of the gods?
and being told, “Yes, wise man,” he said, “For what purpose have you come?
When he replied, “Wise man, it is for the sake of making your wisdom known,” he advised him, saying, “In that case, do not act like this again. Sakka, too, displaying his divine power—
Standing in the air, he praised the wise man, saying, "The wise man has rightly adjudicated the wager," and then departed for his own place.
At that time, the minister himself went into the presence of the king and said, "Great King, the wise man has thus rightly adjudicated the wager for the chariot;
even Sakka was defeated by him. Why, O Lord, do you not recognize such a distinguished person?"
The king asked Senaka, "Senaka, shall we bring the wise man?
Out of a desire for gain, he said, "Great King, one does not become 'wise' by such means alone; wait a while, and after testing him, we shall know.
The Question of the Seven Boys is finished.
The Question of the Donkey:
One day, King Daṇḍa, thinking, "I shall test the wise man," had a khadira-wood staff brought;
then, having measured one span from it, he summoned a skilled carver, had it well-carved, and sent it to the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka.
He sent word, saying: "The inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka are said to be wise;
let them know which is the top and which is the root of this acacia staff. A fine of one thousand [pieces] shall be imposed on those who do not know.
The villagers gathered together, and being unable to determine it themselves, they spoke to the merchant: "Perhaps the wise Mahosadha might know; let us summon him."
“Ask him. The merchant summoned the wise man from the gaming circle, informed him of the matter, and asked, “Dear sir, we are unable to find out; will you be able to do so?
Upon hearing this, the wise man thought, “The king has no need for either the head or the price of this man; he has sent me for the purpose of testing me.”
Thinking, "It will be so," he said, "Bring it, dear son; I shall know.

Having had it brought, and having grasped it with his hand, although he already knew, "This is the top, this is the root," he nevertheless had a water-pot brought for the purpose of winning over the hearts of the great multitude.
He tied the acacia staff with a string in its middle, and grasping the end of the string, [he held] the acacia staff.
He placed it on the surface of the water. Because of its weight, the root sank into the water first.
Then he asked the great multitude, "Is the root of a tree heavy, or is the top? "The root, O wise ones," they replied.
"In that case, look at this which has sunk first; this is the root. With this understanding, he pointed out both the top and the root. The village dwellers—
"This is the top, this is the root," they sent to the king. The king asked, "Who knows this?
and having heard that it was the wise Mahosadha, the son of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, he asked, "Senaka, shall we bring the wise man?
[Senaka replied,] "Consent, Your Majesty; we shall test him by another means as well."
One day, they had two heads brought—one of a woman and one of a man—and sent word: "Let them know which is the woman’s head and which is the man’s head;
those who do not know shall be fined a thousand. The villagers, being ignorant, asked the wise man.
Upon merely seeing them, he knew. How did he know? It is said that on a man’s head, the seam of the hair (*sibbinī*) is straight.
...there was a seamstress who had a crooked head; she walked by turning around.
By this sign, he identified, "This is a woman's head; this is a man's head. The villagers also sent [a head] for the king. The rest is exactly as before. Regarding the snakes:
then one day, having had a male snake and a female snake brought, [he said], "Let them know, 'This is the male snake; this is the female snake.'"
"Those who do not know shall be fined a thousand," they said, and sent word to the village dwellers. The villagers, being ignorant, questioned the wise man.
He knew as soon as he saw it; for the tail of a male snake is thick, while that of a female snake is thin;
the head of a male snake is broad, while that of a female snake is narrow; and the eyes of a male snake are large.
The young snakes belonged to the female snake (*sappinī*), while the *sovattika* was bound to the male snake (*sappa*) and the *vicchinnaka* to the female snake.
By these identifying marks he declared, "This is the male snake; this is the female snake. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the cock: one day, [he saw] the all-white cock of the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka, whose feet and crest were white...

They sent word, saying: "Let them send a bellowing bull that has not exceeded three years of age and possesses a hump on its head; if they do not send one, there shall be a fine of a thousand [pieces of money].
Not knowing the answer themselves, they questioned the wise man. He said: "The king has had you bring a completely white cock.
For, because its claws and comb are like feet, it is called 'Foot-Horned' (pādavisāṇa); and because of the tuft on its head, it is called 'Hump-Headed' (sīsakakudha)."
"Because it rains three times [in a day], it is said that it roars without missing the three seasons;
therefore, send such a firebrand. They sent it.
"The gem" refers to a cluster of gems given by Sakka to King Kusarājā, which was crooked in eight places. Its old thread—
Because it was cut, no one was able to pull out the old thread and insert a new one; therefore, one day they sent word:
"Let them pull out the old thread from this cluster of jewels and insert a new one.
The villagers, being unable to pull out the old thread and insert a new one, informed the wise man. He said: "Do not..."
He thought, "Bring honey," and having had it brought, he smeared the openings on both sides of the gem with honey.
He wound a woolen thread around it, smeared the ends of the thread with honey, inserted it slightly into the opening, and placed it at the spot where the ants would emerge.
Drawn out by the scent of the honey, the ants came forth and [removed] the old thread from the gem.
While eating, they went to the end of the blanket thread, bit it, and pulling it out, they drew him out from one side.
The wise man, realizing he had been drawn inside, said, "Give him to the king," and gave him to the villagers. They sent him to the king.
Having heard the means by which he was brought inside, the king was pleased.

They caused him to give birth: one day, after having fed the king’s auspicious bull for many months, they made his belly large, washed his horns, smeared them with oil, bathed him in turmeric, and sent him to the village dwellers, saying, "You are indeed wise;
this is the king’s auspicious bull who has conceived a calf. Cause him to give birth to it."

“Send someone; for those who do not send one, there shall be a fine of a thousand [pieces of money]. The villagers said, “This cannot be done; what indeed shall we do? and they questioned the wise man.
He thought, “There must be some way to resolve this question,” and asked, “But will you be able to find a confident man capable of conversing with the king?”
He asked. [The king replied,] “This is no burden, O wise ones. “In that case, summon him,” he said. They summoned him.
Then the Great Being said to him, “Come, good man! Scatter your hair upon your back and go to the palace gate wailing various kinds of powerful lamentations.
Even when questioned by others, do not say anything, but continue to wail. However, by the King...”
Having summoned her, although he questioned her regarding the cause of her lamentation, she said, “Your Majesty, my father is unable to give birth;
today is the seventh day. Be my refuge and provide a means for him to deliver. When the king replied, “What are you prattling?
This is impossible; there are no such things as men who give birth,” she said, “If it be so, Your Majesty...”
“There is no such thing; so why would you say, ‘How will the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka cause the auspicious bull to give birth?
He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and did exactly as instructed. The king asked, “By whom was this solution to the riddle conceived?
and upon hearing that it was by the wise Mahosadha, he was pleased.

Regarding "the rice": on the following day, thinking, "We shall test the wise man," they said, "Let the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka cook and send us sour rice porridge endowed with eight qualities. These are the eight qualities:
[prepared] not by means of husked rice, not by water, not by a cauldron, not by a hearth, not by fire, not by wood, and not by a woman."
“Neither by a man, nor by a path. They sent word: “For those who do not bring [the offering], there shall be a fine of a thousand [pieces].
The villagers, not knowing the reason for this, questioned the wise man.
He said, “Do not worry,” and had them take “not with rice grains” as parched grain (kaṇika), and “not with water” as snow, and “not with a pan” as another new earthenware vessel.

"Having had it taken up" means: not having had it pounded at the hearth by means of a stump; not having had it taken up by fire means: having abandoned ordinary fire and having had it taken up by fire produced from kindling wood (*araṇi*);
not having had it [carried] by wood means: having had leaves taken up, cooked with sour rice-gruel, placed in a new vessel, and sealed;
not by a woman or a man means: having had it lifted by a *paṇḍaka*; not by the road means: the main highway.
“Abandoning the path by way of the legs, send him to the king,” he said. They did accordingly. The king asked, “By whom was this riddle known?
and having heard that it was by the wise Mahosadha, he was pleased.
On another day, for the purpose of testing the wise man, they sent word to the villagers: “The king—”
“Desiring to play on a swing, [the prince] said: ‘Let them send an old cord from the royal palace that has been cut, or let them spin one out of sand;
for those who do not send one, there shall be a fine of a thousand [pieces of money]. They questioned the wise man.
The wise man, thinking, ‘This too must be resolved by means of a clever answer,’ reassured the village dwellers and summoned two or three men skilled in speech, saying: ‘Go!”’
"You should say to the king: 'Your Majesty, the village-dwellers do not know whether that cord was thin or thick;
please send a piece of the old sand-cord measuring either a span or four finger-breadths.
Having examined it, they will spin [the new cord] to that same measure. If the king says to you, 'In our house there is no sand-cord...'"

“I have never heard such a thing before,” he said. Then [the king] sent word to them, saying, “If, Great King, you are unable to do such a thing, tell me how the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka will act.
They did exactly as instructed. The king asked, “By whom was this solution to the problem conceived? and upon hearing that it was by the wise Mahosadha, he was pleased.
On another day, thinking it was for the purpose of testing the wise man, they sent a message to the villagers: "The king wishes to enjoy a water-sport;
let them send a lotus pond covered with five kinds of lotuses. A fine of one thousand [pieces] shall be imposed on those who do not send one.
They reported this to the wise man. He thought, "This too must be due to his power of answering riddles."
Having reflected thus, he summoned several men skilled in speech and said:

"Come now, after you have played in the water, with your eyes reddened, your hair wet, your clothes wet, and your bodies smeared with mud, go to the palace gate carrying ropes, sticks, and clods of earth in your hands.
Having announced your presence at the gate to the King, and having been granted permission to enter, say: 'Great King,..."
"It seems you sent us with the message, 'Let the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka send a lotus pond.
We have come bringing a large lotus pond suitable for you;

however, because we are forest-dwellers, upon seeing the city and observing the gates, walls, moats, watchtowers, and so forth, we became terrified and fled, cutting our cords and returning to the very forest."
"Even when we entered and struck them with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth, we were unable to turn them back.
Send us the old lotus pond brought from your forest; having joined [the elephants] with it, we shall take them away.
When they had said this, the king replied, "Has there ever been such a thing as a lotus pond brought by me from the forest? Nor have I ever joined [anyone] with one."
When it was said, “A lotus pond has been sent previously for the purpose of fetching [the flowers],” he replied, “If, O King, you cannot do this, tell them:
‘How will the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka send a lotus pond? Having said this, he sent [the message].
They did exactly as instructed. When the king heard that the wise man had understood the situation, he was pleased.
Regarding the garden: on another day, they sent word, saying, "We wish to enjoy a pleasure excursion in a garden, but our old garden has become dilapidated and fallen into ruin.
Let the inhabitants of the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka send us a new garden covered with trees in full bloom.
The villagers informed the wise man. The wise man thought, "By means of this very same skill in answering questions..."
Having comforted them with the words, "It must be so," he dispatched men and had the matter discussed in the same manner as before.
Again, the king was pleased and asked Senaka, "Senaka, shall we bring the wise man?
Out of stinginess regarding gain, he said, "Your Majesty, one does not become 'wise' by such means; please wait. Having heard those words of his, the king—
He thought, “The wise Mahosadha has captured my mind with his seven riddles concerning children;
even in such secret questions and answers, as well as in his quick-witted responses, his exposition is like that of the Buddha. Senaka does not allow such a wise man to be brought here.
What use have I for Senaka? I shall bring him myself. With a great retinue, he set out for that village.
As he was riding away on that auspicious horse, one of the horse’s hooves struck a crack in the ground and broke.
The king turned back from that very spot and entered the city.
Then Senaka approached him and asked, “Great King, did you go to the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka to bring the wise man? “Yes, the wise man,” he replied.

“Great King, you look upon me as one who desires your harm; for although I said, ‘Wait a moment,’ you departed in great haste, and by that very first journey, the foot of the auspicious horse was broken.
Having heard his words, he remained silent; then on another day, he consulted with him again: “What do you think, Senaka?”
“Let us bring the wise man. “Your Majesty, do not go yourself; send a messenger with this message:
‘Wise man, as we were coming to you, the horse’s hoof was broken. Send us either another horse or one even better.
If he sends another horse, he will come himself. If he sends one that is better, he will send his father—this is one way.”
“There will be no question. The king, having accepted with “Very well,” did so and dispatched a messenger.
Upon hearing the messenger’s words, the wise man thought, “The king wishes to see both me and my father.
He went to his father’s presence, paid homage, and said, “Father, the king wishes to see both you and me; you should go first, surrounded by a thousand merchants.”
"Go; and as you go, do not return with empty hands, but go taking a sandalwood box filled with fresh ghee.
When the king has exchanged greetings with you and says, 'Householder, sit down after choosing a suitable seat,' then you should choose such a seat and sit down. While you are sitting..."
"I shall come; the king will exchange greetings with me and say, 'O wise one, sit having discerned a seat suitable for you.
Then I shall look toward you, and at that sign, you should rise from your seats and say, 'Dear Mahosadha, please sit on this seat. Today, our single question will reach its conclusion."

“He will arrive,” he said. Having accepted this with the words, “Very well,” he went by the same route as previously described and, having announced his presence at the king’s gate, entered when told, “Please enter. After entering and paying homage to the king, he stood to one side.
The king exchanged greetings with him and asked, “Householder, where is your son, the wise Mahosadha?”

He asked, "Is he coming from behind, Your Majesty? Having heard that he was coming from behind, the king was delighted in heart and said, "Great merchant, knowing your appropriate seat, please sit down.
Knowing his own appropriate seat, he sat down to one side. The Great Being also, adorned and prepared, surrounded by a thousand boys, [mounted] a decorated chariot...
Having sat down and entering the city, he saw a donkey walking along the edge of the moat and dispatched a youth endowed with strength,
saying: "My good man, follow this donkey and, so that it does not make a sound,
bind its mouth, wrap it in a palm-leaf mat, cover it with a single blanket, and carry it on your shoulder."
“Come! They did so. The Bodhisatta also entered the city with a great retinue.
The great multitude said, “This, they say, is the son of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, named the wise Mahosadha;
it is said that when he was born, he was born holding a medicinal jar in his hand, and by him, indeed, the answers to so many riddles have been provided.”
Even as he gazed upon the Great Being, praising him, saying, "He is well-known," he could not reach satiety. He went to the palace gate and announced his arrival.
Upon hearing this, the king was delighted and joyful, and said, "Let my son, the wise Mahosadha, come quickly.
Surrounded by a thousand boys, he ascended the palace, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side.
As soon as the king saw him, he was filled with joy and, having offered a sweet welcome, said, "Wise man, please sit down after finding a suitable seat. Then he looked toward his father.
At the sign of that look, his father also rose and said, "Wise man, sit on this seat. He sat down on that seat.
Seeing him seated there, Senaka, Pukkusa, Kāmindadevinda, and other foolish blind men clapped their hands and laughed a great laugh,
saying, "They called this blind fool a 'wise man,' yet he makes his father rise from his seat and sits down himself; it is not fitting to call him a 'wise man,'" and thus they mocked him.
The king also became dejected and displeased. Then the Great Being asked him, "Why, Great King, are you dejected? "Yes, wise one, I am dejected;
while your voice was pleasing to hear, your sight has become unpleasant.
"For what reason, Great King? "Because you have caused your father to rise from his seat and sit down yourself. "But why is that, Great King?"
“Great King, do you think that in all matters the father is superior to his sons? “Yes, wise one,” he replied.
Then the Great Being said, “Great King, did you not send us this message: ‘Send either a better horse or a more excellent man’?
Having said this, he rose from his seat, looked at those young men, and [said], “That which was taken by you...”
Having ordered, "Bring a donkey," and having had it lie down at the king's feet, he asked, "Great King, what is this donkey worth?
"Wise man, if it were useful, it would be worth eight kahāpaṇas.
"What is a mule worth—one born from such a [donkey] and raised in the womb of a noble thoroughbred mare? "It is priceless, wise man."
“Your Majesty, why do you speak thus? Have you not just now said, ‘In all matters, fathers are indeed superior to their sons’?
If that is true, then according to your own doctrine, even a donkey would be superior to a mule.
But how is it, Great King, that your wise men, unable to understand even this much, clap their hands and laugh?”
"Ah, the perfection of wisdom of you wise men! From where have you obtained these?
Having thus ridiculed the four wise men, he addressed the king with this verse from the Ekakanipāta:
"If you, O best of kings, truly think that 'the father is better than the son'..."
“O best of kings, if you think that in all respects the father is superior to the son, then let this donkey be superior even to your mule. Why? Because the father of a mule is indeed a donkey.
Having said this, the Great Being spoke further: “Great King, if the father is indeed superior to the son, [then consider] my father...”
“Take me! If a son is better than his father, take me for your own benefit. The king was filled with joy.
The entire royal assembly, shouting, “Well-spoken is the question by the wise man!
gave thousands of shouts of approval; they snapped their fingers and waved their cloths. The four wise men, however, remained with downcast faces, brooding in silence.
[They] were. Surely there is no one equal to a Bodhisatta who knows the virtue of his parents;
why then did he act in this way? It was not for the sake of insulting his father, but because the King had sent [the message], saying, "Send either a mule or a superior horse.
Therefore, it was for the purpose of clarifying that very question and for the purpose of making known his own wisdom.
And he acted thus for the purpose of rendering the four wise men speechless.
The Donkey Question is finished.
The nineteenth question.

The King, being pleased, took a golden water-vessel filled with scented water and, pouring the water into the merchant’s hand, said, "Let the village of Pācīnayavamajjhaka be enjoyed by you as a royal grant.

He further declared, "Let all the other merchants become his attendants," and sent all manner of ornaments for the Bodhisatta’s mother. Having gained confidence through the question regarding the donkey, he [honored] the Bodhisatta.
Having made Mahosadha his son, he said to the merchant, “Householder, give me Mahosadha the wise man as my son.
“Your Majesty, this boy is still very young; even today the scent of milk wafts from his mouth.
He will be with you when he has grown up. “Householder, from now on, you must have no further concern for him.”
“From this day forward, this is my son; I shall be able to support my son. Go now,” he said, and sent him forth.
He paid homage to the king, embraced the wise man, laid his head upon the man’s breast, and kissed him on the crown.
Then he gave him this exhortation: “Dear son, be diligent. And he too, having paid homage to his father, said: “Father, do not worry.”
