Having comforted his father, he sent him away. The king asked the wise man, "Dear son, will you take your meals inside the palace or outside?

Thinking, "I have a large retinue; therefore, it is fitting for me to be one who takes his meals outside," he said, "I shall take my meals outside, Your Majesty. Then the king had a suitable residence built for him.
Having provided a travel allowance starting with a thousand boys, he gave them all the necessary provisions for their journey. From that time on, he attended upon the king.

The king, however, desired to test him. At that time, not far from the southern gate of the city, there was a jewel-gem inside a crow’s nest in a palmyra tree on the bank of a lotus pond; its reflection appeared in the pond.
The people informed the king, "There is a jewel in the lotus pond. He summoned Senaka and asked, "It is said that a precious jewel is visible in the lotus pond;

how shall we have it taken? When Senaka replied, "Your Majesty, it is proper to take it after having the water drained," the king said, "In that case, teacher, do so," and placed the responsibility upon him alone.
Thus, having caused many people to assemble and have the water and mud removed, he even broke the ground but did not see the gem.
Again, the reflection of the gem appeared in the full lotus pond. He did it once more in that same way, yet still did not see it.
Then the king addressed the wise man, saying, "Dear son, a single gem appears in the lotus pond."
Senaka had the water and mud removed and even broke the ground, yet he did not see it; it appeared once again in the Puṇṇā lotus pond.
[The king] asked, "Will you be able to have that jewel recovered? He replied, "This is no great matter, Great King;
come, I shall show it to you. The king, pleased by his words, thought, "Today I shall see the power of the wise man’s knowledge."
Surrounded by a great multitude, he went to the bank of the lotus pond.
Standing on the bank and looking at the gem, the Great Being realized, "This gem is not in the pond; there must be a gem in the crow's nest in the palm tree.
Having understood this, he said, "Your Majesty, there is no gem in the pond," and continued, "Is it not in the water?"
When he said, "It is visible," [the king] replied, "In that case, bring a water-bowl.

Having had a water-bowl brought, he said, "See, Your Majesty, this gem is not visible only in the lotus pond; it is visible in the bowl as well. When [the king] asked, "Wise man, where then must the gem be?
he replied, "Your Majesty, its reflection is indeed present both in the lotus pond and in the bowl."
"It is seen, but it is not the jewel; however, the jewel is in a crow's nest in the palmyra tree.
Order a man to go and fetch it," he said. The king did so and had the jewel brought. Once it was brought, he gave it to the wise man.
The wise man took it and placed it in the king's hand. Seeing this, the great multitude gave a cry of "Well done! to the wise man and [rebuked] Senaka.
Mocking him, he offered praise to the Great Being, saying: "The jewel-treasure is in the crow’s nest in the palmyra tree;
Senaka’s son caused many people to destroy the lotus pond itself; one must indeed be wise like Mahosadha!
The king, being pleased with him as well, gave him the pearl necklace from his own neck, as well as for the thousand boys.
He caused pearl necklaces to be given. He authorized the attendance upon the Bodhisatta and his retinue with this provision.
The nineteenth question is finished.
The Kakaṇṭaka Question.
On another day, the king went to the pleasure garden together with the wise man. At that time, a certain crane was perched atop a gateway arch.
Seeing the king approaching, it descended and lay down upon the ground.
The king, observing its behavior, asked, "Wise man, what is this crane doing? The Great Being replied, "Your Majesty, you..."
“He serves him,” he said. “If he serves us in this way, let it not be in vain for him;
have wealth given to him. “Your Majesty, he has no need for wealth; a mere amount of food will suffice for him.
“But what does he eat? “Meat, Your Majesty. “How much is required to obtain it? “An amount worth only a kākaṇika coin, Your Majesty. The king—
He gave orders to a certain man: "Rājadāya is not to receive even a single kākaṇika; from now on, bring him meat worth half a māsaka every day and give it to him.
Having agreed, saying "Very well," the man did so from that time forward.
One day, during the Uposatha, when the slaughter had ceased and he could not obtain meat, he pierced that very half-māsaka coin with a thread.
Having fastened it around his neck, he wore it. Then, on account of that, pride arose within him.
On that very same day, the king went to the pleasure garden again together with Mahosadha.

Seeing the king approaching, and because of the pride that had arisen on account of the wealth [he possessed], he said to the king: "Vedeḥa, are you the one of great wealth, or am I? Together with the king...
Making himself level, he lay down without descending, shaking his head right there on top of the gateway.
The king, observing this behavior of his, asked, "O wise one, today you do not descend as you did before; what is the reason for this?
and spoke this verse:
“This kakaṇṭaka bird does not raise its head at the top of the gateway as it did before;
O Mahosadha, find out why the kakaṇṭaka has become stiff.

In this context, “does not raise its head” means that whereas previously it would not descend but would remain right at the top of the gateway shaking its head, it no longer raises its head in that manner. “Why has it become stiff? means: for what reason has it fallen into a state of rigidity?

The wise man, having heard his words and understanding that "Great King, the royal officer who could not obtain meat on the Uposatha day must have become conceited because of that half-māsaka tied to his neck," spoke this verse:
"Having obtained a half-māsaka, a kakaṇṭaka bird— something never obtained before—
Becomes overweening toward the King of Videha, the capturer of Mithilā."
The king, having heard his words, summoned that man and questioned him. He reported the matter to the king exactly as it had happened.
Upon hearing this account, the king was greatly impressed, thinking, "Without having asked anyone else, this wise man has understood the intention of Kakaṇṭaka just like an omniscient Buddha.
Having gained great confidence, he ordered that a toll be levied at the four gates for the sake of the wise man. As for Kakaṇṭaka—
But having become angry, he began to neglect his duties. The wise man, however, stopped him, saying, "Do not neglect them, O Great King.
The Question of Kakaṇṭaka is finished.
The Question of Sirikāḷakaṇṇī.

Now, a certain young brahmin named Piṅguttara, a resident of Mithilā, went to Takkasilā and, while studying a craft under a world-renowned teacher, learned it very quickly. Having completed his studies, he asked the teacher, "I wish to depart.
In that family, however, there was a custom: "If a daughter has reached marriageable age, she must be given to the senior pupil."
It was as if it were his duty; therefore, that teacher had an only daughter who had reached marriageable age, and she was beautiful, resembling a celestial nymph.
Then the teacher said to him, "Dear son, I shall give you my daughter; you may take her and go.
However, that young man was unfortunate and ill-omened, whereas the maiden possessed great merit. Upon seeing her, his mind did not feel any attraction toward her.
Thus, even though she reported this, he accepted it, thinking, "I shall not break my teacher's word. The teacher gave his daughter to him.

At night, while he was lying on a bed adorned with splendor, as soon as she came and stepped onto the bed, he—trembling with fear, shame, and disgust, and shaking—descended and lay down upon the floor. She too descended.
Having gone into his presence, she lay down; he rose and ascended the bed. She also ascended the bed again;
he, descending from the bed once more, lay down upon the ground. One named Kāḷakaṇṇī does not harmonize with prosperity.
The young woman lay down on the very bed, while he slept on the ground.
Having thus spent seven days, he took her with him, paid homage to his teacher, and departed; on the way, there was not even a word of conversation between them.
Without wishing for anything else, they both arrived at Mithilā.
Then Piṅguttara, seeing a fig tree laden with fruit not far from the city, being oppressed by hunger, climbed it and ate the fruits. She too, her heart tormented by hunger, [did the same].
Having gone to the foot of the tree, she said, "Master, please let some fruits fall for me too. He replied, "Do you have no hands and feet?
Climb up yourself and eat them! She climbed up and ate.
Knowing that she had climbed up, he quickly descended, surrounded the tree with thorns, and saying, "I am rid of this ill-omened woman," he fled. She too—
Unable to descend, she sat right there. Then the king, having sported in the park and seated upon the back of his elephant, saw her as he was entering the city in the evening;
his heart becoming bound with passion, he had it asked of her: "Are you married, or are you unmarried? She replied:
"I have a husband, my lord, given to me by my family; however, he has left me sitting here..."
“Having abandoned [him], she has fled,” he said. The minister reported that matter to the king.

The king, thinking, “Property without an owner belongs to the king,” had her brought down, mounted her upon the back of an elephant, led her to his residence, consecrated her, and established her in the position of chief queen.
She became dear and pleasing to him. Because she was found under an udumbara tree, they gave her the name “Udumbaradevī.”
Now one day, when the residents of the gate-village had the road prepared for the king’s excursion to the park, Piṅguttara, working for wages, bound his loincloth and hacked at the road with a spade.
Before the road was finished, the king set out, seated in a chariot together with Queen Udumbarā. Queen Udumbarā [saw] Piṅguttara hacking at the road, a person of ill omen.
Seeing him, she thought, "This ill-omened man was unable to maintain such glory," and looking at him, she laughed.
When the king saw her laughing, he became angry and asked, "Why did you laugh? She replied, "Your Majesty, this woodcutter on the road was my former husband;
he took me up a fig tree, surrounded it with thorns, and then departed."
Having looked at her, she thought, "This ill-omened woman was unable to maintain such splendor," and so she laughed.
The king said, "You are speaking a lie; you must have seen some other man and laughed.
I shall kill you! and he seized his sword. Terrified, she said, "Your Majesty, first ask the wise ones."
The king asked Senaka, "Senaka, do you believe these words? "I do not believe them, Your Majesty;
for who indeed would go away after abandoning such a jewel of a woman? When she heard his words, she became even more terrified.
Then the king, thinking, "What does Senaka know? I shall ask the wise man," spoke this verse while questioning him:
“A woman may be beautiful and she may also be virtuous;
yet a man might not desire her—believe me, Mahosadha.
In this context, “virtuous” means endowed with the qualities of proper conduct.
Having heard that, the wise man spoke this verse:
“I believe you, O Great King; a man may be unfortunate, but Fortune and the Black-Eyed One (Misfortune) never coexist.”
In this context, "they do not meet" means they do not come together, like the near shore and the far shore of the ocean, or like the surface of the sky and the surface of the earth.
When the king heard that reason from his words, he did not become angry with her; his heart was extinguished [of anger]. Being pleased with him, he said:
"If you had not been wise, today I would have [given] such a jewel of a woman to the foolish Senaka."
“I was lowly, yet by relying on him, I have obtained this,” she said, and she performed an offering worth a hundred thousand pieces.
The queen also paid homage to the king and said, “Your Majesty, it is by relying on the wise man that I have regained my life;
I ask for a boon: that he be appointed to the position of my younger brother. “Very well, Queen, take it; I grant you the boon. “Your Majesty, today—”
“From this day forth, I shall not eat any sweet flavor without my younger sister.
From now on, I take the boon that you may grant me permission to have sweet flavors sent to him by opening the gate at any time, whether it be the proper hour or not.
“Very well, Bhaddā; take this boon as well,” he said.
The Question of Sirikāḷakaṇṇī is finished.
On another day, King Meṇḍaka, having eaten his morning meal, was walking back and forth along the long corridor of the palace when, through the lattice window—
Looking about, he saw a goat and a dog engaged in a friendly intimacy.
It seems that the goat had gone to the elephant stable and eaten some untouched grass left before the elephant. Then the elephant-keepers beat it and drove it out.
It bleated and fled; then a man came running after it with speed and struck it on the back with a staff.
He struck him across the chest. Bending his back and overcome by pain, he went and lay down on his back against the great wall of the royal palace.

On that very day, a dog—who had grown fat from eating bones, skin, and other scraps in the king’s kitchen—stood outside while the cook was preparing the meal, watching as the cook wiped the sweat from his body.
Having smelled the scent of fish and meat, being unable to endure his craving, he entered the kitchen, knocked down the lid of a vessel, and ate the meat.
Then the cook, hearing the sound of the vessel, entered, saw him, closed the door, and beat him with clods, sticks, and other objects.
He spat out the meat he had eaten right from his mouth and cried out.
He departed. The cook, having realized that he had left, followed him and struck him across the back with a stick.
Overcome by pain, he bent his back, lifted one foot, and entered the very place where the goat was lying.
Then the goat said to him, "Friend, why do you come here with your back bent? Is it a wind that pierces you?"
He asked. The dog also asked, "You too have been lying with your back bent; is it a wind that pierces you?
They each related their own condition to one another.
Then the goat asked him, "But my dear, will you be able to go back to the food-house again?"
“I will not be able to, my friend; once I have gone, there is no life left for me. “But will you be able to go back to the elephant stable?
“I too will not be able to go there; once I have gone, there is no life left for me.
They thought, “How indeed shall we live now? and they considered a means. Then the goat said to him:
“If we are able to live in harmony, there is a certain way,” he said. “Then tell me,” the other replied.

“Friend, from now on you should go to the elephant stable; since they will not suspect you of eating grass, saying ‘This one does not eat grass,’ you should bring me my fodder. I, too, shall enter the kitchen.”
“The cook will not suspect me of being a meat-eater, and I shall bring you meat,” he said.
They both accepted this, thinking, “It is a clever plan. The dog went to the elephant stable, bit a bundle of grass, and returning, placed it on top of a high wall.
The other also went to the kitchen and [took] a piece of meat.
Having filled his mouth with meat, he brought it back and placed it right there. The dog ate the meat; the goat ate the grass.
By this means, they lived together in harmony and mutual affection upon the great back wall. When the king saw their friendship, he thought:
"Ah, I have seen a cause never seen before! Though these two were once enemies, they now live in harmony."
“They dwell there. Taking this as my reason, I shall pose a question and ask the five wise men;
if they do not know this question, I will banish them from the kingdom, but if they do know it, I will pay great honor to them, saying, ‘There is no other wise man like him.
Today is not yet the right time; I will ask when they come for their audience tomorrow. On the following day, he—
When the wise men had arrived and were seated, he asked a question, reciting this verse:
“Those who have never before shared even a seven-step friendship in this world—
two born as enemies yet acting as companions— on what account do they move together?”
In that context, "having made a resolution" means having gained faith and having applied oneself.
Having said this, he further spoke thus:
"If you are unable to state a question at the time of my morning meal today, then this [shall be so]."
“I shall banish you all from the kingdom, for I have no need for those of such foolish nature.
At that time, however, Senaka was seated in the seat of honor, while the wise man sat on the outskirts.
As he reflected upon that question, failing to see its meaning, he thought: “This king is of dull temperament; having considered this question—”
"I am unable to compose anything at all; he must have seen something. If I get the opportunity one day, I shall produce this answer.
By some means or other, let Senaka allow him to wait for just this one day.
The other four wise men, too, saw nothing at all, like those who have entered a chamber of darkness. Senaka—
“What, indeed, is Mahosadha’s intention? he thought, and looked toward the Bodhisatta. He too looked back at him.
By the very manner of the Bodhisatta’s look, Senaka understood his purpose; thinking, “It does not occur even to a wise man [to come alone];
therefore, he desires an opportunity for one day, and I shall fulfill his wish,” he spoke with confidence to the king.
Breaking into a great laugh, he said, "What, Great King? Will you banish us all from the kingdom because we are unable to answer this question?
You consider even this to be 'a knotty problem,' yet it is not that we are incapable of answering it;
rather, please wait a little longer. This is indeed a knotty problem; we cannot discuss it in the midst of a great crowd."
“Having reflected upon it in private, we shall tell you later; grant us the opportunity,” they said, and looking at the Great Being, they spoke these two verses:
“In this terrible assembly of the great multitude, when a clamor of people has arisen;”
"With distracted minds and many thoughts, we are not able to state this question.
But each one of us, with a one-pointed mind, having gone into seclusion and reflected upon the matter,
and having contemplated it in solitude, O Lord of Men, those wise ones will then speak on this matter."
In that context, "having reflected" means: "These wise ones, established in physical and mental seclusion, will reflect upon this question and then explain its meaning to you.
Although the king was displeased upon hearing his words, he threatened him, saying, "Speak after having reflected well;
otherwise, I shall have you banished. The four wise men descended from the palace. Senaka said to the others:
—“Good sir, the king has asked a subtle question; if it remains unanswered, there will be great danger.
Eat wholesome food and consider it well,” he said. They each went to their own homes.
The wise man also arose, went to Queen Udumbarā, and asked, “Queen, where did the king stand for so long today or yesterday? “Dear son, [he stood] at the mango grove.”
“Or perhaps he is walking back and forth, looking through the window at the distant horizon. Then the wise man thought, “The king must have seen something from this vantage point.
He went there and, looking outside, saw the behavior of the goats and dogs;
having reached the conclusion, “Having seen these, the king formulated this riddle,” he returned home. The others did likewise.
Having reflected on this and seeing no solution, they went into the presence of Senaka. He asked them, "Have you seen the riddle? "We have not seen it, Master.

"If that is so, and the king causes you to be banished, what will you do? "But have you seen it? "I too do not see it. "If you yourselves do not see it, how can we see it? [What will we do] for the king..."
"But we came here thinking, 'Having reflected, we shall speak,' and having let out a lion's roar;
if we do not speak, the King will be angry with us. What shall we do? This question cannot be solved by us;
however, it must have been reflected upon by the wise man, having considered it a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold. Come, let us go to him."
Those four wise men, having been informed that the Bodhisatta had arrived at the door of his house, said, "Let the wise men enter," and upon being told this, they entered the house.
After exchanging greetings, they stood to one side and asked the Great Being, "But what is the problem you have contemplated, O wise man?
"Yes, it has been contemplated; if I do not contemplate it, who else will?"
"In that case, wise one, please tell it to us as well.
The wise man thought, "If I do not tell them, the king will banish them from the kingdom, but he will honor me with the seven treasures.
Let these blind fools not perish; I shall tell them. Having thought this, he [spoke] to them.

Having had all four sit on low seats and join their palms in reverence, and having instructed them not to reveal that they had been seen by the king, he composed four verses for each of them, saying, "When the king questions you, speak thus. Having made them master the text itself, he dismissed them.
On the following day, they went to attend upon the king and sat down on the prepared seats. The king [addressed] Senaka...
He asked, "Senaka, do you know the answer to this question? "Your Majesty, if I do not know it, who else could know it? "Then speak it.
"Listen, O King," he said, and recited a verse according to the method he had mastered:
"The flesh of the ram is dear and pleasing to the sons of nobles and the daughters of kings."
“They do not give meat to the dog; rather, the ram has friendship with the dog.
Even after speaking this verse, Senaka did not understand the meaning. However, the king understood it because he had seen it for himself.
Therefore, he asked Pukkusa, "Was it first known by Senaka? He replied to him, "Why should I be unwise?
and, following the very method he had learned, recited this verse:
"They beat the skin of a sheep for the sake of comfort as a saddle-cloth on a horse's back."
“They do not spread [the skin] for the dog, but rather there is friendship between the ram and the dog.
The meaning of this too was not yet clear. However, because it was familiar to him, the King thought, “This Pukkusa also knows it,” and he questioned Kāminda.
He too, according to the method he had learned, recited the verse: “The ram has curved horns, and the dog has no horns;”
“One who eats grass and one who eats meat—how then can there be friendship between a ram and a dog?
The king, thinking, “He too knows this,” questioned the Lord of Devas.
He, following the very method he had learned, spoke this verse: “The ram eats grass and eats foliage, but the dog eats neither grass nor foliage.”
“A dog might seize a hare, and then a cat [might seize] the dog; then there would be friendship between the ram and the dog.
Therein, *tiṇamāsi palāsamāsi* means one who eats grass as well as one who eats leaves. *No palāsaṃ* means he does not even eat leaves.
Then the king asked the wise man: “Dear son, do you also know this puzzle? “Great King, from the Avīci hell...”
“Who else but me, up to the peak of existence, could know this? “In that case, tell us,” [the king said].
“Listen, Great King,” he replied, and declaring the familiarity he had with that question, he spoke these two verses:
“The ram, with four and a half feet, eight hooves, and invisible—”
“This one brings rice for this person; this one brings meat for that one.

Thus, it is said, the Lord of Men, the preeminent ruler of Videha, having ascended to the excellent palace, witnessed with his own eyes the exchange of various foods between those who were hungry and those whose mouths were full.
In this context, "eight-and-a-half-footed" refers to a sheep, considering its four legs, due to skill in phrasing (*byañjanakusalatā*).
"Meṇḍa" means a sheep. "Eight hooves" is said with reference to the two hooves on each leg.
"Invisible" means not being perceived at the time the meat is being removed. "Chādi" means a roof; that is, grass. "This belongs to him" means...
"Of the dog and the goat": *vītihāraṃ* means "the act of exchanging. "Of those whose food is mutual": this refers to those for whom food is shared reciprocally.
For the ram brings food to the dog, and he (the dog) exchanges it with him; the dog also brings [food] to him, and the other (the ram) exchanges it.
"He saw" means that he witnessed with his own eyes that exchange of their mutual food.
Having made it his own direct experience, he saw it. "Bubhukka" refers to the dog that makes the sound "bhubhū. "Puṇṇamukha" refers to the ram.
"The king himself witnessed this intimacy between these friends.

Not knowing that the others had come to know [the truth] by relying on the Bodhisatta, the king imagined, "The five wise men knew it each through the power of their own wisdom," and being filled with joy, he spoke this verse:
“Truly, it is a gain for me, a manifold gain, that in this world there are wise ones in my family who, through well-spoken words,
penetrate the profound and subtle meaning of the question— those steadfast ones. In this context,
“they penetrate” means that having understood [the meaning] by means of well-spoken words, they explain it.
Then, thinking, "One who is pleased must show an appearance of being pleased," he performed that gesture and spoke this verse:
"A single chariot drawn by mules, and a single prosperous, excellent village—
these I give to all of you wise ones, for my mind is supremely delighted by your well-spoken words."
Having said this, he caused all of that to be given to them.
The Meṇḍaka Question in the Dvādasanipāta is finished.
The Sirimanta Question.
But Udumbaradevī, having learned from the others that the question had been understood by the wise man, thought:
"The King has treated all five with equal honor, as if making no distinction between a bean and a māsa coin; surely it is right for him to show special honor to my younger brother.
Having reflected thus, she went into the presence of the King and asked: "Your Majesty, by whom..."
“Has your question been answered? “By the five wise men, my lady. “Your Majesty, upon whom did those four people rely to know that question?
“I do not know, my lady. “Great King, what do they know?
However, the wise man thought, ‘Let these fools not perish,’ and had them learn the question; you, however, gave equal honor to all of them.”
“Do not do so; it is improper. It is fitting for a wise man to make himself distinguished.
The king, pleased with the wise man because he had not mentioned his own identity, and desiring to show him even greater honor, thought:
“Let it be; I shall ask my son a question, and when he has answered, I will bestow great honor upon him.”
Thus, while reflecting on a riddle, he thought of the *Sirimanta* riddle. One day, having come into the presence of the five wise men, when they were seated comfortably, he said to Senaka:
"Senaka, I shall ask you a riddle. "Ask, O King," he replied.
The king then spoke the first verse of the *Sirimanta* riddle:
“One endowed with wisdom but devoid of glory, or one who is famous but lacks wisdom—I ask you this, Senaka: which of these two is better? So say those who are skilled.
In this context, “which of these two is better? means: which among these two do the wise declare to be superior?
And this question, it is said, was inherited from Senaka’s lineage; therefore, he answered it immediately:

“O Lord of Men, both the wise and the foolish, those possessed of craft and those without craft, even those of noble birth and those of low birth—when they are renowned, they become the servants of others.”
"Having seen this as well, I say: one who is wise but of low status is indeed better than one who is merely illustrious.
Therein, "one who is wise but of low status" means a wise person who is humble; the sense is that even a lord is superior [only by virtue of his position].
Having heard his words, the king, without questioning the other three, spoke to the wise Mahosadha, who was seated there as the youngest member of the Saṅgha:
“I ask you too, O one of matchless wisdom, Mahosadha, seer of the entire Dhamma:
between a foolish man of great renown and a wise man of little wealth, which of these do those skilled in the Dhamma declare to be better?
In this context, “seer of the entire Dhamma” means one who sees all phenomena.
Then the Great Being said, "Listen, O Great King," and spoke:
"The fool commits evil deeds, imagining that 'this world alone is better';
seeing only this world and not the world beyond, the fool has grasped at misfortune in both places."
"Having seen this as well, I say: wisdom alone is better, not the fool who possesses fame.
In this context, "thinking 'this world alone is better'" means he considers worldly sovereignty alone to be the best for himself.
"He took the side of strife" means that the fool, having committed evil deeds out of pride in his power, is reborn in hell and other such realms; and furthermore, from there in the next world...
"Having come from elsewhere and being reborn into a lowly family, one encounters a state of suffering; thus, one meets with defeat in both worlds.
Seeing this reason as well, I say that only he who is endowed with wisdom is supreme, whereas the lord, being foolish, is not supreme.
When this was said, the king looked at Senaka and asked, "Does Mahosadha not say that only the wise man is supreme?"
Senaka said: "Great King, Mahosadha is but a youth; even now the scent of milk still issues from his mouth.
What does he know? Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
"He who bestows wealth upon one who is not his son, nor his kinsman, nor one of handsome form—this is a marvel."
“The ox Pasela-muga, thriving in happiness, is indeed attended by prosperity like a lotus-pond;
seeing this too, I say that one who is wise but lacking in wealth is better than one who possesses prosperity.
In this context, *eḷamūga* means one whose mouth drips saliva. *Goravinda* refers to a certain man in that very city who possessed a fortune of eight hundred million.
The merchant was deformed. He had neither son nor daughter, and he knew no craft whatsoever.

Even as he spoke, streams of saliva flowed from both sides of his jaw. Two women, like celestial nymphs, adorned with every ornament and holding full-blown blue lotuses, stood on either side of him, catching that saliva with the blue lotuses.
Having accepted them, they threw the blue lotuses out through the window.
Even those intoxicated by liquor, when entering a tavern and having need of blue lotuses, would go to the door of his house and call out, "Master Gorinda, the merchant!
Hearing their voices, he would stand at the window and ask, "What is it, dear ones? and then a stream of saliva would flow from him.
Those women, having accepted them with blue lotuses, threw the blue lotuses into the middle of the street.
Drunken scoundrels took them, rinsed them with water, put them on as ornaments, and entered the tavern. Thus he was endowed with glory.
Having made this an illustration, Senaka spoke thus.
Having heard that, the king asked, "My son, what sort of man is the wise Mahosadha? The wise man replied, "Your Majesty, what does Senaka know?
He sees only fame—like a crow at the place where rice grains lie, or like a dog that has begun to drink curds but does not see the great club falling upon its head.
Listen, Your Majesty," and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“One of little wisdom becomes intoxicated when obtaining pleasure, and even when touched by pain, he falls into delusion.
When touched by adventitious pleasure or pain, he quivers like a water-snake in the heat.
Having seen this as well, I declare: wisdom alone is better, not the fame of a fool.”
In this context, "happiness" refers to the happiness of sovereignty; having obtained it, the fool becomes negligent, and being negligent, he commits evil.
"By suffering" means by bodily and mental suffering. "External" means not internal; for the happiness and suffering of sentient beings are indeed adventitious, not something that persists constantly.
"In the heat" means like a fish pulled from the water and cast into the sun.
Having heard this, the king asked, "What kind of teacher is he? Senaka replied, "Your Majesty, what does he know?
Let alone human beings—even in the forest, many birds resort only to those trees that are rich in fruit. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Just as birds from all sides flock to a tree in the forest that has sweet fruit,"
"Thus, many people, for the sake of their own interest, resort even to one who is wealthy, possessing riches and enjoyments.
Having seen this as well, I say: it is better to be wise, even if lacking in fortune, than to be one who possesses glory but is deficient in wisdom.
In this context, "many people" (bahujjana) means the great multitude.
Having heard that, the king asked, "What kind of thing is it, dear? The wise man said, "What does this pot-bellied one know? Listen, Your Majesty," and spoke this verse:
"It is not good for a fool to be powerful, nor is it right for him to acquire wealth through violence;
they drag this witless man, as he cries out, into the terrible hell."
"Having seen this as well, I say: wisdom alone is better; a fool, however famous, is not.

In this context, "by violence" means that by means of violence, having committed a violent deed and oppressed people, one acquires wealth. Then the guardians of hell drag that dull-witted person, while he is still crying out, into hell with powerful agony.
Again, when the King asked, "What is it, Senaka?", Senaka spoke this verse:
“Whatever rivers flow into the Ganges, they all abandon their respective names and lineages;
yet when the Ganges enters the ocean, its distinctness is no longer perceived. Even so, wisdom is not seen to have such power in the world.
Having observed this, I say: one who possesses glory is better than one who is deficient in wisdom.”
In this context, "the rivers" refers to even small streams that, having become downward-flowing, flow into the Ganges.
"They abandon" means they come to be reckoned simply as the Ganges; they abandon their own names and lineages.
"It is no longer seen" means that when even that Ganges enters the ocean, it is no longer perceived; it receives the name "ocean" alone. In the same way, one of great wisdom—
Having reached the presence of the lord, he was neither seen nor perceived; he was like the Ganges river once it has entered the ocean.
Again the king asked, "What, wise man? He replied, "Listen, Great King," and spoke these two verses:
"Into this great ocean, which is called 'the water,' rivers flow incessantly throughout all time; yet it remains unreckonable."
“Thus the ocean, with its ever-mighty surge, never oversteps its shore.
Even so, though the foolish man’s desires are many, glory never oversteps wisdom.
Seeing this as well, I declare: wisdom alone is better than a man of renown who is a fool.”
In this context, "that which you declare" means that which you have declared or spoken. "The incalculable" (*asaṅkhya*) means beyond counting.

"It does not overstep its limit" means that even though it possesses great force and tosses up thousands of waves, it is unable to exceed its boundary; once it reaches the limit, all the waves necessarily break apart.
"Even so are the longings of a fool" means that even the words of a fool are exactly like this.
They are unable to surpass one possessed of wisdom; they break apart only upon reaching him. "He does not transcend wisdom" means that one called "glorious" does not overstep the wise person.

For no human being, when doubt has arisen regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful, goes to the feet of a foolish lord after bypassing the wise person for the sake of cutting through that doubt; rather, [he goes] to the wise person.
"A legal decision is indeed obtained right at the feet [of the king].
Having heard this, the king asked, "How so, Senaka? He replied, "Listen, Your Majesty," and spoke this verse:
"Even if one is unrestrained, if he speaks for the welfare of others while remaining steadfast and possessed of glory..."

"That very thing flourishes for him in the midst of kinsmen; for it is glory (*sirī*) that makes him so, not wisdom (*paññā*). Having seen this too, I say: one who possesses wisdom but is lacking in glory is indeed better than one who is merely glorious. In this context, "even if unrestrained" means even if he is a lord who is unrestrained in body and so forth, and is thus immoral (*dussīla*). "One who has attained endurance" (*sandhānagata*)— [The text continues: ...means one who has reached a state of stability. "He does not tremble" means he does not shake. "He does not fear" means he is not afraid. "He does not quake" means he does not become agitated. "He does not become terrified" means he does not fall into a state of panic. "He does not become despondent" means he does not sink into dejection. "He does not lose heart" means he does not become discouraged. "He does not shrink back" means he does not retreat. "He does not turn away" means he does not flee. "He does not run away" means he does not escape. "He does not seek safety elsewhere" means he does not look for refuge in another place. "He does not seek a protector elsewhere" means he does not look for a guardian in another person. "He does not seek a refuge elsewhere" means he does not look for a shelter in another place. "He does not seek a resort elsewhere" means he does not look for a support in another place. "He does not seek a dwelling elsewhere" means he does not look for a home in another place. "He does not seek a shelter elsewhere" means he does not look for a protection in another place. "He does not seek a retreat elsewhere" means he does not look for a withdrawal in another place. "He does not seek a hiding place elsewhere" means he does not look for a concealment in another place. "He does not seek a fortress elsewhere" means he does not look for a stronghold in another place. "He does not seek a rampart elsewhere" means he does not look for a defensive wall in another place. "He does not seek a moat elsewhere" means he does not look for a ditch in another place. "He does not seek a gate elsewhere" means he does not look for a portal in another place. "He does not seek a watchtower elsewhere" means he does not look for a lookout in another place. "He does not seek a bastion elsewhere" means he does not look for a tower in another place. "He does not seek a parapet elsewhere" means he does not look for a battlement in another place. "He does not seek a bridge elsewhere" means he does not look for a causeway in another place. "He does not seek a ford elsewhere" means he does not look for a crossing in another place. "He does not seek a path elsewhere" means he does not look for a way in another place. "He does not seek a track elsewhere" means he does not look for a trail in another place. "He does not seek a road elsewhere" means he does not look for a highway in another place. "He does not seek a route elsewhere" means he does not look for a path in another place. "He does not seek a journey elsewhere" means he does not look for a travel-path in another place. "He does not seek a destination elsewhere" means he does not look for a goal in another place. "He does not seek a destination point elsewhere" means he does not look for a terminus in another place. "He does not seek a destination limit elsewhere" means he does not look for a boundary in another place. "He does not seek a destination end elsewhere" means he does not look for a finality in another place. "He does not seek a destination conclusion elsewhere" means he does not look for a completion in another place. "He does not seek a destination fulfillment elsewhere" means he does not look for a perfection in another place. "He does not seek a destination attainment elsewhere" means he does not look for a realization in another place. "He does not seek a destination achievement elsewhere" means he does not look for an accomplishment in another place. "He does not seek a destination success elsewhere" means he does not look for a triumph in another place. "He does not seek a destination victory elsewhere" means he does not look for a conquest in another place. "He does not seek a destination triumph elsewhere" means he does not look for a glory in another place. "He does not seek a destination glory elsewhere" means he does not look for a splendor in another place. "He does not seek a destination majesty elsewhere" means he does not look for a grandeur in another place. "He does not seek a destination power elsewhere" means he does not look for a might in another place. "He does not seek a destination strength elsewhere" means he does not look for a force in another place. "He does not seek a destination vigor elsewhere" means he does not look for an energy in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality elsewhere" means he does not look for a life-force in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-sustenance elsewhere" means he does not look for a nourishment in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-support elsewhere" means he does not look for a prop in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-basis elsewhere" means he does not look for a foundation in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-root elsewhere" means he does not look for a source in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-essence elsewhere" means he does not look for a core in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-nature elsewhere" means he does not look for an inherent quality in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-character elsewhere" means he does not look for a trait in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-mark elsewhere" means he does not look for a sign in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-indication elsewhere" means he does not look for a symbol in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-representation elsewhere" means he does not look for a manifestation in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-expression elsewhere" means he does not look for a display in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-manifestation elsewhere" means he does not look for an appearance in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-revelation elsewhere" means he does not look for a disclosure in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-unveiling elsewhere" means he does not look for an exposure in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-disclosure elsewhere" means he does not look for a manifestation in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-explication elsewhere" means he does not look for an explanation in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-elucidation elsewhere" means he does not look for a clarification in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-illumination elsewhere" means he does not look for a light in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-radiance elsewhere" means he does not look for a glow in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-luster elsewhere" means he does not look for a brilliance in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-splendor elsewhere" means he does not look for a radiance in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-glory elsewhere" means he does not look for a majesty in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-fame elsewhere" means he does not look for a renown in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-praise elsewhere" means he does not look for a commendation in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-celebrity elsewhere" means he does not look for a notoriety in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-distinction elsewhere" means he does not look for a distinction in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-excellence elsewhere" means he does not look for a superiority in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-preeminence elsewhere" means he does not look for a pre-eminence in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-supremacy elsewhere" means he does not look for a supremacy in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-sovereignty elsewhere" means he does not look for a sovereignty in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-autonomy elsewhere" means he does not look for a self-rule in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-independence elsewhere" means he does not look for a freedom in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-mastery elsewhere" means he does not look for a mastery in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-possession elsewhere" means he does not look for a possession in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-determination elsewhere" means he does not look for a determination in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-direction elsewhere" means he does not look for a direction in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-guidance elsewhere" means he does not look for a guidance in another place. "He does not seek a destination vitality-self-leadership elsewhere" means he does not look for a leadership in another place
Standing in a court of law, one speaks for the sake of others;
yet, having uttered a falsehood in that assembly while surrounded by a great retinue, even though one makes the owner ownerless, that word of theirs prevails.
For it is *siri* (fortune) that causes this to happen, not wisdom (*paññā*). Therefore, I say that one with wisdom is inferior, and one possessed of fortune alone is superior.
When the king asked again, "What is it, dear? the wise man said, "Listen, Your Majesty, what does a foolish soldier know? and spoke this verse:
"Whether for the sake of another or even for himself, the fool of little wisdom speaks falsehoods;
he is censured in the midst of the assembly, and later he goes to a state of misery."
"Having seen this as well, I say: wisdom alone is better than a man of renown who is a fool.
Then Senaka spoke this verse:
"Even if one of vast wisdom speaks of wealth, he may be without property, lacking means, and poor."
"That does not take root for him in the midst of kinsmen, and glory does not belong to one possessed of wisdom.
Having seen this as well, I say: it is better to be wise even if lacking in glory.
In this context, "atthampi" means if one speaks even a reason. "Ñātimajjhe" means in the midst of an assembly. "Paññāṇavato" means of one possessing wisdom.
“Great King, when one approaches a person possessed of wisdom who has attained the pinnacle of glory, even the natural splendor one possesses ceases to exist.
For in his presence, one appears like a glowworm at the rising of the sun; thus he shows.
When the king asked again, “Of what sort is it, dear sir? the wise man said, “What does Senaka know? He looks only toward this world, not toward the world beyond,” and spoke this verse:
“Whether for the sake of another or even for himself, one of vast wisdom does not speak falsehood;
he is honored in the midst of the assembly, and in the end, he goes to a happy destination.
Seeing this as well, I declare: wisdom alone is better, not the fame of a fool.”
Then Senaka spoke this verse:
“Elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, earrings, and women born of wealthy families—
all these are enjoyments for a man of power who lacks such power himself.”
"Having seen this as well, I say: one who possesses wisdom is better than even a glorious man of low intelligence.
In this context, "of the powerful" means of the lord. "One without psychic power": not only those women, but indeed all beings lacking psychic power become objects of enjoyment for him.
Then the wise man, saying "What does he know?", spoke this verse while bringing forward a supporting reason:
“Fortune abandons the foolish person of dull wit who has failed to prepare for his work and lacks wise counsel,
just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
Having seen this as well, I say:”
“Wisdom alone is better; the fool has no glory.
Regarding that, the meaning of the phrase “Fortune deserts him” should be illustrated by means of the *Cetiya Jātaka*.
Then, when the king asked, “Of what sort? Senaka said, “Your Majesty, what does this young boy know? Listen! and, thinking, “I shall render the wise man speechless,” he spoke this verse:
“We five are wise, O Blessed One, and all stand here with palms joined;
you are our sovereign, surpassing us all, like Sakka, the Lord of Beings, the King of the Gods.
Having seen this as well, I say: one who possesses glory is better than one who is deficient in wisdom.”
Having heard this, the king thought, "A sound reason has been brought forward by Senaka;
will my son perhaps be able to refute his argument and bring forward another? Thinking thus, he asked, "What sort of wise men are they?
It is said that when Senaka had presented this case, no one other than the Bodhisatta was able to refute that argument.
There was no one capable [of refuting him]; therefore, the Great Being, shattering his argument by the power of his own knowledge, said, "Great King, what does this fool know?
He looks only for honor; he does not understand the distinction of wisdom. Listen! and spoke this verse:
"Like a slave to the wise and illustrious man is the fool when such matters arise."
"That which the wise man plans with skill, the fool falls into confusion regarding;
seeing this as well, I say: wisdom is better than the fame of a fool.
In this context, "atthesu" means when duties have arisen. "Saṃvidheti" means he plans or arranges.
Thus the Great Being demonstrated the method of reasoning, like one drawing up golden sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, or like one raising the full moon in the vault of the sky.
When the Great Being had thus spoken, demonstrating the power of his wisdom, the king said to Senaka:
"Tell me further, Senaka, if you are able. He [Senaka] [replied regarding] the grain stored in the granary...
Having exhausted his memorized material, he sat there speechless, humiliated, and brooding.
For had he brought forth another reason, this Jātaka would not have been concluded even with a thousand verses.
But while he remained speechless, the Great Being, as if leading him across a deep flood, further extolling wisdom, spoke this verse:
“Truly, wisdom alone is praised by the virtuous; men who delight in wealth find beauty desirable.
But the knowledge of the Buddhas is of incomparable nature; beauty never surpasses wisdom.
In this context, “the virtuous” refers to the True Persons (sappurisa) such as the Buddhas and others. “Men who delight in wealth,” O Great King, refers to those who are blind fools.
O you who delight in enjoyments, therefore glory is dear to them. Furthermore, this meaning—that fame is censured by the wise but is dear to fools—should be illustrated by the *Bhisajātaka*.
"Of the Buddhas" refers to the knowledge of the omniscient Buddhas.
"At any time" means that at no time whatsoever does glory ever surpass one who possesses wisdom, O Deva.
Having heard that, the king was delighted by the Great Being’s answer to his question. Showering him with wealth as if raining down a heavy downpour, he honored the Great Being with these verses:

“Since you have explained to us that which we asked, O Mahosadha, you who see the Dhamma in its entirety—here are a thousand cows, a bull, a noble elephant, and ten chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses.”
“Satisfied by the answer to my question, I shall give you sixteen excellent villages.
Therein, “I give you an elephant named Usabha”—having made that elephant the leader of his thousand cattle, he gives him as a mount, adorned and prepared.
The Sirimanta Question in the Vīsatinipāta is concluded.
The Question of the Covered Path.
From that time forth, the Bodhisatta’s fame became great. Queen Udumbara alone managed all of it.
When he reached the age of sixteen, she thought: "My younger brother has grown up; his fame is also great."
“There has been; it is fitting to hold his marriage ceremony. She reported this matter to the king. The king said, “Very well, inform him.
Having informed him and received his consent, she said, “In that case, dear father, I shall bring you a maiden.
Then the Great Being thought, “Perhaps one brought by these people might not please me; let me first examine her myself.”
Having reflected thus, he said: "Queen, for a few days do not say anything to the king;
I shall seek out a young maiden myself and, having found one who pleases my heart, I will announce her to you. "Do so, dear friend," she replied.
He paid homage to the queen and went to his own home, where he gave notice to his friends and, in the guise of a stranger, [prepared] the implements of a tailor.
Taking it, he went out alone by the northern gate and set out for Uttarayavamajjhaka.
At that time, however, there was an ancient merchant family there that had become impoverished. The daughter of that family was named Amarādevī;
she was beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, endowed with all auspicious marks, and possessed of great merit. On that day, she rose early in the morning and cooked rice-gruel.
Taking her with him and thinking, "I shall go to my father's field," he set out and followed that very same path.
Seeing her approaching, the Great Being thought, "This woman is endowed with every auspicious mark;
if she is unmarried, it would be fitting for her to become my foot-attendant."
She too, upon seeing him, thought: "If I were to be in the house of such a man, I would be able to establish a household.
Then the Great Being thought: "I do not know whether she has a husband or not;
I shall ask her with my clenched fist. If she is wise, she will understand; if not, she will not understand. Right here..."
Thinking, "I shall go away, leaving him behind," he stood at a distance and made a fist with his hand.
She, perceiving that he was asking whether she had a husband or not, extended her hand.
Knowing she was unattached, he approached and asked, "Noble lady, what is your name? "My lord, as for me, whether in the past, the future, or the present..."
“Or rather, it is named after that which does not exist. “Bhadde, there is no such thing as ‘immortal’ (amarā) in the world;
you shall be named Amarā. “Yes, my lord. “Bhadde, for whom will you carry the rice-gruel? “For the former deity, my lord.
“Bhadde, the so-called ‘former deity’ refers to one’s mother and father; I suppose you will carry rice-gruel for your father. “Yes, my lord.”
“Bhadde, what does your father do? “Master, he divides one into two. “Dividing one into two is called plowing;
your father plows. “Yes, Master. “But in what place does your father plow?
“In that place, Master, where those who have once gone do not return. “A place from which those who have once gone do not come back.”
“There is a cemetery; he plows near the cemetery, Bhaddā. “Yes, Master. “Bhaddā, will you go this very day? “If he goes, I will not go.
If he does not go, I will go, Master. “Bhaddā, I suppose your father plows on the far side of the river;
you will not go when the water rises, but you will go when it subsides. “Yes, Master. This much—
The Great Being engaged in conversation with him.
Then Queen Amarā invited him, saying, "Sir, will you drink rice-gruel?
The Great Being thought, "To refuse at the very outset is indeed inauspicious," and said, "Yes, I shall drink. She then poured out the jar of rice-gruel.
The Great Being thought, "If she gives it without having washed the bowl or offered water for washing the hands, I shall leave it right here and depart.
However, she washed the bowl, brought water in the bowl, and offered water for washing the hands;
then, placing the empty bowl in her hand and setting it on the ground, she stirred the jar and filled it with rice gruel.
There, moreover, the grains were large. Then the Great Being said to her, "My dear lady, why is the rice-gruel so thick?
"Water was not obtained, master," she replied. "I suppose water was not found in the field, was it? "That is so, master.
She set aside her father's portion of gruel and gave it to the Bodhisatta. Having drunk the gruel and rinsed his mouth, he—
“Bhadde, I shall go to your mother’s house; show me the way,” he said.
She replied, “Very well,” and while showing him the way, she recited this verse from the Ekakanipāta:
“Where the *sattubilaṅgā* and the double-leaved *palāsa* are in flower;”
“I speak by that which I give; I do not speak by that which I do not give.
This is the path of Yavamajjhaka; know this to be his way of eating.
The meaning of this is: “Master, having entered the village, you will see a flour shop, and from there, a shop selling sour gruel.”
In front of them stands a flowering *koviḷāra* tree with twice as many leaves;
therefore, go to where the *sattubilaṅgā* and the *koviḷāra* are in bloom, stand at the foot of the *koviḷāra*, and take the right hand and release the left.
This is the path leading to our house in the village of Yavamajjhaka, situated in the midst of barley fields; having hidden yourself in this manner—
"I said 'the covered path'—understand this as a concealed path, or rather, a path hidden by reason.
For here, "with which I give" refers to the hand with which I give; this was said with reference to the right hand, while the other is the left hand.
Having thus pointed out the way to him, she took her father's rice-gruel and departed.
The Question of Channapatha is finished.
The Search for Queen Amarā:
He too went to that house by the very path she had described. Then, seeing him, the mother of Queen Amarā offered him a seat.
Having given it, she said, "Sir, you shall drink the rice-gruel. He replied, "Mother, my younger sister, Queen Amarā, has already given me a little gruel.
Hearing this, she realized, "He must have come for the sake of my daughter.
Although the Great Being knew their state of poverty, he said, "Mother, I am a tailor; is there anything that needs to be sewn?"
She asked, "Is there [cloth], Master? But there is no money. He replied, "Mother, there is no work for one who has no money;
bring it, and I will sew it. She brought worn-out rags and gave them to him. The Bodhisatta finished each piece as soon as it was brought.
For indeed, the undertaking of one who possesses merit succeeds. Then he said to her, "Mother, you should announce this along the street. She—
He announced it throughout the entire village. Having performed the work of a tailor, the Great Being earned one thousand kahāpaṇas in a single day.
His mother cooked and gave him his morning meal, and then asked, "Dear son, how much shall I cook for the evening meal?
He replied, "Mother, prepare as much as will suffice for all those who eat in this house. She then prepared many kinds of soups and condiments.

She cooked a great deal of food. In the evening, Queen Amarā, having returned from the forest carrying a bundle of firewood on her head and leaves in her lap, set down the bundle at the door of the house in the city and entered through the back door.
Her father also arrived later in the evening. The Great Being partook of various kinds of choice delicacies. After the other woman had fed her parents, she...
After he had eaten himself, he washed the feet of his parents and then washed the feet of the Great Being.
Examining him, he stayed right there for several days. Then, testing him one day, he said:
"My dear, take half a nāḷika measure of rice and cook from it my rice-gruel, cakes, and a meal."
Having accepted with the words, “Very well,” she pounded the rice; she prepared a meal from the best grains, rice-gruel from the medium grains, and cakes from the broken grains.
Having prepared a corresponding curry and condiments, she gave the Great Being the rice-gruel along with the condiments.
As soon as that gruel was placed in his mouth, it pervaded the seven thousand channels that carry the vital flavors.
Thus, in order to test her, he said as if angry, "Bhadde, since you do not know how to cook rice-gruel, why have you ruined my rice?
and spat upon it with saliva, throwing it onto the ground.
Without becoming angry at him, she said, "Husband, if the gruel is not good, eat some cake," and gave him a cake. He did the same with that as well. "If..."
“Master, the previous [food] was not good; please eat this meal,” she said, and gave him the food.
He did the same with that meal as well, and as if angry, he said, “Bhadde, since you do not know how to cook, why have you ruined what belonged to me?
Then, as if in a rage, he crushed all three together, smeared it from his head down over his entire body, and said, “Go, sit at the door!”
She said, "Very well, my lord," and without becoming angry, she went and did as he asked.
Knowing that her pride had been subdued, he said, "Come, dear lady. Without becoming angry, she came at his single word.
Meanwhile, the Great Being, as he was coming, had brought a pair of single garments and a betel-roll pouch along with a thousand kahāpaṇas. Then he—
Having removed that garment and placed it in her hand, he said, "Bhadde, go bathe with your companions, put on this garment, and come back. She did accordingly.
The wise man gave all the wealth he had produced as well as the wealth he had brought to her parents, and having comforted them, [departed].
Having taken leave of her father-in-law and taking him with her, she set out toward the city.
On the way, for the purpose of testing her, he gave her a sunshade and sandals, saying, "My dear, take this sunshade and protect yourself;
put on these sandals and go. She took them, but instead of doing so, she remained in the open air under the scorching heat of the sun.
She went along holding her parasol in the forest and putting on her sandals on dry ground, then, upon reaching a body of water, she stepped into them and proceeded.
Seeing this, the Bodhisatta asked, "Why, lady, do you put on your sandals on dry ground and step into them when you reach the water? Is it because of the heat of the sun?"
“Why do you not hold the umbrella over yourself, but instead hold it at the edge of the forest? She replied:
“Master, on dry land I see thorns and such things, but in the water I do not see fish, turtles, or aquatic thorns; if my feet were to enter those, there would be painful sensations.
However, in the open air there are no thorns from dry trees, whereas for those who have entered the interior of the forest, there are dry trees, stumps, and so forth.”
"If they were to fall upon my head, there would be painful sensation; therefore, I do this for the sake of warding them off.
Having heard her words, the Bodhisatta was pleased for two reasons and, as he continued on his way, saw at one spot a jujube tree laden with fruit.
He sat down at the foot of that jujube tree. [She saw] the Great Being sitting at the foot of the jujube tree.
Seeing him, she said, “Master, climb up, take some jujube fruit and eat; give some to me as well.
He replied, “My dear, I am weary and cannot climb; you yourself must climb.
Having heard his words, she climbed the jujube tree, sat upon a branch, and plucked the fruit. The Bodhisatta said to her: “My dear...”

“Give me a fruit,” he said. Thinking, “I shall test whether this man is wise or unwise,” she asked him, “Husband, will you eat a warm fruit, or a cold one? Not understanding her intention, he replied, “My dear, I have need of a warm fruit.
She then threw the fruits onto the ground and said, “Husband, [this is what you get].”
"Please eat," she said. The Bodhisatta took it and ate it while chewing.
Examining her further, he said, "My dear, give me something cool. Then she threw jujube fruits onto the grassy ground.
He took them, ate them, and was pleased, thinking, "This girl is exceedingly wise. Then the Great Being—
He said to her, "Bhadde, descend from the jujube tree.
Having heard the Great Being’s words, she descended from the tree, took a water jar, went to the river, brought water, and gave it to the Great Being.
The Great Being drank, rinsed his mouth, and rising from there, proceeded until he reached the city itself.
Then, having placed her in the gatekeeper’s house for the purpose of testing her and having informed the gatekeeper’s wife, he went to his own residence.
He summoned his men and said, "I have come after placing a woman in such-and-such a house;
take this thousand pieces of money, go, and test her. Having given them the thousand, he sent them off. They did exactly as instructed.
She said, "This is not even worth the dust on my husband's feet. They went and reported this to the Wise One.
Again, having sent her forth up to three times, on the fourth occasion the Great Being said to them, "In that case, bring her here, dragging her by the hand.
They did so. She [did not recognize] the Great Being established in such great prosperity.
She recognized him; and upon looking at him, she both laughed and wept. He asked for the reason for both [reactions]. Then she said to him:

"Husband, laughing, I looked upon your prosperity and thought, 'This was not obtained without cause, but was obtained by performing wholesome deeds in a previous existence; oh, what a fruit indeed is that of merit! Thus I laughed. But as for my weeping—"
"He wept out of compassion for you, thinking: 'Now, by offending against another's guarded and protected property, he will go to hell.
Having tested him and known his purity, he said, "Go and lead him right back there," and sent him off.
Then, again assuming the guise of a tailor, he went and lay down with her; on the following day at dawn, he went to the royal palace.
Having entered, he informed Queen Udumbara. She, in turn, informed the king;
then, having adorned Amarādevī with all her ornaments and seated her upon a great palanquin, she escorted her with great honor to the Great Being’s house and performed the auspicious rites.
The king sent a gift worth a thousand pieces of gold to the Bodhisattva. Starting from the gatekeepers, all the inhabitants of the city...
They sent gifts. Queen Amarā, for her part, divided the gift sent by the king into two parts and sent one portion back to the king.
By this means, she sent gifts to all the inhabitants of the city and won them over.
From that time forth, the Great Being lived in harmonious union with her and instructed the king in both worldly prosperity and the Dhamma.
The search for Amarādevī is finished.
Now, as for the commentary on the theft of all the jewels:
one day Senaka addressed the other three who had come into his presence, saying, "Friends, we [must act] regarding the son of the householder..."
“It was not so with Mahosadha himself; however, he has now brought home a wife even more clever than himself.
How can we cause a rift between her and the king? “Teacher, what do we know?
You alone must know. “Very well, do not worry. There is a certain plan: I shall steal the king’s crest-jewel and bring it back, Pukkusa.”
“‘Kāminda, you bring the golden garland; Devinda, you bring the woolen blanket; [and] you, bring the golden sandals.
In this way, all four of us will obtain those items through stratagem, and then, having set them aside in our own house, we will send for the householder’s son.
Then those four did exactly so. Among them, Senaka first [took] the crest-jewel.
Having placed the jar of buttermilk in the hand of a maidservant, he sent her forth with these instructions:
“Without giving this jar of buttermilk to anyone else who asks for it, if they take it at Mahosadha’s house, give it to them along with the jar itself.
She went to the door of the wise man’s house and wandered back and forth, crying out, “Buttermilk! Buttermilk! “Take some buttermilk! Take some buttermilk!”
Amarādevī, standing at the door, having seen her action, thought, "She does not go elsewhere;
there must be a reason for this. By means of a sign from her gesture, she had the maidservants withdraw and called out herself, "Come, my dear, let us take some buttermilk.
When she arrived, she gave a signal to the maidservants, and as they did not come, she said, "Go, my dear."
“Call the female slaves! Having sent her off, he dipped his hand into a jar of buttermilk, saw the jewel, and asked that slave, “Mother, whose slave are you?
“Noble lady, I am the slave of the wise man Senaka.
Then, having asked her name and her mother’s name, when she replied, “I am named So-and-so,” he asked, “Mother, what is the price of this buttermilk?”
She asked, "Noble lady, is it four *nāḷikas*? "In that case, my dear, give me this buttermilk," she said.
When [the other] replied, "Noble lady, while you are taking it, what need have I for the price? Take it along with the jar itself," [the first] dismissed her, saying, "In that case, go.
Then she [went to] the teacher Senaka on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, [saying], "The slave girl named so-and-so..."
Having written on the letter, “I have sent the king’s crest-jewel by the hand of my daughter named Asukā for the purpose of being sent,” he took the ink-pot.
Pukkusa also, having placed a golden garland in a basket of *sumana* flowers and covered it with *sumana* flowers, sent it in the same manner.
Kāmin also, having placed a woolen blanket in a leaf-tray, [sent it] with letters.
She sent it after having wrapped it up. The Lord of Devas also sent the golden sandals, having tied them within a bundle of barley stalks.
She took all of these, wrote letters upon the leaves, informed the Great Being of their contents, and set them aside.
Those four wise men also went to the royal palace and asked, "Why, O King, do you not wear your crest-jewel?"
They said: "The king said, 'Bring them, for I shall wear them,' and he spoke thus to his men. They did not see the gem, nor indeed did they see the others either.
Then those four wise men said, 'Your Majesty, your ornaments are in the house of Mahosadha;
he himself uses them. O Great King, that householder’s son is your adversary.'"
They broke it. Then his attendants went quickly and reported it.
Thinking, "I shall know after seeing the king," he went to wait upon the king. The king, becoming angry, said, "Who knows? What will happen? What will he do?
and would not allow himself to be seen. The wise man, perceiving that the king was enraged, [thought] regarding himself—
He went straight to his residence. The king ordered, "Seize him!

Having heard the words of his ministers, the wise man thought, "It is necessary for me to depart," and after signaling his intention to Queen Amarā, he left the city in disguise and went to the village of Yavamajjhaka in the south, where he took up the work of a potter. In the city, a great clamor arose: "The wise man has fled!"
Senaka and the other three men, having learned of his flight, said to one another, "Do not worry;
are we so unwise? and without informing each other, they sent a gift to Queen Amarā.
She accepted the gifts sent by those four and, saying, "Let him come at such-and-such a time," she had a well dug and filled it with a heap of excrement.
Having filled it with water, he covered the surface of the cesspool with mechanical planks, concealed it with a mat, and completed everything.
Then, in the evening, Senaka bathed, adorned himself, ate various choice foods, and went to the Bodhisatta’s house. Standing at the door of the house, he [addressed] himself...
She made it known that he had arrived. She said, "Come, Teacher. He went and stood near her. She spoke thus:
"My lord, now that I have come under your power, it is not fitting for me to lie down without having bathed my body.
Having heard her words, he consented, saying, "Very well. She went out and took a jar filled with water.
As if she had been sitting there, she said, "Come, teacher, climb onto the planks for the sake of bathing.
When he had climbed onto the planks and was standing there, she entered the house, stepped on the edge of a plank, and caused him to fall into a cesspool.
Pukkusāti, having bathed in the evening, adorned himself, and eaten various kinds of choice food, [approached] the Bodhisatta.
Having gone to the house and standing at the door, he made known his arrival. A female attendant informed Queen Amarādevī.
Upon hearing her words, she said, "Come, teacher; it is not fitting for you to lie down without having bathed your body.
He consented, saying, "Very well. She went out and [took] a jar filled with water.
Taking hold of him as if pouring water over him, she said, "Come, teacher, climb onto the planks for the sake of bathing.
When he had climbed onto the planks and was standing there, she entered the house, dragged the planks back, and threw him into a cesspool.
Senaka asked Pukkusa, "Who is this? He replied, "I am Pukkusa. "What is your name, man? "I am..."
"Senaka! they said, and having questioned one another, they stood there. In that same manner, she caused the other two as well to fall right there.

They all stood in that loathsome cesspool. When the night had turned to dawn, she had them lifted out from there, had the four men shaved bald, had rice taken and soaked with water, had it pounded, and [prepared] a thick gruel of flour.
Having had it cooked and ground, she had him smear his entire body starting from the head;
then, having had cotton wool taken and sprinkled over him in the same manner starting from the head, she caused him great suffering.
Having laid him down on a mat and bound him up, desiring to inform the king, she had them take the four jewels and went into the presence of the king together with them.

Having gone and paid homage to the king, he sat down to one side and said, "Your Majesty, please accept this great gift called the 'White Monkey,'" and having spoken thus, he placed four mats at the king's feet.
Then the king had them opened and saw four men who resembled white monkeys. Thereupon all the people cried out, "Oh, never before seen! Oh!"
Having said, "The great white monkeys," they laughed a great laugh. Those four were filled with great shame.
Then Queen Amarā, explaining her husband’s innocence, said to the king: "Your Majesty, the wise Mahosadha is not a thief;
these four alone are the thieves. For among them, Senaka is a jewel-thief, Pukkusa is a gold-garland thief, and Kāmindu—"

“Kambalacora, Devinda, and Suvaṇṇapādukācora—these thieves, on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, have sent these jewels by the hands of such-and-such a daughter of a slave and such-and-such slaves. Look at this letter;
take what belongs to you, O King, and receive these thieves. Having thus brought all four men into great distress, she...

Having paid homage to the king, they went to their own homes. Because of the Bodhisatta’s flight, his suspicion toward them, and the absence of other wise counselors, the king said nothing to them but sent them away, saying, "Wise men, go to your own homes after bathing.
Having met with great misfortune, the four men paid homage to the king and returned to their own homes.
The *Sabbaratanathena* is finished.
Regarding the question of the firefly:
a deity dwelling in the Bodhisatta’s parasol, not hearing his teaching of the Dhamma, thought, "What indeed..."
Reflecting on "the cause," and having understood that cause, she thought, "I shall provide the reason for bringing the wise man.

Then, in the middle of the night, she opened the umbrella-stand and asked the four questions—beginning with "He strikes with hands and feet"—which had been posed by the deity to the king in the *Catukkanipāta*. The king, not knowing [the answers], said, "I do not..."
“I know; I shall ask other wise men. Having requested an opportunity one day, he sent a message to the four wise men on the following day, saying, “Let them come.

When they replied, “We are ashamed to go out onto the street with our heads shaved,” the king sent four bamboo hats, saying, “Let them come placing these upon their heads. At that time, it seems, they...
Reed-mats appeared. They arrived and sat down on the prepared seats.
Then the king said, "Senaka, during the night today, a deity residing in my parasol asked me four questions. Not knowing the answers, I said, 'I shall ask the wise ones.
Tell me those questions," and he spoke this verse:
“He strikes with his hands and feet, and he bites with his mouth;
such a person, O King, is indeed beloved—what do you see in him?
Senaka, not knowing what was meant by “he strikes” or “how he strikes,” lamented this and that, yet he saw no end to it.

He saw the answer. The others, too, were left speechless. Then the king, feeling remorseful, was questioned by the deity at nightfall as to whether he had understood the problem; he replied, "I asked four wise men, yet even they did not know it.
The deity said, "What could they have known? Aside from the wise man Mahosadha, no one else is capable of explaining these questions."
“There is no one capable [of answering]. If you do not have him summoned and make him answer these questions, we shall split your head with this flaming iron mallet,” he threatened the king.
Then, saying, “Great King, when there is need for fire, it is not right to blow on a glowworm;
when there is need for milk, it is not right to milk a horn,” he spoke as follows:
In the Pañcaka-nipāta, he recited the Khajjopana-question:
“Who indeed, while there was a lamp, went about searching for fire?
Seeing a glow-worm at night, he thought it was the fire born of fuel.”
“With cow-dung powder and grass he smeared it,
yet because of his perverted perception, he was unable to set it ablaze.
Even so, by an improper means, the deer does not achieve his goal.”
One might milk a cow from its horns where no milk is to be found.
"By various means, young men attain their goal:
by subduing their enemies and by supporting their friends."
“By the acquisition of release from armies, and by the policy of those who are dear, the protectors of the world dwell upon the earth, O Vasundharā.
In this context, *santamhi pajjote* means while the fire is present. *Caranti* means they move about. *Addakkhī* means he saw; having seen—
Furthermore, because of their similarity in color, he thought, "This glow-worm will be fire. "Svassa" means:
upon that glow-worm, there were fine particles of cow-dung and grass. "Abhimattham" means:
rubbing with his hands and scattering [the fuel], while kneeling on the ground and blowing with his mouth, he thought, "I shall kindle it."
Later, even though he strove with a perverted perception, he was unable to kindle it.
Like a deer—a fool resembling a deer—one who seeks in such an unskillful manner does not obtain the goal.
"Where" means that just as one milking a cow from which there is no milk at all finds no benefit, so too he does not find the goal. "By the release of the army" refers to the soldiers' liberation.
By means of the gain of ministers; and by way of dear and beloved, trustworthy ministers.
