Regarding the earth: because it holds the treasures known as *vasu*, it has acquired the name "Vasundharā," and kings, the protectors of the world, dwell upon that earth.
They are not like you, who, while the fire is still present, fan the glow-worm. Great King, you ask about Senaka and the others— asking what they know—
like one who fans a glow-worm while the fire is there, like one who weighs with his hand after having discarded the scale,
or like one who milks from the horn when the need for milk has already been met.
"These are like glow-worms. Mahosadha shines with wisdom like a mass of fire; summon him and ask him.
There is no life for you if you do not know these questions. Having thus threatened the king, he vanished.
The Question of the Glow-Worm is finished.
The Questions of Bhūri:
Then, on the following day, the king, terrified by the fear of death, summoned four ministers and said,
"Sirs, you four, mounting four chariots, shall depart from the four city gates and [search] wherever my son—
"Behold the wise Mahosadha! Having paid him due honor right there, bring him back quickly," he commanded.
Those four men then departed, each by a different gate. Three of them did not find the wise man;
however, the one who had gone out by the southern gate saw the Great Being in the village of Dakkhiṇa-yavamajjhaka, bringing clay for his teacher’s wheel.
He saw him sitting on a bed of straw, his body smeared with clay, eating barley-rice with little sauce, having formed it into small morsels one by one. But why did he perform this work?

It was because the king, fearing that "the wise man will undoubtedly seize the kingdom," had become apprehensive; however, upon hearing that "he lives by the work of a potter," he became free from fear.
Thinking, "It shall be so," he acted accordingly. Upon seeing the minister and realizing that he had come into his presence, he thought, "Today my reputation will be restored to its former state;
I shall eat only the food of various exquisite flavors prepared by Queen Amarā.
Having discarded the morsel of barley-rice he had taken, he rose and rinsed his mouth.
He sat down. At that moment, the minister approached him. Being a partisan of Senaka, he tried to persuade him, saying:
"O wise one, the words of Master Senaka are leading to liberation.
When your fame had declined, such wisdom as yours was unable to remain established; now, smeared with mud and sitting on a bed of straw, you speak such things as this."
Having said, "Do you eat alms-food?", he recited the first verse in the *Bhūripañha* of the *Dasakanipāta*:
"Is it true, O Bhūripañña, that even such glory, steadfastness, and wisdom as yours do not protect one who,
though brought to wealth and power, eats barley with little sauce?"
In this context, "saccaṃ kira" means that what the teacher Senaka said is indeed true. "Sirī" means sovereignty.
"Dhitī" means unceasing energy. "Na tāyate bhāvavasūpanitaṃ" means that which is brought under the power of non-existence—that is, lack of growth—does not protect it, does not guard it;
it is unable to serve as a foundation. "Yavakaṃ" means barley-food.
Then the Great Being said to him, “O blind fool, desiring to restore that glory to its former state through the power of my own wisdom,
I act in this way,” and spoke these two verses: “Bringing happiness to maturity through suffering, discerning the right and wrong time while shrouded by desire,
opening the doors to what is beneficial— it is for this reason that I am satisfied with barley-gruel.”

“Having known the right time for awakening, and having brought the purpose to fruition through mantras, I shall stretch out my limbs like a lion’s stretch; by that very psychic power, you shall see me once again.
Therein, by the word “with suffering,” it means by means of this physical and mental suffering, through the restoration of his own former happiness to its natural state.
"Bringing to maturity" means causing to increase. "Time and non-time" means discerning thus: "This is the time to wander in concealment;

this is the time not to be concealed. Knowing that one must wander in concealment when the king is angry, he—being "concealed" (channa) by his own will (chanda), that is, by his own preference—lived by the work of a potter for the sake of his own welfare while remaining hidden.
The meaning is: "I dwell opening the doors known as causes; for that reason, I am satisfied with barley-rice.
*Abhijīhanāya* means for the sake of exerting effort (*vīriyakaraṇassa*). "Having brought the purpose to maturity through mantras" means:
having increased my glory by the power of my own knowledge, I shall stretch out like a lion stretching on a slab of emerald; by means of that psychic power (*iddhi*).
"Will you see me again?
Then the minister said to him: "O wise man, the deity dwelling in the royal parasol asked the king a question.
The king questioned four wise men, yet not even one among them was able to explain that question; therefore, the king [sought] you..."
“...sent me to his presence. “This being so, why do you not see the power of wisdom?
For at such a time as this, sovereignty does not provide a firm footing; only one endowed with wisdom provides a firm footing. Thus the Great Being praised the power of wisdom.
The minister [was told by the king]: “Having shown honor to the wise man in the very place where he was seen, bring him here.”
He placed a thousand kahāpaṇas in the hands of the Great Being.
The potter fell into fear, thinking, "It seems the wise Mahosadha has been made by me to perform the work of a weaver. Then the Great Being comforted him, saying, "Do not fear, teacher;
you have been very helpful to us," and having given him the thousand coins, [he departed] with his body still smeared with clay.

Having mounted his chariot, he entered the city. The minister informed the king, and when the king asked, "Dear man, where have you seen the wise man?", he replied, "Your Majesty, having heard that he lives by working as a potter in the village of Yavamajjhaka in the south, he came immediately upon hearing the summons, without even bathing and with his body still smeared with clay. The king said, "If he were my enemy..."
Thinking, "He might act according to the ritual for sovereignty; this man is not my enemy," he said, "Tell my son:
'Go to your own home, bathe, adorn yourself, and come back according to the procedure given by me.
Having heard that, the wise man did so. Upon his arrival, when told, "Enter," he entered, paid homage to the king, and—
He stood to one side. The king, having offered him hospitality and wishing to test the wise man, spoke this verse:
“Some do not commit evil even when they are happy; others do so out of fear of ill repute or social disapproval.
Being wealthy and contemplating great aims, for what reason do you not cause me suffering?”
In this regard, O wise one, as for those who are happy: some do not commit evil for the sake of further power, thinking, "We are happy and possess great sovereignty; this much is sufficient for us";
others do not commit it out of fear of ill repute and social censure, thinking, "If we offend such a master who bestows honor upon us, we shall incur blame. Yet another is simply incapable.
"He is one of dull wisdom, whereas you are both capable and a thinker of vast purpose; if you so desired, you could even rule over the whole of Jambudīpa.
For what reason do you not take my kingdom and put an end to this suffering?
Then the Bodhisatta said to him:
“Wise people do not perform evil deeds for the sake of their own happiness;
even when touched by suffering and fallen into misfortune, they do not abandon the Dhamma out of desire or hatred.

In this context, “even when fallen” means that although they have fallen from prosperity and exist in a state of adversity, they do not abandon the Dhamma—neither the Dhamma of the tradition nor the Dhamma of good conduct.
Again, for the purpose of testing him, the king spoke this verse while recounting the traditional wisdom of the kṣatriyas:
“By whatever means possible, whether gentle or harsh, one should rescue one’s own wretched self;
afterwards, one may practice the Dhamma.”
In this context, "the wretched" means: "Having rescued myself from misfortune, I shall establish myself in prosperity.
Then, showing him the simile of the tree, the Great Being spoke this verse:
"In the shade of whose tree one might sit or lie down..."
"One should not break its branch, for he who betrays a friend is evil.

Having spoken thus, he continued: "Great King, if even one who breaks a branch of a tree that has been enjoyed becomes a betrayer of friends, then those by whom my father was established in such exalted sovereignty, and myself with great favor..."
“Having been favored by you, how could I, who do not offend you, be a betrayer of friends?
Having thus declared in every way his own lack of treachery toward friends, he spoke this verse to challenge the king’s mental disposition:
“Even for one whose Dhamma a man may understand, and whose doubts the virtuous dispel;”
"For that indeed is his island and his refuge; one wise with wisdom should not let friendship with him wear away.

Its meaning is this: O Great King, from whichever teacher a person might learn even a small portion of the Dhamma or its reasoning, and who remove the doubts that have arisen in him—him he should regard as his island in the sense of being his firm foundation.
And with such a teacher as a final resort, a wise person should not let their friendship decay or perish.
Now, advising him, he spoke these two verses:
“A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good; one who has gone forth but is unrestrained is not good.”
“A king who acts without reflection does not do well; even if he is wise, one who is prone to anger does not do well.
A noble ruler should act with reflection, not without reflection, O Lord of the Earth.
For a king who acts with reflection, his glory and fame increase.”

In this context, "not good" means not beautiful. "One who acts without reflection" refers to one who, having heard something, acts upon it without investigating or making it a matter of personal experience. "Fame and renown" means that both the retinue of power and the reputation for virtue increase exclusively.
The *Bhūri-pañha* is concluded.
The *Devatā-pañha*.
When this was said, the King had the Great Being seated upon a royal couch beneath a raised white parasol, while he himself sat on a low seat and said:
"O wise one, a deity dwelling in the white parasol asked me four questions which I do not know.
Even the four wise men did not know them; tell them to me, dear father. "Great King," [the Bodhisatta replied].

"Whether it be a deity residing in the Chattiya Shrine, or one belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings and so forth—it matters not who it is—I am able to answer whatever question has been asked.
Speak, O Great King, regarding the question asked by the deity. Then the King, speaking in accordance with the manner in which the deity had questioned him, recited the first verse:
“He strikes with his hands and feet, and he bites with his mouth;
yet he indeed becomes dear to the king—what do you see in him that you look upon him thus?
In this context, *hanti* means he strikes; *parisumbhati* means he likewise strikes. *Sa ve* means he who acts in such a way is indeed dear.
"It exists. "Whom do you regard as dear because of that? "O King, whom do you regard as a beloved person because of that reason for striking?
Upon hearing those words from the Great Being, the matter became as clear as the full moon in the sky. Then—

The Great Being said, "Listen, Great King: when a young child lying on his mother's lap plays joyfully and contentedly, striking his mother with his hands and feet, pulling her hair, or hitting her face with his fist, then his mother, out of the influence of affection and love, says things such as, 'O little thief!
Why do you strike us like this? and thus she expresses her love."
Unable to hold him back, she embraced him, laid him upon her breast, and kissed his face.
Thus, even at such a time, he was dearer to her, and likewise to his father.
Having thus explained the question clearly, like the sun rising in the midst of the sky, the deity uncovered the handle of the parasol and emerged.
Displaying half his body, he gave a cry of approval in a sweet voice, saying, "The question has been well answered by the wise man.
Filling a jeweled casket with divine flowers, perfumes, and ointments, he honored the Bodhisatta and vanished.
The king, too, having honored the wise man with flowers and other offerings, requested the other question. When told, "Speak, Great King," he recited the second verse:
“He reviles him as he pleases, yet he desires his favor;
indeed, such a person is dear to a king—what do you see in him that you look upon him so?
Then the Great Being said to him: “Great King, my mother has a son aged seven or eight years who is capable of carrying out her verbal commands.”

Having told her son, "Dear, go to the field; go to the marketplace," and so forth, when he says, "Mother, if you will give me this and that solid food and soft food, I shall go," she replies, "Very well, my son, take it," and gives it to him.
That boy, having eaten it, goes outside, plays with the other boys, and does not heed his mother's summons.
He departed. When his mother said, "Dear son, go," he replied to her, "Mother, you sit in the cool shade of the house;
why then should I do the work of a messenger for you outside? I am deceiving you!
Having spoken thus, he made gestures with his hands and face and went away. Seeing him depart, she became angry and took up a staff.
Rebuking him, saying, “Having eaten what belongs to me, you do not wish to do the work in the field,” she pursued him as he fled in haste;
being unable to catch him, she reviled and abused him at will, saying things such as, “May thieves cut you into pieces!
Furthermore, whatever she spoke with her mouth, even the slightest bit remained in her heart.
He did not wish to come, yet he desired his arrival; having played for part of the day, being unable to enter his home in the evening, he went to the presence of his relatives.
His mother, watching the path of his arrival and seeing that he did not come, thought, "I suppose he is unable to enter," and her heart was filled with grief, her eyes brimming with tears.

While searching in the house of her relatives, she saw her son; she embraced him, kissed him on the head, and grasping him firmly with both hands, she felt an even greater surge of love, saying, "Dear beloved son, have you kept my words in your heart?
"In this way, Great King, even when a mother is angry, her son is indeed more beloved," he said, answering the second question.
The deity worshipped him in the same manner.
The king, having also worshipped her, requested a third question. When she said, "Speak, O Great King," he uttered this third verse:
"He accuses with what is untrue, and pursues with falsehood."
“He indeed becomes dear to the king; what do you see in him?

Then the Great Being said to him: “O King, when both husband and wife, having retired in private to sport in the world’s delight, falsely misrepresent one another by saying, ‘My dear, you have no love for me; your heart has gone elsewhere,’ at that time—”
“When they bring a case forward with falsehood and accuse one another, then they love each other all the more.
Know the meaning of this question thus,” he said. The deity honored him accordingly.
The king also, having honored him, requested the other question; when told, “Speak, O Great King,” he recited the fourth verse:
“Those who take away food and drink, clothing and lodgings,
and who live as plunderers of others’ wealth— verily they, O King, are dear to you.
Why do you look upon them so?”
Then the Great Being said to him: "Great King, this question was asked with reference to righteous recluses and brahmins.
For families endowed with faith, having conviction in both this world and the world beyond, give gifts and desire to give;
even when seeing such recluses and brahmins begging, taking what is received, and consuming it, they think: 'They are begging from us alone; they are [taking] from us alone.'"
“They feel even greater affection for those who consume their food, drink, and other provisions.
“In this way, Great King, those who take what belongs to others, who beg unilaterally and carry off what they have received, become beloved,” he said.
When this question had been answered, the deity, having likewise honored him, gave a cry of approval.
He threw a jeweled spittoon filled with the seven precious gems at the feet of the Great Being, saying, “Take this, O Great Sage.
The king, having performed even greater honor for him and being exceedingly pleased, granted him the position of commander-in-chief.
From that time forth, the fame of the Great Being became great.
The Question of the Deity is finished.
The Question of the Five Wise Men:
Again, those four wise men said, "Friends, the householder’s son has now grown even greater; what shall we do?"

They deliberated. Then Senaka said to them: "Let it be; I have seen a stratagem. Let us approach the householder’s son and ask him, 'To whom is it proper to tell a secret? He will say, 'It should not be told to anyone.
Then we shall cause a rift by saying, 'Your enemy, O King, has become the householder’s son.'"
Those four wise men went to his house, exchanged greetings, and said, "Wise sir, we wish to ask you a question.
When he replied, "Ask," Senaka asked: "Wise sir, where should a man establish himself?
"He should establish himself in truth. "What should one who is established in truth produce? "Wealth should be produced."
“Having acquired wealth, what should be done? “A spell should be learned. “Having learned the spell, what should be done?

“One’s own secret must not be told to another. Saying, “Excellent, wise ones,” they were delighted in heart and, thinking, “Now we shall see the back of the householder’s son,” they went into the presence of the king and said, “Great King, ...”
“The son of a householder has become your adversary,” they said.
“I do not believe your words; he will not become my adversary. “It is true, Great King; believe it.
But if you do not believe me, ask him himself: ‘O wise one, to whom should one’s own secret be told? If he is an adversary...”
"He will not say, 'It should be told to such-and-such a person. If he becomes an adversary, he will say, 'It must not be told to anyone; it should be told when one's wishes are fulfilled.
Then, having faith in our words, you should be free from doubt. Having accepted this with "Very well," one day...
When they had all come together and were seated, he recited the first verse in the *Pañcapaṇḍita-pañha* of the *Vīsati-nipāta*:
“Five wise men have gathered here; a question occurs to me, so listen to it.
Regarding that which is blameworthy or praiseworthy—whose secret matter would one not reveal?”
When this was said, Senaka thought, "I shall include the king himself within our own circle," and spoke this verse:
"Reveal yourself, O protector of the earth; speak as one who is your husband’s comrade and capable of bearing his burden.
Having considered your desires and inclinations, O lord of men, the five wise ones will then speak."
"In this matter, 'husband' means you are both our master and the one capable of bearing the burden that has arisen;
first, let you yourself say what it is. Then, after considering your own desire as well as the reasons for your preference, these five wise men will speak."
Then the king, due to his own mastery over the defilements, spoke this verse:
“She who is virtuous, not unfaithful, obedient to her husband’s will, dear and pleasing;
she would reveal the secret matter of her wife, whether it be blameworthy or praiseworthy.”
In this context, *anaññatheyyā* means she must not be stolen away by another through the influence of defilements (*kilesa*).
Then Senaka, satisfied with the thought, "Now we have placed the king within our own circle," spoke this verse while pointing out the very deed he himself had performed:
"He who becomes a refuge, a resort, and a final destination for one who is afflicted and fallen into distress..."
"One should reveal a secret matter to one who is blameworthy, or to one who is praiseworthy, or to a friend.
Then the King asked Pukkusa, "How do you see it, Pukkusa? To whom should a secret matter—whether blameworthy or praiseworthy—be told? While explaining, he spoke this verse:
"The eldest, the middle, or the youngest—whoever is established in virtue, composed, and firm in self."
“Whether it be a matter of blame or praise, one should reveal a brother’s secret.
In this context, “one who stands firm” means one whose nature is stable and free from guile.
Then the King asked Kāminda, “Kāminda, how do you see it? To whom should a secret be told? As he spoke, he recited this verse:
“He who follows at the father’s heels, born after his father with peerless wisdom—he would reveal the secret matter of a son, whether it be blameworthy or praiseworthy.
In this context, “one who follows at the heels” means one who acts as a messenger;
he carries out his father’s errands and acts according to the will of his father’s mind.

The meaning is that he is capable of receiving instruction. Regarding "born after" (*anujāta*): there are three kinds of sons—the over-born (*atijāta*), the born-after (*anujāta*), and the under-born (*avajāta*).
One who brings about unarisen fame is over-born; one who is a burden to the family is under-born; but one who protects the lineage of the family is born-after.
It is with reference to such a person that this was said.
Then the king asked the Lord of Devas: “How do you see it, Lord of Devas? To whom should a secret be told? Speaking of his own experience, he recited this verse:
“The mother, O best among the two-footed folk, who nourishes one with her will and affection— one should reveal a secret matter to such a mother, whether it be something blameworthy or praiseworthy.”
In that passage, "O best of two-footed beings, O lord of men" means: "O best among bipeds, O ruler of people. "With desire and affection" means with both longing and love.
Having thus questioned him, the king asked the wise man: "Wise one, how do you regard this? To whom should a secret be told? [The wise man replied:
"Great King, as long as one's own purpose has not been accomplished, a wise person should remain patient; to no one..."
“He should not speak,” he said, and uttered this verse:
“It is better that what is secret remain secret; for the disclosure of a secret is not praised.
A wise man should endure it as long as it remains unaccomplished; once it is accomplished, he may speak as he pleases.”
"In this matter, O Great King, as long as one's own desire has not been fulfilled, a wise man should endure it and speak to no one.
When the wise man had spoken thus, the king became displeased. Senaka looked at the king, and the king also looked at Senaka’s face.
The Bodhisatta, seeing their behavior, knew at once: "These four men [will surely harm me] from the very beginning."
“They have created a rift within the king; he will likely ask a question as a means of testing me.
While they were still speaking, the sun set and the lamps were lit. The wise man thought, “Royal affairs are indeed grave;
it is not known what might happen. It is best to depart quickly. Having risen from his seat, he approached the king.
Having paid homage and departed, he thought: "One among these said, 'It is right to tell my friend';
another said, 'It is right to tell my brother'; another said, 'It is right to tell my son'; and another said, 'It is right to tell my mother.

I believe that whatever they have said must be what actually happened, for they speak only of what they have seen. Well then, I shall find out the truth this very day. Then those four, regarding others...
Every day, after departing from the royal palace, they would sit on the rim of a single food-vessel at the gate of the king’s residence,
consult regarding their duties, and then go home. Therefore, the wise man thought,
"I shall be able to learn their secret by lying beneath this vessel," and so he had that vessel lifted up.

Having had the mat spread out, he entered beneath the mango tree and gave a signal to the men, saying, "When you four wise men have finished consulting together and departed, come back and take me away.
They accepted, saying, "Very well," and departed. Then Senaka said to the king, "Great King, you do not believe our words; now—"
"What will you do? he asked. Having taken his words to heart and without even reflecting on them, the king became terrified and trembling, and asked, "What shall we do now, wise Senaka?
"Your Majesty, without making a delay and without letting anyone know, it is right to kill the householder’s son," replied Senaka.
The king said, "Senaka, apart from you, there is no one else who desires my welfare."

“There is no one else; take your own wives, stand at the gateway, and when the householder’s son comes for his morning visit, cut off his head with this sword,” he said, giving them his precious sword.
They replied, “Very well, Your Majesty; do not fear, we shall kill him,” and having departed, they saw their enemy.
They sat down on the back of the rice-pounding mortar. Then Senaka said, "Friends, who will kill the householder’s son?
The others replied, "Teacher, you yourself must kill him," and thus they placed the burden upon him alone.
Then Senaka asked them, "You say that a secret must be told to such-and-such a person."
“Was this done by you, or was it seen or heard? “It was done, Teacher.
“You say that a secret must be told to a friend; was this done by you, or was it seen or heard?
“It was done by me. “Tell me, Teacher. “If this secret were known by the king, my life would be at risk.”
“There is none. “Do not be afraid, teacher; there is no one here who would betray your secret, so speak,” he said.
Then, scratching the ground with his fingernail, he asked, “Is there perhaps a householder’s son beneath this?
“Teacher, a householder’s son would not enter such a place by his own authority; he is now intoxicated with his own glory.”
"It will happen; tell me your secret," he said. First, Senaka spoke, revealing his own secret:
"Do you know a certain courtesan by the name of So-and-So in this city? "Yes, Teacher. "Is she visible now?
"She is not visible, Teacher. "I performed the act of a man with her in the Sālavana grove, and of her—"
Out of greed for her ornaments, I killed her, wrapped her body in her own cloth, and brought it back.
I hung it on a peg in a certain room on a certain floor in our house;
I do not dare to use it, but I merely look upon it to observe its state of decay. Having committed such a criminal act, I told it to one of my friends.
"He has never spoken of this to anyone before; for that reason, I said, 'A friend's secret must be told.
The wise man carefully analyzed and observed his secret.
Pukkusāti, as he was telling his own secret, said: "I have leprosy on my thigh; my younger brother, early in the morning..."
Without letting anyone know, he washed it, smeared it with medicinal ointment, placed a piece of cloth over it, and bound it up.
"The king, having a soft heart toward me, called out to me, 'Come, Pukkusa,' and for the most part lay upon my thigh;
but if the king were to know of this, he would have me killed. Aside from my younger brother, no one else knows."
“There is no other reason; for that reason I said, ‘The secret must be told to one’s brother.
Then Kāmindī, telling her own secret, said: “On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, a yakkha named Naradeva seizes me, and I howl like a mad dog. I have told this matter to my son.”
"Knowing that I had been seized by a *yakkha*, he laid me down inside a chamber within the house, closed the door, and went out.
For the purpose of concealing my cries, he held a festival at the gate.
It was for this reason that I said, 'A secret must indeed be told to one's son. Thereupon, the three of them questioned the Lord of Devas (*devinda*). He [related] his own...
Speaking in secret, he said: "While I was performing the work of polishing the jewel, Sakka gave me a jewel belonging to the king;
I then stole the auspicious *maṅgala-maṇi-ratana* used for entering the royal palace and gave it to my mother.
Whenever she entered the royal palace without letting anyone know, she would give that jewel to me, and with that jewel, I would enter the palace."
"I am going to the royal palace. Without speaking with you, the king spoke with me first.
Every day he gives me eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four kahāpaṇas for my maintenance.
If the king were to discover the secret concealment of that jewel-treasure, I would have no life."
"For this reason I said, 'A secret must be told to one's mother.

The Great Being made his secret known directly to them all. They, as if cutting open their own bellies and turning their insides outward, told the secret to one another and said, "Be diligent; come back early in the morning."
“Let us kill the householder’s son,” they said, and rising up, they departed.
When they had gone, the wise man’s men arrived, lifted up the basket, took the Great Being with them, and departed.
He went home, bathed, adorned himself, ate a fine meal, and thought, “Today my sister, Queen Udumbara, will send a message from the royal palace.”
Having understood this, he stationed a man at the gate with these instructions: "When someone arrives from the royal palace, you must admit them quickly and show them to me.
Having spoken thus, he lay down upon his bed. At that very moment, the king, while still lying on his bed, recalled the virtues of the wise Mahosadha, thinking:
"Since the time I was seven years old, the wise Mahosadha has served me..."
"He has done nothing harmful to me; even when the deity asked the question, had there not been a wise man, I would not have regained my life.
By taking the words of enemies and foes and giving him a sword, saying, 'Kill this peerless wise man,' I have acted improperly;
now tomorrow I shall no longer be able to see him," he said in grief.
He broke into tears; sweat broke out from his body. Overwhelmed by grief, he found no peace of mind.
Queen Udumbarā, who was lying on the same bed with him, seeing this state of affairs, thought:
"Is there perhaps some fault on my part, or has some cause for sorrow arisen for the King? I shall ask him now. She then spoke this verse:
“Why are you dejected, O best of kings, lord of bipeds? Let us hear this word of yours.
Thinking what are you so sorrowful? Surely, O Lord, there must be some fault on my part.
Then the king spoke this verse in reply:
“‘Mahosadha is to be executed for his answer,’ so was I commanded by you, O lady of great wisdom.
Thinking of that, I am dejected; for there is no fault on your part, O Queen.
In this passage, “commanded” means: “O Lady, the four wise men said, ‘Mahosadha is my enemy.’”

“Without having investigated the truth of the matter, I, though possessed of vast wisdom, was commanded to execute him, saying, ‘Kill him! It is because I am reflecting on that reason that I am dejected.
Upon hearing his words, a sorrow as great as a mountain arose within her out of affection for the Great Being.
Then she thought: “By some means, I shall comfort the king; and when the king has fallen asleep, [I will take] my younger brother...”
“I shall send a message. Then she said, “Great King, it was you who did this by establishing that householder’s son in great power;
he was appointed to the position of commander-in-chief by you, yet now, it seems, he has become your very own enemy. There is no such thing as a minor enemy—one must simply be slain. You—”
"Do not worry," he reassured the king. His grief having subsided, the king fell asleep.
The queen rose, entered her chamber, and said, "Dear Mahosadha, the four wise men have slandered you;
the king, being enraged, has ordered your execution at the city gate tomorrow. Do not come to the royal palace tomorrow; however, if you do come..."

“Having brought the city into your hands and become capable, you may come,” he wrote in a letter, placed it inside a sweetmeat (*modaka*), wrapped the sweetmeat with thread, put it in a new vessel, covered it, and sealed it.
He then gave it to his attendant maidservant, saying, “Take this sweetmeat and give it to my younger brother. She did so. [At night...]
"One should not wonder, 'How did she depart? For the king had already granted the queen a boon at the very beginning;
therefore, no one restrained her. The Bodhisatta, having accepted the gift, sent her away. She returned and reported that it had been given.
At that moment, the queen came and lay down with the king. The Great Being, for his part, broke open the sweetmeat."
Having read the leaf, understood the matter, and deliberated on what was to be done, he lay down upon his bed.
The other four men also took up their swords at dawn and stood by the doorway;
not seeing the wise man, they became dejected and went into the presence of the king. When the king asked, "Was the householder’s son killed by you, wise men? they replied:

“We do not see him, Your Majesty,” they replied. The Great Being, having brought the city into his own hands at the very break of dawn, established guards here and there, and surrounded by a great multitude, mounted his chariot and proceeded with a vast retinue to the royal gate.
The king stood watching outside, having opened the lion-window. Then the Great Being—
Having descended from his chariot, he paid homage to the king and stood before him. Seeing him, the king thought, "If this man were my enemy, he would not pay me homage.
Then, having summoned him, the king sat upon his throne.
The Great Being also sat down to one side, and the four wise men likewise sat down right there. Then the king, knowing nothing of him, [asked...]
As if saying, "Dear one, you went away yesterday and now you have returned; why do you abandon me? she spoke this verse:
"You have come back now after going at the end of the day; what have you heard that your mind is so anxious?
Who said what to you, O one of vast wisdom? Pray, let us hear it; tell us this."

In this context, "arrived at the end of the day" means he arrived just now after having gone [yesterday] during the first watch of the night. "What does he fear? means what does he suspect? "What did someone say? means that someone said to him, "Do not go into the presence of the king.
Then the Great Being, reproaching him, saying, "Great King, you took the word of the four wise men and ordered my execution; for that reason I do not come," spoke this verse:
"If it was your counsel, O Lord of Men, that Mahosadha was to be executed for a fault in answering a question..."
"I have heard from you a secret that was disclosed to me while you were in private with your wife.
Therein, "if by you" means because of you. "Counselled" means spoken. "At nightfall" means at the time of evening;
this is the meaning. To whom was it spoken? To his wife. For yesterday, while in private, you spoke this matter to her.
"Revealed her secret" means that she revealed such a secret of her own. "I heard it from her" means that I heard this at that very moment.
Upon hearing this, the king, thinking, "She must have sent a message at that very instant," looked at the queen with anger.
Having understood this, the Great Being said, "Why, O King, are you angry with the Queen? I know everything—past, future, and present.
Your own secret has been told to the Queen, but by whom was the secret of the teacher Senaka or of Pukkusa and the others told to me? I know their secrets as well. Thus he spoke first to Senaka.
While speaking of the secret matter, he spoke this verse:
“That evil deed which Senaka committed in the Sāla grove—
an unseemly act that he confided to his friend alone in private— that secret has been disclosed and heard by me.”
In that context, "unseemly" means he committed an ignoble, base, and unwholesome deed. For in this very city,
having performed sexual intercourse with a certain courtesan named So-and-so in the Sālavana grove, he killed her, took her ornaments,
made a bundle out of her very garment, and hung it on a peg in such-and-such a place in his own house.
He set it down. "As for 'by a friend,' O Great King, he then told this to one of his companions in private;
that too was heard by me. I am not the king's adversary; Senaka alone is. If you have business with an adversary, then have Senaka seized."

The king looked at Senaka and asked, "Is it true, Senaka? When Senaka replied, "It is true, Your Majesty," the king ordered him to be cast into prison. Then the wise man, while speaking of Pukkus's secret, spoke this verse:
"O Lord of Men, a disease has arisen for you that is unbecoming of a king;
what was spoken by your brother in private has been heard by me as a secret made public."
"In this regard, O Great King, 'unfit for the king' means that leprosy has arisen in him;
he is unfit to approach the king and is not worthy of being touched. And you, thinking 'Pukkusa's thigh is soft,' mostly lie down upon his thigh.
But this, O Lord, is merely the touch of a bandage-cloth over a wound."

The king, having observed him as well, asked, "Is it true, Pukkusa? When he replied, "It is true, Your Majesty," the king had him too cast into the prison. While the wise man was disclosing Kāmindaka’s secret, he spoke this verse:
"This is an unseemly affliction that Kāmindaka has suffered at the hands of the god among men;
what he told his son in private, that secret, has been heard by me and made public."

In that regard, "unseemly" means: "That disease by which he, when afflicted, cries out like a mad dog—that disease of humans, gods, and *yakkhas* is of an unseemly nature, wretched, and unfit for entering the royal palace, O Great King," he said.

The king, having looked at him as well, asked, "Is it true, Kāmindā? When she replied, "It is true, Your Majesty," he had her too cast into prison. While the wise man was telling the secret even to Devinda, he spoke this verse:
"Sakka gave you that noble eight-curved jewel, O Grandfather."
"Today that [jewel] has come into the hand of the Lord of Devas; in private, you spoke with my mother;
this secret, which was heard by me, has been made manifest.

In this context, "of the grandfather" means of your grandfather, King Kusa. "Today it has come into the hand" means that today, O Great King, that jewel-gem, esteemed as auspicious, has come into the hand of the Lord of Devas.
The king, having observed him as well, asked, "Is it true, O lord of gods? When he replied, "It is true, O King," the king had him too cast into prison.
Thus, intending to kill the Bodhisatta, they all entered the prison together.
The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, for this reason I say: 'One's own secret must not be told to another.'"
"I say this: those who speak [of such things] have met with great ruin. Having said this, he spoke these verses while further teaching the Dhamma:
"It is indeed good for a secret to remain secret; it is not praised to disclose a secret.
A wise person should endure what has not yet come to fruition; only when it has come to fruition should one speak as one pleases."
“One should not disclose a secret matter; one should guard it like a treasure.
For a wise person, a secret matter is not good when made public.
A wise man should not tell a secret to a woman, nor to an enemy.”
The man who is led astray by material gain, and the man who is a heart-thief;
the man who makes known a secret matter that was not understood— out of fear of the disclosure of his counsel,
one remains submissive and endures him as a servant.
“As many as there are counselors who know a man’s secret purpose, so many are his anxieties;
therefore, one should not disclose a secret.
One should speak of a secret during the day in seclusion, but at night one should not let one’s voice go beyond [the bounds of silence].”
"For eavesdroppers hear the secret counsel; therefore, counsel quickly leads to division.
In this context, "and to an enemy" means one should not speak to a woman or an adversary.

"To a flatterer" means one who is led astray by any kind of material gain, who praises one for the sake of favor, and who seeks to win one over—one should not confide in such a person either. "To one who has a hidden motive": [one should not speak].
And one should not confide even in a friend who is not a true friend but merely a counterfeit friend—one who says one thing with his mouth while thinking something else in his heart.
"Unknown" (*asambuddha*) means not known by others. There is also a reading, "unawakened" (*asambodha*), which means it is improper to awaken others [to that secret].
"He endures" means that he endures their abuse, insults, and even blows, acting like a slave.
He consents. "Counselors" (*mantinaṃ*) means those who have deliberated (*mantitaṃ*), or the meaning is: as many as there are among the counselors who know [the secret].
"So many" means that depending on those who know the secret, so many pangs of anxiety and terrors arise for him.
"Does not disclose" means he would not disclose it; he would not let another know. "In seclusion" means if, during the day, he wishes to deliberate on a secret matter, [he goes] to a secluded place.
Having obtained permission, one should consult in a well-sheltered place. Regarding "not excessively":
when speaking in secret at night, one should not release one's voice with excessive loudness that oversteps the bounds of propriety.
"Eavesdroppers" refers to those who, having approached the place of consultation, stand behind walls and so forth to listen. Therefore, O Great King, by that...
"For that reason, the counsel quickly came to ruin.
When the king heard the Great Being's words, he became enraged, thinking, "These men, being themselves enemies of the king, are making my wise counselor their enemy as well.
He then commanded, "Go, expel them from the city, impale them on stakes, or else cut off their heads!"

“Cut them off! he commanded. As they were being led away, their hands tied behind their backs and given a thousand lashes with whips at every four-way junction, the wise man said to the king, “Your Majesty, these are your former ministers; please forgive their offense.
Having heard his words, the king said, “Very well,” summoned them, and made them his own slaves.
Having done so, he gave them away. He, however, made them free men right there. The king, saying, "In that case, let them not dwell within my realm," ordered an act of banishment against them.
The wise man, saying, "Forgive, O King, the fault of these blind fools," asked for their pardon and restored their former positions. The king [thought], "Even toward his enemies..."
"Since such loving-kindness exists even toward these people, how could it not exist toward other beings? Thus he became exceedingly confident in the wise man.
From that time on, the four wise men became like venomless snakes whose fangs had been pulled out;
they were unable to say anything at all.
The Question of the Five Wise Men is finished. And the Discourse on Divisive Talk is finished.
The Section on Defeat in Battle.
From that time on, the wise man alone instructed the king in both worldly affairs and the Dhamma. He thought: "The king possesses only the white parasol;
as for the administration of the kingdom, I myself manage it. Therefore, I must be diligent.
He had a great wall built around the city, as well as an inner wall, gate-towers, intermediate towers, a moat of water, and a moat of mud.
Sukkha-parikhanti caused three moats to be constructed; he had dilapidated houses within the city repaired;
having caused great lotus ponds to be made, he established water reservoirs in them; he filled all the storehouses in the city with grain;
and from the Himalayan region, he had his personal ascetic attendants bring back seeds of kudrūsa and kumuda grass, as well as drainage channels for water.
Having had it cleaned, he had trees planted there; he also had the work of repairing dilapidated halls done outside the city. For what reason?
To ward off future dangers. He would ask the merchants who arrived from here and there, "Good sirs, from where have you come?
and when they replied, "From such-and-such a place," he would ask, "What is dear to your king?"
When he had been told, “He is named so-and-so,” [the king] honored them and sent them away. Then, having summoned his own one hundred warriors, he said:
“Gentlemen, take these gifts given by me, go to the one hundred royal capitals, and out of a desire for their friendship, present these gifts to those kings.
While attending upon them, learn either their conduct or their secret counsel.”
"Stay right there while sending word to me; I shall support your wives and children," he said.

Then, having engraved inscriptions upon the earrings of some, the sandals of others, the swords of others, and the golden garlands of others, saying, "When I have need of you, let these be recognized," he placed them in their hands and sent them forth.
Having gone here and there and presented gifts to those various kings, when they asked, "For what purpose have you come?", they replied, "We have come to attend upon you yourselves.
When asked, "From where have you come?", instead of stating their place of origin, they mentioned other places.
Once it was accepted with the words, "Very well then," they remained as attendants and became their intimate associates.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kapila, a king named Saṅkhabālaka prepared weapons and assembled an army.
A man stationed near him sent a message to the wise man:
"Sire, we do not know what will happen here—that 'this will be done'—but he is preparing weapons and assembling an army; you [should bring] distinguished men..."
"Having sent him, you must understand this situation as it truly is. Then the Great Being addressed the young parrot:
"Friend, in the kingdom of Kapila there is a king named Saṅkhabālaka who is preparing weapons;
go there, find out exactly what he is doing, and after wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, bring back news of my condition to me."
Having spoken thus, he had him fed with honey-lājās, given honey-water to drink, and anointed his wings for a fortnight with oils refined a hundred and a thousand times;
then, placing him in an eastern lion-cage, he released him.
He too, having gone there and learned the news of that king from the man exactly as it was, began surveying the whole of Jambudīpa and arrived in the kingdom of Kapila.
He arrived at the city of Uttarapañcāla. At that time, a king named Cūḷanibrahmadatta reigned there.
A brahmin named Kevaṭṭa served as his counselor for both worldly affairs and the Dhamma; he was wise and competent.
Having awakened at dawn and looking with the light of a lamp upon the royal chamber, which was adorned and prepared, he beheld his own great glory.
Having seen him, he thought, "Whose glory is this? Whose is it? Then he reflected, "It does not belong to anyone else; it belongs to Cūḷanibrahmadatta.
It is fitting that I make such a king, the bestower of such glory, the preeminent king of all Jambudīpa, and that I myself become his chief priest.
Having thought thus, he bathed, ate, and adorned himself early in the morning, and went into the presence of the king.

Having gone there, he asked after the king’s well-being, saying, "Great King, are you sleeping in comfort? When the king replied, "Yes, wise one," he said to the king, "Your Majesty, there is something that must be deliberated.
"Speak, teacher," [the king said]. "Your Majesty, it is not possible to find privacy within the city;
let us go to the park. "Very well, teacher," [said] the king, and he went with him.
Having gone to the park, he stationed his army outside, established a guard, and entered the park with the brahmin;
there he sat down upon the auspicious stone slab.
At that time, the young parrot, seeing this activity, thought: "There must be a reason for this; today something worthy of being told should be explained to the wise one."
Thinking, "I shall hear something," he entered the garden and sat down, hiding himself among the leaves of an auspicious *sāla* tree.
The king said, "Speak, teacher. "Great King, turn your ear toward this; the spell shall become four-eared.
If you, Great King, would act upon my words, you will become the preeminent king in all of Jambudīpa."
“I shall do so. Hearing his words, he was overcome by great craving and, filled with joy, said, “Speak, teacher;
I will do as you say. “Your Majesty, we shall assemble our army, first besiege the small city, and capture it.
For I myself will enter the city through the small gate and say to the king: ‘Great King, ...’”
“There is no need for you to fight; simply become a subject of our king, and your kingdom shall remain yours alone.
However, if you do fight, you will certainly be defeated because of the vastness of our army and forces. [He thought:
“If he follows my advice, we shall win him over. If not, having fought, I shall bring about his death.”

"Having seized two armies, we shall capture another city; from there, yet another"—by this means, having taken the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, they said, "We shall drink the wine of victory.
Having brought one hundred and one kings to our city and having had a drinking-pavilion constructed in the park, they seated them there, gave them liquor mixed with poison, and [all of them...]
“By bringing the kings to the end of their lives, we shall place sovereignty over the one hundred and one royal capitals into our own hands.
In this way, you will become the supreme king over the whole of Jambudīpa. He replied, “Excellent, teacher; I shall do so. [The teacher said:
“Great King, there is what is called the ‘Four-Eared’ mantra; for this mantra cannot be known by anyone else, therefore—”
“Without making delay, depart quickly! The king, being pleased, accepted it, saying, “Very well.
When the young crow heard this, at the conclusion of their counsel, as if letting down a hanging from a branch, he dropped a lump of dung onto the head of the fisherman.
As the fisherman opened his mouth, asking, “What is this? and looked upward, [the crow] let another [lump fall].
Having fallen into his mouth, crying out the sound "kiri kiri," he leapt from the branch and said, "Keṭṭha, you think you are a four-eared mantra;
but this very moment you have become six-eared, and having become eight-eared, you shall even become many hundreds of eared!
While they were still saying, 'Seize him! Seize him!', he went by the force of the wind to Mithilā, to the wise man."
He entered his residence. Now, this was his custom: if a message brought from anywhere was to be told only to the wise man, it would alight upon the shoulder of his neck;
if it was also to be heard by Queen Amarā, it would alight in her lap;
if it was to be heard by the great multitude, it would alight on the ground. At that time, it alighted upon the shoulder of the wise man.
"Let us descend. Because of that sign, the great multitude thought, "It must be a secret," and they departed.
The wise man took him, ascended to the upper terrace of the palace, and asked, "What have you seen or heard, my dear?
Then he replied to him, "Your Majesty, as I was wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, I saw no secret whatsoever in the presence of any other king; however, in the city of Uttarapañcāla—"
"But the brahmin named Kevaṭṭa, the chaplain of Cūḷani-Brahmadatta, led the king to the park and took up a four-cornered spell.
Then, sitting among the branches, I listened to their spell; at the conclusion of the spell, I dropped a lump of dung on his head and in his mouth, and then I came back.
Having said this, he told the whole story. "It was accepted by the king," [he added].
When this was said, he replied, “I accept it, O King.

Then the wise man, having performed the appropriate honors for him, laid him down comfortably upon a soft mattress within a golden cage and thought, “I suspect the fisherman does not know of my wisdom as Mahosadha; I shall—”

Thinking, "I shall show him how to bring this counsel to its ultimate conclusion," he had the poor families removed from the city and settled outside, while bringing wealthy and influential families from the gates of the kingdom and the country villages and settling them within the city;
he also caused much wealth and grain to be collected. Cūḷanibrahmadatta, too, having accepted the words of the fisherman—
Surrounded by his army, he went and besieged a certain small city.
Keṭaka, likewise entering there in the same manner, persuaded that king and made the city his own. Combining the two armies into one, they then held another city.
By this method, they captured all those cities in succession. Thus...
Cūḷanibrahmadatta, abiding by the advice of the fisherman, took possession of all the kings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, with the exception of the King of Vedeha.
Meanwhile, the spies stationed with the Bodhisatta constantly sent word back, saying: "So many cities have been seized by Cūḷanibrahmadatta; be vigilant! He, too, [acted] upon their [report].
“I dwell here with diligence; you too should dwell without longing and with diligence,” he sent back as a reply.
After seven years, seven months, and seven days, having abandoned the kingdom of Videha, Cūḷanibrahmadatta seized the remainder of the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
He then said to Kevaṭṭa: “Teacher, the kingdom of Videha in Mithilā—”
“Let us seize it. “Great King, we shall not be able to seize the kingdom in the city where the wise Mahosadha dwells.
For he is thus endowed with wisdom and thus skilled in expedients,” he said, explaining in detail and praising the virtues of Mahosadha as if raising up the lunar disk.
For he himself was likewise skilled in expedients; therefore, [he spoke of] the city of Mithilā...
"Your Majesty, sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa is but a trifle for us; what need have we for this?"—thus he made the king perceive the situation through skillful means.
The other kings also said, "We shall drink the wine of victory only after seizing the kingdom of Mithilā.
Kevaṭṭa restrained them as well, saying, "What shall we do with the kingdom of Videha? That king too belongs to us..."
"He is indeed your own; therefore, turn back. In this way, he awakened them through a skillful means. Having heard his words, they turned back.

The men stationed near the Great Being sent a message saying, "Brahmadatta, while on his way to Mithilā surrounded by one hundred kings, turned back and went to his own city. He too [instructed] them: "From now on..."
“Let them know his deed,” he sent word. Brahmadatta, too, consulted with the fisherman, “What shall we do now?
When the fisherman said, “We shall drink the drink of victory,” he had the pleasure garden adorned and commanded his servants:
“Place liquor in hundreds and thousands of jars, and bring various kinds of fish, meat, and other foods. Then the men stationed there—
They reported that news to the wise one. However, they did not know that he had mixed the liquor with poison, intending to kill the kings.

But the Great Being, having heard it from the young parrot and knowing it as it truly was, sent back a message saying, "Having learned the exact day on which they drink the liquor, send word to me. They did accordingly.
The wise man thought, "While one such as I is still living, it is improper for so many kings to die; I shall be their support.

Having reflected thus, he summoned his thousand co-born warriors and said, "Sirs, it is said that Cūḷanibrahmadatta has had a pleasure grove decorated and, surrounded by a hundred and one kings, desires to drink liquor. You should go there and [seize] the kings from their seats..."
While they are still seated at any of the designated seats, even before they have sat down, you should say, “Give this very costly seat next to that of Cūḷanī Brahmadatta to our king.
When those men ask you, “Whose men are you? you should say, “We are the men of the King of Videha.
Then, together with them, [you should say], “We [have been away] for seven days and seven months plus...”
"Those who have held the kingdom for seven years do not see even a single day's rule of the King of Videha; what is this so-called 'king'?
Go and take a seat at the edge!"—speaking thus, they will engage in quarreling.
Then you, increasing the dispute by saying, "Apart from Brahmadatta, there is no one else here superior to our king," [will cause trouble] for us.
Not receiving even a mere seat for the king, they cried out, "Now we shall no longer give you liquor to drink or fish and meat to eat!
Roaring, clamoring, and making a great din, they struck terror into them, smashed all the jars with large clods of earth and sticks,
scattered the fish and meat about, and rendered them unfit for use, then quickly entered the midst of the army.
"Having entered the city of the gods like Asuras who have caused a tumult to arise, announce your arrival by saying, 'We are the men of the wise Mahosadha in the city of Mithilā; seize us if you can!
and then come back. They accepted his words, saying "Very well," and after paying him homage, they equipped themselves with their five weapons.
Having departed and gone there, they entered the decorated park which was like the Nandana Grove;

and having seen the royal splendor prepared and adorned—beginning with the one hundred and one royal thrones under raised white parasols—they performed everything according to the procedure prescribed by the Mahāsatta.
Having agitated the great multitude, they set out toward Mithilā. The king’s men also...
They reported that occurrence to those kings. Cūḷanibrahmadatta was angry, thinking, "An obstacle has been placed in the way of such a victory for my realm.
The other kings were also angry, thinking, "He did not give us wine to drink in our triumph.
The army as well was angry, thinking, "We were not allowed to drink strong liquor without cause."

Having addressed those kings, Cūḷanibrahmadatta said, “Come, sirs, let us go to Mithilā, cut off the head of the King of Videha with a sword, trample it with our feet, sit down, and drink the wine of victory; meanwhile, prepare the army for the march.
Having spoken thus, he went into private again and told this same matter to Keṇiya as well, saying, “For one such as ours...”
"Let us seize the enemy who is creating obstacles for our counsel;
let us go surrounded by an army numbering one hundred and eight akṣauhiṇīs. Come, Master! he said. The brahmin, reflecting on his own wisdom, thought:
"It is impossible to defeat the wise Mahosadha; we ourselves shall be the ones to suffer shame. I will make him turn back."
"No," he replied. Then they said to him: "Great King, this is not the power of the King of Videha;

it is the stratagem of the wise Mahosadha. He is of great majesty, and Mithilā, protected by him, is like a cave guarded by a lion—it cannot be captured by anyone. It will only bring us shame; enough with going there."
But the King, intoxicated by the pride of his kshatriya status and the madness of sovereignty, said, "What can he do?
and set out surrounded by one hundred kings and accompanied by an army numbering eighteen akṣauhiṇīs.
Keṭubha, unable to make his own words accepted, thought, "It is improper for me to act in opposition to the king," and set out together with him. Those warriors also—
Having reached Mithilā in a single night, they informed the wise man of what had been accomplished.
They also sent a message to the man previously stationed there: "Cūḷanibrahmadatta, intending to capture the King of Videha, is approaching surrounded by one hundred and one kings;
let the wise man be vigilant! Today he has arrived at such-and-such a place; today he has arrived at such-and-such a place."
“Today he will reach the city,” they continued to send word to the wise man. Upon hearing this, the Great Being remained vigilant.
Meanwhile, King Videha heard through a succession of rumors that Brahmadatta was indeed coming to seize this city.
Then Brahmadatta, arriving at the very first watch of the night while a hundred thousand torches were being carried [before him], surrounded the entire city.
Having caused it to be encircled by ramparts of elephants, ramparts of chariots, and so forth, he stationed military units at various locations.
The people shouted, clapped their hands, whistled, danced, roared, and threatened.
They stood there making a great clamor. By the light of the lamps and the radiance of the ornaments, the entire city of Mithilā, extending for seven yojanas, was filled with a single glow.
With the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, and musical instruments, it was as if the very earth were about to split apart.
Hearing the tumultuous noise, the four wise men went into the presence of the king, not knowing [the cause], and said: "Great King,..."
"A tumultuous sound has arisen; we do not know what this is, but it is right to investigate," they said.
Hearing this, the king thought, "Could Cūḷanibrahmadatta have arrived?
Opening the lion-window and looking out, he recognized his arrival and, trembling with fear, cried, "There is no life for us; all of us are facing the end of our lives!"
“...he will bring [me] back,” he sat down conversing with them. But the Great Being, having realized her arrival, remained as fearless as a lion;

having arranged for protection throughout the entire city and thinking, “I shall comfort the king,” he ascended the royal residence and stood to one side. Upon seeing him, the king regained his composure and said, “Except for me...”
Thinking, "There is no one else capable of releasing me from this suffering except my son,
the wise Mahosadha," he spoke to him as they conversed:
"Brahmadatta has arrived here with his entire army, O Pañcāla!"
In the evening, the army of Pañcālī arrived, with Mahosadha as its immeasurable leader.
It was equipped with chariots and infantry, skilled in every form of combat;
it carried banners and sounded musical instruments, awakened by the beat of drums and the blast of conchs.
“Adorned with the ornaments of the science of metalwork, possessing banners and mounting on the left;
well-provided with craftsmen, it is firmly established by heroes.
Ten wise men of vast intelligence, who frequent secluded places, are said to be here.”
Mātā Ekādasī rules over Pañcālī for the king. Now,
there were one hundred illustrious kṣatriyas here who,
having been driven from their kingdom and being distressed, came under the sway of Pañcālī.
“As long as the king’s assailants, though they speak kindly against his will,
pursue the people of Pañcāla, they have gone there helplessly,
yet remaining in control. By that army, Mithilā was besieged on three sides.”
“The capital of the Videhas is being besieged on all sides by a trench.
Like stars appearing in the sky, it is surrounded on every side.
O Mahosadha, understand this: how will there be liberation?”

In that context, "with the entire army" means he had reportedly come together with the entire royal host of one hundred and eight kings, numbering eighteen *akṣauhiṇīs*. "Of Pañcālī" means belonging to King Pañcāla.
"Possessing streets" means it was provided with a multitude of carpenters who moved about taking building materials brought along the streets. "Possessing boats" means...
"Endowed with a body of troops moving in formation. "Skilled in all battles" means proficient in every kind of combat.
"Carrying away" means capable of entering the midst of the enemy army and bringing back the heads of the foe without being detected.
"Possessing sound" means not devoid of the ten sounds. "Awakened by drums and conchs" refers to [the cries] such as "Come! Go! Fight! and so forth, occurring therein.

Because it is impossible to make oneself understood through the breaking of words, but such tasks here are made known by the sounds of drums and conchs, it is called "awakening by drums and conchs" (*bherisaṅkhappabodhana*).
Regarding "the brilliance of metal-science ornaments" (*lohavijjālaṅkārābhā*): here, "metal-science" (*lohavijjā*) refers to the crafts of metalworking.

This is the name for items such as armor, leather mail, chain-mail, and bronze helmets, which are adorned with the seven precious gems. "Ornaments" (*alaṅkāra*) refers to the ornaments of kings, high ministers, and so forth.
Therefore, because she shines with both metallurgical arts and ornaments, the meaning here is "shining with metallurgical arts and ornaments" (*lohavijjālaṅkārābhāti*).
"Possessing banners" (*dhajinī*) means being endowed with banners raised upon chariots and other vehicles, which are brightened by various cloths and adorned with images of gold and so forth.
"Riding on the left" (*vāmarohinī*) means that those riding elephants and horses mount them from the left side; hence she is called "riding on the left."
They are so called because they are endowed with them; the meaning is that it is filled with immeasurable elephants and horses.
"By craftsmen" means it is well-endowed and well-filled by those who have attained mastery in the eighteen crafts, such as the craft of elephant-riding and the craft of horsemanship.
"By heroes," [the king says], "father, this army is indeed well-established by heroic warriors whose prowess is equal to that of lions."
They say that ten oblations were offered here for the army by the wise ones. "Of vast wisdom" means they were endowed with a wisdom as extensive as the earth.
"Fond of solitude" means they were habituated to going into seclusion; having sat in private, they were habituated to deliberating.
It is said that, being permitted to reflect for one or two days, they were capable of overturning the earth and grasping the sky. "On the eleventh."
It is said that the mother of the King of Pañcāla possessed even greater wisdom than those wise men. Acting as their chief on the eleventh day, she governed and commanded the army of the Pañcālas.
One day, it is said, a certain man took a measure of rice, a portion of cooked food, and a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Thinking, "I shall cross the river," he descended into the water; but having reached the middle of the river and being unable to cross, he spoke thus to the people standing on the bank:
"O friends, in my hand there is a bundle of rice, some cooked food, and a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Whatever among these pleases me, I will give away. Whoever is able, let him ferry me across. Then one man, endowed with great strength—
A man, having dressed himself in thick garments, waded into a river; [another] man took him by the hand, helped him across to the other shore, and said, "Give me what you owe me.
[The first man replied,] "Take a measure of rice or a bundle of cooked food.
"Friend, I rescued you without regard for my own life; I have no need for these things, give me a kahāpaṇa coin. [The second man said,] "I—" from here...
"I will give you whatever pleases me," he said; now, giving me whatever pleases me, he takes it if I desire it.
He spoke to someone standing nearby, who said to him, "He is giving you what he himself likes; take it.
He replied, "I will not take it," and taking it with him, he went to the court of justice to the judges.
He reported it. Having heard everything, they said exactly the same thing.
Unsatisfied with their judgment, he went into the presence of the king and reported the matter to him.

The king, having summoned the judges and heard the statements of both parties from them, being unable to decide the case, entrusted the matter to one who had entered the river and sacrificed his own life.
At that moment, the king’s mother, Queen Calākādevī, was sitting nearby.
Knowing that the king had reached a difficult decision, she said, "Dear son, having understood this case, you have judged it well. "Mother, I know only this much.
If you know more than that, then you yourself should judge it. She replied, "I shall do so," and...
Having summoned that man, he said, "Come, dear son, place all three things you hold in your hand upon the ground.
After having them placed one after another, he asked, "Dear son, what did you say about this while you were being carried away by the water?
When he replied, "I said, 'This is for my mother,'" he said, "In that case, take whichever you prefer. He [took] the purse of a thousand [pieces].
He took it. Then, after he had gone a short distance, she summoned him and asked, "Dear son, would a thousand [pieces] please you?
When he replied, "Yes, it would please me," she asked, "Dear son, did you not say to this man, 'I will give him whatever pleases me from here'?
When he said, "I did say so, Your Majesty," she said, "In that case, give this thousand to him."
Having said, "Give it," she caused it to be given. Weeping and lamenting, she gave it away. At that moment, the king and his ministers were pleased and broke into applause.
From then on, her wisdom became renowned everywhere.
Referring to her, the King of Videha said, "The Queen is the mother of the King."
“Khattiyā” means nobles. “Whose kingdoms were seized” means whose kingdoms had been seized and taken by Cūḷani Brahmadatta.
“Distressed” means terrified by the fear of death, seeing no other recourse to be taken.
“Fell under the power of the Pañcāla king” means they fell under the control of this King of Pañcāla; for here the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive. As far as—
"Those who act" (*takkarā*) refers to those who are able to carry out what the king says with their mouths.
"Have come under his control" (*vasino gatā*) means that they were previously independent, but now they have come under his power.

"Threefold-walled" (*tisandhi*) means it was first surrounded by a wall of elephants, then by a wall of chariots, then by a wall of horses, and then by a wall of infantry; it is [so called] because of these.

It is surrounded by four divisions and three junctions. For there is one junction between the elephants and the chariots, one junction between the chariots and the horses, and one junction between the horses and the infantry. "It is being dug around" (*parikhaññati*) means it is being excavated.
Indeed, they are digging all around as if desiring to uproot and seize this [fortress] right now. "The stars are appearing above," O dear one.
That army, surrounded on all sides, appears as if filled with stars above because of its many hundreds of thousands of torches.

"Understand this, dear Mahosadha Paṇḍita! From the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, there is no other wise man so skilled in means as you. True wisdom is indeed manifested in such situations; therefore—"
“You yourself must know how we may be delivered from this suffering.
Having heard these words of the king, the Great Being thought: “This king is exceedingly terrified by the fear of death.
Now, for one who is ill, a physician is a refuge; for one who is hungry, food; for one who is thirsty, water. For him as well, I—”
"There is no other refuge; I shall comfort him. Then the Great Being, roaring like a lion upon the surface of the emerald stone, said: "Do not fear, O Great King! Enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty.

Just as one might seize a clod of earth and drive away a crow, or take up a bow and drive away a monkey, I shall rout this army of eighteen akkhobhaṇīs, making it ownerless even as to the loincloths on their bellies. Having spoken thus, he uttered the ninth verse:
“Stretch out your feet, O King, enjoy sensual pleasures, and take your delight;
having abandoned the army of Pañcāla, Brahmadatta has fled.
The meaning of this is: “O King, stretch out your feet at your pleasure—those feet which are designated as the bliss of your own sovereignty—and while stretching them out...”
“Do not set your heart on battle; enjoy yourself and take delight in sensual pleasures. This Brahmadatta will abandon this army and flee.
Having thus reassured the king, the wise man paid his respects, departed from the royal palace, and had the festive drum beaten throughout the city.
He then addressed the citizens: “O sirs, do not worry. For seven days, [provide] garlands, perfumes, ointments, drinks, food, and so forth.”
Having prepared it, let the festival games begin. Let people here and there drink as much strong liquor as they wish;
let them play music, play instruments, shout, clap their hands, roar, dance, sing, and slap their arms.
Furthermore, the expenses for this shall be from my own resources. I am the wise man named Mahosadha; you shall see me!
"Let us show our power," they said. They did accordingly. At that time, those standing outside the city heard the sounds of singing, instrumental music, and so forth;
people entered the city through the small gate. Except for their enemies, they would not seize anyone they saw;
therefore, the movement of people was not cut off, and those who had entered the city saw the crowds intent on festive games.
Cūḷanibrahmadatta, too, having heard the clamor in the city, spoke thus to his ministers:
"Sirs, while we stand with an army of eighteen akkhobhiṇīs surrounding the city, there is no fear or trepidation among the city-dwellers;
instead, they are joyful and filled with gladness, clapping their hands, shouting, whistling, dancing, and singing. What is this? Then—
The men stationed there spoke falsely, saying: "Your Majesty, while we were entering the city by the small gate on some business, we saw a great crowd gathered for a festival and asked them:
'Friends, the kings of the whole of Jambudīpa have arrived and are standing surrounding your city; yet you are so utterly heedless—what is this?'"

They said this: “Friends, when our king was a prince, he had a wish that, while the entire city of Jambudīpa was surrounded by kings, he would hold a festival. Today that wish has reached its fulfillment;
therefore, having caused the festival drum to be beaten, he himself drinks the great draught upon the upper terrace.”
Having heard their words, the king became angry and commanded his army: "Sirs, go!
Quickly surround the city from every side, breach the moats, crush the ramparts, and break down the gates and watchtowers.
Having entered the city, take the heads of the multitude like gourds with carts—[the heads] of the King of Videha."
“Bring his head! Hearing this, the brave warriors, weapons in hand, approached the gate;
but being harassed by the wise man’s men through the pouring of gravel, sand, and mud, and the throwing of stones and other means, they retreated.
Even when they descended into the moat thinking, “We shall break down the wall,” those stationed on the inner battlements pierced them with spears, javelins, lances, and the like.

They bring about great destruction. The warriors of the wise [king] displayed hand gestures and other such signs to the warriors of Cūḷani-Brahmadatta, reviling, insulting, and threatening them in various ways:
"When you are exhausted and receive no food, you shall drink and eat a little! And they gave them lumps of fermented grain and spits of fish and meat.
Stretching out their necks, they drank and ate by themselves and walked back and forth on the terrace. The others, unable to do anything,
went to Cūḷanibrahmadatta and said, "Your Majesty, it is impossible for anyone other than those possessing psychic power to drive them out."
The king, having stayed for four or five days and seeing nothing worth seizing, asked the fisherman: "Teacher, we are unable to take the city;
not even one person is capable of approaching it. What should be done? The fisherman replied:
"Be at ease, Great King. A city is like water on the outside; we shall take it by means of exhausting its water. People..."
“Exhausted by the water, they will open the door,” he said. He agreed, thinking, “This is a means.
From that time on, they did not allow water to enter. The men stationed with the wise man wrote a letter, tied it to an arrow, and sent word of the situation.
By him, too, it had been commanded from the very beginning: “Whoever [finds] a letter on an arrow...”
“Whoever sees it, let him bring it to me. Then a certain man, having seen it, showed it to the wise man.
Understanding the situation, [the wise man thought], “They do not know my wisdom.
He split a sixty-cubit bamboo pole in two, had it cleaned until it was perfectly pure, then joined the two pieces back together again, bound them with hide, and smeared the top with mud.
Having had seeds of *kudrūsa* and water-lily brought from the Himālaya by powerful ascetics, he planted them in the mud on the bank of a lotus pond;
having had bamboo stakes placed over them, he filled [the area] with water.
In a single night they grew, and the flower, rising from the top of the bamboo, stood a cubit in height.
Then, having had it uprooted, he had his own men give it to them, saying, "Give this to Cūḷani-Brahmadatta.
They made a staff and a bracelet out of its stalks and threw them [to him], saying, "O you who serve at the feet of Brahmadatta, do not die of hunger!
Take this lotus, put it on as an ornament, and eat the stalk until your belly is full!"
One of the men placed at the disposal of the wise man stood up and seized him; then, having brought him before the king, they said, "Behold, Your Majesty, this man's staff!
Never before have we seen such a long staff.
When [the king] said, "Measure it," the wise man’s men measured the staff at sixty cubits and eighty cubits.
Having done so, they reported it. Again, when the king asked, "Where was this born?", one man told a lie and spoke thus:
"Your Majesty, one day, being thirsty, I entered the city through the small gate thinking, 'I will drink liquor.
I saw a great lotus pond prepared by the citizens for the purpose of water-sports; the great multitude sat upon boats..."
He gathers flowers. There, this [tree] has grown on the bank; however, for one grown in deep water, its trunk will be a hundred cubits long.
Having heard this, the king said to the fisherman: “Teacher, it is not possible to take this by means of draining the water; let us go by boat.”
“They will come,” [they said]. “In that case, Your Majesty, we shall take it when the grain is exhausted; for a city, by its very nature, has its grain outside.

“Let it be so, Teacher,” [the king replied]. The wise man, having understood the situation through his previous methods, thought, “The brahmin fisherman does not know my wisdom,” and so he made a mud-bank right on the edge of the rampart and had rice sown there. Of the Bodhisattas...
"The intention indeed succeeds": this means that after the rice had been harvested in a single night, it appeared blue upon the top of the rampart.
Seeing this, Cūḷanibrahmadatta asked, "Ho there! What is this that appears blue upon the top of the rampart?
The man stationed near the wise minister [replied], his tongue hanging out from his mouth at the king's words.

As if plucking it out, he seized him and said, "Your Majesty, the wise Mahosadha, having foreseen a future danger, previously had grain brought from the kingdom and filled the storehouses; he then had the remaining grain placed against the walls of the rampart.
It is said that those ears of grain, drying in the sun, were moistened by the rain and produced a crop right there. One day, I—"
