He reported: “One day, having entered through the small gate by means of a certain deed, I saw people standing on top of the wall taking rice from a heap with their hands and throwing it onto the street. Then, mocking me, they said, ‘I suppose you are hungry;
tie up some rice at the end of your robe, carry it home, pound it, have it cooked, and eat it! Thus he spoke.
Having heard this, King Kevaṭṭa said, "Teacher, it is not possible to capture him even by means of exhausting the grain; this too is no effective method.
"In that case, Your Majesty, we shall capture him by exhausting the timber; for a city, as it were, has its timber outside," he replied.
"So be it, Teacher," the king agreed. The wise man, having understood the situation through the previous method, [placed] rice upon the top of the rampart.
Having passed beyond it, he had a visible pile of wood constructed.
The men of the wise man, joking with the men of Cūḷani Brahmadatta, threw down very large logs, saying, "If you are hungry, cook and eat gruel and rice.
The king asked, "The wood is visible along the top of the wall; what is this?"
Having inquired, and having heard the report from those who had been left in charge— "Sire, it is said that the wise Mahosadha, having foreseen a future danger,
had timber brought and stored in the back rooms of the houses of various families, and the surplus was stored against the wall"—

and having thus heard the words from those very persons to whom the goods had been entrusted, he said to the fisherman: "Teacher, even by the exhaustion of the timber, we shall not be able to seize them."
“Bring forth a single stratagem,” [the king said]. “Do not worry, Great King; there is another stratagem,” [the teacher replied].
“Teacher, what indeed is this so-called stratagem? I see no end to your stratagem; we will not be able to capture Vedeha.
We shall simply go back to our own city. “Your Majesty, Cūḷanibrahmadatta, together with one hundred kṣatriyas...”
"It will be a source of shame for us if we are unable to capture the King of Videha;
however, while Mahosadha alone is wise, I too am indeed wise, so I shall devise a stratagem. "What is this 'stratagem,' teacher?
"We shall engage in what is called a 'righteous battle' (dhammayuddha), Your Majesty. "And what is this so-called 'righteous battle'? "Great King..."
The armies will not fight; rather, two wise men from the two kings will be in one place.
Whichever of them he pays homage to, that one shall suffer defeat. However, Mahosadha does not know this spell.
"I am old and he is young; upon seeing me, he will surely pay homage. Then Videha will be known as the defeated one."
"Now, having defeated Videha, we shall go back to our own city; in this way, there will be no cause for shame.
This is what is called a 'righteous war' (dhammayuddha).
The wise man, having understood that secret as well through the same method as before, thought: "If I am defeated by Kevaṭṭa, I am not a wise man."
He thought thus. Cūḷanibrahmadatta also said, “A splendid plan, teacher! and had a letter written stating: “Tomorrow there shall be a battle of righteousness;
the victory or defeat of both wise men shall be according to righteousness. Whoever does not engage in the battle of righteousness shall also be considered defeated.
Having thus written the letter, [he sent it] to the King of Videha through the small gate.
He sent [the message]. Having heard it, Vedeha summoned a wise man and explained the matter to him.
Upon hearing the news, the wise man said, “Excellent, Your Majesty! Tomorrow morning at dawn, they will prepare the arena for the Dharma-battle at the western gate;
send word saying, ‘Let them come to the arena of the Dharma-battle. Having heard this, the king [sent the message] to the messenger who had already arrived.
He placed the betel leaf in his hand. On the following day, the Wise One prepared a circle for a righteous battle at the western gate, thinking, "Let there be defeat for the fisherman alone.

Those one hundred men, wondering "Who knows what will happen?", surrounded the fisherman for the sake of protecting the Wise One. Those one hundred kings [also went] to the circle for the righteous battle.
Having gone there, they stood looking toward the eastern direction; the Brahmin Kevaṭṭa did likewise.

But the Bodhisatta, having bathed early in the morning with scented water, put on a Kāsika cloth worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, adorned himself with all his ornaments, and eaten various kinds of choice food, went to the palace gate with a great retinue.
Having gone there, when he was told, "Let my son enter," he entered, paid homage to the king, and stood to one side.
When asked, "Where are you going, dear? he replied, "I am going to the arena of the Dhamma-battle.
"What do you wish to obtain? [the king asked]. "Your Majesty, I wish to deceive the brahmin Kevaṭṭa with the jewel-treasure; I wish to obtain the eight-curved jewel-treasure."
“It is fitting,” he said. “Take it, dear one,” [the king replied].

Having taken it and paid homage to the king, he descended from the royal palace and, surrounded by his kinsmen and a thousand warriors, mounted an excellent chariot yoked with white Sindh horses worth ninety thousand kahāpaṇas.
At the hour of the morning meal, he arrived near the city gate. Meanwhile, Kaṭṭhavaṇṭa thought, “He will arrive now.”
Thinking, "He will arrive now," he stood waiting for her arrival;
from his constant gazing, he appeared as if he had grown a long neck, and beads of sweat were released by the heat of the sun.
The Great Being, like the great ocean overflowing due to his vast retinue, remained undaunted and free from horripilation like a maned lion, and having caused the gate to be opened—
Having departed from the city and descended from his chariot, he set forth, stretching out his limbs like a lion.

When even the one hundred and one kings beheld the splendor of his form, they raised thousands of shouts of acclaim, saying, "This is indeed the son of the merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, the wise Mahosadha, who is peerless in wisdom throughout all Jambudīpa."
He too, like Sakka surrounded by a host of gods, went toward the fisherman, holding that jewel-treasure in his hand with incomparable splendor and majesty.
Upon seeing him, the fisherman was unable to maintain his composure; he went out to meet him and said:
"O wise Mahosadha, we two are both wise men, and it is by depending on you that we have attained all this."
“Kāla, during your time as residents here, you have never before sent even a mere token gift; why have you acted thus?
Then the Great Being said to him, “O wise one, while looking for a gift worthy of you, we have today obtained this jewel-treasure.
Come, take this jewel-treasure; indeed, there is no other such as this.”

“There is no jewel-treasure,” he said. Seeing the flaming jewel-treasure in his hand, the other thought, “He must wish to give it to me,” and extending his hand, said, “In that case, wise one, give it.
The Great Being said, “Take it, Teacher,” and having hurled it, caused it to fall upon the fingers of the outstretched hand. The brahmin [caught] the heavy jewel-treasure...
He was unable to hold it with his fingers. The jewel slipped away and fell at the feet of the Great Being.
Out of greed, the brahmin bent down at his feet, thinking, "I shall take it.
Then the Great Being, not allowing him to rise, seized him by the collarbone with one hand and by the back of the neck with the other, saying, "Rise up, Teacher!"
"Stand up, teacher! I am far too young for you, being merely your grandson; do not bow down to me," he said.
As he spoke, he rolled back and forth, striking his face against the ground until it was smeared with blood.
Then, saying, "You blind fool, you expect a salutation from me! he seized him by the neck and threw him down. He fell at a distance of the length of a bull.
Having fallen down, he rose and fled. As for the jewel-treasure, the men seized it for the Great Being himself.
But the voice of the Bodhisatta’s words—“Rise up, Teacher! Rise up, Teacher!
Do not worship me!”—stood resounding, covering the entire assembly. The men also [recognized him], thinking, “The Brahmin fisherman is prostrating at the feet of Mahosadha.”

All at once, they raised a great clamor and so forth. Starting with Brahmadatta, all those kings saw Keṭaka bowing down at the feet of the Great Being. Thinking, "Our wise minister Mahosadha has been saluted;
now we are defeated, and he will not spare our lives," they each mounted their horses and set out toward Uttara-Pañcāla.
They began to flee. Seeing them fleeing, the men of the Bodhisatta raised a great shout once more, crying out, "Cūḷanibrahmadatta is fleeing, having seized a hundred and one khattiyas!
Hearing this, those kings, terrified by the fear of death, broke ranks as they fled even more desperately.
The men of the Bodhisatta also roared and shouted even more loudly.
A great clamor arose. The Great Being, surrounded by his military forces, entered the city itself.
Cūḷanibrahmadatta’s army also advanced for a distance of three leagues.
Kevaṭṭa, having mounted his horse and wiping the blood from his forehead, reached the army while still seated upon the horse's back.
“Sirs, do not flee! Sirs, do not flee! I am not bowing to the householder’s son; stop, stop! he cried.
The army, not believing him, did not halt but continued on, reviling and abusing the fisherman as he approached:
“O man of evil nature, wicked brahmin! Having said, ‘I will wage a righteous war,’ you have not even waited for the night to pass.”
"Pay homage; there is nothing more for you to do," they said, and continued on their way as if they had not heard his words.
He went with great speed, reached the army, and said, "Sirs, believe my words! I did not pay homage to him; he deceived me with that jewel-treasure.
Having thus awakened all those kings by various means, he caused them to accept his account.

In that manner, he turned back the broken army. Now, if that vast army had taken up each handful of dust or each clod of earth and thrown it toward the city, it would have formed a heap as large as the ramparts, filling the moat.
However, the intentions of the Bodhisattas always succeed; therefore, not even a single handful of dust [was lost].
Nor was there anyone who threw a clod of earth toward the city; indeed, they all turned back and returned to their respective camps.
The King asked Ke vaṭṭa, "What shall we do, Teacher? "Your Majesty, for anyone to exit through the small gate—"
“Let us cut off the passage without giving it; when the people, unable to exit, become distressed, they will open the gate, and then we shall capture our enemies.
The wise man, having understood that situation in the same manner as before, thought:
“If these people remain here for a long time, there will be no peace at all. It is necessary to make them flee by some stratagem.”
Thinking, "I shall cause him to flee by means of a charm," he looked for someone skilled in charms.
Seeing a brahmin named Anukevaṭṭa, he summoned him and said, "Teacher, it is necessary for us to perform a certain rite.
"What shall we do, wise one? Speak," [the other replied]. "Teacher, standing on the bank of the Anupākāra river, [you must act] toward our people..."
Observing their negligence, he would from time to time throw cakes, fish, meat, and other foods to Brahmadatta’s men, saying:
"Ho! Eat this and that; do not be despondent. Strive to stay for another few days;
like city-dwellers’ chickens bound in a cage, you will soon become weary, and they will open the door for you. Then you..."
“...you shall seize both Vedeha and the wicked householder’s son.
When our men heard those words, they reviled and threatened you, and right before the eyes of Brahmadatta’s men, they seized you by your hands and feet as if striking you with bamboo splinters;
they shaved your hair, had the five top-knots bound, and [covered you] with brick-dust.

Having had him smeared with [ashes], having placed a garland of *kaṇavīra* flowers upon his ear, having given him several blows so as to show streaks on his back, having made him climb over the wall, and having placed him in a swing-basket and lowered him down by means of a rope, they will say, "Go, you traitor! You are a thief!
and they will present him to the people of Cūḷani-Brahmadatta. They will bring him into the presence of the king. The king—
Upon seeing me, he will ask, "What is your offense? Then you should say to him: "Great King, previously my reputation was great;

[the king], having become angry with me for being a householder’s son who betrayed his counsel, told the king and confiscated all my wealth, saying, 'I shall have the head of this householder’s son, who betrayed my reputation, taken.'"
“By releasing you humans from your longing, I shall give these standing ones either soft food or hard food.
It was because of this that he, harboring ancient enmity in his heart, brought me to such calamity.
‘Your people know all of that, O Great King’—having made him believe this through various means, when confidence has arisen, you should speak.”
“Great King, from the moment you obtained me, do not worry. Now the life of both Vedeha and the householder’s son is at an end.
I know the strong and weak spots of the city walls here, as well as where crocodiles and other predators exist in the moat and where they do not; before long, we shall capture your city.”
“I will give it. Then that king, having placed his trust in you, will honor you and assign you the command of his army.
You should then lead his army into places inhabited by fierce crocodiles. His army, out of fear of the crocodiles, will not advance;
at that time, you should approach the king and say, “O King, [the son of a householder] from your army...”
"Bribery has been given; indeed, there is no king, starting from the royal preceptor and the courtiers, who has not taken a bribe.
These men merely follow you as your retinue, but they all belong to the householder’s son alone;
I am the only one among you who is truly yours. If you do not believe me, let all the kings adorn themselves and come to see me."

“Let them come,” you should send [messengers]. Then, when they have seen the letters on the garments, ornaments, swords, and so forth—which the householder’s son had written with his own name and form and given to them—they should reach a conclusion, you should say.
He, having done so and seeing those [letters], reached a conclusion; then, terrified and trembling, he dismissed those kings and thought, “Now what shall we do?”
If he asks you, "Are you wise?", you should say to him: "Great King, this householder’s son is full of deceit.
If you stay for a few more days, he will bring your entire army into his own hands and capture you.
Therefore, without delay, this very day, during the middle watch of the night, mount the backs of horses..."
“Having sat down, we shall flee; let there not be death for us at the hands of others. Having heard your words, he will do accordingly.
At the time of his fleeing, you must turn back and inform our men.
Hearing this, the brahmin Anukevaṭṭa said, “Excellent, wise man! I shall do as you say. “In that case—”
“Only a few blows are worth enduring,” he said. “O wise one, setting aside my life and my hands and feet, do with the rest as you please.
He then had the people in his house perform an honorific reception for him, but following the previously mentioned method, he brought about a state of ruin.
Having lowered him by means of a rope, he had him handed over to the men of Brahmadatta. Then—
They took him and presented him to the king. The king, having tested him and gained confidence in him, paid him honor and assigned him the army.
He, too, landed them in the very places where the fierce crocodiles dwelt.
While being devoured by the crocodiles and pierced by spears, javelins, and lances from men stationed on the watchtowers, the people met with great destruction.
From that time on, no one was able to approach out of fear. Anukevaṭṭa approached the king and said, "There are none who will fight for your sake;
everyone has taken bribes. Do not believe them, but summon them and examine the letters on their undergarments and other clothes.
The king did so, and [he saw] the letters on the clothes of all of them.
Having seen the letters and reaching the conclusion, "Surely a bribe has been taken by these men," he asked, "Teacher, what should be done now? [The teacher replied:
"Your Majesty, there is nothing else to be done. If you make a delay, the householder’s son will seize you;
even the teacher Ācariyaka-vaṭṭa wanders about with nothing but a wound on his forehead, yet even he took a bribe."
“He has been captured. For he took this jewel-treasure and caused you to flee three leagues; then, having inspired confidence in you again, he brought you back—this man too is a traitor.
Even staying for a single night is not pleasing to me; it is fitting to flee this very day, immediately following the middle watch of the night.
There is no one else so well-disposed toward you as I am. When this was said, [he replied]: “In that case,”
"Teacher, please prepare my carriage yourself," he said.

Knowing from his resolve that the king intended to flee, the brahmin comforted him, saying, "Do not fear, Great King," and then went outside to instruct the guards stationed there: "The king will flee today; do not fall asleep!"
Just as a horse that has been broken in by the king runs even better when pulled, so too, having prepared him through this training, he said at the end of the middle watch:
"The horse is ready, Your Majesty; know the time. The king mounted the horse and fled.
Anukēvaṭṭa also mounted the horse and, as if going along with him, traveled a short distance.
He turned back. Having had his horse prepared for the escape, he fled while being dragged along, seizing the king.
Anukevaṭṭa entered the midst of the army and raised a shout, crying out, "Cūḷanibrahmadatta has fled!
The men stationed as scouts also shouted together with their own people. Hearing this, the remaining kings said, "The wise Mahosadha has opened the gate..."
“Having opened [the gates], he will come out; now he will not spare our lives. Terrified and trembling, they fled hither and thither without even looking back at their goods for enjoyment and use.
Hearing this, the people shouted all the more loudly, crying, “The kings are fleeing!
Upon hearing that, even those standing at the gates, watchtowers, and other places raised a great clamor and clapped their hands. Thus, at that moment, the earth—
As if splitting apart and as turbulent as the ocean, the entire city, both inside and out, became one great roar.

Eighteen *akkhobhaṇī* (one hundred and eighty million) people, terrified by the fear of death at the thought that "the wise Mahosadha has captured Brahmadatta and the one hundred and one kings," fled, abandoning even the loincloths they wore around their waists.
The royal camp became empty. Cūḷanibrahmadatto took one hundred khattiyas and returned to his own city.
On the following day, however, at dawn, they opened the city gates;
the military forces emerged from the city and, seeing the great devastation, cried out, "What shall we do, O wise ones? and informed the Mahāsatta. He said: "By these..."
“The abandoned wealth shall come to us; that which belongs to all other kings shall belong to our king. Give it!
Bring to us what belongs to the merchants and to the brāhmaṇa fisherman, but let the remaining citizens take for themselves.
While they were bringing only the most precious jewel-treasures, half a month passed. As for the rest—
However, they brought them after four months. The Great Being paid great honor to Anukevaṭṭa.
From that time on, it is said, the inhabitants of Mithilā became very wealthy in gold and bullion.
A year also passed while Brahmadatta was living with those kings in the city of Uttarapañcāla.
The section on Brahmadatta’s defeat in battle is finished. Now, as for the section on the fisherman:
one day, while the fisherman was looking at his face in a mirror, he saw a scar on his forehead and thought, “This belongs to the householder’s son.”
Thinking, "This is the result of my own karma; for that reason, I have been put to shame in the presence of so many kings," he became filled with anger.
Pondering, "When indeed shall I be able to see his back? he thought, "There is this means:
our king has a daughter named Pañcālacandī, who possesses supreme beauty and resembles a celestial nymph. To the King of Videha..."
Having said, "We shall give it," they resolved, "By enticing Vedeha with desire, we will bring him here together with Mahosadha like a fish that has swallowed a hook;
then, having killed them both, we will drink the drink of victory. Approaching the king, they said, "Your Majesty, there is a certain incantation.
[The king asked,] "Teacher, relying on your incantation, even for one whose loincloth is bound to his belly..."
“Since you have been born without a master, what will you do now? Be silent! “Great King, there is no other means like this.
“In that case, speak it. “Great King, it is fitting that we two alone should be together. “So be it.
Then the brahmin, having led him up to the upper terrace of the palace, said: “Great King, [regarding] the King of Videha...”
“Having enticed her with passion and brought her here, we shall kill her together with the householder’s son. “It is a clever plan, teacher;
but how shall we entice her and bring her here? “Great King, your daughter Pañcālacandī possesses supreme beauty.
Having had poets compose songs about the excellence of her form and her graceful charms, [recite] those—”

Having had verses composed in Mithilā, I shall go there myself and settle the matter on the day [of his marriage], knowing that his heart is already bound by the mere sound of those verses, thinking, "What is the use of sovereignty to the King of Videha if he does not obtain such a jewel of a woman?
When I have settled the day and arrived, he will be like a fish that has swallowed the hook.
“Once we have captured the householder’s son, we shall then put them both to death.
When the king heard his words, he was pleased and accepted the proposal, saying, “A clever stratagem, teacher; we shall do so.
However, the female myna bird who guarded the bedchamber of Cūḷanī Brahmadatta overheard that counsel and made it known to him directly. The king—
Having summoned skilled poets and given them much wealth, he showed his daughter to them and said, "Sirs, compose verses based upon her physical beauty.
They composed most enchanting songs and recited them for the king.
The king was pleased and gave them much wealth. Having learned from the presence of the poets, the actors...
They sang in the center of the assembly. Thus, those [songs] became widespread.
When they had become widespread among the people, the king summoned the singers and said:
"Sirs, having caught large birds, you climbed a tree during the night and sang while seated there; then at dawn, you fastened bronze cymbals around their necks."
“Lift them up and descend! It is said that he caused this to be done in order to make it known that even the deities sing of the beauty of the daughter of the King of Pañcāla.
Again, the king summoned the poets and said, “Sirs, now you must declare:
‘A maiden of such beauty as this is not fit for any other king on the surface of Jambudīpa; she is worthy only of the King of Videha in Mithilā.’”
“Compose songs that are appropriate, extolling both the king’s sovereignty and her beauty,” he said.
They did so and reported it to the king.
The king gave them wealth and, having summoned the singers again, said, “Sirs, go to Mithilā and there, with this very [method]...”
“Sing with skill,” he sent them. Singing those songs, they gradually reached Mithilā and sang in the arena of the festival.
Hearing them, the great multitude raised thousands of shouts of acclaim and gave them much wealth.
At nightfall, they sang even among the trees, and at dawn, they tied bronze cymbals to the necks of birds.

They descended. Upon hearing the sound of bronze cymbals in the sky, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city, saying, "Even the deities are singing the praises of the beauty of the daughter of the King of Pañcāla!
When the king heard this, he summoned the singers and held a festival within his palace;
being delighted by the thought, "It is said that King Cūḷani desires to give me such a daughter, endowed with the most excellent form," he was satisfied.
He gave them much wealth. They returned and reported this to Brahmadatta.
Then Kevaṭṭa said to him, “Now, Great King, I shall go for the purpose of making arrangements for the day. “Very well, Teacher; what should be obtained?
“A small gift,” he replied. “Then take it,” the king ordered, and had it given to him. He took it and departed.
With a great retinue, he arrived at the kingdom of Videha. Upon hearing of his arrival, a great clamor arose in the city:
"It is said that King Cūḷani and the King of Videha will establish a bond of friendship;
King Cūḷani will give his daughter to our king, and Keṭaka comes to fix the auspicious day. Both the King of Videha and the Great Being heard this as well.
Upon hearing this, he thought: "Her arrival does not please me; I shall find out the truth of the matter.
He sent a message to the men stationed near Cūḷani, saying: "Having ascertained this matter as it truly is, send word back to me.
Then they replied: "We do not know this as it truly is; King Keṭaka and [Cūḷani] are in the bedchamber."
“Having sat down, they will deliberate; however, the parrot bird who is the king’s bed-guardian will know this matter,” they sent back in reply.

Hearing that, the Great Being thought: “I shall not allow Keṭaka to see the city, which has been so well-apportioned and well-prepared, unless I ensure that no opportunity arises for my enemies. He [then left] from the city gate.
From the royal palace to his own residence, and from the royal palace back to his own residence, he had the path for travel enclosed on both sides with screens of reeds,
covered at the top with reed screens, had murals painted upon them, scattered flowers on the ground,
set out full water-jars, tied up plantain trees, and raised victory banners.
Kevaṭṭa, having entered the city and not seeing it properly laid out, thought, "The king has had the road decorated for me," and did not realize that the city had been made invisible.
He went on, saw the king, presented his gift, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side; then, having received the honor and hospitality shown by the king, he stated the purpose of his visit.
Proclaiming this, he spoke two verses:
“The king, desiring your friendship, bestows these jewels upon you;
let messengers come from here, sweet-voiced and pleasant of speech.”
“Let them speak gentle words, words that are welcomed in return;
let both Pañcāla and Videha become one.
Therein, “desirous of intimacy,” O Great King, means that our king wishes to establish a friendship and intimacy with you.
"Under the 'Policy of Jewels,' beginning with his own daughter, the Jewel of Women, he will show you all his jewels.

Let them come!"—this means that from now on, let messengers who speak sweet words and pleasant speech come here from the city of Uttarapañcāla taking gifts, and let them go from here to there. "Let them be one"—this refers to the water of the Ganges.
“...as if merging with the waters of the Yamunā, let them become exactly one and the same. Having spoken thus, he said:

“Great King, although our king wished to send another high minister, thinking, ‘No other will be able to deliver the message so pleasingly,’ he sent me, saying: ‘Teacher, you [must go] to the king...’”
"Having thoroughly awakened her, take her and come! he said. "Go, O best of kings; you will obtain a maiden of beautiful form, and our friendship with the king will be firmly established.
Having heard his words, the king was delighted in mind, thinking, "I shall indeed obtain a maiden possessing supreme beauty," through the influence of what he had heard.
Having bound him, he said, “Teacher, it seems there was a dispute between you and the wise man Mahosadha in a battle of wits.
Go and see my son; let both wise men apologize to one another, consult together, and then return.
Hearing this, Kevaṭṭa thought, “I shall see the wise man,” and went to see him. The Great Being also—
On that day, thinking, "May there be no conversation with that man of evil character," she drank a little ghee early in the morning;
she had her house smeared thickly with fresh cow dung, anointed the pillars with oil,
and having set aside his bed for him to lie upon, she had all the other beds, chairs, and such removed.
So he gave instructions to the people: "Sirs, when the brahmins begin to speak, you should say, 'Brahmin, do not converse with the wise man;
today he has drunk sharp ghee. And even while I am engaged in conversation with him, you should say to me, 'Your Majesty, you have drunk sharp ghee; do not speak.'"
“...keep him away. Having reflected thus, the Great Being put on his crimson robe, stationed men at the seven gate-towers, and lay down upon the first couch at the seventh gate-tower.
Keṇiya stood at the first gate-tower and asked, “Where is the Wise One? Then those men said to him, “Brahmin, do not make a noise; even if...”
"Desiring to come, come silently; today the wise man has drunk sharp ghee, so it is not permitted to make a loud noise," they said.
They spoke to him in the same manner at all the other gate-towers as well.
Having passed through the seventh gate-tower, he went into the presence of the wise man. The wise man made a sign for him to speak. Then those people—
“Your Majesty, do not speak; you have drunk sharp ghee. What is the use of speaking with this wicked brahmin?
Having said this, they restrained him. Thus, when he went into his presence, he could find neither a place to sit nor a spot to stand leaning against a seat;
he stood there having stepped upon fresh cow dung.
Then, having observed him, one closed his eyes, another raised his eyebrows, and another scratched his elbow.
Observing their behavior, he became abashed and said, "I am going, O wise ones. When another replied, "Hey, you wicked brahmin!
Though told 'do not make a sound,' you make even more noise; I shall break your bones! he became terrified and trembling with fear.

Having offered the oblation, he turned back and looked. Then another struck him on the back with a bamboo scraper, another seized him by the neck and threw him down, and another struck him on the back with the palm of his hand.
Like a deer released from the jaws of a leopard, he emerged terrified and trembling and went to the royal palace.
The king thought, "Today my son must have been delighted upon hearing this news."
"Something great will happen; there must be a great discussion on the Dhamma between these two wise men. Today they will both ask one another for forgiveness.
What a gain this is for me! Seeing Kevaṭṭa, he spoke this verse, asking about the manner of his meeting with the wise man:
“Tell me now, Keṭubha, how was the meeting with Mahosadha? Pray, tell me this:
has he been appeased by you, and is Mahosadha satisfied? In this context, *paṭinijjhatto* means:
was he appeased for the sake of pacifying the conflict that had arisen on the field of the righteous battle (*dhammayuddha*)?
"You [were] appeased by him, and he was appeased by you. "Is he pleased? means: "Is he pleased having heard the news sent by your king?
Having heard that, the fisherman spoke this verse: "Great King, you wander about taking him along, thinking 'he is wise'; yet there is no one more of an unvirtuous person than he."
“O Lord of Men, this man is of ignoble form: he is unfriendly, stubborn, and unrefined;
like one who is mute and deaf, he did not speak a single word of meaning.

In this passage, “unrefined” means one of an unintelligent nature. “He did not speak a single word of meaning” means he did not discuss any matter with me; for that very reason, [the king] spoke of the Bodhisatta’s lack of virtue, thinking, “I consider him to be unintelligent.”

The king, neither rejoicing in his words nor rejecting them, provided him and those who had come with him with travel expenses and lodging, and having dismissed him, saying, "Go, teacher, rest," he thought:
"My son is wise and skilled in hospitality; it is said that he did not even offer such hospitality to this man."
He did not express his satisfaction. "He must have seen some future danger," [the king] thought, and he himself initiated the conversation:
"Surely this line of the mantra is very difficult to perceive; its pure meaning has been seen by the heroism of a man.
For even my body trembles; having abandoned it myself, who would deliver it into the hands of another?"
In this context, "this" refers to that which was seen by my son; surely this line of the mantra is very difficult for any other ordinary man to perceive.
"By human effort" means that the wise Mahosadha, being possessed of heroic energy, must have perceived the pure meaning.
"He himself"—having abandoned his own kingdom, who else would go into the hands of another?
"Something must have been seen by my son regarding the coming of the brahmin. For he is not coming out of friendship;

rather, having come with the intention of luring me with desire, leading me to the city, and taking me away, that wise man must have perceived this future danger. Having reflected on this matter, he became terrified and trembling.

While he was seated, the four wise men arrived. The king asked Senaka, "Senaka, do you approve of going to the city of Uttarapañcāla to bring back the daughter of King Cūḷani? "What would you say, Great King?
It is not right to strike away prosperity when it arrives with a staff. If you go there and take her, setting aside—"
"O Cūḷanibrahmadatta, there shall be no one else on the surface of Jambudīpa equal to you. Why is that?
Because his eldest royal daughter has been taken by you. For he thought, 'The other kings are my subjects;

Vedeha alone is my equal,' and thus he became desirous of giving his daughter, who possesses the most excellent beauty in all of Jambudīpa, to you. You must follow his word. We too [shall support] you..."
“Relying on this, we shall obtain clothes and ornaments. The king questioned the others as well, and they spoke in the same manner.

Even as he was conversing with them, the brahmin Kevaṭṭa emerged from his own residence and, arriving with the thought, “I will go after addressing the king,” said: “Great King, we cannot afford to delay; we must go.”
“We are your subjects, O Lord of Men,” he said. The king, having paid him honor, dismissed him.
The Great Being, knowing that he was about to depart, bathed, adorned himself, and came to attend upon the king; having paid homage to the king, he sat down to one side.
The king thought: “My son is the wise Mahosadha, the great minister who has mastered the sciences and possesses knowledge of the past, future, and present.”
“He knows the matter. A wise man will know whether it is appropriate or inappropriate for us to go there.
Without stating his own initial thought, being intoxicated by passion and deluded by folly, he asked him, speaking this verse:
“For those who are wise, having attained the highest and most abundant success, their judgment is indeed one and the same.”
“Whether it be a vehicle, a non-vehicle, or even a standing place, you too, Mahosadha, should apply your mind.
In this regard, O wise one, “of the six”— that is, of the brahmin Kevaṭṭa, myself, and these four—
our single thought and our single intention flow together and coincide like the waters of the Gaṅgā with the waters of the Yamunā.
"We six wise men, who have attained the highest and most abundant success, all agree that the bringing of Cūḷanī, the daughter of the king, is desirable.
As for the 'place,' our residence shall be right here. Make your decision"—meaning, "our own preference is not the sole authority;
you too must consider whether there should be a vehicle for us to go there for the sake of the marriage, or rather no vehicle."
“‘To dwell right here is what pleases me.

Having heard this, the wise man thought: ‘This king is excessively greedy for sensual pleasures and, out of blind folly, accepts the words of these four men. I shall speak of the dangers in going and cause him to turn back. Having thus reflected, he spoke these four verses:
“You surely know, O King of great majesty, that Cūḷani Brahmadatta is exceedingly powerful.”
And the king desires his death, just as a hunter seeks a deer by following its tracks.
Just as a fish, greedy for raw flesh, does not perceive its own death when it swallows the hook concealed by meat.
“Just so, O King, you who are greedy for the daughter of Cūḷaneya do not realize your own death, like a fish [baited by] a hook.
If you go to Pañcāla, you will quickly abandon your life.”
“Just as a deer following a path, great danger will come upon you.
In this context, “King” is an address to the King of Videha. “Of great power” means of great renown.

“Possessed of great strength” means endowed with an army numbering eighteen akṣauhiṇīs. “For the purpose of killing” means for the sake of slaughter. “By one who wanders for a mate” refers to a female deer seeking a mate.
A hunter, having trained a single doe, bound her with a rope, led her into the forest, and placed her in the feeding ground of the deer.
Desiring to bring a young buck to her side, she cried out, generating passion through the perception of him as her own kind.
Hearing her sound, the young buck—who was lying in a forest thicket surrounded by a herd of deer—[directed his] perception toward the other does.
Without having done so, bound by the contact of hearing her voice, he rises and goes out;
lifting his neck, he approaches that doe under the influence of defilement and stands there, giving the hunter an opening.
Then the hunter pierces him with a sharp spear and brings about the end of his life. In this context, King Cūḷani is like the hunter, and the female companion is like the doe.
The fisherman was like a weapon in the hands of a hunter;
the meaning is that just as a hunter wandering in the forest desires a deer for the sake of killing it, so too did that king desire him.
"Greedily attached" means that even though he dwelt in water a hundred fathoms deep, [the hook] concealed the bend of the baited line within it.
Having become greedy for the bait known as "the fish," it swallows the hook and does not know its own death.
"The daughter" refers to the bait-like words of the fisherman-brāhmaṇa Cūḷani-bāḷisika, which stood there concealing the hook.
Greedy for the king’s daughter, the fish—like a fish [greedy for] bait—did not [perceive] what was called its own death.
"You know. "Pañcāla" refers to the city of Uttarapañcāla. "Self" (*atta*) means oneself. "Following the path" (*panthānubandha*):

just as a deer following the road to a village gate will encounter great danger—for when people go out bearing weapons for the purpose of killing that deer, whoever sees it kills it—so too [is it with] Uttarapañcāla city.
"Even as he goes, that great fear of death will come upon him; it will approach him.
Thus the Great Being, having rebuked the king with these four verses, spoke. That king, being exceedingly rebuked by him, thought, "This man regards me as if I were his own slave;
he does not even acknowledge me as a king. By this supreme king, [he has been told] regarding my daughter..."
"Knowing that he has been sent to me with the thought, 'I shall give [it],' he does not utter even a single word concerning an auspicious blessing;
instead, he says to me, 'Like a foolish deer, like a fish that has swallowed the hook, like a deer following a path to its end, you will meet with death.
Having spoken thus in anger, he immediately recited this verse:
“We alone are fools and mutes, who have prattled on about the highest goals to you.
What indeed do you know of these matters, like one who has grown up at the tip of a ploughshare, as others do?
In this context, *bālamhase* means “we are fools. *Eḷamūgā* means “we are indeed mutes with drooling mouths. *Uttamatthāni* refers to the causes for obtaining the supreme jewel of women.
*Tayī lavimhā* means "we spoke in your presence. *Kimeva* is a particle used in the sense of reproach.
*Naṅgalakoṭivaḍḍho* refers to the son of a householder who grows up from his childhood carrying only the tip of a plough;
with reference to that fact, he spoke thus with the underlying intention: "You know only the work of a householder, not the auspicious rites of the kṣatriyas."

"Aññe" means: "Do you know these auspicious rites for the Khattiyas as other wise men—such as the fisherman (Kevaṭṭa) or Senaka and others—know them? Knowing only the work of a householder is suitable for you.
Having thus reviled and reproached him, he spoke this verse in order to have him expelled, saying: "The son of a householder is creating an obstacle to my auspicious ceremony; throw him out!"
“Seize him by the throat and cast him out from my kingdom—
he who speaks thus to create an obstacle to my acquisition of the jewel.
Perceiving the king’s anger, he thought, “If anyone were to take the king’s word and seize me by the hand...”
“Or if he were to seize me by the neck, that would be enough for me to feel shame for as long as I live; therefore, I shall depart of my own accord.

Having thought thus, he paid homage to the king and went to his own home. The king spoke only out of a surge of anger, but because of his deep respect for the Bodhisatta, he did not command anyone to do anything to him. Then the Great Being [thought]: “This...

The king is a fool; he does not know what is for his own benefit or harm. Being greedy for sensual pleasures, thinking "I shall certainly obtain his daughter," and failing to perceive future danger, he will go and meet with great ruin.
It is not right to take his words to heart. He has been very helpful to me, a bestower of great fame; it is right that I should act as a support for him.
"First, however, I shall send the young parrot; having learned the truth from him, I will go afterwards," he thought, and sent the young parrot.
To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
"And then, departing from the presence of the King of Videha..."
Then he addressed his messenger, Mādhara, who was very wise:
"Come, friend Haritapakkha, perform a service for me;
the King of Pañcāla has a myna bird that guards his bed."
“Ask her while she is bound, for she is skilled in all things;
she knows everything concerning both the king and Kosiya.
Having replied, “So be it,” the very wise Mādhava departed.
The green-winged parrot arrived at the side of the sāḷikā.
Then that wise Mātali, having gone there,
addressed his beautiful-voiced domestic sāḷikā.
“Is it bearable for you in your fine home? Is all well with you, O Vessa?
Do you receive parched grain with honey in your fine home?
“It is indeed well with me, my dear friend, and I am free from ailment.”
“Furthermore, O most wise one, parched grain with honey is obtained by me.
“From where have you come, my friend, or by whom were you sent?
For neither before nor now have you been seen or heard of by me.”
In this context, "of the same side as green" means having a side similar to green leaves. "Service" (veyyāvacca):
when he said, "Come, good sir," she came and sat on his lap; then he said, "Good sir, perform for me one service that cannot be performed by any other human being.
When he asked, "What shall I do, my lord? she replied, "Good sir, except for the reason for which the Keṭubha brahmin has come as a messenger..."
Neither King [Bimbisāra] nor Kevaṭṭa knew of one another; both were seated in the king’s bedchamber and consulted together.
Now, the King of Pañcāla had a female parrot who guarded his bed. It was said that she knew this secret;
you should go there, establish a confidential intimacy with her regarding sexual matters, and [learn] that secret of theirs.
"Ask him while he is bound. Ask that sāḷika bird in a concealed place so that no one may know;
for if anyone hears your voice, you will have no life left. Therefore, ask slowly in a hidden spot.
She told them all this—that is, she told them everything regarding both the king and the fisherman of the Kosiya clan.
He knows all the secrets of both people.
"Yes, monks," [the Buddha said], "that young parrot, having been sent by the wise man after being honored in the same manner as before,
replied 'Yes' to him, paid homage to the Great Being, circumambulated him, and went out through the open lion-window."
Driven by the force of the wind, he went from the royal capital to the city named Ariṭṭhapura; having observed the situation there, he went into the presence of the sāḷikā.
How so? For he sat upon a golden mound at the king’s residence and uttered a sweet cry inspired by passion.
Why? Because upon hearing this sound, the sāḷikā would respond with a call, and by that signal—
"I shall go to her presence. She too, having heard his voice, sat within a golden cage near the royal bed;

with her mind colored by passion, she cried out three times in response. He went a short distance, making the sound again and again, and following the direction of the sound she had made, he eventually stood at the threshold of the lion-window and, after ensuring there was no danger, looked in.
He went into her presence. Then she said to him, "Come, dear friend, sit in the golden cage.
He went and sat down. "He addressed her" means that, having gone there and desiring to establish a confidential intimacy connected with sexual union, he addressed her.
"Sughara" means a beautiful house because of his dwelling in a golden cage. "Vessa" means a courtesan (*vessikā*), one of the *vessa* class.
It is said that among birds, the sāḷika is known as one of the merchant class; therefore, he addresses her thus. "Tuva" means:
"O lady of the beautiful home, I ask you: do you receive parched grain together with honey? "Āgamma" means: "Friend, from where have you come to enter here?
He asks this. "Kassa va" means: "By whom were you sent to come here?"
Having heard her words, he thought: "If I say, 'I have come from Mithilā,' she will not place her trust in me even if she were to face death.
However, having observed Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, I have come from there;
therefore, by telling a lie, I shall say that I have been sent from there by the King of Sivi. Having reflected thus, he said:
“I was the bed-keeper in the palace of King Sivi;
then that righteous king released all those bound from their fetters.
In this context, “bound” means that by virtue of his own righteousness, he released everyone who was bound from their bonds. While releasing them in this way—
Having placed faith in me as well, he had me released, saying, "Release him!
Having emerged from the open golden cage, I take my food wherever I wish on the palace grounds, yet I continue to dwell within the golden cage itself.
It is not as you are; I do not remain in the cage at all times.
Then she gave him honeyed parched grain and sweet water placed upon a golden tray for her own use, and asked, "Good sir, you have come from afar; for what purpose have you come here?
Having heard her words and desiring to hear the secret, he spoke a falsehood, saying:
“I had a single companion there, a sāḷika bird of sweet voice;
while I was looking on in my own fine home, a hawk killed her.
In this passage, *tassa mekā* means “of that mine, one”; *dutiyāsī* means “she was my former companion.”
Then she asked him, "But how did the hawk kill your wife? As he explained it to her, he said, "Listen, my dear:
one day, while our king was going for a water-sport, he summoned me as well. Then I took my wife and went with him;
after sporting together, we returned with him at evening time, and by the king—"
Having ascended the palace together with my wife, and having gone out through the lion-window for the purpose of drying our bodies, I sat down inside the upper chamber.
At that moment, a hawk emerged from the upper chamber and swooped down to seize us.
Terrified by the fear of death, I fled with great speed; she, however, was then heavily pregnant.
Because he was so heavy, he was unable to flee with speed. Then, even as I watched, he killed her, took her [body], and departed.
Seeing me weeping out of grief for her, our king asked, "Friend, why do you weep?
and having heard the matter, he said, "Do not weep excessively, friend; seek another wife."
Having said this, when she replied, "My lord, what is the use of bringing back a wife who is ignorant, immoral, and unchaste?
It would be better even to wander alone than that," he said, "Friend, I have heard of a female bird endowed with virtue and good conduct, exactly like your wife.
For such was the maina who was the bed-guardian for King Cūḷani; go there."
“Having asked her for permission and obtained leave, she said, ‘If it pleases you, come and tell us;
then we shall perform your marriage ceremony and bring you here with a great retinue. It was for this reason that she sent me here, and that is why I have come,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“Indeed, I am devoted to him; who would say, ‘I have come to you’?
If he would grant me the opportunity, we both shall dwell together.
Having heard his words, she was filled with joy. Nevertheless, without making known her own affection, as if unwilling, she said:
“A parrot should desire a parrot, and a maina a maina;
what kind of union can there be between a parrot and a maina?
In this context, “parrot” means: O wise parrot, a parrot indeed should desire a parrot. “What kind” refers to those of a different species.
“What kind of thing is cohabitation? For even a sparrow, upon seeing another sparrow of its own kind, will abandon a mynah bird despite a long-standing intimacy;
that separation from what is dear will lead to great suffering. Indeed, cohabitation with those of a different kind does not harmonize.
Hearing this, the other thought, “He does not reject me; he is merely making an excuse. He certainly desires me; I shall convince him by means of various similes,” and said:
“Whoever desires sensual pleasures—even a Caṇḍāla woman—everyone is indeed the same;
there is no one who is not the same in regard to sensual pleasures.

In this context, “even a Caṇḍāla woman” means even a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste. “The same” means that because of the sameness of their minds, every cohabitation is indeed the same. For in the matter of sensual pleasure, the mind alone is the measure, not birth.
Having spoken thus, and in order to show how various classes among human beings can share a common nature, he brought forward the past and spoke the following verse:
“There was a woman named Jambāvatī, the mother of King Sivi;
she was the wife of Vāsudeva, the beloved chief queen of Kaṇha.”
In this context, "Jampāvatī" refers to the mother of King Sivi; she was a Caṇḍālī named Jampāvatī.
She was the beloved chief queen of Vāsudeva, the eldest of the ten brothers of the Kaṇhāyana clan.
It is said that one day, while he was departing from Dvāravatī on his way to a pleasure garden, he saw a beautiful Caṇḍālī woman standing to one side as she was entering the city.
Having seen her, his mind became bound with passion; he had it asked, "What is her caste?

and even upon hearing, "She is of the Caṇḍāla caste," because his mind remained bound with passion, he had it asked whether she was without a master. Hearing that she was "without a master," he took her, turned back from there, led her to his residence, and made her his chief queen.
She gave birth to a son named Sivi. After his father’s passing, he...
He reigned in Dvāravatī; it was with reference to him that this was said.
Thus, having brought forward this example, he thought: "If even a khattiya of such a kind lived in cohabitation with a caṇḍālī woman, what need be said of us who are like animals?
The mere fact of consenting to live together with one another is sufficient."
Having said this, bringing forward another illustration, he said:
“The Kimpurisa woman Raṭṭhavatī also desired a young fawn;
a human being with a doe—there is nothing that is not similar in its desires.”
"Let us go there to that ascetic of such-and-such a name. But how did she desire him?
In the past, a certain brahmin, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, abandoned great fame and went forth as an ascetic.
He built a leaf-hut in the Himalayas and lived there. Not far from his leaf-hut, many kinnaras dwelt in a cave.
Right there, a single monkey lived at the door. Having drawn back the net, he would split their heads and drink their blood.
The kinnaras were indeed weak and of a timid nature. That monkey was also exceedingly large.
Being unable to do anything against him, they approached the ascetic; after exchanging greetings, they were asked the reason for their visit.
“Your Majesty, a single monkey is taking our lives; apart from you, we see no other refuge for ourselves.
Slay him and bring us safety,” they said. Upon hearing this, the ascetic dissuaded them, saying, “Go away;
those like me do not commit the taking of life. Among them was a Kinnarī named Raṭṭhavatī, who was exceedingly beautiful.

She was lovely and without a master. They adorned her, led her to the presence of the ascetic, and said, "O Lord, let this woman be your attendant; slay our enemy. As soon as the ascetic saw her, his heart became bound to her.
Having lived in union with her, he stood at the entrance of the cave and [saw] a monkey that had gone out for the sake of food.
Having struck him with a pestle, he brought him to his death. Living in harmonious union with her, he increased through sons and daughters and passed away right there.
Thus she lusted after him. Having cited this example, the parrot chick said:
"The ascetic Vaccha, being a human, entered into a life of cohabitation with a kinnarī who was an animal."
"What then of us? For we are both merely winged animals among the beasts," he said, demonstrating this by saying, "A human with a doe.
Thus he spoke, explaining that humans live in harmonious cohabitation with animals;
there is nothing indeed unequal in sensual pleasures, for the mind alone is the measure.

Having heard his words, she said, "My lord, the mind is not always the same; I am afraid of separation from what is dear. He too was skilled in the wiles of women, and desiring to test her, he spoke this verse again:
"Come now, I shall depart, O sweet-voiced *sāḷikā*;
surely you despise me because of this rejection?"
In this context, regarding what you call "the reason following upon the renunciation": all of this is indeed following upon the renunciation;
it is the cause of the renunciation, a constituent part of the renunciation. When you say, "Surely he despises me," you think, "He surely desires me," and thus you disregard me;
you do not know my true worth. For I am one who is honored by kings.
"A wife is not difficult for me to find; I shall seek another wife.

Upon hearing his words, as if her heart were breaking, and as if she were being consumed by the passion that arose at the mere sight of him, she nevertheless—out of her feminine artifice—acted as if she did not desire him and spoke this verse and a half:
"O Mādhava, O wise one, fortune does not come to one who is in a hurry."
"Stay right here for now until you see the king;
you shall hear the sound of the drums and witness the majesty of the king.
In this regard, "no glory," my dear wise friend, means that there is no such thing as glory for one who is hurrying; by one who is hurrying, no work is accomplished.
"It does not shine; this so-called household life is exceedingly heavy"—having thought and weighed these things, it should be undertaken.
"Stay right here for now, until you see our king endowed with such great glory.
"You have heard" refers to the evening time, when drums are being beaten by women of supreme beauty who possess the playful grace of *kinnarīs*.
"You will hear the sounds of other singers and musicians, and you will see the great power and glorious splendor of the king.
"My dear, why are you in such a hurry? Do you not know even a fraction [of what is to come]? Wait for now; we shall find out later.
Then, immediately after evening, they engaged in sexual intercourse, living together in harmony, joyfully, and in mutual affection.
They lived there. Then the young parrot, thinking, "She will not keep my secret from me now;
it is time to ask her and then depart," said, "Sāḷikā! "What is it, Master? "I wish to say something to you.
"Speak, Master. "Very well; today is an auspicious day for us; we shall know on another day."
“If there is to be talk connected with blessings, speak; if not, do not speak, Master. “This is indeed talk about blessings, my dear,” he said.
“In that case, please speak. Then, having told her, “My dear, if you wish to hear it, I shall tell it to you,” he spoke one and a half stanzas while questioning her about the secret:
“This intense sound which has been heard across the countryside—
[it is said] the daughter of the King of Pañcāla, beautiful as a medicinal herb,
will be given to the Videhas; that shall be the wedding.”

The meaning of this is as follows: "This sound which is indeed intense and thick, heard across the countryside, renowned, famous, well-known, and widespread throughout foreign lands and other kingdoms—what is it?
There is one who shines like the star Osadhītārakā, the daughter of the King of Pañcāla;
there is one of identical beauty to her whom he will give to the Videhas, and that shall be the marriage. He who...
Such was the sound that spread abroad; having heard it, I thought: "This maiden possesses supreme beauty, and even the King of Videha has become an enemy to King Cūḷani.
There are many other kings who are under the command of Cūḷani-Brahmadatta;
for what reason would he give his daughter to the King of Videha instead of giving her to them?"
Having heard his words, she said to him: "My lord, for what reason do you speak of inauspiciousness on an auspicious day?
"My dear lady, I speak of 'the auspicious,' yet you speak of 'the inauspicious'; what indeed is this?
"My lord, may such an auspicious rite never happen even to our enemies! "Tell me then, my dear lady."
“Master, it cannot be told,” she said. “Bhadde, from the moment that secret known by you was not told to me, there has been no harmonious living between us.
Being thus pressed by him, she said, “In that case, Master, listen,” and spoke this verse:
“Let there not be such a marriage for our enemies, nor for our kin, as that which shall take place between the King of Pañcāla and the Princess of Videha.
Having spoken this verse, when he was asked again, “Bhadde, why do you speak such words? she replied, “In that case, listen; I shall explain the fault in this matter to you,” and spoke this verse:
“Having brought the King of Videha here, the bull among charioteers of Pañcāla will then have him executed; perish, O friend, you shall not exist.
In that context, “he will then have him executed” means that when he has arrived at this city, then—along with him—
"He will not act with friendship or the duty of a friend, nor will he allow me to see his daughter.
However, he has a wise counselor named Mahosadha who instructs him in matters of state and dharma;
[the king] will have him killed along with [the prince]. Having had both men executed, we shall drink the wine of victory"—having thus consulted with the king, the fisherman went to seize him.
Thus, having disclosed the secret in its entirety, she told it to the wise bird.
Upon hearing this, the wise bird praised the fisherman Kevaṭṭa, saying, "The teacher Kevaṭṭa is skilled in means; it is marvelous how that king was slain by such a stratagem.
Then he said, "What use have we for such an ill omen? Let us remain silent."
Having spoken thus and knowing that the purpose of his journey was accomplished, he stayed with her that night and said to her,
in order to obtain permission to depart: "Bhadde, I shall go to the kingdom of Sivi and inform King Sivi and his queen that I have obtained a pleasing wife."
“Come now, grant me leave for seven nights,
until I have informed King Sivi that the Great Sage has found lodging in the vicinity of Sāḷikā.”
In this context, *mahesi* refers to the Great Seer’s wife. *Āvasatha* means a dwelling place. *Upantikaṃ*:
then, having said to them, "Come, let us go into her presence," he thought, "On the eighth day I will bring her here and depart with a great retinue;
until my return, do not be despondent."
Having heard this, the female myna bird—though unwilling to be separated from him and unable to refuse his words—spoke the following verse:
“Very well, I grant you leave for seven nights;
if you do not return to my side within those seven days, [I shall go with you].”
“I think you will come when I am dead, for I perceive that you have entered upon death.
Therein, “I think you will come when I am dead”: this being so, I observe that you are one whose life has departed. Since you do not come on the eighth day, you will come when I am dead;
therefore, do not delay. The other replied, “Bhadde, what are you saying? If I do not see you on the eighth day, how shall I live?”
Having spoken with his voice, but thinking in his heart, "Whether you live or die, what is it to me?", he rose and walked a short distance toward the camp.
Then, turning back and going to Mithilā, he alighted upon the shoulder of the wise man.
However, having been raised to the upper terrace by the Great Being through that signal, the wise man was asked about the entire occurrence, and [the messenger] told him everything.
He reported it. He too, in the same manner as before, performed every honor for him. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, having gone there, that wise Mādhava parrot reported these words of the sāḷika to Mahosadha.”
Therein, he spoke by explaining in full: "This is the parrot's speech" means "this is the speech of the parrot.
The Section on the Parrot is finished.
The Great Section on Omens.
Having heard this, the Great Being thought: "The king will depart even though I am unwilling; and having gone, he will meet with great destruction.
Furthermore, the reproach will arise against me: 'Though such a king who bestows honor spoke these words, you did not take them to heart nor show him favor,' while a wise man like myself exists."

For what reason would he perish? I shall go before the king, see Cūḷanī, and having laid out the city with its divisions for the Videha king to dwell in, I will have a footpath of one *gāvuta* and a great highway half a *yojana* constructed;
then, having consecrated Cūḷanī’s daughter as my king’s consort, she shall serve at his feet.

"Even while one hundred kings stand surrounding me with armies numbering eighteen akkhobhaṇis, it is my burden to rescue our king from Rāhu’s mouth and bring him back, like the moon from the jaws of Rāhu.
As he thought thus, joy arose in his body. With the force of that joy, uttering an inspired exclamation, he spoke this half-stanza:
“Whatever wealth a man may enjoy in the house of another, he should act for the benefit of that very person.

This is its meaning: when a man, having obtained great power in the presence of a king, enjoys wealth—even if the king reviles him, strikes him, or drags him away by the throat—he should act for the welfare and benefit of that very king.
“A wise man should conduct himself through the three doors—the body and so forth—with growth in mind. For a deed of treachery against friends is not to be committed by the wise.
Having reflected thus, he bathed, adorned himself, and went to the royal palace with great splendor.
After paying homage to the king, he stood to one side and asked, “Sire, will you go to the city of Uttarapañcāla? “Yes, my son,” [the king replied].
“What is the use of sovereignty to me if I do not obtain Pañcālacandī? Do not abandon me; come along with me.
For our going there, two purposes will be accomplished: I shall obtain the jewel of a woman, and friendship will be established between me and the king.
Then the wise man said to him, “In that case, Your Majesty, I [shall go] before...”
"Having gone, I shall have dwellings built for you; you should come when sent by my message," he said, and spoke these two verses:
"Come then, O Lord of Men, I shall go to the most delightful city of the King of Pañcāla."
“Build dwellings for the illustrious Vedeha.
“Having built dwellings for the illustrious Vedeha,
when I send word to you, then you should come, O Khattiya.”
In that context, "of the Videhan" means "of you, the King of Videha. "Eyyāsi" means "you should come.
Having heard this, the king—thinking, "It seems the wise man does not abandon me"—became joyful and satisfied, and said:
"Dear son, what should be obtained for you as you go to your own city? "A powerful army, Your Majesty," he replied. "As much as you desire," [the king said].
“Take as many as you wish, dear one. “Your Majesty, have the four prisons opened and the shackles of the thieves broken;
let them also go with me. “Do as you please, dear one.
The Great Being had the doors of the prisons opened and summoned brave, great warriors capable of accomplishing the task in the place where they had gone.
Having had them removed and saying, "Attend upon me," he performed honors for them;

then, taking eighteen divisions consisting of carpenters, smiths, leather-workers, masons, stonemasons, painters, and others skilled in various crafts, and having them take many implements such as axes, adzes, mattocks, and spades, he departed from the city surrounded by a great army. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then Mahosadha departed from Pāyāsi toward the most delightful city of the King of Pañcāla,
to construct dwellings for the illustrious Vedehiputta.
As the Great Being proceeded, he established a village at every league’s interval and appointed a minister to each.
Having said, "When you have taken Pañcālacandī from the king and are returning, you should prepare elephants,
horses, and chariots, take the king with you, ward off the enemies, and quickly reach Mithilā," he gave his instructions and sent them forth.
Upon reaching the bank of the Ganges, however, he summoned Prince Ānanda and said, "Ānanda, taking three hundred carpenters with you, go up the Ganges..."
"Go, have heartwood cut, construct about three hundred boats, and having had them fashioned right there for the sake of the city,
fill the boats with light timber and return quickly," he sent. He himself, however, having crossed the Ganges by boat,
began counting by footprints from the place where he disembarked, thinking, "This is half a yojana."
Having demarcated the site, saying, "There shall be a great elephant-enclosure here; in this place there shall be the king’s residential city;
and from here for a distance of one *gāvuta* up to the royal palace, there shall be a foot-enclosure," he entered the city.
King Cūḷani, hearing of the Bodhisatta’s arrival, thought, "Now my heart's desire has reached its fulfillment."
"He will arrive; I shall see the backs of my enemies. When he has come, Vedeha will also arrive before long.
Then, having slain both of them, we shall exercise sole sovereignty over the entire surface of Jambudīpa.
Thus he attained the highest satisfaction. The whole city was thrown into agitation: "It is said that this is the wise Mahosadha; it is said that by him [one hundred and one kings...]"
“Like crows driven away by a clod of earth.
While the citizens were still beholding the Great Being’s perfection of form, he went to the king’s gate and announced himself to the king.
When told, “Enter,” he entered, paid homage to the king, and sat down to one side. Then the king greeted him with words of welcome.
Having done so, he asked, "Father, when will the king arrive? "At the time I have sent for him, O King.
"But for what purpose have you come? "To construct a dwelling for our king, O King. "Very well, father," he replied.
Then, having provided his army with travel expenses and having ordered great honors to be shown to the Great Being, [he prepared] a residence house.
Having had it given, he said, “Dear son, until the king returns, stay here without longing for home, doing whatever is appropriate for us.
It is said that as he was ascending the royal palace, he stopped at the foot of the great staircase and observed, “Here will be the Jaṅghomaṅga gate. Then this thought occurred to him: “The king—”
“If he says, ‘Do what is appropriate for us as well,’ you should ensure that when the trench is being dug, this staircase does not sink. Then he said to the king:
“Your Majesty, while entering, I stood at the base of the stairs and, observing the construction work, I saw a flaw in the great staircase. If it pleases you, [let me fix it].”
“Having obtained timber, I shall fashion it into something pleasing and spread it out. “Very well, wise man, you may spread it out,” he replied.

He then observed, “This will be the location for the side door,” and having removed that old staircase, he had a wooden floor laid down where the side door would be, so that no dust would fall there. As he was doing this...
He did not let the ladder slip down; having thus made it steady, he spread the ladder out. The king, not knowing the reason for this, thought, "He is doing this out of affection for me.
Having spent that day occupied with that very same construction work, on the following day he said to the king: "Your Majesty, if..."
“Let us know the dwelling place of our king; having made it pleasant, we shall guard it. “Very well, wise one;
with the exception of my own residence, you may take whichever house you desire in the entire city.
“Great King, we are newcomers, and you have many beloved warriors; if they were to take houses for themselves...”
“They will quarrel with us. “Then, Your Majesty, what shall we do with them? “Do not heed their words. Have them take whatever place you desire.
“Your Majesty, they will come back again and again and speak to you; because of that, you will find no peace of mind. But if—”
“If you so desire, let our own men serve as gatekeepers for as long as we occupy our residences;
then, being unable to gain entrance, they will not come. This being the case, you too will obtain peace of mind.
The king accepted this, saying, “Excellent.”
The Mahāsatta, having stationed his own men at every place—the base of the stairs, the top of the stairs, and the great gate—commanded them, saying, "Do not allow anyone to enter.
Then, having gone to the residence of the king’s mother, he ordered her attendants, "Show the manner of breaking [the wall].
They began from the threshold of the doorway and [took up] bricks and clay...
And they began to demolish it. When the Queen Mother heard of this occurrence, she came and said, "Why, dear ones, are you tearing down my house?
"The wise Mahosadha has had it demolished because he wishes to build his own residence for his king.
"If that is so, stay right here," she said. "Our king possesses a great army and transport; this place is not sufficient for him."
“We shall build another large house. “You do not know me; I am the queen mother.
Now I shall go to my son’s presence and find out. “We are breaking [the agreement] at the king’s command; if you can, stop us!
She became angry and said, “Now I shall see what you have to do,” and went to the palace gate. Then they told her, “Do not enter.”
The gatekeepers stopped her. "I am the king's mother," she said. "We do not know you;
we have been commanded by the king, 'Do not let anyone enter,' so go away," they replied.
Seeing no way to gain entry, she turned back and stood looking toward her own residence. Then a certain man said to her, "What are you doing here? Go!"
“You are not going! she said, and seizing him by the neck, she threw him to the ground.
She thought, “Surely these men must have been commanded by the king; otherwise, they would not have been able to do such a thing.
I shall go to the presence of the wise man himself. Having gone there, she said, “Dear Mahosadha, why did you [leave] my residence?”
“...he had it demolished,” she said. He did not speak with her; however, a man standing near him asked, “Queen, what were you saying?
“Dear one, why does the wise Mahosadha have my house demolished?
“To make a dwelling place for King Vedeha. “What, dear one? In such a great city, why seek a dwelling place elsewhere?”
"He thinks, 'It cannot be obtained. [The king says: 'Take this bribe of one hundred thousand and have another house built elsewhere.
[The minister replies: 'Very well, Queen, I shall cause your house to be relinquished; do not tell anyone that a bribe was taken.
Lest others, by giving us bribes, should also desire to have their houses relinquished. 'Very well, father,' [she says]. 'To the King..."
“My mother gave me a bribe,” he thought, “which is indeed shameful even for me; therefore, I will not tell anyone.
Saying, “Very well,” he took a hundred thousand from her, had his house vacated, and went to the fisherman’s house.
He too went to the door, and having received the stripping of his back skin with bamboo splinters, he saw no way to take what was to be taken.

Returning home again, he gave exactly one hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas]. By this means, as he took possession of houses throughout the entire city while accepting bribes, nine crores of kahāpaṇas were acquired from those very payments.
Having traversed the entire city, the Great Being went to the royal palace. Then the king asked him, "What is it, O wise one?"
“Have you found a place to dwell? “Great King, there are none who would not give; however, when their homes are taken, they suffer.
It is improper for us to cause them the pain of separation from what is dear to them.
At a distance of one *gāvuta* outside the city, in such-and-such a place between the Ganges and the city, we shall build a dwelling-city for our king.”
Having heard this, the king was pleased and said, "It is difficult to fight within the city; neither one's own army nor the enemy's army can be distinguished there.
However, it is easy to wage war outside the city; therefore, we shall besiege and kill them right there outside the city.
He added, "Excellent, wise man! Have it done exactly in the place you have identified. [The minister replied,] "Great King, as for me..."
“I shall have it built; however, your men must not come to our construction site for the sake of wood, leaves, and so forth.
For if they come, they will cause quarrels, and because of that, there will be no peace of mind for either you or us.
“Very well, wise man; have the access road made by that side. “Your Majesty, as for us...”
“The elephants delight in water; they will play in the water itself.
If the citizens should become angry, thinking, ‘Since the arrival of Mahosadha, we have not been able to drink clear water because the water has become turbid,’ you must endure that as well.
The king said, “Let your elephants play as they please,” and had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “Whoever from here...”
"Having departed, he shall go to the place where the city for Mahosadha is to be built; his penalty shall be a fine of one thousand [pieces of gold].
The Great Being, having paid homage to the king and taken his own retinue, departed and began to build the city at the designated location.
Having established a village named Vagguli on the further bank of the Gaṅgā, he provided it with elephants, horses, chariots, and other vehicles.

Having established there a cattle-pen and deliberating on the construction of the city, he assigned all the tasks, saying, "Let so many do this," and began the work of the Great Moat. The gate of the Great Moat was at the ford of the Ganges.
About sixty hundred warriors dug the Great Moat; carrying away sand and earth in large leather bags, they worked.
They throw [dust] into the Ganges. The elephants trample the dust that has been thrown, and the Ganges flows in a turbulent state.
The city dwellers say, "Ever since Mahosadha arrived, we have not been able to drink the clear water;
the Ganges flows turbulently—what indeed is this? Then, the men stationed by the wise man inform them.
“It is said that Mahosadha’s elephants, while playing in the water, stirred up mud in the Ganges, and because of that, the Ganges flows turbid.
The intention of the Bodhisattvas indeed succeeds; therefore, the roots, stumps, sand, and stones in the marsh all sank into the ground.
The gate of Jaṅgha-umaṅga was in that very city.
There were three hundred men digging a great pit; having gathered earth with leather bags, they threw it into that city.
As each portion was thrown in, they had it trampled down with water and built a rampart, or performed other such works.
At the entrance to Mahāumaṅga’s gate into the city, there was a gate equipped with a mechanical device, eighteen cubits high.
It was so equipped that it would close when one bolt was pushed in and open when another bolt was pushed in.
Having built up the two sides of the great gateway with bricks, he had the plastering work done;
having had the top covered with wooden planks and the ceiling smeared with clay, he had the whitewashing and the decorative painting work completed.
In this place, there were eighty great gates and sixty-four small gates, all of which were equipped with mechanical devices.
By the pressing of a single bolt, all were closed; by the pressing of a single bolt, all were opened.
On both sides, there were hundreds of lamp-holders, which were also equipped with mechanical devices. When one was opened...
When all were opened, they were revealed; when one was closed, all were closed. On two sides, there were one hundred bed-chambers for one hundred khattiyas.
In each chamber was a single great couch spread with multicolored coverlets and raised with a white parasol; beside each great couch stood a single female figure.
He stood there, possessing a most excellent form. Without even touching him with one's hand, it would not have been possible to know him as "human form";

rather, on both sides of the mountain Umanga, skilled painters executed various kinds of painted work depicting Sakka’s splendor, Mount Sineru, the seven surrounding mountain ranges, the Cakkavāḷa world-system, the seven great oceans, the seven great lakes, the four great continents, the Himavanta mountains, Lake Anotatta, and the surface of the Manosilā rock.
All the splendors of the moon, the sun, and the six classes of deities belonging to the realm of sense-desire, beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, appeared as if within a single courtyard.
Silver-colored sand was strewn upon the ground, and lotuses were displayed suspended above.
On both sides, various kinds of market stalls were shown, and in various places, garlands of perfumes and flowers were displayed.
Having suspended them, they adorned the inner apartments like the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas.

Then those three hundred carpenters, having moored three hundred boats and filled them with building materials for which the preparation was complete, brought them by way of the Ganges and informed the wise man. He brought them into the city and [said]: "By me..."
"Bring it on the very day you are commanded," he said, and had the ship placed in a concealed location.
