He caused three moats to be made around the city: a water-moat, a mud-moat, and a dry-moat.

A rampart eighteen cubits high, with gate-towers, watchtowers, royal residences, elephant stables and other buildings, and lotus ponds—all this was brought to completion. Thus ended the great consecration ceremony.
The legs, the body, and the city—all this was completed within four months.
Then, at the end of the four months, the Great Being dispatched a messenger for the purpose of inviting the King. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
"Having constructed the dwellings for the illustrious Videha..."
Then he sent a messenger to Vedeha, the ruler of Mithilā, [saying]:
"Come now, Great King, your residence has been built.
Therein, *pāhiṇī* means he dispatched.
Having heard the messenger’s words, the king, with a joyful heart, set out from the city with a great retinue. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then King Pāyāsi set forth with his fourfold army to see the prosperous city of Kapilavatthu and its infinite array of vehicles.”
In that context, "Anantavāhana" means possessing an immeasurable array of vehicles such as elephants and horses. "The city of Kapila" refers to the town built in the kingdom of Kapila.
Having traveled by stages, he reached the bank of the Ganges. Then the Great Being went out to meet him and led him into the city he himself had built.
There, having entered an excellent palace and partaken of various foods of exquisite flavor, he rested for a short while.
In the evening, he sent a messenger to King Cūḷani to inform him of his arrival. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then, having gone there, he sent word to Brahmadatta:
‘I have come, O Great King, to pay homage at your feet.’”
“Now give me your wife, a woman beautiful in every limb, covered in gold, and attended by a retinue of female servants.
Therein, “having been saluted” means that the Elder of Vedeha was such that King Cūḷani was not even his grandson, yet [the king acted] out of defilement.
But having become infatuated, he thought, "A father-in-law indeed ought to be saluted by his son-in-law," and without knowing the other's mind, he sent a message requesting a salutation.
He sent the message: "Give her now! I was summoned by you with the words 'I will give my daughter,' so give her to me now. "Covered with gold" means adorned with golden ornaments.
Having heard the messenger’s words, King Cūḷani was filled with joy and thought, “Now where will my enemy go?
Having cut off the heads of both of them, I shall drink the drink of victory!
Displaying only his joy, he paid honor to the messenger and spoke the following verse:
“Welcome to you, O Vedeḥ, and a most hearty welcome;
inquire about the auspicious stars, for I shall give my daughter to you—
covered in gold and preceded by a retinue of handmaidens.”

In that context, "speak to the Vedeha" means he addresses him as if the Vedeha were standing right before him after hearing his message. Alternatively, he spoke thus while commanding the messenger: "Tell him, 'Speak thus as was said by Brahmadatta.
Having heard this, the messenger went into the presence of the Vedeha and said: "Your Majesty, please ascertain an auspicious constellation suitable for the performance of the marriage rites;
the King intends to give you his daughter. He replied, "Today the constellation is indeed auspicious," and again—
He sent a messenger. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then King Videha inquired about the auspicious constellations;
having inquired about the constellations, he sent word to Brahmadatta.”
“Now give me your wife, a woman beautiful in all her limbs,
covered in gold and attended by a retinue of slave-girls.
And King Cūḷani replied:
“I now give you this wife, a woman beautiful in every limb,
covered in gold and attended by a host of maidservants.
Having spoken this verse, he uttered the falsehood, “I am sending her now, I am sending her now,” and gave the signal to one hundred and one kings.
He gave the order: “Let everyone set forth together with an army numbering eighteen akkhobhaṇas, fully equipped for battle;
today we shall sever the heads of both our adversaries, and tomorrow we shall drink the wine of victory.
They all departed. But having himself set out, he [took] his mother, Queen Calākā, and his chief queen, Queen Nandā.
Having settled his son Pañcālacanda and his daughter Pañcālacandī—these four people—along with the women of the harem in the palace, he departed.
The Bodhisatta, for his part, rendered great honor to King Vedeha and the army that had come with him.
Some people drank liquor; some ate fish, meat, and other foods.

Some, exhausted from having traveled a long distance, lay down to rest. But the King of Videha, taking the four wise men beginning with Senaka and surrounded by his retinue of ministers, sat upon a decorated great terrace.
King Cūḷani also, with an army numbering eighteen akkhobhaṇīs, entered that entire city with its three gates and four divisions.
Having surrounded himself while hundreds of thousands of torches were being held aloft, he stood ready for battle as the dawn was just breaking.
Knowing this, the Great Being dispatched three hundred of his warriors, saying:
"Go by way of the Jaṅgha-ambush; having brought the King’s mother, the chief queen, the son, and the daughter by way of the Jaṅgha-ambush, [bring them] by way of the Mahā-ambush."

"Having led him out from the entrance of the inner apartment, but not having left him outside, place him right there within the inner apartment and remain stationed there guarding him until our arrival.
Then, at the time of our arrival, lead him out from the inner apartment and place him in the great, spacious hall at the entrance of the inner apartment.
Having accepted his word, they went by way of the lower courtyard and spread a plank-covering at the foot of the stairs.
Having opened [the door], she stationed guards and female attendants such as hunchbacks at these places— the base of the stairs, the top of the stairs, and the great hall—
binding their hands and feet and covering their mouths, placing them in various concealed spots; then,
having eaten some of the king’s prepared solid and soft food and having broken up the rest, she reduced it to powder and fragments.
Having rendered it unusable and having discarded it, they ascended to the upper terrace of the palace.
At that time, Queen Calākā, taking Nandādevī, the prince, and the princess, and thinking, "Who knows? What might happen?
she had them lie down on the same bed as herself. Those warriors stood at the door of the chamber and called out. She went out.
“What is it, father? she asked. “O Queen, our king has brought both Vedeha and Mahosadha to their deaths and established sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
Today, surrounded by one hundred kings and drinking the great victory-wine with great glory, he has sent us to bring you four people here. Thus he dispatched us.
Having trusted their words, they descended from the palace and went to the foot of the stairs. Then, taking hold of them, they entered the inner chamber.
They said, "While living here for all this time, we have never before come down this street.
[The king replied,] "Queen, they do not descend this street at all times; this is called the Maṅgala Street (the Auspicious Street). Today—"
“Because it was an auspicious day, the king ordered that they be brought by this path. They believed their words.

Then some of them took those four and departed. Others turned back, opened the treasure-chambers in the royal palace, took as much of the finest jewels as they desired, and returned. The other four nobles also [proceeded] in front.
Having reached the great palace and seeing the palace adorned like the assembly hall of the gods, they perceived that it had been prepared for the sake of the king.
Then, having led them to a place not far from the Ganges and seated them within the palace itself in decorated chambers,
some remained there taking up guard duty, while others went to inform them of their arrival.

They informed the Bodhisatta. Having heard their words, he thought, "Now my heart's desire will reach its fulfillment," and filled with joy, he went into the presence of the king and stood to one side. The king, too, being afflicted by his defilements, thought, "Now he will send his daughter;
now he will send his daughter," and rose from his couch and [looked out] through the window.
Beholding the city, which had become a single mass of light through many hundreds of thousands of torches and was surrounded by a great army, he became apprehensive and suspicious.
Thinking, "What indeed is this?", he spoke this verse while consulting with his wise ministers:
"Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—the army stands arrayed in full armor."
"The torches are burning and glowing; what do the wise think of this? Therein, "What do they think? means:
"Is King Cūḷani pleased with us, or is he angry? What indeed do the wise think?"—thus he asked.
Having heard that, Senaka said: "Do not worry, Great King; very many torches are visible. The King [is] yours..."

"He seems to be coming to take his daughter away. Pukkusaka also said, "He will be stationed there to provide protection while you perform the hospitality due to a guest. Thus they spoke of whatever each of them preferred.
But the king said, "Let the army remain at such-and-such a place; take up your positions for protection at such-and-such a place; be vigilant!"
Hearing the sound of those speaking and looking out, he saw an army equipped with the fivefold armor;
terrified by the fear of death and longing for the Great Being’s word, he spoke this other verse:
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—the army stands arrayed in mail.”
“The torches are burning and glowing; what indeed will the wise do?
Therein, “What indeed will the wise do? means: “O wise one, what are you thinking? What will these armies do to us?
Having heard that, the Great Being thought, “I shall first frighten this blind fool a little, and afterwards, by displaying the power of my wisdom, I will reassure him,” and he said:
“O Great King, Cūḷaneyya, who is possessed of great strength, protects you;
yet, being incensed by Brahmadatta, he will have you executed at dawn.

Upon hearing this, they were all overcome with the terror of death. The king’s boil dried up, saliva ceased to flow from his mouth, and a burning fever arose in his body. Terrified by the fear of death, he lamented and spoke these two verses:
“My heart trembles and my mouth goes dry;
I find no peace, like one scorched by fire in the heat.
Just as the flame of a blacksmith’s bellows burns within and not outside,” so too does my mind burn within and not outside.
"Even so, my heart burns within, not without.
Therein, "it trembles" means: "O dear Mahosadha Paṇḍita, my heart quivers like a sprout shaken by a great wind.
"It burns within" means: "Like a torch, it burns inside my heart-flesh; without—"
"But he does not meditate," he lamented.
Hearing his lamentation, the Great Being thought, "This foolish man did not follow my words on other days; I shall restrain him even more. He then said:
"Negligent and having overstepped counsel, you are one whose counsel has been shattered, O Kṣatriya!"
Now let those wise and prudent people protect you!
Having failed to follow the words of the counselor who desired his welfare and sought his benefit,
the king— delighting in his own pleasure— is like a deer caught in a trap.
“Just as a fish, greedy for raw meat, does not perceive its own death when it sees a hook curved and covered with flesh; even so,
O King, you [do not perceive the danger] regarding Cūḷanī’s daughter.”
“Greedily attached to sensual pleasures, you do not realize your own death, like a fish [on the hook].
If you go to Pañcāla, you will quickly abandon your life;
like a deer following a path, great danger will come upon you.”
“A man who is unrighteous in form, O Lord of Men, might bite like a snake that has crept into one’s lap;
a wise person should not form friendship with him, for association with a base man is indeed painful.
But when one knows a man, O Lord of Men, to be virtuous and learned...”
"Therefore, a wise person should make friends; for indeed, association with a true person is pleasant.
In this regard, O Great King, you are "negligent" because you are negligent due to sensual desire.

You are "one who has overstepped counsel" because you are transgressing the counsel that was deliberated by me after seeing the future danger and determining it through wisdom. You are "one whose counsel has been broken" precisely because of having overstepped that counsel.
"Broken in counsel" means that the counsel you received together with Senaka and the others has been broken; thus, you have become one whose counsel is broken.
"The wise"—he indicates this by saying, "Let these four men, Senaka and the others, protect you now; I shall observe their strength.
"Without doing the minister's bidding" means without following the word of my chief minister. "Delighting in self-pleasure" refers to oneself...
"Having become delighted by the joy of defilement (*kilesapīti*). "Like a deer caught in a snare":

just as a deer that has come for the sake of bait is bound in a trap, so too, having disregarded my words and come out of greed for defilement thinking, "I shall obtain Pañcālacandī," you have now become like a deer bound in a snare.
The two verses beginning with “Just as a mortal” were spoken to show: “At that time, this simile was brought forward by me.
The verse beginning with “If you go” was also spoken to show: “It is not only this much; I have also cited this one.
“One of ignoble form” means a person of the same kind as the Kevaṭṭa Brahmin, a base-born individual, a shameless man. “Not a friend because of him” means...
One should not form a bond of friendship with such a person; however, you formed a bond of friendship with the fisherman and accepted his word.
"Suffering" means that even a single instance of association with such a person brings great suffering both in this world and in the next;
therefore, it is called suffering. "Yadeva" means "whatever"; it is this very thing.
Or this is another reading. "Sukha" means he is happy indeed both in this world and in the next world.
Then, restraining him even more strictly with the thought, "He might do such a thing again," [the king] brought forward and presented the words previously spoken by the king himself:
"You are a fool, O King, you are like a mute donkey, you who have prattled about the highest goals to me!"
“What does it matter to me that I am but a plowman? I know matters of state no less than others.
‘Seize him by the throat and destroy him, my conqueror!
He speaks for the sake of creating an obstacle to my acquisition of the jewels.’”
Having spoken these two verses, he said: "Great King, I am the son of a householder.
Just as your other wise men, such as Senaka and the rest, understand matters, how could I possibly know them? This is not my domain; I know only the craft of a householder.
This matter is well known to the wise men such as Senaka and the others. Today, for you who possess eighteen akṣauhiṇīs..."
“Let Senaka and the others be the ones to provide support for one surrounded by an army;
but he has ordered me to be dragged away by the neck—why do you ask me now? In this way, he rebuked him with a well-founded rebuke.
Hearing this, the king thought: “This wise man speaks exactly as I have said. For indeed, this future danger was [foreseen] long ago.”
"I know him; therefore he restrains me excessively. However, he will not remain idle for so long;
surely he will ensure my safety. Then, examining him, he spoke these two verses:
"O Mahosadha, the wise do not pierce the truth by means of the past."
"Why do you pierce me like a horse tethered by the goad?
If you see liberation or even safety, instruct me with that;
why do you pierce me with what is past?"
In this context, "they do not pierce" means they do not pierce him with the weapons of their mouths by seizing upon past faults.
"Like a horse well-tethered": like a horse that has been firmly bound and stationed because it is surrounded by an army of attendants—why do you pierce me?
"By that very [means]," meaning: instruct and reassure me with that very state of safety, saying, "In this way will there be your release; in this way will there be security."
"For apart from him, I have no other refuge.

Then the Great Being thought, "This king is exceedingly blind and foolish; he does not recognize a distinguished man. Having fatigued him for a short while, I shall afterwards become his support," and said:
"The past human deed is difficult to perform and hard to accomplish;..."
Even Sakka could not release him; understand this well, O Khattiya:
“There are nāgas who travel through the air, possessing psychic power and renown;
they too would depart taking with them only one for whom such [powers] exist.”
“There are horses that travel through the air, possessing psychic power and renown;
they too would take [the rider] away, for whomsoever such as these belong.
There are winged birds that travel through the air, possessing psychic power and renown.”
They might take him away, for such are those who possess them.
Or there are *yakkhas* who travel through the air, possessing supernormal power and renown;
they too might take him away, for such are those who possess them.
“Past human action is difficult to undo and hard to overcome;
I am not able to release you from that by way of the air, O Kṣatriya.
Therein, O Great King, this so-called release of yours from here is past human action (*manusya-karma*). It is the deed that ought to have been performed by humans.
"Past. "Difficult to do, difficult to accomplish" means it is neither possible to perform nor possible to achieve.
"I am not able to do that" means I am not able to release him from this. "You shall understand, O Khattiya," [means] O Great King, you alone must know what is to be done here.
"Vehāyasa" means capable of traveling through the air. "Nāgas" means elephants. "Yassa" means of whom.
"Of the king. "Of such a kind" means elephants born in the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage;
they might take that king and depart. "Horses" means horses born in the lineage of Valāhaka, the king of horses. "Birds" he says with reference to the Garuḷas.
"Yakkhas" refers to yakkhas such as Sātāgira and others. "Through the air": "I am not able to release him through the air"—that [is what he said].
The meaning is that he thought, "I am unable to take him through the air and lead him to Mithilā.
When the king heard this, he sat there speechless. Then Senaka reflected:
"Now, for both the king and ourselves, there is no other refuge except for this wise man; yet having heard his words, the king is terrified by the fear of death."
“He is unable to say anything at all; I shall ask the wise man,” he thought. And as he was asking, he spoke these two verses:
“A man who cannot see the further shore in the vast expanse of water finds happiness wherever he gains a firm footing.”
“Thus you are our support and that of the king, O Mahosadha;
you are the best among those possessed of wisdom, so release us from our suffering.
In this context, *atīradassī* means one whose ship has been wrecked in the ocean and who does not see the shore. *Yattha* means where [the ship] was struck by the force of the waves.
"Roaming about, he finds a firm footing in whatever place he enters. "Release us!
they entreated, saying, "Previously, when we were surrounded by [the enemy] at Mithilā, it was by you alone that we were released; now too, may you alone deliver us from this suffering.
Then, restraining them, the Great Being addressed them with a verse:
“Past human karma is difficult to undo and hard to overcome;
I am not able to release him—understand this, Senaka.
In that context, “understand this, Senaka,” means: “Senaka, I am not able; but you, take this king through the air to Mithilā.”

Seeing no way to seize what ought to be seized, and terrified by the fear of death, the king was unable to speak with the Great Being. Thinking, "Perhaps Senaka might know some means; I shall ask him first," he spoke this verse while questioning him:
"Listen to these words of mine; behold the great danger, Sena! Now I ask Senaka: what do you think should be done here?"
"In this matter, what task do you consider appropriate to be done here? I have been entrusted to Mahosadha; if you know, speak.
Hearing this, Senaka thought, "The king asks me for a stratagem; whether it be good or not, I shall tell him one. Having reflected thus, he spoke this verse:
"Either we give him fire from the door, or we take his share of the sale-price."
"Having struck one another down, we shall quickly take each other's lives;
let not King Brahmadatta kill us with prolonged suffering.
In this context, "by way of the gate" means that having closed the gate, we shall set fire there. "Mutilating" means mutilating one another.
“Let us take up weapons; we shall slay him. By this they meant, “We shall quickly abandon life; our very decorated palace will become our funeral pyre.

Hearing this, the king was displeased and said, “Prepare such a pyre for your own children and wives,” and then he questioned Pukkusa and the others. They too spoke only words suited to their own [station], mere childish talk.
Therefore it is said: “Listen to these words of mine; behold this army, a source of great terror!”
Now I ask you, Pukkusa, what do you think should be done here?
"Let us eat poison and die; let us quickly end our lives, lest King Brahmadatta kill us with long-lasting suffering."
“Listen to these words of mine; behold this army of great terror!
Now I ask the Lord of Desire: what do you consider to be the duty here?
We are being killed while bound by ropes; we are falling down precipices.”
“May King Brahmadatta not kill us with long-lasting suffering!
Listen to these words of mine: behold this army, a source of great terror!
Now I ask you, Lord of the Devas: what do you think should be done here?”
“Or we shall give ourselves to the fire at the gate, or we shall accept the stake;
having slain one another, we will quickly end our lives.
Mahosadha is not able to release us in peace.”
Furthermore, O Lord of Devas, among these [deities], they thought: "What is this king doing? While there is a fire, he is fanning a glowworm!
There is no one else capable of ensuring safety here except Mahosadha.
He asks us without having asked him; what do we know? Seeing no other means, they [replied] exactly as Senaka had said.
Having spoken thus, he praised the Great Being and uttered two verses. The intention here is this: “Great King, we all likewise entreat only the Wise One.
But if, even when entreated, Mahosadha is unable to liberate us easily, then we shall follow the word of Senaka.”
Having heard this, the king recalled the faults previously pointed out by the Bodhisatta; unable to converse with him, he lamented even as the Bodhisatta listened and said:
"Just as one seeking the core of a plantain tree finds none, so too, though we have searched for it, we have not attained the answer to that question."
“Just as one seeking the core of a śimbalī tree does not find it,
so too, though we have sought him, we have not attained this answer.
Truly, it has rained upon us in the wrong place, like rain upon the elephants in the forest water.”
In the presence of wicked men, fools who lack understanding:
“My heart trembles, my mouth goes dry;
I find no peace, like one scorched by fire in the heat.”
“As a smith’s furnace glows within, not without;
even so my heart glows within, not without.
In this context, regarding the word *kadali*: just as a person seeking pith, though searching, finds none in a plantain trunk because it is devoid of pith...
Thus, one does not find the essence; likewise, although we questioned the five wise men while searching for the means by which we might be released from this suffering, we did not obtain the answer.
We became as if we had neither known nor heard the means we inquired about;
we did not attain that answer. The same method applies to the second verse as well. [Regarding] elephants...
Regarding "in the forest and by the water": just as for elephants, staying in a place devoid of water is called "staying in an improper place";

for while dwelling in such a waterless, dense forest region, they quickly fall under the power of their enemies, so too, by our staying in the presence of these wicked, foolish men, we have stayed in an improper place. Among so many...
“Indeed, now there is not even a single wise man who is my refuge,” he lamented in various ways.

Hearing this, the wise man thought, “This king is exceedingly distressed. If I do not comfort him, he will die of a broken heart. Having reflected thus, he comforted him. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Then that wise and steadfast Paṇḍita, Atthadassī Mahosadha...”
Seeing Vedeha suffering, he spoke these words:
“Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O bull among charioteers!
I shall deliver you, just as Rāhu released the moon.”
"Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!
I shall release you, as the sun releases itself from the grasp of Rāhu.
"Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!"
“I shall release you, like an elephant sunk in the mud.
“Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!
I shall release you, like a serpent bound within a basket.”
"Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!
I shall deliver you, like a bird released from a cage.
"Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!"
“I shall deliver you, like a fish caught in a net.
“Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O Bull among Charioteers!
I shall deliver you, along with your horses, troops, and vehicles.”
"Do not fear, O Great King; do not fear, O bull among charioteers!
I shall drive toward Pañcāla as one would strike a flock of crows with a clod of earth.
Of what use is such wisdom, or even a minister like that?"
“He who would not release you from suffering when you have fallen into that strait.
Therein, the words beginning with “Do not fear, O Great King,” were spoken to comfort him like one pouring down a heavy rain in a forest already scorched by a wildfire.
Therein, *sannaṃ* means stuck; *peḷābaddhaṃ* means bound in a box.
"A snake that has gone inside a basket. "Pañcāla" refers to the army of the King of Pañcāla, even though it is so vast.
"I shall drive away" means I shall cause it to flee. "Adū" is a particle used in the sense of "not"; the meaning is: "Of what purpose is wisdom?
"Or even such a minister"—of what purpose is even a minister who is endowed with such wisdom, he who [acts] thus toward it?
"Though he has reached the straits of death, suffering cannot release him. Great King, you might think, 'Why did he come so early?
What is his purpose? Do not fear; I shall release you from this suffering," he reassured him.
Having heard those words, he too gained confidence, thinking, "Now my life is saved. Thus [it was said] by the Bodhisatta.
When the lion’s roar was uttered, everyone was satisfied. Then Senaka asked him, “O wise man, by what means will you go when you take us all with you?
He replied, “I shall lead you by way of a decorated *umaṅga* (procession); you must be ready for the journey.
Having said this, he spoke a verse while commanding his warriors to open the gates of the *umaṅga*:
“Come, young men, arise! Cleanse the gateway!
Vedeha, together with his ministers, will pass through the tunnel.
In this context, “young men” (māṇavā) is a term for youths. “Cleanse the gateway” (mukhaṃ sodhetha) means: open the entrance to the tunnel. “Sandhino” means...
“Cleanse the doors of the inner chambers; open the doors of the one hundred sleeping rooms; open the doors of the many hundreds of lamp-holders.
They arose and opened the doors of the inner apartments.
The entire inner apartment shone with a single radiance, like the adorned assembly hall of the gods. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard those words of his, the attendants of the wise man opened the Umanga gate and the bolts fitted with mechanical devices.
In this context, *anucārino* refers to the servants (*veyyāvaccakarā*). *Yantayutte ca aggaḷe* refers to the door-panels equipped with pins and bolts.
They opened the door of the inner chamber and informed the Great Being. He gave the king a signal, saying, "It is time, Your Majesty;
please descend from the palace. Upon hearing this, the king descended. Then Senaka removed the turban from his head, took off his upper garment, and tightly girded his loins.
When the Great Being saw him, he asked, "Senaka, what are you doing?"
He asked: “O wise man, when entering through a narrow passage, one must indeed loosen one’s turban, bind one’s waist-folds firmly, and then proceed.
“Senaka, do not imagine that you will enter the narrow passage by bending down and placing your knees on the ground.
If you wish to go by elephant, mount the elephant and go. If you wish to go by horse—”
“You wish to go; mount a horse and proceed. There is a high palanquin, eighteen cubits in height, with wide doors;
you may go before the king, adorned and prepared as you please,” he said.
It is said that the Bodhisatta, having deliberated on Senaka’s departure, placed the king in the middle and himself remained behind. Why?
For what reason? [Because] the king, looking at the decorated *umaṅga* (palanquin), thought, "Let him not go slowly.

In the *umaṅga*, there was an immeasurable amount of rice gruel, boiled rice, hard food, and so forth for the great multitude of people. Those people went along, eating and drinking while looking at the *umaṅga*.
The Great Being went behind, urging them on, saying, "Go, Great King! Go, Great King! [Meanwhile,] the king [was looking at] the decorated celestial assembly hall...
He goes along looking at every limb as if it were his own. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Senaka goes in front, and Mahosadha behind;
And in the middle is King Videha, surrounded by his ministers.”
Knowing that the king had arrived, those young brahmins brought the queen mother, the queen, the son, and the daughter out from the inner apartments and placed them in a large, spacious hall.
The king also emerged from the inner apartments together with the Bodhisatta.
Seeing both the king and the wise man, they thought, "Without a doubt we have fallen into the hands of others; surely those who came taking us away..."
“Men must become wise!”—thus they cried out with a great roar, terrified by the fear of death.
It is said that King Cūḷani, out of fear of fleeing from King Vedeha, had stationed himself one *gāvuta* away from the Ganges.
When the night had settled and he heard their shouting, although he wished to say, “This is the sound of Queen Nandā,” he [asked], “Where is Queen Nandā?”
“Will you go? he asked, but out of fear of being ridiculed, the other said nothing.
However, the Great Being, having placed the maiden Pañcālacandī upon the heap of jewels at that spot and consecrated her, said: “Great King, you have come for her sake;
let her be your chief queen. Three hundred ships were made ready, and the king descended from the spacious pavilion.
He boarded the decorated ship. Those four kṣatriyas also boarded the ship. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having departed from Ummaṅga, Vedeha boarded the ship;
and knowing that he had boarded, Mahosadha gave him instruction.”
“This is your father-in-law, O King, and this is your mother-in-law, O Lord of Men;
let your conduct toward your mother-in-law be just as it is toward your own mother.
Just as one’s own biological brother, born of the same womb, [is dear]...”
“Thus, O bull among chariot-warriors, this Pañcālacandī must be cherished by you.
This princess Pañcālacandī is desired by you;
do as you wish with her, O bull among chariot-warriors—she shall be your wife.”
In that context, "he instructed" means this was his thought: "Perhaps he might, out of anger, kill the mother of Cūḷanī-rāja;
or he might take up a life of cohabitation with the beautiful Queen Nandā; or he might kill the prince. I shall obtain a promise from him.
Therefore, saying "This is for you," and so forth, he instructed him. In that passage, "this is your father-in-law" refers to this [person].
This son of your father-in-law, King Cūḷanī, the younger brother of Pañcālacandī, is now your father-in-law.
This is your mother-in-law—this woman, his mother, named Queen Nandā, is your mother-in-law. "As toward a mother":
just as sons perform services and counter-services for their mother, so let it be for you toward her; having established a powerful perception of her as a mother.
"Do not look upon her at any time with a mind of greed. 'Niyaka' means one's own, born from the same father.
'Ekamātuka' means born from the same mother. 'Dayitabba' means she is to be cherished; 'bhariyā' means this is your wife—do not treat her with contempt.
Thus he took a formal promise from the king.
The king accepted, saying, "Very well. However, he said nothing concerning the queen mother.
For what reason? Because of her advanced age. But the Bodhisatta spoke all of this while standing on the shore.
Then the king, wishing to depart because he was freed from great suffering, said, "Dear son, you spoke while remaining on the shore," and recited this verse:
“Having boarded the ship and hastening across, why indeed do you stand on the shore?
We have been released from hardship and suffering; let us go now, O Mahosadha!
The Great Being said, “Your Majesty, it is not fitting for me to travel together with you,” and spoke thus:
“O Great King, it is not my duty as the leader of this army to abandon a division of the forces and seek my own deliverance.
O Deva, within your own residence, a division of the forces has already been abandoned.”
"That was given by Brahmadatta; I shall bring it, O bull among chariot-warriors.

In this context, *dhamma* means intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "In the dwelling" (*nivesanasmim*) is said with reference to that city. "I shall deliver" (*parimocaye*) means I shall cause to be released.
"Neglected" (*parihāpitaṃ*) means abandoned. For among those people, because they had come along a long road, some were exhausted and fell asleep.
Some who had entered were eating and drinking and did not even know that we had departed; others were ill.
Many people there had been my assistants, having worked with me for four months;
it was impossible for me to go leaving even a single person behind. However, I shall turn back and [bring] that entire army of yours.
"I shall bring back that which was given by Brahmadatta but not yet understood.
Your Majesty, proceed quickly without lingering anywhere. I have stationed elephant-vehicles and other conveyances along the way;
leaving behind those that are exhausted, enter Mithilā swiftly with those who are still capable."
Then the king spoke this verse:
“How will you stand in conflict with a great army while having only a small one?
Being weak against the powerful, you will be overcome, O wise one.”
Therein, "having quarreled" means having spread out [the conflict]. "You will be afflicted" means you will be struck down.
Then the Bodhisatta said:
"Even if he be a minister with a small army, if he does not counsel a king who has a great army..."
“The king conquers other kings, as the rising sun [conquers] the darkness.
In this context, “counselor” (*mantī*) means one endowed with counsel, wise, and skilled in means.
He “conquers the uncounseled” (*amantim*) means that the wise man conquers the unwise; even a single king of such a nature conquers many unwise kings.
"He simply conquers. How so? Just as the rising sun dispels darkness—just as the rising sun, having destroyed the darkness, displays light—so too does he conquer and shine forth like the sun.
Having said this, the Great Being paid homage to the king, saying, "Go, you," and dismissed him. [The king thought: "I am indeed liberated!"
"Having recovered her from the hands of my enemies, my heart's desire has reached its ultimate fulfillment," he said.
Reflecting thus upon the virtues of the Bodhisatta, filled with joy and gladness, he spoke this verse while recounting the qualities of the wise Senaka:
"O Senaka, how truly happy is the dwelling together with the wise!"
"Like a bird bound in a cage, like a fish caught in a net, like one fallen into the hands of an enemy—Mahosadha has not released us.
In this context, "susukhaṃ vata" means "it is indeed exceedingly happy," namely, this dwelling together with the wise. "Iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.
This is an interjection. This is what is meant: "Because Mahosadha liberated her when she had fallen into the hands of her enemies, therefore, Senaka, I say:
'How truly happy indeed is this, which is association with the wise.
Having heard that, Senaka also spoke, praising the virtues of the wise man:
“So it is, Great King; for the wise bring happiness.
Just as Mahosadha liberated a bird bound in a cage and a fish caught in a net, he has now set us free from falling into the hands of our enemies.”
Then the King of Videha, having crossed the river, arrived at a village established by the Great Being at intervals of one *yojana* each.
There, the men appointed by the Bodhisatta gave him elephant-vehicles and the like, as well as food and drink.
Having set aside his weary elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, he took the others and reached another village together with them.
By this means, having traversed a road of eighty *yojanas*, he entered Mithilā early the next morning.
The Great Being also went to the gate of the inner palace, removed the sword with which he was armed, and after scattering sand at the gate of the inner palace, he set it down.
Having thus left the sword, he entered the inner palace, proceeded through it, and entered the city to reach the palace.

Having mounted [the palace], bathed with scented water, and partaken of various foods of the finest flavors, he went to his excellent bed and lay down reflecting, "My desire has reached its fulfillment.
Then, at the end of that night, King Cūḷani, while inspecting his military divisions, arrived at that city. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:
Having guarded the meditation object throughout the night,
the mighty Cūḷaneyya approached his benefactor as the dawn was rising.
Mounting a noble, powerful elephant sixty years of age, he went forth.
King Pañcāla Cūḷaneyya, possessed of great strength, spoke thus:
“Girt with a jewel armor and taking an arrow in his hand,
he addressed Pesiya when the two great hosts had come together.”
In this context, *kasiṇa* means entire and without remainder. *Udentam* means while it was rising.

*Upakāriṃ* refers to that city which had received the name "Upakāri" because it had been built by the Great Being (Mahāsatta) starting from the city of Pañcāla; he went to that city. *Avoce* means he spoke to his own army.
*Pesiyā* means to those who were his messengers. *Ajjhabhāsittha* means he addressed them; [the prefix] *adhi-* is used here in the sense of "previously."
It was said, "Puthugumba" means one established in many arts, that is, one who knows numerous crafts.
Now, in order to show these [crafts] in their specific form, he said:
"Elephant-riders, cavalrymen, charioteers, and infantrymen;"
"In archery, when the hair-splitting [shot] has been mastered.
Herein, "in archery" means in the science of the bow. "With a skilled hand" means having perfected the hand through unerring shooting.
Now, the King, commanding that the Videhan be captured alive, said:
“Drive forth the tusker elephants, powerful and sixty years of age;
let the elephants trample the city well-built by the King of Videha.
With their faces like calf-teeth, white, with sharp tips and eight piercing goads,”
Driven by the force of the bowstring, they fell upon one another. "Let the young men, skilled archers and heroes, equipped with weapons and variegated staffs—
those leaping great elephants— stand face to face with the enemy elephants."
“Let the spears, washed with oil, blazing and radiant,
stand shining like stars together with the sun.
[Let them belong] to those powerful with weapons, wearing bracelets and armlets.”
“From where can Vedeha escape, when he faces such warriors who do not flee in battle, even if he acts like a bird?
‘I have thirty-nine thousand men, all of them individually armored;’”
“As I wander over this entire earth, I do not see anyone who is their equal.
There are well-trained, tusked elephants, powerful and sixty years of age,
upon whose shoulders shine youths of lovely appearance.”
“Adorned with yellow ornaments, clad in yellow garments, with yellow upper robes,
they shine upon the elephant trunks like sons of the gods in the Nandana grove.
The *nettiṃsa* fish are the color of pāṭhīna, bright and shining, as if washed with oil.”
These have been completed by the wise men, even-balanced and well-fastened.
Made of strong bamboo, free from blemish, and fashioned with a cord,
they are grasped by the powerful who deliver them with a firm stroke.
“Endowed with golden spears and bearing crimson shields,
they shine as they wheel about, like flashes of lightning amidst thick clouds.
These brave warriors, skilled in sword and shield, carry banners and quivers.”
“O archers, most highly trained, who can strike down even the bodies of elephants!
Surrounded by such as these, there is no escape for you from here.
I see no power in you by which you might reach Mithilā.”
In this context, *dantī* means those who possess excellent tusks. *Vacchadantamukhā* means those whose mouths resemble the snouts of calves.
*Paṇunnā* means discharged. *Sampatantutarītarā* means "let such arrows as these fly hither and thither, let them come together";
he thus commanded: "Rain down a shower of arrows like the rain from a thick cloud. *Māṇavā* refers to young warriors. *Vammino*... [text fragment]
"Armored hands. "Equipped with variegated-staff weapons" means they were endowed with weapons provided with variegated staffs. "Pakkhandino" means those who charge into battle.

"Great elephants" refers to warriors capable of standing motionless even when great elephants approach letting out trumpeting cries, and of seizing and tearing out their tusks. "Like the sun among the stars" refers to the sun.
Like the star Osadhi. "Possessing the strength of weapons" means those endowed with and possessed of the power of weaponry. "Wearing breastplates and armlets":
*guṇi* refers to armor; thus it means those wearing both armor and armlet ornaments, or those wearing armlets that are counted as armor.
"If he should act like a bird" means even if he should leap into the sky like a bird.
"Even if he does so, will he nevertheless be released? he asks.
"Thirty-nine hundred men" (*tiṃsa me purisanāvuti*) means thirty thousand nine hundred men; they are called "thirty-nine hundred.
"All of them individually equipped" means that this many [men] of mine, having taken weapons from the hands of others, [stand against] the enemies.
This shows that these warriors, each selected individually, were capable of felling a sal tree and would not retreat.
"They roam the entire earth alone"—this shows that as they roam this whole earth, I see no one equal to them; how much less anyone superior?
"These alone are my warriors, so many. "Beautiful to behold" (*cārudassanā*): *cāru* means gold; thus, it means "having a golden complexion."
Meaning: "Yellow ornaments" means golden ornaments of yellow color. "Yellow garments" means clothes of yellow-colored gold.
"Yellow upper robes" means those clothed in yellow *uttarāsaṅga* robes. "The color of a pāṭhīna fish" means resembling a stone-fish.
"Swords" (*nettiṃsa*) means blades. "By wise men" (*naradhīrehi*) means by learned persons. "Well-sharpened" (*sunissitā*) means very sharp and keen.
"Fluttering" means shining like the sun at midday as it stands [in the sky].
"Made of leather thongs" means made from leather thongs obtained after having fed them to cranes seven times. "By those who strike with easy-to-aim blows" means by warriors who deliver firm strikes.
"Bearing red armpits" means endowed with a red-colored lining. "Banners" means in the sky.
"Capable of maneuvering. "Brave" means naturally brave. "Skilled in sword and shield" means expert in seizing these.
"Archers" means those who are archers. "Highly trained" means extremely well-trained in this art of archery.

"Capable of striking down from the neck of an elephant" means capable of cutting down with a sword from the neck of an elephant and bringing it to the ground. "There is no escape," [said] "O friends!"
"Videha," he said, "first you were released by the power of the householder’s son; but now there is no escape for you.
By this he meant: "I see no royal majesty in you now by which you might go quickly to Mithilā;
you have become like a fish caught in a net."
King Cūḷani, goading the King of Videha and thinking, "Now I shall capture him," urged on his elephant with a golden hook and commanded his army, saying, "Seize him!
Break him! Pierce him! He approached as if about to besiege the city of Upaka.
Then the men stationed near the Great Being said, "Who knows? What will happen?"

Taking their own attendants, they surrounded him. At that moment, the Bodhisatta rose from his glorious couch, attended to his person, and having eaten his morning meal, he dressed himself in full regalia.
He put on a Kāsika cloth worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold, draped a red woolen blanket over one shoulder, and took up a walking staff adorned with the seven precious gems.
Having ascended his golden sandals, fanned by an adorned woman like a celestial nymph with a yak-tail whisk,
he opened the lion-window of his decorated palace and paced back and forth with the majestic grace of Sakka, the king of the gods, displaying himself to King Cūḷani. King Cūḷani, however,
was unable to compose his mind even as he gazed upon the splendor of his form, thinking, "Now— "
"I will capture him," he thought, and he sent the elephant away with great haste. The wise man reflected:
"This man is coming in great haste under the impression that 'I have captured Vedeha'; he does not know that our king has already departed taking his own wife and children.
I shall speak with him after showing him my face, which resembles a golden mirror."
Thus, standing at the window, he let out a sweet voice and, conversing with him, said:
"Why indeed did you send the elephant, the great tusker, as if in such haste?
You have come here with a joyful appearance; do you think, 'I am Siddhattha'?"
“Withdraw that drawn bow; withdraw the arrow;
remove that beautiful armor, inlaid with beryl and jewels.
In this context, *kuñjara* means excellent. *Pahaṭṭharūpo* means one whose mind is joyful, glad, and filled with happiness. *Āpatasi* means... [approaching].
"You are coming. You think, 'I am one whose goal is accomplished' (siddhattha), meaning my purpose is fulfilled; I imagine that my desire has reached its peak.
"Take it away"—take this bow known as a *cāpa*, remove it, cast it aside; what need have you for it?
"Withdraw it"—having removed it, give it to another, or place it in a hidden spot; what is the use of an arrow-head?
"You will do so. This is armor; remove even this armor as well. This must have been fastened by you yesterday;
cast it off, lest your body become pale, and enter the city early in the morning without tiring yourself.
Thus she played with the king.
Having heard his words, [the monk thought], "The householder’s son is playing with me; today I shall know what must be done for you. Intimidating him, he spoke this verse:
"You have a bright complexion and speak with a smile;
such a perfection of complexion occurs indeed at the time of death."
"In that regard, 'having previously laughed' means: having first laughed and then speaking afterwards, you speak only after having laughed;
you do not take me into account at all. 'Indeed it happens' means: at the time of death, there is indeed the perfection of complexion;
therefore you shine so brightly. Today, having cut off your head, we shall drink the wine of victory."
Thus, while he was conversing with him, a great body of troops, having seen the splendor of the Great Being’s form, thought, "Hey, our king is consulting with the wise Mahosadha;
what indeed is he saying? We shall listen to their conversation.
They went right back to the presence of the king. The Wise One, too, having heard his words, [thought], "He does not know me as 'the wise Mahosadha'..."
"You know [the truth]. I will not allow myself to be killed. Your spell, O King, has been broken.
What was intended by Keṭaka and by you in your hearts has not come to pass; only what was spoken with the mouth has come to pass," he said, making it clear:
"Your thundering was in vain, O King; your spell is broken, O Kṣatriya."
"The king is difficult for you to catch, like a thoroughbred steed by a wild colt.
For yesterday the king, together with his ministers and his retinue, crossed the Ganges;
like a vulture following a king of swans, you shall fall behind."
In this context, "your spells are broken" means: do not imagine that you no longer know the spell which you learned together with Kevaṭṭa in the bedchamber;
rather, it was already known by me, and thus your spells have become broken.
"You are difficult to catch," O Great King, means: by you our king has been made as difficult to catch as a wild Sindhu horse is by a stallion; [like] a wild colt...
The meaning is that it is impossible to catch [him], just as one who has mounted [a horse] cannot catch a noble thoroughbred while riding it.
He shows that the fisherman is like a wild colt, you are like the man who has mounted it, I am like the swift Sindhu horse, and our king is like the man who has mounted that horse.
"Crossed yesterday" (*tiṇṇo hiyyo*) means he crossed already yesterday. And furthermore...
"He did not flee alone, but went accompanied by his ministers and his retinue.
However, if you pursue him—if you follow after him—then just as a vulture pursuing the king of golden swans would fall midway, so too will you fall;
you will meet with destruction along the way," he said.
Now, like a fearless maned lion, he spoke, bringing forward an illustration:
“Jackals, in the middle of the night, having seen a blooming *kiṃsuka* tree,
thinking it was a piece of meat, rushed toward it— those lowest of beasts.”
“When the nights have passed away and the sun has risen high,
what beautiful flower did you see in bloom that the lowest of deer would sit upon with their mouths cut off?
In just this way, O King, you have surrounded the Prince of Videha.”
“You will go with your entrails cut out, like a jackal to a *kiṃsuka* tree.
Therein, “having seen” means having looked by the light of the moon. “Surrounded” means they stood encircling [him], thinking, “We will eat this lump of flesh as soon as morning comes.
“In which nights” means in whichever successive nights they had thus stood.
"When the nights have passed. "Having seen" means: having seen the *kiṃsuka* tree by the light of the sun, and knowing "this is not meat," they fled with their hopes shattered.

"Jackals": just as jackals, having surrounded the *kiṃsuka*, departed with their hopes shattered, so too you, having learned here of the absence of King Vedeha, will depart with your hopes shattered, taking your army with you.
He indicates that you will flee.
Having heard his fearless words, the king thought, "This son of a householder speaks as one who is exceedingly brave;
without doubt, Vedeha must have fled. Becoming extremely angry, he [said], "Previously, we [spoke to] the son of a householder..."
“By relying on him, even our own stomach-cloths have become ownerless; now that enemy who had fallen into our hands has been driven away by him.
Alas, he has done us much harm! We shall do for this very man what ought to be done for both of them,” he said, as he gave orders to carry out his purpose.
“Cut off his hands and feet, and his ears and nose—
him who has liberated from my hand my enemy, the prince of Videha!
Let him be impaled on a stake and roasted like this meat!”
“He who liberated from my hand the Vedeha, my enemy who had fallen into my grasp.
Just as the hide of a stallion is stretched out upon the earth,
so too is the skin of the lion and the tiger lashed with whips.”
“Having thus stretched it out, I shall pierce him with my spear—he who liberated from my hand my enemy, the prince of Videha.
In this context, “to be drunk” (*pātabya*) means that he is to be cooked, fit for cooking, like the meat of deer and other animals; [thus] this son of a householder.
“Having impaled them on a stake, cook them! Let the skins of the lion and the tiger be stretched out like a drum!
Hearing this, the Great Being smiled and said, “This king [speaks] regarding his queen, his kinsmen, and me...”
"He does not know that my heart is set on Mithilā; therefore, he has this legal case brought against me.
Out of anger, he might pierce me with an arrow or do whatever else pleases him.

I shall explain the reason for this, so that he may leave me here, afflicted by grief and overcome by pain, and have me laid down unconscious right there upon the back of the elephant. Having thought thus, he said:
“If you cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose,
even so will the King of Videha cut off the hands and feet, and the ears and nose, of the Moon of Pañcāla.
“If you cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose...”
In this way, Vedeha will cause the cutting off of Pañcālacandī.
“If you cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose;
in this way, Vedeha will cause the cutting off of Queen Nandā.”
“If you cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose,
then Vedeha will likewise cut off those of your wife and children.
If my flesh must be eaten, you shall roast it after impaling me on a stake.”
In this way, Vedeha will cause Pañcālacanda to be cooked.
"If meat must indeed be eaten, you shall cook me after impaling me on a spit;
in this way, Vedeha will cause Pañcālacandī to be cooked."
“If flesh must indeed be eaten, you shall roast it on a spit;
thus will King Vedeha cause Queen Nandā to be roasted.
“If flesh must indeed be eaten, you shall roast it on a spit.”
"In this way, the King of Videha will cause harm to your wife and children.
'If you pierce me with a spear after drawing back [the bow],
then the King of Videha will pierce the Moon of Pañcāla in the same way.'"
“If, having drawn back, you pierce me with a spear,
even so will the King of Videha pierce Pañcālacandī.
If, having drawn back, you pierce me with a spear...”
Thus will Vedeha pierce Queen Nandā with his spear:
“If you pierce me with your spear after drawing it back,
then Vedeha will likewise pierce your wife and children.”
Thus we deliberated in secret, the Videhan and I:
“Just as a hide weighing a hundred palas, well-prepared by a skilled tanner,
serves for protection against the cold and for warding off arrows.”
“Bringing happiness and dispelling suffering for the illustrious Videha,
I shall strike down your intellect as one strikes an arrow with a hundred blades.
Therein, “he will have it cut off” means that upon hearing, “It is said that the hands and feet of the wise man were cut off by Cūḷani,” he will indeed have them cut off.
"Regarding 'Puttadārassā' (of son and wife): on account of my execution, our king will execute all three of us—your two sons as well as your chief queen.
Thus, O Great King, was it deliberated by us in secret; that is, by me and the King of Vedeha, thus deliberated in private:
'Whatever the King of Cūḷani causes to be done here to me...'"

"Whatever [work] is to be done there for his wife and children. *Palasatanti* means leather that has been brought to a state of softness after being treated with many alkaline substances measuring a *palasata*.
*Kontimantāsuniṭṭhitan’ti*: *kontimantā* is said to be the leather-worker’s knife;
it is "well-finished" because it was made by means of cutting and carving with that [knife]. *Tanutāṇāyāti*...
Just as that shield, when used in battle to ward off arrows, serves as protection for the body— having warded off the arrows,
it protects the body— so too, O Great King, I am a bringer of happiness because I act as a defense against our king’s enemies,
just like that protective arrow-shielding shield. And I am a dispeller of suffering, bringing both physical and mental happiness.
"I bring [it] and I dispel suffering. Therefore, thinking, "I shall counter your mind—your wisdom—with my own mind, as one might strike a hundred-palmed hide with an arrow," he spoke.
Hearing this, the king thought: "What is the householder’s son saying? It seems that I shall do for him exactly as he says."
"In this way, the King of Videha will subject my wife and children to torture; he does not know how well their protection has been arranged.
He laments out of fear of death, thinking, 'He will kill me now,' yet I do not believe his words.
The Great Being, thinking, "He imagines that I am speaking out of fear of death; I shall make him understand," said:
“Come now, see, Great King, how empty is your inner palace!
Your eunuchs and princes, and even your mother, O Kṣatriya, have been led out and presented to the King of Videha.”

"In this matter, O Great King, I sent my own young men, had them descend from the palace, had them bring [the goods] by way of the lower limbs, had the great bundles brought out, and presented those bonds to the King of Videha.
Hearing that, the king thought: "This wise man speaks with extreme firmness.
And during the night, by the banks of the Ganges, I heard a sound like that of Queen Nandā; perhaps this highly wise and learned man might speak the truth."
Thus, although his grief had arisen with great force, he established mindfulness and, as if not grieving at all,
summoned a minister and sent him forth to find out the truth,
speaking this verse: “Come now, go into my inner palace and search for her;”
"Whether his word be true or whether it be false.

Having said this, he went with his retinue to the royal palace; having opened the gate and entered within, they bound his hands and feet, covered his mouth, and suspended him from the rafters, as did the guards of the inner apartments and the hunchbacks, dwarfs, and others.
Having broken the vessels and scattered the various kinds of hard and soft food here and there,
and having opened the doors of the jewel-house, he saw the plundering of the jewels and the inner chamber with its doors wide open; and as he moved about,
he saw flocks of crows entering through the windows left just as they were, while the house was devoid of splendor like a deserted village or a cemetery ground.
Having seen the royal residence and returned, he reported to the king, saying:
"It is even so, Great King, as Mahosadha said;
the entire inner palace is empty, like a settlement of crows."
In this context, "like Kākapaṭṭanaka" refers to a deserted village on the seashore, crowded with flocks of crows that have gathered there because of the smell of fish.
Upon hearing this, the king, trembling with grief born from the separation from those dear to him, thought, "This suffering of mine has arisen because of the householder’s son.
Like a venomous snake struck by a staff, he [turned] toward the Bodhisatta.
He became exceedingly angry. Seeing his reaction, the Great Being thought: "This king is of great renown;
perhaps, out of a fit of anger or through his pride as a kshatriya, he might think, 'What use have I for these? and harm me.
What if I were to describe Queen Nandā’s physical beauty to him as if she had never been seen before? Then, remembering her, if he thinks, 'If I [do not honor] Mahosadha..."
Thinking, "I shall kill her; I will not obtain such a jewel of a woman [again], but by not killing her,
I might obtain her once more," and considering that out of affection for his wife she would do nothing to him,
he, for the sake of protecting himself, remained on the palace roof, drew forth his golden-colored arm from within a red woolen cloak, and spoke while describing the path she had taken:
“From here she has gone, O Great King, this woman beautiful in every limb,
with hips as lovely as a *kosamba* fruit, speaking with a voice like a swan’s cry.
From here she has been led away, O Great King, this woman beautiful in every limb.”
Clad in silk garments, her hair braided, with a beautiful girdle of gold;
with feet beautifully dyed, she was lovely, with a golden gem-studded girdle;
with eyes like the *pārevata* bird, a slender body, lips like the *bimba* fruit, and a delicate waist.
“Sujātā is like a graceful vine, her waist slender like an altar;
long are her dark locks, slightly curled at the tips.
Sujātā is like a deer’s eye, like the crest of a winter fire.”
Like a river in mountain fastnesses, overgrown with small reeds:
“Beautiful as an elephant’s trunk, with thighs like the finest *timbaru* fruit;
neither too tall nor too short, neither hairless nor overly hairy.”
In this context, "there" (*tatra*) indicates the vicinity. "With beautiful hips like a *kosamba* fruit" means she has lovely hips resembling a broad, golden slab.

"Speaking with a voice like that of young swans" means she is endowed with a sweet, resonant tone like that of cygnets wandering about for grazing. "Clad in silk garments" means she is dressed in silken cloth inlaid with gold.
"Sāmā" means golden-hued. "Pārevatakkhī" means one whose eyes, in the place where they are red among the five types of clear-sightedness (pasāda), resemble those of the *pārevata* bird.
"Sutanū" means one with a beautiful body. "Bimboṭṭhā" means one whose lips have a beautifully reddened and polished edge like the *bimba* fruit.
"Tanumajjhā" means one with a waist as slender as a reed. "Sujātā bhujalaṭṭhīvā" means her creeper-like arms are lovely, like tender sprouts reddened by the wind when she stretches them out.
Her well-formed creeper-like arms shine forth. Her slender waist is like a golden altar-platform (*vedī*).
"Slightly curved at the tips" means slightly bent at the ends; or alternatively, it means bent like the tip of a bowstring (*nettimsa*).
"Like a deer’s bow" means she is endowed with graceful movements, like a well-born one-year-old female tiger cub on a mountain ridge.
“Like a flame of fire in winter”: because of its perfection of radiance, it shines like a crest of fire in the winter season.
“Like a small reed-stream”: just as a river covered with small water-reeds shines, so too does she shine with a line of hair that is fine and thin.
“Beautiful” (*kalyāṇī*): she is endowed with the fivefold beauty consisting of skin, flesh, hair, sinews, and bones.
"Paramā timbarutthanī" means her breasts are like the *timbaru* fruit; they are supreme and excellent.
Like two *timbaru* fruits of golden hue placed upon a golden plate, her pair of breasts was perfectly formed and closely set.

While the Great Being was thus describing the beauty of her form, it was as if she had never been seen by him before, and he felt a powerful surge of affection. Then, knowing that affection had arisen within him, the Great Being spoke the following verse:
“O Sirivāhana, you surely rejoice at Nandā’s death;
surely both I and Nandā shall go to the same destination.
Therein, “Sirivāhana” means O Great King, you whose vehicle is endowed with glory; surely you [rejoice] because she possessed such supreme beauty.
She said, "You are called Nanda because of your delight in death. "If you kill me saying 'I am going,' then our King will certainly kill Nanda as well.
Thus, both Nanda and I shall go into the presence of Yama;
and when Yama sees us both, he will give Nanda to me alone. Therefore, by killing me, you have lost such a jewel of a woman."
“What is the use of kingship to one who does not obtain it? O King, I see no loss for myself in my own death.
Thus, at this point, the Great Being praised Nanda alone and not the other three people. For what reason?
Indeed, sentient beings do not place their attachment on others as they do on their beloved wives; even when remembering their mother, they [remember] their sons and daughters as well.
Thinking, "He will remember," he therefore praised him alone; however, because she was elderly, he did not praise the Queen Mother.
While he was praising the Great Being, who was endowed with wisdom, in a sweet voice, Queen Nandā arrived and stood as if before the King.
Then the King thought, "Apart from Mahosadha, there is no one else capable of bringing back my wife."
As he was remembering her, sorrow arose within him. Then the Great Being comforted the king, saying, “Do not grieve, O Great King;
your queen, your son, and your mother—all three shall come. My departure alone is the measure here;
therefore, take heart, O lord of men. Then the king thought: “I [myself]...”
Having caused this city to be well-guarded and well-protected, he remained encircling this city of Upakāra with such a force and army.

Yet this wise man, despite my city being so well-guarded, brought away my queen, my son, and my mother, and gave them to the King of Videha. And while we stood thus surrounded, not even a single one of us—
"Without knowing his science, he caused him to flee along with his army and chariots. Does he perhaps know celestial illusion, or is it a 'confusion of the eye'?
Then, questioning him, he said:
"Do you study celestial illusion? You have performed a confusion of the eye."
“He who liberated from my hand the Vedeha who had fallen into the grasp of his enemy.

Having heard this, the Great Being said, “I know divine illusion; for those truly called wise, having mastered divine illusion, liberate both themselves and others from suffering when danger arises,” and he spoke further:
“O Great King, here in this world the wise study divine illusion;”
Those wise and thoughtful people saved themselves, saying:
"I have sons who are young brahmins, skilled at cutting through walls;
by a tunnel they have made, the fire has reached Mithilā."

In this context, *dibbamāyidha* means "divine illusion here. *Māṇavaputtā* refers to the young warriors who were his attendants. *Yesaṃ katenā* means "by those who had done. *Maggena* means "by way of the decorated gateway.
Having heard that he had gone by way of the decorated gateway, the king wondered, "What kind of gateway is it?
and became desirous of seeing it. Then, perceiving the king's desire, the Great Being, thinking, "The king wishes to see the gateway; I shall show him the gateway," spoke while showing it to him:
“Come now, Great King, behold this well-constructed gateway;
for elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
it stands like a beacon of light, a well-constructed gateway.”

"In that regard, O King, behold this pleasure-park (umaṅga) which stands resplendent with rows of these elephants and other figures made by means of brickwork and mural painting; it resembles the decorated assembly hall of the gods and exists as a single uniform mass.

Having spoken thus, he continued: "Great King, in this decorated pleasure-park laid out by my wisdom—which is as manifest as the rising places of the moon and the sun—there are eighty great gates, sixty-four small gates, and one hundred sleeping chambers."
"Behold, O gods! Entering Upakāra City together with me, in harmony and full of mutual joy, enter it with your own forces.
Having said this, he had the city gates opened. The king, accompanied by a retinue of one hundred and one kings, entered the city.
The Great Being descended from the palace, paid homage to the king, and taking him along with his retinue, led them into the inner apartments.
He entered. Seeing the inner chamber like a decorated celestial hall, the king, praising the virtues of the Bodhisatta, said:
"What a gain for the people of Videha that such wise men as you, O Mahosadha, dwell in their homes within their kingdom!"
In this context, "of the Videhas" means: what a gain it is for the country of the Videhas, which is a source of such wise men and a place where they arise!

"For whomsoever these"—meaning for whomsoever such wise men, skilled in means, dwell nearby, or in the same house, or in the same province, or in the same kingdom—for him too it is a gain! "Just as you are."
They are fortunate indeed those inhabitants of the kingdom of Videha and the city of Mithilā who get to live together with a wise man such as you, whether in the same kingdom,
the same district, the same city, or the same house. Thus he spoke.
Then the Great Being showed him one hundred and one sleeping chambers. When the door of one was opened, the doors of all were opened;
when the door of one was closed, the doors of all were closed. The king went forward, looking about the palace interior, while the wise man followed behind.
The entire army entered the palace interior alone. The king emerged from the palace interior, and the wise man [followed].
Knowing that he had departed, he himself went out, prevented others from leaving, and while closing the door of the inner chamber, stepped upon the bolt.
At that very moment, the eighty great doors, the sixty-four small doors, the hundred doors of the bed-chambers, and the hundreds of doors of the lamp-chambers all closed simultaneously.
The entire inner chamber became like the Lokantariya hell.
It became like darkness. The great multitude was terrified and trembling.

For the Great Being, taking the sword he had placed on the sand yesterday while entering the inner palace, leaped from the ground eighteen cubits into the air, descended, seized the king by the hand, and brandishing the sword, threatened him, saying, "Great King, [the sovereignty] over the whole of Jambudīpa..."
He asked, "Whose kingdom is it? Terrified, he replied, "It is yours alone, O Wise One," and added, "Grant me safety.
"Do not fear, Great King; I did not grasp my sword with the desire to kill you. I grasped it only to demonstrate the power of my wisdom," he said, and returned the sword to the king.
Then, as the king stood there holding the sword, [the Teacher said], "Great King..."
“If you wish to kill me, then kill me right now with this sword. But if you wish to grant me safety, then grant me safety,” he said.
“O wise one, I have already granted you safety as well; do not worry,” he replied.
Setting aside his sword, they both made an oath to each other that neither would harm the other.
Then the king said to the Bodhisatta: "O wise one, being so endowed with the power of knowledge, why do you not take up the kingship?
"Great King, if I so desired, I could slay all the kings throughout the entire Jambudīpa this very day and seize the kingdom.
However, seizing glory by means of killing others is not praised by the wise. "Wise one," [the king replied].
“The great multitude, unable to find the gate, is lamenting; open the side-gate and grant the gift of life to the people!
He opened the gate, and the entire side-street became one mass of light. The great multitude regained their composure.
All the kings, together with their own armies, went forth and came into the presence of the wise man. The king—
He stood together with them in the spacious courtyard. Then those kings said to him, "O wise one, it is by depending on you that we have obtained our lives;
had you not opened the gate of the inner palace for even a moment, all of us would have perished right there. [The wise man replied:
"Great Kings, it is not only now that you have obtained your lives by depending on me; in the past as well, you certainly obtained them."

“When, O wise ones? “When, after having seized the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa with the exception of our own city, we have gone to the city of Uttarapañcāla and are prepared to drink the victory-drink of liquor in the park, O charioteer. “Yes, wise ones.
Then this king, together with Keṭaka, through that ill-advised [plan], [partook] of the liquor mixed with poison and of the fish and meat.
And he performed the deed to kill you. Then I thought, "While a wise man such as I am living,
let these not die an orphan's death," and so I dispatched my own warriors, had all their vessels broken, and by breaking their secret counsel,
I granted you the gift of life.
All of them, their minds filled with agitation, asked King Cūḷani, "Is it true, O Great King?
"Yes," he replied, "I acted upon the advice of the fisherman; what the wise man said is indeed the truth.
Then they all embraced the Great Being, saying, "Wise one, you have become the support for us all; relying upon you, we..."
"We have regained our lives! they cried, and they performed an offering for the Great Being with all their ornaments.
The Wise One said to the king: "Great King, do not grieve; this was the fault of association with evil friends. You should ask these kings for forgiveness. The king said:
"It was through reliance on a wicked person that I did such a thing to you; this is my own [fault]."
“Forgive my fault; I shall not do such a thing again,” he said, seeking forgiveness. Having confessed their transgressions to one another, they became reconciled and lived in harmony.

Then the king, having had many kinds of solid and soft foods, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings brought, spent seven days sporting together with everyone in the pleasure garden itself. After entering the city, [he honored] the Great Being...
Having performed great honors and seated himself upon the great terrace surrounded by one hundred and one kings,
he spoke out of a desire to have the wise man live in his own presence:
"I shall grant you double the provisions, maintenance, food, and wages."
“I give you vast riches; enjoy pleasures and take your delight in them.
Do not go back to Videha—what will Videha do for you?

Therein, “mode of livelihood” (vutti) refers to a way of life dependent on misfortune. “Maintenance” (parihāra) refers to the granting of villages and market towns. “Food” (bhatta) refers to provisions. “Wages” (vetana) refers to travel expenses. “Riches” (bhoga): I give you those other vast riches as well.
The wise man, rejecting that, said:
"O Great King, he who would abandon his master for the sake of wealth is to be censured by both himself and by another."
“As long as Vedeha lives, no other man shall be his husband.
“O Great King, he who would abandon his husband for the sake of wealth is blameworthy both by himself and by others.”
“As long as Vedeha lives, he shall not remain under the sway of another.
In this context, regarding the phrases “of oneself and of another”:
thinking, “For the sake of wealth, I have committed evil by abandoning my own husband,” one reproaches oneself; and [thinking], “For the sake of this wealth, my husband has been abandoned...”
"Others too will reproach him, saying, 'This man is of evil character. Therefore, as long as he remains alive, it is not possible for me to dwell here in another's realm.
Then the king said to him, "In that case, wise man, give your promise that you will come here when your own king has passed away.
He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty; I shall come while I am still living. Then the king provided him with great honors for seven days.
After seven days had passed, at the time of making his request again, saying, "O wise man, I give you this and that," he spoke this verse:
"I give you a thousand *nikkhas*, and eighty villages in Kāsi;
I give you four hundred female slaves and a hundred wives."
“Taking all your troops with you, go in safety, O Mahosadha!
In that context, “a thousand *nikkhas* of gold” means a thousand *nikkhas*, where each *nikkha* is made of five pieces of gold. “As for the villages”:
those villages which yield a thousand [pieces of gold] each year—those villages I give to you. “In Kāsi” means in the kingdom of Kāsi.
That was near the kingdom of Videha; therefore, he gave him eighty villages there.
That man also said to the king: "Great King, do not worry about your kinsmen. At the very time my king was departing, I said:
'Great King, you should establish Queen Nandā in the position of mother, and Pañcālacanda in the position of younger brother.'"
“Having had my daughter consecrated, I shall dismiss the king; I will send his mother, the queen, and their son here very quickly.

Saying, “Excellent, wise one,” he entrusted the Great Being with the items to be given to his daughter—female and male slaves, clothing, ornaments, gold, silver, and decorated elephants, horses, and chariots—saying, “You should give these to her. Then, while considering the duties to be performed for the army and the transport, he said:
“Let them give double rations for the elephants and horses;
let them satisfy the chariot-drivers and the infantry with food and drink.
In this context, “as much as” (yāva) means not only double, but as much as is sufficient—namely, barley, wheat, and other such fodder for the elephants and horses.
He says, "Let them eat. By "let them eat," he means: let them eat by giving as much as is necessary so that they may travel along the road without becoming weary.
Having spoken thus, he said while sending off the wise man:
"O Wise One, go taking with you elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry."
"Let the Great King see him, O Vedehe, once he has reached Mithilā.
In this context, "reached Mithilā" means let him see him having arrived safely at that city of Mithilā.
Thus, having paid great honor to the wise one, he sent him forth. Those one hundred and one kings [also honored] the Mahāsatta...
Having paid him great honor, they presented him with many gifts. The men stationed near them also surrounded the wise man alone.
Surrounded by a large retinue, he set out on the road;
while still on the way, he dispatched men from the village given by King Cūḷani to bring in revenue, and thus he reached the kingdom of Videha. Senaka also—
However, she stationed her own man on the road between them, saying, "Once you have learned whether King Cūḷani is coming back again or not, report the arrival of anyone at all to me.
Having seen the Great Being from as far as three *yojanas* away, he returned and informed Senaka, "A wise man is approaching with a great retinue. He [Senaka]—

Having heard this, he went to the royal palace. The king, standing on the terrace of his palace and looking out through a window, saw the vast army and thought, "The army of the wise Mahosadha is small, yet this army appears exceedingly large;
could it be that King Cūḷani has arrived? Terrified and trembling, he asked about the matter, saying:
“Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—a great army is seen there, fourfold and fearsome in appearance. What do you think, wise one?
Then Senaka, explaining the matter to him, said:
“O Great King, Ānanda will appear as your supreme adversary;
yet Mahosadha, taking his entire fourfold army with him, has returned in safety.
Hearing this, the king said: “Senaka, the wise man’s army was small, but this one is vast. “Great King, [it is so].”
“King Cūḷani must have been pleased by him, and it must have been given to him out of that pleasure.
The king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “Let the citizens decorate the city and go out to meet the wise man.
The citizens did so. The wise man entered the city, went to the royal palace, and paid homage to the king.
He sat down to one side. Then the king, rising and embracing him, sat upon his excellent couch and, exchanging greetings, said:
