"Just as these four people have abandoned this body here in the charnel ground, so too, O Lady of Kapila, have we abandoned you and come here."
“By what means, by what cause, or by what kind of purpose did you liberate yourself?
Therein, “four persons” refers to the wise man; just as four people carry one who has passed away on a bier to the cemetery.
"Having led [him] there and abandoned him, they go away without looking back"; thus the meaning is: "Having abandoned him in the kingdom of Kapilavatthu, we have come here.
"By what praise? means by what reason. "By what cause? means by what condition. "By what matter? means by what purpose.
"He liberated himself" means: having fallen into the hands of enemies, by what reason, by what condition, or by what purpose [did he do so]?
He asks, "Have you liberated yourself?
Thereupon the Great Being said:
"O Knower of Truth, truth by means of truth; O Khattiya, counsel by means of counsel."
“I surrounded the king, as the ocean surrounds Jambudīpa.
The meaning of this is: O Great King, I surrounded the purpose he had conceived with my own conceived purpose, and the counsel he had deliberated upon with my own deliberated counsel.
And it was not merely this much; [I surrounded him] together with a retinue of one hundred kings.
But they will surround that king, as the ocean surrounds Jambudīpa.
He then related in detail all the deeds he had performed.
Upon hearing this, the king was exceedingly pleased. Then the wise man spoke, describing the gift bestowed upon him by King Cūḷani:
“A thousand pieces of gold were given to me, and eighty villages in Kāsi;
four hundred female slaves and one hundred wives were given to me.
Having taken my entire army with me, I have returned here in safety.”
Then the king, exceedingly joyful and delighted, praising the Great Being’s virtue, uttered this inspired utterance:
“O Senaka, how very happy indeed is the dwelling with the wise!
Like birds confined in a cage, or like fish caught in a net.”
“Mahosadha rescued us when we had fallen into the hands of our enemies.
Senaka, accepting his words, spoke this very same verse:
“It is even so, Great King; for the wise bring happiness.”
“Just as one might release a bird bound in a cage, or a fish caught in a net, or one who has fallen into the hands of an enemy, so did Mahosadha set us free.

Then the king, having had the festive drum beaten throughout the city, gave this command: “Let there be a great festival for seven days! Let all those who have affection for me pay honor and respect to the wise man. Thus he spoke.
“Let all lutes be struck; let kettledrums and cymbals resound;
let the Magadhan conchs blow; let the drums roar sweetly.
In this context, “let them be struck” means let them be played. “Magadhan conchs” refers to conchs produced in the kingdom of Magadha. “Drums” refers to large kettledrums.

Then those city-dwellers and country-folk, who were already by nature desirous of honoring the wise man, upon hearing the sound of the drum, did even more so. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher said:
“Eunuchs and princes, merchants and brahmins, Brought forth abundant food and drink for the wise man.”
“Elephant-riders, chariot-warriors, cavalrymen,
and foot-soldiers brought much food and drink to the wise man.
The people of the countryside gathered together, and the merchants also assembled.”
They brought much food and drink for the wise one:
"The multitude has become inspired upon seeing the wise one arrive;
now that the wise one has come, the tossing of garments has ceased."
In this context, "the women of the harem" refers to the ladies of the inner apartments, beginning with Queen Udumbarā. "They brought forth" means they had them brought forth;

the sense is that they sent them. "A great multitude," monks, refers to the people residing in the city, those residing in the villages of the four gates, and those residing in the countryside—a great multitude who were inspired with faith.
"Having seen the wise man arrive" means having seen the wise man come to Mithilā.
When the wise man had arrived at Mithilā, the people were delighted and said, "He has come back having first liberated our king who had fallen under the power of his enemies and sent him away;

afterwards, he reconciled one hundred and one kings with one another, made them harmonious, and appeased Cūḷanī, taking back the great glory bestowed by him. Thus they spoke to the wise man who had arrived at Mithilā.
The waving of the handkerchief was set in motion.
Then, at the conclusion of the festival, the Great Being arrived at the royal palace and said, “Great King, it is fitting that you send the mother, the queen, and the son of King Cūḷani immediately.
“Very well, dear one, send them,” he replied. He [then sent] those three...
Having rendered great honor to the people and having ensured that his own escort who had come with him was also properly honored and respected,
he sent those three persons along with a vast retinue and his own men.
He also sent the hundred wives given to him by the king and the four hundred female slaves together with Queen Nandā, as well as the army that had come with him.
He sent them off together with those very people. With a great retinue, they reached the city of Uttarapañcāla.
Then the king asked his mother, "Mother, has the King of Vedeha shown you favor? "What are you saying, dear son?
He placed me in the position of a deity and paid me honor; he even placed Queen Nandā in the position of a mother."
“He appointed Pañcālacanda in the position of his younger brother. Upon hearing this, the king was exceedingly pleased and sent many gifts.
From that time forth, the two of them lived together in harmony and mutual affection.
The section on the Great Auspicious Ceremony is concluded.
In the *Dakarakkhasapañha*, Pañcālacandī was beloved and pleasing to the King of Videha. In her second year, she gave birth to a son.
In his tenth year, the King of Videha passed away. The Bodhisatta raised the royal parasol over him.
“Your Majesty, I shall go into the presence of your grandfather, King Cūḷani,” he requested.
“Wise one, do not leave me behind while you are young; I will establish you in your father’s place and pay you honor.
Pañcālacandī also said to him, “Wise one, when you have gone, there will be no other refuge for us; do not go!”
He entreated him. He too, saying, "I have given my word to the king;
it is not possible for me to go," took his own attendants and departed from the city even as the great multitude was lamenting piteously, and went to the city of Uttarapañcāla.
When the king heard of his arrival, he went out to meet him, led him into the city with great honor, provided him with a large residence, and settled him there.
Of the eighty villages given on the first day, he gave no other wealth [to anyone else]. He attended upon that king.
At that time, a female wanderer named Bherī was eating at the royal palace; she was wise and clever.
The Great Being had never seen her before, but he heard only the report: "It is said that the wise Mahosadha attends upon the king. By him also—
She had never seen her before; she heard only the report: "A female wanderer named Bherī is eating at the royal palace.
Queen Nandā, however, became displeased with the Bodhisatta, thinking, "She has caused us distress by creating this separation from what we love.
She commanded five hundred favorite women: "Find some fault in Mahosadha and [report it] to the king."
"Strive to break them apart! Thus they wandered about, watching for his weak points.
Then one day, after that female wanderer had eaten and departed from the royal palace, she saw the Bodhisatta coming to attend upon the king in the royal courtyard.
He paid homage to her and stood aside. She thought, "This man is said to be wise; I shall find out..."
“Is he wise or unwise? she asked, looking at the Bodhisatta and extending her hand as if asking the question by means of a hand-gesture.

It is said that she asked the question mentally, thinking: “Wise man, how is it that the king now supports you after bringing you here from a foreign land—does he support you or not? The Bodhisatta [perceived] that this was by means of a hand-gesture...
Knowing that he was asking her this question, she made a fist as she answered the question.
It is said that he, thinking, "Lady, having taken my promise and summoned me, the king has now become tight-fisted;
he gives me nothing new," answered the question only in his mind. She, understanding the reason for this, raised her hand and [said] of herself—
She touched her head. By this she showed: "O wise one, if you are weary, why do you not go forth [into homelessness] like us?
Knowing that, the Great Being touched his own belly. By this he showed: "Noble lady, I have more children and wife to support;
for that reason I do not go forth. Thus, having asked the question by means of hand gestures, she—of her own...
He went straight to his own residence. The Great Being, having paid homage to him, went to attend upon the king.
The favorite women employed by Queen Nandā, standing at the lattice window, saw that deed;
they went into the presence of King Cūḷani and said, "Your Majesty, Mahosadha has joined together with the female ascetic Bherī against you."
“Desiring to seize the kingdom, he has become your enemy,” they slandered him.

The king asked, “What have you seen or heard? “Great King, when a female wanderer was descending after eating and saw Mahosadha, she leveled the king like the palm of her hand and like a threshing floor, thinking, ‘The kingdom is now in my own hands.’”

"Are you able to do it? he asked, extending his hand. Mahosadha, showing the gesture of grasping a sword, clenched his fist, thinking, "In a few days I shall cut off his head and bring the kingdom into my own hands.
She raised her hand, touching her head and saying, "Cut off my head instead! Mahosadha thought, "I shall cut him right in the middle."
“...and she touched her belly. ‘Be heedful, Great King; it is necessary to have Mahosadha put to death,’ she said. Having heard their words, he thought:
‘It is not possible for that wise man to feel ill-will toward me; I shall ask the female wanderer.
On the following day, after the female wanderer had finished her meal, he approached her and asked: ‘Lady, is the wise Mahosadha well?’”
“Was he seen? “Yes, Great King; we saw him yesterday as he was departing after having eaten here.
“But did you have any conversation with him? “No conversation, Great King.
Having heard that he was wise, we thought, ‘If he is wise, he will know this,’ and so we asked him a question by means of hand gestures: ‘Wise man, is all well with you?’”
The king extended his hand; it was not a clenched fist. "Does he welcome you? I asked, and extended my own hand.
The wise man thought, "The king took my promise and summoned me, yet now he gives me nothing," and he clenched his fist.
Then I touched my head and said, "If you are weary, why do you not go forth into homelessness like us? He—
“I have many children and wife to support; for that reason I do not go forth,” he said, as he touched his own belly.
“Is Mahosadha wise, lady? “Yes, Great King, there is no one on the surface of the earth equal to him in wisdom.
When the king heard her words, he paid homage to her and dismissed her. After she had departed, the wise man—
He entered the royal audience hall. Then the king asked him, "Have you seen that female wanderer named Bherī, wise man?
"Yes, Great King; yesterday I saw her as she was departing from here.
She questioned me with a sign of her hand, and I answered her in exactly the same way," he replied, recounting the matter according to the sequence she had described. The king—
Having been pleased on that day, he granted the wise man the position of general and entrusted all affairs of state to him alone.
His fame became great.
Immediately after the king had bestowed this honor upon him, he thought: "The king has granted me an exceedingly vast sovereignty all at once."
“It has been given. Moreover, kings will do exactly this even when they wish to kill someone.
What if I were to test the king to see whether he is kind-hearted toward me or not? No one else will be able to find out;
the female wanderer Bherī is endowed with wisdom, and she will know by means of a certain stratagem. Taking many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he went to the female wanderer.

Having gone to her residence, having honored and paid homage to her, she said: "Noble lady, from the day you spoke of my virtues to the king, the king has overwhelmed me and bestowed upon me excessive fame.
However, I do not know whether he bestows it out of his own true nature or not; it would be well indeed if, by some means, you could [ascertain] the king's state of affection toward me."
“You should know,” he said. She replied, “Very well. On the following day, as she was going to the royal palace, she thought of the "Riddle of the Water-Demon.

It occurred to her: “Acting like a spy, I will ask the king a question by means of a stratagem, and thus I shall know whether the wise man is kind-hearted or not. Having gone there and finished her meal, she...
She sat down. The king also, having paid homage to her, sat down to one side. It occurred to her:
"If the king becomes hostile toward the wise man, he will reveal his hostility when questioned about the matter right in the midst of the great assembly;
that would be improper. I shall question him in private. She said, "I desire privacy."
“Great King,” she said. The king had his men step back. Then she said to him, “Great King, I shall ask you that question.
“Ask, noble lady; if I know it, I shall answer. Then she spoke the first verse regarding the water-demon:
“If you seven were being carried away in the middle of the ocean...”
“Seeking human flesh, a rākṣasa would seize a boat;
by giving him a series of offerings, how was he released from the water-demon?”—
in this context, “of the seven” refers to your mother, Queen Nandā, Prince Tikhiṇamanti, and his companion Dhanusekha.
“Of these seven: the chaplain, Mahosadha, and yourselves. “In the water-ocean” means in deep and vast waters. “Seeking a human offering” means searching for a human sacrifice.
“He might seize it” means that the powerful water-demon (udaka-rakkhasa), having split the water in two and emerged, might seize that boat; and having seized it, [he would say], “Great King, these—”
"Give six people to me in succession, and I will release you," he might say.
Then, having given them one after another, by giving whom first... [and so on] ...by giving whom sixth would you be released from the water-demon?
Having heard this, the king, speaking according to his own inclination, spoke this verse:
“First one should give one’s mother; having given one’s wife, then one’s brother;
then, having given one’s friend, one should give a brahmin as the fifth;
sixth, I would give myself—but I would not give Mahosadha.”
"In that regard, noble lady, on the sixth day—after the fifth had been eaten—I said, 'O water-demon, open your mouth!
When he had opened his mouth, I would have fastened my girdle tightly and, disregarding this royal glory, fallen into his mouth saying, 'Now eat me!';
but I would never, while still alive, have given Mahosadha the wise man."
With this much, this question was concluded.
Thus, the female wanderer came to know the great compassion of the Great Being toward the king; yet, by this alone, the virtue of the Wise One did not become as manifest as the moon.
Therefore, it occurred to her: "In the midst of the great multitude, I shall [reveal] their virtue..."
“I shall speak; the king, having described their faults, will describe the virtues of the wise man, and thus the virtue of the wise man will become manifest like the full moon in the sky.
She, having assembled all the people of the inner palace, asked the king that same question again from the beginning, and when he had answered it in exactly the same way, she said: “Great King, ...”
“You say, ‘I will give my mother first. Now, a mother indeed possesses great virtue, and your mother is not like the mothers of others.
She has been of great benefit to you. Speaking thus, he spoke these two verses while describing her virtues:
“She is your nourisher and your mother, who has shown compassion for you for a long time.”
Chabbhi was intent on harming you, she who is wise and discerning of what is beneficial;
by providing another means, she delivered you from death.
"To her, such as she was, the giver of life, your own flesh-and-blood mother who bore you in her womb—"
“For what fault would you give your mother away, O protector of the young?
In this context, “she nourished” means that during her childhood, she nourished her by bathing, feeding, and clothing her two or three times [a day].
“Compassionate for a long time” means compassionate with a gentle and benevolent heart for a long duration. “One who is timid toward you would offend” means when one who is timid toward you...
A certain brahmin became enamored [of her]; then that wise woman, who perceived the true purpose, fashioned another likeness of you and thereby saved him from execution.
It is said that Cūḷani’s father was named Mahācūḷani; she [was his daughter], and during this boy’s childhood, she [lived] together with the family priest.
Having engaged in sexual intercourse and having caused the king to be killed with poison, she raised the royal parasol for the brahmin and became his chief queen.
One day, when her son said, "Mother, I am hungry," she had him given a cake with molasses.
Then flies swarmed around it; he thought, "I will eat this after making it free of flies."
Stepping back a short distance, he dropped drops of molasses on the ground; having driven away the flies near himself, he scattered them.
They went and swarmed around the other pot of molasses.
Having cleared it of flies, he ate his snack, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, and departed. The brahmin [observed] that deed of his.
Seeing this, he thought: "This boy is now eating molasses free of flies;
once he has grown up, he will not give me my kingdom. I shall kill him right now. He reported this matter to the queen.
She said: "Very well, my lord. Out of affection for you, I even killed my own husband; what need have I for this?"
“Great King, without letting even a single person know, we shall kill him in secret.
Having thus deceived the brahmin, he summoned the wise and skillful cook, saying, “This is the means,” and said to him:
“Friend, my son, Prince Cūḷani, and your son, Prince Dhanusekha, were born on the same day and have grown up together, reared with the same princely upbringing.”
“O dear friend, the brahmin Chabbhi wishes to kill my son; please grant him the gift of life.

When she was told, “Very well, Queen, what shall I do? she replied, “Let my son stay frequently in your house, and you and he should sleep in the kitchen itself for a few days so that there may be no suspicion. Then, having ascertained that there is no suspicion...”

“Place some sheep bones in your sleeping place; then, at the time when people are going to bed, set fire to the kitchen without letting anyone know, take my son and your son, exit by the main gate, and go to another kingdom.
There, without disclosing my son’s status as a prince, protect his life,” he said.
"So be it," he agreed. Then she gave him the essence of her jewels.
Having done so, he took the prince and his son and went to the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda, where he waited upon the king.
The king dismissed his former cook and gave that position to him. Both boys also went with him to the royal palace.
The king asked, “Whose sons are these princes? The cook replied, “They are my sons.
“Are they not two who are unlike one another? “They are the sons of two different women, Your Majesty.

As time passed, they became intimate with one another and played together right in the royal palace with the daughter of King Madda. Then, because of their frequent meetings, Prince Cūḷani and the princess—
Their hearts became bound to one another. At the place of play, the prince had the princess bring him a ball and a dice-cube.
When she did not bring them, he struck her on the head; she wept. Then, hearing her cry, the king asked, "Who has struck my daughter?
The nurses came and questioned her. The young girl said, "If I say, 'I have been struck by this man,'..."
"I shall speak; my father will inflict royal punishment upon him," thinking thus, she did not speak out of affection and said, "I was not struck by anyone.
Then one day, King Madda saw him striking her. Upon seeing this, it occurred to him: "This prince is not like an ordinary cook;
he is handsome, pleasing, and exceedingly fearless. It cannot be that he [struck her] himself."
“He must be treated as a son. From that time forth, he took charge of him.
When the nurses brought food for the princess at the playground, she would give it to the other children as well.
They would take it by kneeling down and bending over; however, Prince Cūḷani would snatch it from her hand while standing upright. The king also—
He observed that deed. Then one day, Prince Cūḷani’s ball went under the king’s small bed.

While attempting to retrieve it, the prince, out of his own pride and arrogance, thought, "It shall not enter under the bed of this frontier king," and so he pulled it out with a stick and took it. The king, having seen that deed as well, [thought], "This man is certainly..."
"He is not the son of the cook. Having summoned him, he asked, "Whose son is he?
"He is my son, Your Majesty," he replied. "I know both your son and your non-son; tell me the truth.
If you do not speak, you shall have no life," he said, brandishing his sword. Terrified by the fear of death, he said, "I will tell you, Your Majesty, but in secret."
Having said, "I am seeking refuge," and being granted leave by the king, he requested immunity from fear and related the matter as it truly was.
The king, knowing it for what it was, adorned his own daughter and gave her to him as a handmaid.
On the day these men fled, however, [the king thought], "The cook, Prince Cūḷani, and the cook’s son..."
“The kitchen has been set on fire and is burning!”—such was the great clamor that arose throughout the entire city.
When Queen Calākā heard this news, she informed the brahmin: “Your Majesty, your heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment;
it is said that all three of them have been burnt right there in the dining hall. He became overjoyed and elated. Queen Calākā [then spoke] regarding Prince Cūḷani...
Having had the bones of a sheep brought and shown to the brahmin, she had them discarded.
With reference to this matter, the female wanderer said: "Having made another pretext, she delivered you from death.
For she had delivered him from death by showing the bones of a sheep as "human bones. *Orasaṃ*: that which you [hold] against your chest (*uraṃ katvā*).
"She was raised by you; she is your own, dear, and beloved.
As for the one who bore you in her womb—by what fault would you give such a mother as this to the water-demon?

Hearing this, the king said, "Noble lady, my mother has many virtues, and I recognize her state of being helpful to me; nevertheless, my own virtues are even more numerous. Thus speaking of his mother's faults, he recited these two verses:
“A young girl, wearing ornaments and finery,
laughs excessively at the gatekeepers and the soldiers. Furthermore,
she herself issues commands to the envoys of rival kings.”
"Because of that fault, I would give my mother to the guard of the water.
In this context, "as if she were young" means that although she was old, she appeared like a young woman.
"She wears ornaments" means she wears decorations unsuitable for wearing. It is said that she had put on a golden girdle filled with diamonds and [presented herself] to the king.
While she was seated on the great terrace with her ministers, she walked back and forth;
by the sound of her girdle, the royal palace resounded as one single noise.

"She laughs excessively" means that she addressed even the gatekeepers, elephant trainers, and other military officers—those who were unfit even to eat her leftovers—and laughed excessively with them.
He laughs a great laugh. "The rival kings" means other kings. "He himself sends messengers with instructions" means that he writes a letter in his own hand and dispatches messengers, saying:
"My mother is still at an age when she enjoys sensual pleasures;
it is said that such-and-such a king has come, so let him take her away. They [the messengers] say: "We are the king's attendants; why do you speak to us in this way?"
They sent forth counter-arguments. While these were being recited in the midst of the assembly, it was as if my own head were about to be cut off;
I thought, "I shall give my mother to that water-demon for this offense.

Then the female wanderer, speaking in praise of her virtues, said two stanzas: "Great King, you may indeed hand over your mother for this offense, but your wife has been of great service to you. Thus she spoke these two verses.
“The most excellent woman of the clan, speaking ever so kindly;
virtuous and well-behaved, she follows like a shadow that never departs.
Free from anger, meritorious, wise, and perceiving the true goal.”
“For what fault did you, noble lady, follow after this young man?
In this context, “of the group of women” (*itthigumbassa*) means of the company of women. “Followed from childhood” (*anuggatā*) means she has followed him since her own youth.

By the words beginning with “free from anger,” he describes her virtues. Even when struck while living in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda, she [obeyed] out of fear of carrying out your command.
"Out of affection for you, she did not tell her parents; thus, she is free from anger, meritorious, wise, and discerning of what is beneficial.
This was said with reference to her state of being free from anger and so forth during her childhood. "Ubbari" means a female attendant.
He says this to express: "By what fault would you give Nandā-devī, who is thus endowed with such virtues, to the water-demon?"
Thus, speaking of her lack of virtue, he said:
“Absorbed in the pleasure of sport, fallen under the sway of what is harmful,
she begs for wealth from me, even though she has her own sons.”
“Full of passion, I give away much wealth of various kinds;
having given what is so difficult to give, I later grieve with a dejected mind.
Because of that fault, O protector of the gift, I would give even my wife.”

Therein, "having come under the power of what is harmful" means having recognized that I had fallen under the sway of those defilements which cause harm through that play and delight in sensual sport.

"She" refers to Queen Nandā. "To her own children" means that whatever jewelry she had given to my own sons and daughters, as well as to my wives—being of a nature not to be asked for—she said, "Give it to me."
She begs [for them]. Thinking, "I shall grieve later," on the following day she says, "These ornaments were given to me by the king;
bring them back! and while they are weeping, she takes them off and seizes them. Then, seeing them come into my presence weeping, I grieve afterward.
Thus she is a doer of harm. Because of this offense, I shall give her to the water-demon.
Then the female wanderer, asking him, said: "Give this one first for that fault; but as for your younger brother, Prince Tikhiṇamanti, he was a benefactor—on what fault would you give him away?
"He who brought together the provinces, and brought them as a bridegroom's gift;
who, having conquered, brought back vast wealth from foreign realms."
"For what fault would you give away your brother, the best of archers, a hero with sharp counsel, who protects the weak? In this passage:

*ocitā* means "reared" or "brought up. *Paṭiggaṇha* refers to that by which you, while living in a foreign land, were brought back home again. *Abhiṭṭhāya* means "having overcome. *Tikhiṇamantim* means "possessing sharp wisdom."
It is said that he was born while his mother was living with a brahmin.
When he had reached maturity, the brahmin gave him a sword in his hand and said, "Take this and attend upon me. He attended upon the brahmin, perceiving him as his father.
Then a certain minister said to him, "Prince, you are not his son; at the time you were in your mother's womb—"
“Queen Calākā, having killed the king, raised this very parasol; you are the son of King Mahācūḷani,” he said.

Becoming angry, [he thought], “I shall kill him by some means. As he was entering the royal palace, he gave that sword to one of the footmen and told another, “At the palace gate, you must say to him, ‘This is my sword.’”
Having said, "You might start a quarrel," he went inside. They began to quarrel. He sent a man, asking, "What is this quarrel?
The man returned and said, "It is for the sake of a sword. Upon hearing this, the brahmin asked, "What is this?
The man replied, "The sword you gave me was claimed by another. The brahmin asked, "What are you saying, dear? By him—"
“Bring it here,” he said, “and I shall recognize it. Having had it brought and drawn out from its sheath, as if to make him recognize it by saying, “Look!
he approached and severed his head with a single stroke, dropping it at his own feet.
Then, having restored the royal palace and decorated the city, when the time for his consecration arrived, his mother—

She explained that Prince Cūḷani was living in the Madda kingdom. Upon hearing this, the prince, surrounded by his army, went there, brought his brother back, and had him installed in the kingship. From then on, they came to know him as "Tikhiṇamantī" (the Sharp-witted One).
The female wanderer asked her, "By what fault did you give such a brother as this to the water-demon?"
Speaking of his fault, the king said:
“By whom the provinces were conquered, and who brought them as tribute;
who brought back vast wealth from foreign realms, having triumphed over them.”
“The preeminent among archers, the hero with the sharp sword—
this child treats this happy king as if he were of no account.
Even my attendance upon him, noble lady, he does not come to as he did before.”
“For that fault, I would give my brother to the water-wardens.
In this context, “from a foreign kingdom” means that much wealth was brought from a foreign kingdom by him;
and while he was living in a foreign kingdom, he has now brought him back to this house and says, “He has been established by me in great glory. Just as...
“Previously she used to come early in the morning, but now she does not come in that way. Because of this fault, I shall give her to the Water-Demon.

Then the female wanderer, speaking of his virtues, said: “First, let there be some fault in your brother; but Prince Dhanusekha is bound to you by the bond of affection and has been very helpful to you.
And she added: “For a single night, both you and Dhanusekha—”
"Both Pañcālā and Sahāya were born here together in their youth.
You followed his conduct, sharing in his sorrow and happiness;
eager for him day and night, you were occupied with all his affairs."
“For what fault would you give an assistant who guards the water?
In this context, “dhanusekhā” means both a pupil of archery and the youth Dhanusekhaka. “Ettha” means right here in this city.
“Pañcālā” is a designation because they were born in the city of Uttarapañcāla. “Susamāvayā” means those of perfectly equal age.
"He followed you in your wanderings" means that during your youth, when you had set out on a journey through the countryside, he followed you, never leaving you like a shadow.
"He was ever eager" means that day and night he was intent upon your affairs, filled with zeal, and constantly occupied [on your behalf].
"Why, for what fault, would you give him to the young ogress? means why would you hand him over to the young female demon?
Then the king, speaking of her fault, said:
"This conduct of yours, noble lady, was laughed at by me;
even today, because of that appearance, you laugh excessively."
“O noble lady, I shall speak to you in private, Ubbarī:
He enters uninvited and without having been previously announced.
Having gained access and being granted leave, he is shameless and disrespectful.”
“For that fault, I would give a companion to the protector of the water.

Regarding this, “even today with that same appearance” means: just as previously, while following me according to my conduct, eating and sleeping together with me who was without a protector, and having struck my hand, he laughed a great laugh—even today it is exactly the same.
"He laughs because he thinks of me as if I were in times of poverty.

'Without having informed me' means that even while I am consulting in private with Queen Nandā, he enters abruptly without letting me know. Because of this fault, I shall give him to the water-demon, for he is shameless and disrespectful.
Then the female wanderer said, speaking of his virtues: "Great King, let this fault belong to your companion for now; however, the chaplain has been of great service to you."
“Skilled in all signs, knowing their meaning, and possessed of the traditional scriptures;
adept in portents and dreams, in both departure and entry;
a traveler on land and in the sky, and an expert in the courses of the constellations.”
“For what fault would you give a brahmin who guards his wealth?
In this context, *sabbanimittānaṃ* means one who is skilled in all signs (*nimitta*), such as thinking, “By this sign this will happen; by that, that.
*Rutaññū* means one who knows every sound. *Uppāte* refers to portents such as lunar eclipses, solar eclipses, meteors, and conflagrations in the quarters of the sky.
Regarding *uppāte*: "Appropriate for dreams" means he is skilled in knowing the results produced by dreams. Regarding "In departure and entry":
by this he knows that one should depart under this constellation and enter under this [other] constellation.

"Expert" (*paṭṭha*) means clever and capable, able to discern the faults and virtues both on the earth and in the sky. "Skilled in the movements of the constellations" refers to the twenty-eight [constellations].
"He is skilled in the divisions of the constellations. For what fault would you give him to the water-demon?
The king, explaining his fault, said:
"Even in my assembly, noble lady, he gazes at me with eyes wide open."
"Therefore, O protector of the gift, I would give even to one with eyebrows raised excessively, fierce, and like a hunter.
The meaning of this is: "Noble lady, even though he is looking at me in the midst of the assembly, he gazes at me with his eyes wide open as if angry;
therefore, to one who stands thus with eyebrows raised so high that they are unpleasant—as if his brows were knit in anger—and who is fierce and terrifying..."
"I shall give her to the water-demon.
Then the female wanderer said, "Great King, you say, 'Beginning with my mother,
I give these five to the water-demon,' yet you disregard such royal splendor and give even your own life to Mahosadha."
Asking, "What benefit do you see in that?", she spoke these verses:
"He dwells upon the earth, which is encompassed by the oceans and girt by the sea,
the bearer of wealth, surrounded by his ministers."
“You are the great king of the four quarters, victorious and possessed of great power;
you are the sole monarch of the earth, and your fame has spread far and wide.
You have sixteen thousand women adorned with jeweled earrings.”
Women from various lands, as beautiful as celestial maidens—
“Such a life, O Khattiya, they say is long, pleasant, and full of happiness for one who is endowed with all limbs and has all desires fulfilled.”
“By what praise, or by what cause, do you,
protecting the wise man, sacrifice life which is so difficult to give up?
In this context, “as far as the ocean’s boundary” means endowed with the ocean’s perimeter, which is defined as the limit of the sea.
"Sāgarakuṇḍala" means that which has become like a circular earring (kuṇḍala) of the ocean surrounding [the world]. "Vijitāvī" means one who has conquered in battle.
"Ekarājā" means he alone is the king, because there is no other king equal to himself.
"Sabbakāmasamiddhinam" means of those endowed with the fulfillment of all things, both sensual objects (vatthukāma) and defilements (kilesakāma). "Sukhitānam" refers to such persons as these.
"For beings who are happy, such a life—endowed with all its factors—is long indeed and dear;
they do not desire a short life," so say the wise. "Why then do you, while protecting your own life which is of such a nature, cause it to perish?
Having heard her words, the king, speaking of the wise man's virtue, spoke these verses:
“Since Mahosadha came into my hands, noble lady,
I do not recall even the slightest misdeed on the part of that wise man.
And if at any time death should come to me before his,”
“May Mahosadha bring happiness to my sons and grandsons.
He sees everything— both the future and the present—
and since his actions are free from fault, O guardians of the gift, you should not withhold the gift.”
In that context, "at some time" (*kismiñci*) means at any time whatsoever. "One should establish in happiness" (*sukhāpeyya*) means one should establish [the person] in happiness itself.
"He sees all meaning" (*sabbamatthaṃ*) means that he, like an omniscient Buddha, perceives all meaning—past, present, and future.
"Faultless action" (*anāparādhakammantaṃ*) refers to bodily action and so forth that is free from fault. "Noble lady, they would not give such an unequal burden."
"I will not give the wise man to the water-demon"—thus he spoke of the Great Being's virtues, lifting them up as if drawing out the orb of the moon.
Thus this Jātaka reaches its natural conclusion. Then the female wanderer thought: "Even by this much [I have seen] of the wise man’s..."
Thinking, "His virtues are not yet manifest; I shall make his virtues known among all the inhabitants of the city,
like oil poured upon the surface of the ocean so that it spreads abroad," he took the king down from the palace, prepared a seat in the royal courtyard,
seated him there, and having assembled the citizens, began once more from the beginning to [describe] the water-demon to the king.
When he had asked the question and spoken according to the method previously explained by him, he addressed the citizens and said:
“Listen to this, O Pañcālas, the speech of Cūḷaneyya:
‘Protecting the wise man, he gives up his life, which is so hard to give.’”
“For his mother, his wife, his brother, his friend, and the brahmin,
as well as for himself— Pañcāla gives up his life for these six.
Thus is wisdom of great benefit, subtle, and rightly reflective.”
“For the sake of welfare in this very life, and for happiness in the future life.

In this context, “of great benefit” means they stand having grasped a great purpose. “For the sake of welfare in this very life” means it serves for the welfare in this very selfhood and for the sake of happiness in the world beyond.
Thus, as if seizing the peak of the jewel-house with a mass of gems, she seized the peak of the teaching through the virtues of the Great Being.
The Question of the Water-Demon is finished.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise; in the past as well, he was indeed wise,” and while identifying the Jātaka, he spoke these concluding verses:
“The drum was Uppalavaṇṇā, and Suddhodana was the father;”
Mahāmāyā was his mother, and Bimbasundarī was his nurse.
Ānanda was Suva, and Sāriputta was Cūḷanī;
Devadatta was Kevaṭṭa, and Thullanandā was Calākā.
“Pañcālacandī was Sundarī, Sāḷikā was Mallikā;
Ambaṭṭha was Kāminda, and Poṭṭhapāda was Pukkusa.
Pilotika was Devinda, and Senaka was Kassapa.”
Udumbarā Maṅgalikā, Vedeho Kāḷudāyako,
Mahosadho Lokanātho— thus should you remember this Jātaka.
The commentary on the Umaṅga Jātaka is the fifth.
(The sixth part is finished.)
